source: operator refresh from production catalog + species_field_guide for hand-coded species
note: Merged into static species entries at build time (src/lib/static-species-overlay.ts). The build never fetches Supabase.

aardvark.spotlight: Aardvark teaches Persistence through a night digger proving that valuable things are often buried. Heavy claws, long ears, termite mounds, burrows, and a sticky tongue make hidden food accessible through repeated effort.
aardvark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, grasslands, scrub, open woodland, termite-rich plains, and diggable soils.
signatureTraits: Powerful digging claws used for termite mounds and burrows.
Long sticky tongue specialized for ants and termites.
Large ears and nocturnal movement across dry ground.
Burrow building that creates shelter for itself and many other animals.
interestingFacts: Aardvarks are the only living species in their order, Tubulidentata.
They can dig quickly into hard ground when escaping or foraging.
Their abandoned burrows provide shelter for many other species.
Despite looking like several other animals mixed together, aardvarks have their own unique lineage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Termites and ants dominate the diet, with occasional fruit such as aardvark cucumber in some areas.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, leopards, hyenas, pythons, wild dogs, humans, and burrow collapse can threaten aardvarks. Digging, night movement, and retreat burrows protect them, turning the same tool toward food and safety.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Aardvarks are nocturnal, resting in burrows by day and foraging at night. Their rhythm is sleep underground, emerge, listen, dig, lick, and keep moving.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Zoo animals often reach their early twenties, and a few have approached 30 years. Lifespan in the wild is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single young in a burrow, where the baby is protected before following the mother.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be somewhat larger.

aardwolf.spotlight: The Aardwolf is specialized humility: a hyena relative that chooses termites over drama. Its quiet feast proves that the humble job can feed you best when the body is built for it.
aardwolf.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Aardwolves live in dry grasslands, savannas, and open scrub where termite colonies are abundant. This habitat fits Specialized Humility because the animal's success depends on a quiet food source underfoot, not on dramatic large-prey hunting.
signatureTraits: Long sticky termite-feeding tongue
Hyena relative with reduced hunting jaws
Nocturnal grassland foraging
Mane raised in defensive display
interestingFacts: Aardwolves are hyena relatives but feed mainly on termites.
They can consume thousands of termites in a night.
They usually do not destroy termite mounds, allowing the food source to continue.
Their name means earth wolf in Afrikaans/Dutch roots.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat mainly harvester termites, licking them from the ground with a long sticky tongue. The diet fits the lesson perfectly: a narrow, humble food path becomes reliable when followed with patience.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators such as lions, leopards, hyenas, and humans may threaten them, especially young. Their defense is denning, night activity, mane display, and strong-smelling anal gland secretions, showing that a gentle specialist still has boundaries.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mainly nocturnal, resting in burrows by day and foraging at night when termites are active. Their rhythm fits the principle because the quiet feast appears only to the one willing to work the right hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aardwolves may live around 8 to 12 years in the wild and longer in care. Their lifespan shows that specialization is not a limitation when the resource renews.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in dens, often to two to four cubs, and both parents may help guard territory or young. Offspring are raised near the termite-rich ground that will define adult life.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, with the same striped yellowish coat, dark legs and erectile mane, and are very similar in size. The sexes cannot usually be told apart in the field.

abyssinian-ground-hornbill.spotlight: Standing about a metre tall, this is one of the largest hornbills, and it lives on the ground across the belt of dry country just south of the Sahara, from Senegal to Ethiopia. Pairs and small family parties walk steadily through the grass for most of the day, flying well but seldom.
abyssinian-ground-hornbill.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Abyssinian Ground Hornbills usually live in savannas, grasslands, and open woodland.
signatureTraits: Ground walking and thunderous calls
Adapted to savannas
Black plumage with white primaries visible only in flight
Tall casque on top of the bill, open at the front
Bare blue skin around the eye
interestingFacts: Abyssinian Ground Hornbills are closely tied to savannas, grasslands, and open woodland.
Their food is mainly insects, reptiles, small mammals, birds, and carrion.
Major pressures include large carnivores, raptors for chicks, and habitat loss.
Long, stiff eyelashes shield its eyes from dust and grit while it feeds on the ground.
Birds have been seen following grazing herds and the edges of grass fires to catch the small animals that are flushed out.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on insects, reptiles, small mammals, birds, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults are big enough to have few enemies beyond leopards and other large carnivores. Eggs and chicks are more exposed, to nest robbers and to birds of prey. Clearance of wooded savanna and hunting reduce numbers. A disturbed bird takes to the air and perches high in a tree.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active from soon after sunrise, it rests in shade through the hottest part of the day. At dusk the birds fly up to roost in trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured. Zoo birds have lived about 35 to 40 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One or two eggs are laid in a hole in a large tree such as a baobab, or among rocks, and the female incubates for about five to six weeks while the male brings her food. She is not walled into the nest. When two chicks hatch, the younger usually dies within days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have blue and red throat skin; females more blue.

ackie-monitor.spotlight: Ackie Monitor teaches Spiny Boundary through a small desert monitor locking itself into stone. Spiny tail, wedge posture, rocky crevices, and heat-loving alertness make boundary a physical anchor, not just a warning.
ackie-monitor.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Arid rocky outcrops, desert scrub, spinifex, stone cracks, and hot basking surfaces.
signatureTraits: Spiny tail used to block or brace inside rock crevices.
Compact monitor body suited to arid rocky habitats.
Strong claws and alert movement near shelter.
Heat-loving daytime activity balanced with quick retreat.
interestingFacts: Ackie Monitors are small Australian monitor lizards with spiny tails.
They often retreat into rock cracks when threatened.
Their tail can help make them harder to pull from a crevice.
They are active hunters of insects and small animals in hot habitats.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, roaches, beetles, small lizards, spiders, eggs, and occasional small vertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, larger monitors, cats, foxes, and humans threaten them. Wedging and tail armor make the boundary real, forcing danger to deal with stone as well as skin.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Ackie Monitors are diurnal, basking before hunting and retreating into rock when risk or temperature demands it.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Well-kept captive lizards commonly live 15 to 20 years. Lifespan in the wild has been little studied.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected warm sites such as burrows or soil chambers.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and more robust than females.

addax.spotlight: Addax teaches Desert Sparing through a pale antelope that survives by spending slowly in hard heat. Its light coat, broad hooves, spiral horns, and water-saving body show endurance as discipline under the sun.
addax.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Saharan desert, gravel plains, dunes, dry grassland, and sparse scrub fit Addax because every feature is built around heat, distance, and scarcity.
signatureTraits: Pale coat that reflects desert heat
Broad hooves for walking on soft sand
Long spiral horns in both sexes
Ability to survive with little free water
interestingFacts: Addax are among the most desert-adapted of all antelopes, living in remote sandy parts of the Sahara.
They can get much of their water from plants.
Their coat changes with the seasons, being greyish-brown in winter and turning nearly white in the hot summer.
They are critically endangered, with very few addax believed to survive in the wild, mainly in Niger.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Desert grasses, shrubs, leaves, seeds, and succulent plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions historically, hyenas, wild dogs, and humans can threaten addax, with human pressure now the major danger. Open distance and herd movement help defense.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Addax may feed in cooler hours and rest during extreme heat. Their rhythm is conservation: move when the desert costs less.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In zoos addax commonly live into their late teens and have reached about twenty-five years. Sahara desert ages for free herds remain unmeasured as wild numbers collapse.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single calf, which must stand and follow or hide quickly. Milk and shade carry the first stage of desert survival.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes have spiral horns, but males are often larger and more robust. The shared horns make sparing strength visible across the species.

adelie-penguin.spotlight: Adelie Penguin carries Hardiness through cheerful-looking motion in brutal ice. Marching feet, strong flippers, dense plumage, and colony grit make cuteness inseparable from Antarctic endurance.
adelie-penguin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southern_ocean, arctic_antarctic. Antarctic coasts, sea ice edges, rocky nesting colonies, and cold Southern Ocean waters.
signatureTraits: Dense waterproof feathers protect against freezing water and wind.
Strong flippers turn awkward land movement into underwater speed.
Colonies share the burden of breeding in harsh open ice landscapes.
Stone nests show how small materials matter when the world is mostly ice.
interestingFacts: Adelie penguins breed all around the Antarctic coast, nesting on ice-free rocky ground in summer.
They collect stones for nests, which can make pebble stealing part of colony drama.
They are agile swimmers even though they waddle on land.
Their black-and-white body suits both water and ice-edge life.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Krill, fish, and squid.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopard seals, skuas, giant petrels, orcas, storms, and shifting ice threaten them. Colony life and relentless feeding trips keep chicks alive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal during long summer breeding light, with foraging rhythms shaped by chick hunger, sea access, and weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 10 to 20 years; endurance becomes a lifetime of returning to ice, mate, nest site, and dangerous water.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay usually two eggs in stone nests, and both parents share incubation and feeding, turning hardiness into family labor.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, with males slightly larger on average.

african-bullfrog.spotlight: African Bullfrog teaches Rain Readiness through a giant frog storing force underground until temporary water returns. Dry-season dormancy, protective cocooning, explosive feeding, male guarding, and rain-pool breeding make patience muscular.
african-bullfrog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry savannas, grasslands, temporary pools, and burrowable soil.
signatureTraits: Dry-season burrowing lets the frog survive long periods without surface water.
A large mouth and powerful body allow intense feeding after rains.
Breeding happens rapidly in temporary pools when conditions finally arrive.
Males can be highly protective and aggressive around breeding sites and young.
interestingFacts: African Bullfrogs can spend dry periods underground in a dormant state.
They are opportunistic predators and may eat surprisingly large prey for a frog.
Males are much larger than females and may defend breeding areas.
Their tadpoles must develop quickly because temporary pools can vanish.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, rodents, birds, reptiles, amphibians, other frogs, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, snakes, mammals, larger frogs, drought, humans, and habitat change threaten African Bullfrogs. Burrowing protects during scarcity, while size, bite, and timing protect when the wet season becomes crowded and competitive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Bullfrogs can remain inactive underground during dry periods, then become active after heavy rains.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespans are poorly measured, but captive bullfrogs commonly pass 20 years and a few are reported beyond 35.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay large numbers of eggs in temporary water, while males may guard territories and sometimes protect channels or access to water for tadpoles. Offspring survival depends on speed, water timing, and parental defense.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are far larger and more heavily built than females, especially around breeding contests and defense.

african-bush-elephant.spotlight: African Bush Elephant is known for matriarchal groups, long-range movement, water knowledge, and immense strength.
african-bush-elephant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, woodlands, deserts, wetlands, and mixed African landscapes where water and forage shift seasonally.
signatureTraits: Largest living land animal
Trunk used for touch, smell, food, and water
Matriarch-led social herds
Very large ears, flapped to shed heat
Tusks in both sexes, heavier in bulls
interestingFacts: African Bush Elephants communicate with low-frequency rumbles, some below human hearing, that other elephants can detect kilometres away.
They dig for water and can shape habitat for other species.
Older females often guide herds through drought decisions.
Since 2021 the IUCN has assessed African Bush Elephants separately from forest elephants, listing them as Endangered.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Herbivorous, eating grasses, leaves, bark, fruit, roots, and branches.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few predators; calves may be threatened by lions, hyenas, or drought stress.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sleeps in short periods, often resting less than many mammals because feeding demands are high.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live around 60-70 years in the wild under good conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry calves through a long pregnancy and raise them with help from the herd.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and often leave natal herds, while females remain in family groups.

african-civet.spotlight: African Civet teaches Scented Adaptation through a striped nocturnal omnivore keeping its pattern while changing menu. Scent glands, bold markings, edge foraging, and flexible food choices make adaptation identifiable rather than shapeless.
african-civet.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Forest edges, savanna, thickets, farmland, riverine cover, and villages.
signatureTraits: Bold striped and spotted coat that keeps identity visible.
Nocturnal movement through forests, edges, and open habitats.
Scent-marking glands used to communicate presence and territory.
Flexible omnivorous diet that changes with opportunity.
interestingFacts: African Civets are nocturnal omnivores, not cats, despite their cat-like look.
They use scent marking as an important part of communication.
Their diet can include fruit, insects, small animals, eggs, and carrion.
Their bold pattern stays recognizable even though their habits are highly flexible.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, insects, rodents, reptiles, birds, eggs, carrion, and plant matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, hyenas, pythons, dogs, humans, and road traffic threaten civets. Night movement and scent marking organize risk, turning the dark into a familiar map.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Civets are nocturnal, resting hidden by day and moving after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive civets commonly reach 15 to 20 years. Wild animals are thought to live less long, but their lifespan has not been measured well.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to young in sheltered dens or hidden cover.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be larger.

african-clawed-frog.spotlight: Tongueless and flat-bodied, this frog of southern Africa lives almost wholly under water. Rows of pale, stitch-like sense organs along its flanks pick up movement in murky water, as the lateral line of a fish does, and the long fingers sweep food into the mouth. Most frogs lose these organs when they stop being tadpoles; this one keeps them for life.
african-clawed-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Ponds, slow streams, pools, ditches, and still freshwater fit African Clawed Frogs because sensing works through water movement.
signatureTraits: The body is flattened, with a small wedge-shaped head.
Small eyes sit on top of the head and look upward.
Hind feet are large and fully webbed; the fingers are unwebbed.
Skin is smooth and slippery, mottled olive-grey above and pale below.
It rises briefly to gulp air, then sinks back to the bottom.
interestingFacts: From the 1930s to the 1960s it served as a pregnancy test: a female frog injected with a pregnant woman's urine laid eggs within about a day.
John Gurdon's cloning experiments, which later earned a Nobel Prize, were carried out on this species.
When a pond dries out it can bury itself in the mud and wait, or cross land in wet weather to reach new water.
Males have no vocal sacs; they call under water with rapid clicks made in the larynx.
Escaped and released animals have founded wild populations on several continents outside Africa.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, crustaceans, tadpoles, small fish and carrion. Lacking a tongue, it finds prey by touch, smell and the lateral-line system that senses water movement, then pushes food into its mouth with its forelimbs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, birds, snakes, mammals, and larger frogs can threaten them. Aquatic hiding and clawed feet help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly aquatic and often active at night or in low-light water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 10 to 15 years in captivity, with some individuals reported at 25 or more; lifespans in the wild are less well known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After heavy rain, females release many eggs into water during breeding. The eggs, from several hundred to a few thousand, are stuck singly or in small groups to plants and stones and get no care. The filter-feeding tadpoles hang head-down in mid-water and have a pair of long barbels.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are clearly larger and plumper than males and have small fleshy flaps beside the vent. Breeding males develop dark, rough pads along the inner arms and fingers.

african-fish-eagle.spotlight: African Fish Eagle teaches Lake Dominion through voice, perch, and strike aligned over the same water. Its ringing call, tall waterside perch, sharp vision, and fish-gripping talons show power made clear by owning one domain.
african-fish-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Lakes, rivers, wetlands, reservoirs, and tall waterside trees.
signatureTraits: Ringing territorial call that carries over water
High waterside perches used for scanning fish
Strong talons built for seizing slippery prey
Bold white, chestnut, and dark plumage with commanding presence
interestingFacts: African Fish Eagles are famous for a call often treated as a signature sound of African lakes and rivers.
They may catch fish but also steal food or scavenge when opportunity appears.
Pairs often hold territories around productive water and may stay on the same stretch of shore year-round.
Their talons have to grip prey that is wet, moving, and difficult to hold.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish are central, with birds, reptiles, carrion, and small animals sometimes taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large raptors, crocodiles, nest predators, humans, and disturbance may threaten eggs or young. High nests and territorial defense make dominion protective rather than just dramatic.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Fish Eagles are diurnal, calling, scanning, and hunting in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually put at about 12 to 24 years in the wild, although few birds have been followed for life.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests near water, and both parents help guard and feed the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males, while both share territory defense and parenting.

african-forest-elephant.spotlight: African Forest Elephant teaches Forest Pathmaking through strength that opens room for other lives. Its trunk, straight downward tusks, seed dispersal, trail making, and rainforest movement show leadership as ecological service rather than noise.
african-forest-elephant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Central and West African rainforests, forest clearings, mineral-rich bais, swamp forest, and dense trails fit African Forest Elephants because their strength works inside thick vegetation.
signatureTraits: Large forest body that clears trails through dense vegetation
Straight tusks used while feeding and moving in rainforest
Major seed disperser for many forest plants
Social intelligence and long memory in matriarchal groups
interestingFacts: African Forest Elephants are a distinct species from African Savanna Elephants.
They help create trails used by many other animals.
Their dung spreads large seeds across rainforest landscapes.
They are generally smaller than savanna elephants but vital to forest structure.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, leaves, bark, branches, mineral soil, and aquatic plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult forest elephants have few natural predators, but calves may face big cats and humans are the major danger. Herd protection and dense forest help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They may feed and travel by day or night depending on disturbance, heat, and fruiting. Their rhythm is slow movement that changes the forest behind them.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Forest elephants can live for many decades. The long lifespan makes pathmaking cumulative: old animals remember routes and shape forests over time.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry calves through long pregnancies and raise them with help from related females. Calves learn migration paths, feeding sites, and social signals from the herd.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger and often live more solitarily as adults, while females remain in family groups. That difference makes forest strength both solitary and matriarchal.

african-grey-parrot.spotlight: This parrot of West and Central African rainforest goes on learning new sounds throughout its life instead of hatching with a fixed set of calls. In decades of laboratory work by Irene Pepperberg, a bird named Alex used spoken English labels for objects, colours and shapes and answered simple questions about number.
african-grey-parrot.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. African Grey Parrot usually lives in African rainforests, forest edges, plantations, and tall trees.
signatureTraits: vocal mimicry
grey plumage
red tail
problem-solving mind
interestingFacts: Flocks have been watched gathering in swampy forest clearings in the Congo Basin to eat soil and drink.
The smaller, darker Timneh parrot of the far west of Africa, with a maroon tail, was treated as the same species until 2012.
In a 2020 experiment, grey parrots passed tokens to a neighbour who could trade them for food, although the giver gained nothing at the time.
Young birds have dark grey eyes; the iris turns pale yellow as they mature.
Surveys in Ghana published in 2016 estimated that the population there had fallen by at least 90 per cent since the early 1990s.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: African Grey Parrot feeds on seeds, nuts, fruit, berries, and palm foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds of prey, including palm-nut vultures, have been recorded taking grey parrots, and monkeys and snakes are thought to raid nest holes. Flocks keep to the high canopy and are wary when they come to the ground. Trapping for the pet trade, with forest loss, is by far the greatest threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Grey Parrot is diurnal, roosting communally and feeding by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive birds have lived 40 to 60 years, though many die younger. Lifespan in the wild is poorly measured and is thought to be considerably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In the wild, females lay eggs in tree cavities and both parents help. Clutches are of 2 to 5 eggs, which the female incubates for about 30 days while the male feeds her. Chicks leave the nest at around 12 weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look similar to most observers. Males average slightly larger, with a broader and flatter head, but the overlap is too wide for the difference to be used in the field.

african-jacana.spotlight: African Jacana teaches Light Footing through toes that spread pressure across floating leaves. Its long toes, lily-pad walking, wetland balance, and reversed parenting pattern show that impossible crossings become possible when weight is carried carefully.
african-jacana.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Lily pads, marshes, wetlands, floodplains, and shallow vegetated water.
signatureTraits: Extremely long toes that spread weight over floating plants
Light stepping across lily pads and wet vegetation
Wetland life built around unstable surfaces
Male-heavy parental care after females lay clutches
interestingFacts: African Jacanas are sometimes called lily-trotters because they appear to walk on floating leaves.
Females are larger than males and may mate with several males.
Males commonly incubate eggs and care for chicks.
The chicks can hide under a parent’s wings while only their long legs show.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, snails, seeds, aquatic invertebrates, and plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish eagles, snakes, monitor lizards, crocodiles, and mammals threaten eggs or chicks. These pressures make careful footing protective: the same floating maze that feeds the jacana also helps it keep danger at a distance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Jacanas are diurnal, walking and feeding on floating vegetation in daylight. Their rhythm is constant pressure management: step gently, read the leaf, move before it sinks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: African Jacanas can live for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs, but males usually incubate and care for the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and more competitive, while males are smaller and do much of the parental care.

african-openbill.spotlight: African Openbill teaches Shell Skill through a stork whose bill is shaped for the gap force misses. Curved mandibles, visible opening, snail handling, and wetland feeding turn extraction into the lesson.
african-openbill.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Marshes, floodplains, papyrus swamps, rice fields, shallow lakes, and seasonal wetlands.
signatureTraits: Specialized open bill with a gap between mandibles
Wetland feeding focused strongly on freshwater snails
Careful shell handling rather than brute-force feeding
Long-legged stork body suited to shallow water
interestingFacts: African Openbills are named for the visible gap in the closed bill.
Their bill shape helps them handle aquatic snails.
They often feed in marshes, floodplains, and rice fields.
They may gather where snail abundance is high after rains or flooding.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Freshwater snails are central, with mussels, frogs, insects, crabs, and small aquatic animals sometimes taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, crocodiles, monitor lizards, snakes, mammals, and nest predators threaten openbills or chicks. Colonies reduce risk, while the specialized bill keeps adults tied to productive wetland timing.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: African Openbills are diurnal, feeding in shallow wetlands by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Published mean ages are lacking; storks that prise apple snails with gap-billed forceps in African wetlands have scant lifespan datasets.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick nests, often in colonies near wetlands.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may average larger.

african-rock-python.spotlight: Africa's largest snake, a non-venomous python that is commonly 3 to 5 metres long and exceptionally more. It hunts from ambush, lying motionless beside a game trail or in shallow water, and detects warm-blooded prey in the dark with heat-sensing pits along its lips.
african-rock-python.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savanna, grassland, open woodland and forest edge across West, Central and East Africa, generally near rivers, lakes or swamps. Rocky outcrops, thickets and reedbeds give cover, and it also lives in farmland and around villages where rodents are plentiful.
signatureTraits: A dark spearhead mark on top of the head is edged with pale stripes.
Dark brown blotches, often joined into a chain, run along a tan back.
The body is very thick for its length, with smooth, glossy scales.
Large individuals crawl forward in a straight line, caterpillar-fashion.
interestingFacts: After a very large meal, such as an antelope, a python may not need to feed again for several months.
Trade in its skin and in live animals is regulated under CITES Appendix II.
Attacks on people are rare but have been recorded, including a small number of deaths.
The two halves of the lower jaw are joined at the front by an elastic ligament, letting it swallow prey wider than its own head.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, birds, monitor lizards, monkeys and small to medium antelopes, with the largest snakes taking prey as big as warthogs. Prey is seized with backward-curving teeth, killed by constriction and swallowed whole, usually head first.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hatchlings and young snakes fall to birds of prey, mongooses, monitor lizards and other snakes. Adults are most at risk when sluggish after a large meal, when hyenas or wild dogs may kill them. People hunt them for skin and meat. A cornered python hisses and strikes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active at dusk and during the night, although it often basks in the morning sun. Days are spent in burrows, rock crevices, hollow logs or thick vegetation, and in the driest months it may stay inactive underground for weeks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive individuals have lived more than 25 years. Lifespan in the wild is not well known and is probably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female lays roughly 20 to 100 eggs in an old burrow, termite mound or hollow. She coils around them for the two to three months of incubation and guards them without feeding. Hatchlings are about half a metre long.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow larger and heavier than males. Males have bigger spurs, small claw-like remnants of hind limbs beside the vent. Colour and pattern are the same in both sexes.

african-wild-dog.spotlight: African Wild Dog is Pack Relentlessness painted in motion. Its endurance, communication, and shared chase make the hunt belong to the group rather than to one heroic body.
african-wild-dog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. African Wild Dogs live in savannas, open woodland, grassland, and scrub where long pursuit is possible.
signatureTraits: Painted coat patterns unique to each individual
Large rounded ears for heat loss and communication
Cooperative endurance hunting in packs
Strong social care around pups and injured members
interestingFacts: Each African Wild Dog has a unique coat pattern.
They are among the most cooperative mammalian hunters.
Packs may feed pups and even injured adults after a hunt.
Their large ears help with both hearing and cooling.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly medium-sized antelope: impala over much of the range, with kudu, reedbuck, gazelles and wildebeest calves elsewhere, and smaller prey such as duikers and hares. Prey is run down in a long chase and eaten quickly, before lions or hyenas arrive.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include lions, hyenas, disease from domestic dogs, snares, vehicles, and habitat fragmentation. Their defense is distance, social cohesion, speed, and the pack's ability to watch many angles at once.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Often active in cooler daylight hours, especially morning and evening, resting during heat. Their rhythm shows discipline: relentless movement works only when energy is saved for the chase.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 10 to 12 years in the wild if disease and conflict are avoided. The lifespan why is social persistence: survival depends on the pack staying functional through hunts, pups, and losses.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Usually the dominant female breeds, with the pack helping raise and feed pups.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar in appearance, and roles are social rather than heavily ornamental.

agile-wallaby.spotlight: The most common wallaby of tropical northern Australia and southern New Guinea, a medium-sized kangaroo relative of river flats and coastal plains. It feeds in loose groups that can number dozens where the grass is good. An alarmed animal often thumps the ground with its hind feet before the group scatters in long, low bounds.
agile-wallaby.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Tropical woodland, grassland, savanna edges, and open scrub fit Agile Wallabies because hopping is efficient across broken ground.
signatureTraits: Coat is sandy brown above and whitish below.
A pale stripe runs across each hip.
A whitish stripe runs along the cheek.
A dark line runs down the middle of the forehead.
Ear edges and tail tip are black.
interestingFacts: On some northern rivers agile wallabies dig drinking holes in the sand back from the water's edge, behaviour thought to reduce the risk from crocodiles.
During the dry season it scrapes up the roots of grasses and sedges when green feed is scarce.
It has taken readily to pasture and sugar cane, and is treated as a pest in parts of Queensland.
It was long placed in the genus Macropus; Notamacropus is now used for this and several other wallabies.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, leaves, herbs, fruits, and shoots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dingoes, large pythons, raptors, dogs, and humans can threaten wallabies. Speed, alertness, and cover help them escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They often feed in cooler hours and rest during heat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably around 10 to 12 years at most in the wild, where few animals have been followed for life; captive animals have reached about 16.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding continues all year. A single young is born after about a month's pregnancy and spends seven to eight months in the pouch, suckling until around a year old. A female mated soon after the birth carries a dormant embryo until the pouch is free.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are much the larger, reaching about 85 centimetres in head and body length and up to about 27 kilograms, against roughly 15 kilograms or less for females. Males also have heavier forearms and chests.

aldabra-giant-tortoise.spotlight: The last of the giant tortoises that once lived on islands across the western Indian Ocean; those of the Mascarene islands were wiped out by the mid-1800s. Around 100,000 survive on Aldabra atoll in the Seychelles. It can drink through its nostrils, drawing water from rain pools too shallow for the mouth.
aldabra-giant-tortoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, indian_ocean. Aldabra Giant Tortoise usually lives in Aldabra atoll scrub, grassland, mangrove edges, and island shade.
signatureTraits: Massive shell and body built for island endurance
Slow grazing that shapes vegetation over long periods
Heat-management through shade, wallows, and timing
Centuries-scale presence that makes patience visible
interestingFacts: Aldabra Giant Tortoises are among the largest tortoises alive.
Some individuals can live for more than a century.
Their grazing can shape island plant communities, cropping grasses and herbs into short lawns known as tortoise turf.
Aldabra Giant Tortoises have been introduced to islands such as Mauritius to replace extinct native giant tortoises.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aldabra Giant Tortoise feeds on grasses, leaves, woody plants, fallen fruit, and low vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crabs, rats and birds eat eggs and hatchlings. Adults have no natural predators, though sailors once carried them off by the thousand as ship's provisions. On a low, dry atoll the present dangers are drought and rising sea level.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active but rests during heat, using shade, wallows, and slow rhythms so endurance does not waste itself.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live well over 100 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil nests, leaving hatchlings to begin the long life alone under sun, shell, and chance.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with longer tails and more concave plastrons, while females carry the slow future into island soil.

alligator-gar.spotlight: Alligator Gar carries Ancient Strength in slow rivers. Armor-like scales, air-gulping ability, a toothy snout, and ambush patience prove that old designs endure when they still solve present water.
alligator-gar.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Large slow rivers, bayous, oxbows, reservoirs, floodplains, and brackish coastal waters fit Alligator Gar because ancient strength works where oxygen, depth, and cover change.
signatureTraits: Ganoid scales form hard armor that protects the body.
Long toothy jaws suit sudden grabs in slow water.
Air-breathing ability helps in warm or low-oxygen habitats.
Ambush style makes patience more valuable than constant chase.
interestingFacts: Alligator gar belong to an ancient lineage of fishes.
They can surface to gulp air using a vascularized swim bladder.
Their eggs are toxic to many animals, adding another old defensive layer.
They are among the largest freshwater fishes in North America.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, waterbirds, turtles, crustaceans, and opportunistic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators besides humans and large alligators, while eggs and young face fish, birds, and reptiles. Armor takes time to become full protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly crepuscular or nocturnal in many settings, but can be active whenever prey and temperature make ambush favorable.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth rings in the ear bones show that many adults live several decades. The oldest females have been aged at well over 60 years, and males tend to die younger.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs in vegetated shallow water during floods or warm seasons, and the young begin as small vulnerable versions of a future armored giant.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are typically larger, especially as they age, making long life and reproduction part of the species' heavy endurance.

alligator-snapping-turtle.spotlight: The largest freshwater turtle in North America, confined to rivers that drain into the Gulf of Mexico. Large males commonly reach 70 kilograms or more. It can stay under water for 40 to 50 minutes between breaths and almost never comes out to bask.
alligator-snapping-turtle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Alligator Snapping Turtle usually lives in slow rivers, swamps, oxbows, and deep muddy channels.
signatureTraits: Worm-like tongue lure that brings curious fish close
Massive head and hooked beak for sudden close-range capture
Ridged shell that resembles old submerged debris
Extreme stillness that turns patience into hunting design
interestingFacts: Its lure is a real moving part of the tongue, not a separate bait.
The shell can look like a piece of ancient river bottom.
Adults rarely need to chase; they make the feeding zone come to them.
Despite the name, it is a turtle, not an alligator.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Alligator Snapping Turtle feeds on fish, frogs, snakes, turtles, birds, carrion, and prey drawn by its tongue lure.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons dig up many nests, and hatchlings are eaten by large fish, wading birds and other turtles. Adults have no regular predator except people, who trapped them heavily for meat. A cornered turtle gapes and bites; its small lower shell leaves the limbs exposed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends long inactive periods submerged and often becomes more active at night, letting the river come close before effort begins.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often several decades and may exceed 70 years; Attraction here is not charm, but a lifetime of designing the trap so opportunity swims inward.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females leave water to bury clutches in sandy or loose soil, placing the next generation outside the ambush world until it can return to water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger with longer tails, while females invest in risky nesting trips away from the safety of mud and depth.

alpaca.spotlight: Alpaca teaches Reassurance through a herd animal whose quiet humming keeps social distance from becoming fear. Soft fleece, alert ears, group grazing, and contact calls show communication as steady warmth rather than loud control.
alpaca.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. High Andean grasslands, cool pastures, and open herd spaces fit alpacas because they are grazing animals shaped by altitude, cold, and group awareness. The setting makes reassurance practical.
signatureTraits: Soft humming maintains contact between herd members without turning every concern into alarm.
Dense fleece reflects a highland history where cold, altitude, and patience shaped the body.
Herd awareness makes calm a social behavior, not just an individual mood.
interestingFacts: A baby alpaca is called a cria and typically arrives after a pregnancy of roughly eleven months.
Alpacas were domesticated in the Andes for fine fleece.
They communicate with hums, alarm calls, clucks, posture, and ear position.
Alpacas in a herd often share communal dung piles rather than scattering droppings across their pasture.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grazes mainly on grasses, sedges and other low pasture plants, supplemented with hay in managed herds. Food is chewed as cud and digested by fermentation in a three-compartment stomach, which extracts nutrients efficiently from poor forage.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pumas, foxes, dogs, and other predators make herd communication important. A calm contact hum can shift quickly into alarm when the group needs to respond.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Alpacas are mainly active by day, grazing, resting, and ruminating in social groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Alpacas often live 15 to 20 years with good care. That lifespan makes long-term herd bonds, routine handling, and repeated calm communication central to the animal’s story.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single cria is born after a gestation of about 11 to 11.5 months; twins are very rare. Births usually happen in the morning, and the cria, weighing about 6 to 9 kilograms, stands and suckles within a few hours. Weaning comes at around 6 months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may be larger and can develop fighting teeth, while females are shaped by pregnancy and cria care. Most visual differences are subtle, so behavior and herd role matter more than obvious display.

alpine-ibex.spotlight: Alpine Ibex teaches Cliff Balance through a mountain body treating danger as ordinary ground. Rubber-edged hooves, strong legs, massive horns, and near-vertical movement turn balance into confidence.
alpine-ibex.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe. Alpine cliffs, rocky slopes, high meadows, mountain ledges, and mineral-rich terrain.
signatureTraits: Specialized hooves that grip steep rock
Powerful legs for cliff and ledge movement
Large curved horns, especially in males
High-mountain confidence on terrain that punishes mistakes
interestingFacts: Alpine Ibex can move across very steep rocky slopes with surprising calm.
Their hooves have hard edges and softer gripping pads.
Males carry much larger, ridged horns than females, sometimes approaching a metre in length.
Steep cliffs can protect them from many predators.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Alpine grasses, herbs, shrubs, mosses, and lichens.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, lynx, bears, golden eagles for young, avalanches, winter, and humans threaten ibex. Steep ground becomes protection, proving that danger can become shelter when the body is built for it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Alpine Ibex are diurnal, often feeding in morning and evening while resting on safer ledges. Their rhythm follows temperature, footing, and mountain exposure.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 10 to 16 years in the wild. The oldest animals, usually females, reach about 19 or 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to kids that must quickly learn mountain footing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have much larger horns and heavier bodies, while females are smaller and highly agile.

alpine-newt.spotlight: A newt 8 to 12 centimetres long whose belly is plain and unspotted. In the pond the male turns blue-grey above, with a band of black spots on white along each flank and a low, smooth-edged crest barred yellow and black. Once breeding is over the skin turns dark, dull and velvety for the months on land.
alpine-newt.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe. Mountain ponds, forest pools, damp woods, meadows, and cool terrestrial cover fit Alpine Newts because their life moves between water season and land season.
signatureTraits: Orange belly gives a warning flash beneath the body.
Breeding colors become strongest during pond season.
Land-and-water life changes with moisture and season.
interestingFacts: Alpine Newts move between ponds and damp terrestrial shelter.
Their orange belly can signal toxic skin defenses.
Breeding males develop more striking seasonal color and cresting.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small crustaceans, insect larvae, worms, tadpoles, and tiny aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, birds, snakes, mammals, larger amphibians, and aquatic insects threaten eggs, larvae, or adults. Toxic skin secretions and seasonal cover help reduce danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Alpine Newts are most active in damp conditions and during breeding seasons around ponds.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly around 10 years. Age studies from bone growth rings suggest some high-altitude animals reach about 20, and captive newts have lived about as long.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs one by one on aquatic plants or submerged material, often folding leaves around them. Each egg is placed carefully inside the breeding pond season.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males become more colorful in breeding condition, while females are usually fuller-bodied with eggs. Sex difference is most visible during the glowing pond season.

alpine-salamander.spotlight: The Alpine Salamander is cool fit and hidden patience. Its dark body, mountain moisture, and live-bearing reproduction show that some lives are not built for speed or spectacle, but for quiet weather and deep timing.
alpine-salamander.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe. Alpine Salamanders live in cool, moist mountain forests, alpine meadows, and rocky areas of Europe.
signatureTraits: Cool mountain habitat specialist
Smooth dark warning-toned skin
Gives birth to developed young
Moisture-dependent slow movement
interestingFacts: Alpine Salamanders are unusual because females give birth to fully formed young rather than laying eggs in water.
Development inside the mother can take a very long time compared with many amphibians.
They are most often seen in damp weather or moist mountain conditions.
Their black coloration helps absorb heat in cool habitats.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat small invertebrates such as insects, worms, spiders, and slugs found in damp ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators may include birds, snakes, and small carnivores, though skin secretions help discourage attacks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are most active in wet, cool conditions and often hide under logs, stones, or vegetation during dry periods. This rhythm shows the wisdom of fit: the salamander moves when the weather belongs to it.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: At least 10 years in the wild, and probably 15 or more in some individuals. Exact figures are scarce.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to one or two fully developed young after a long internal development period.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, with subtle size or body-shape differences at most. The important distinction is reproductive role, especially the female's remarkable live-bearing strategy.

amazon-milk-frog.spotlight: Amazon Milk Frog teaches Canopy Vigilance through a tree frog watching hidden water above the forest floor. Large eyes, sticky toe pads, tree-hole breeding, and milky secretion make awareness vertical.
amazon-milk-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Amazon rainforest canopy, tree holes, bromeliads, humid trunks, and water-filled cavities.
signatureTraits: Large striking eyes suited to nocturnal canopy awareness.
Sticky toe pads for climbing trunks, branches, and tree holes.
Breeding tied to water-filled cavities above the ground.
Milky defensive secretion that helps deter predators.
interestingFacts: Amazon Milk Frogs breed in water-filled tree holes and cavities.
Their name comes from a milky defensive secretion produced when stressed.
They are arboreal, spending much of life above the forest floor.
Their large eyes suit a nocturnal life among branches.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, moths, crickets, roaches, and small arthropods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, spiders, drying tree holes, and habitat loss threaten frogs or tadpoles. Adhesion, height, secretion, and careful breeding-site choice help protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Amazon Milk Frogs are nocturnal, calling and hunting at night from trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity these frogs commonly live about 8 to 10 years, sometimes longer. No reliable figure exists for wild animals.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in water-filled tree holes or similar cavities, where tadpoles develop above the forest floor.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though females are often larger in many frogs. The shared canopy body plan carries the principle, while male calling adds the breeding signal.

american-alligator.spotlight: American Alligator teaches Patience through armored stillness at the water’s edge. Eyes above water, hidden body, powerful tail, crushing jaws, and explosive strike show strength held back until the world comes close enough.
american-alligator.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Swamps, marshes, lakes, rivers, ponds, bayous, and wetland edges fit American Alligators because water hides the body while shorelines deliver prey. The habitat turns waiting into strategy.
signatureTraits: Eyes and nostrils sit high, allowing the body to stay mostly submerged.
Armored scutes and a muscular tail support both defense and sudden movement.
Ambush hunting turns patience into explosive force at close range.
interestingFacts: Alligators create small wet depressions that can hold water for other animals in dry periods.
Temperature during egg incubation can influence the sex of hatchlings.
Mothers guard nests and young more actively than many reptiles.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, turtles, birds, mammals, frogs, snakes, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult alligators have few natural predators, but eggs and young face raccoons, birds, snakes, larger alligators, and mammals. Nest guarding and water refuge protect the next generation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Alligators are most active in warm conditions and often hunt from dusk into night, while basking by day to regulate temperature. Their rhythm mixes solar recharge with hidden ambush.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild adults are thought to reach about 35 to 50 years, though ages are hard to confirm in the field; zoo animals have lived past 70.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build mound nests and guard eggs and hatchlings, sometimes carrying young gently in the mouth. Offspring matter because the same jaws used for power also become careful transport and defense.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger than females and may defend territories or display with bellows.

american-avocet.spotlight: American Avocet teaches Elegant Sifting through an upturned bill turning repetition into grace. Long legs, shallow water, side-sweeping arcs, and seasonal plumage show that the right tool can make patient work beautiful.
american-avocet.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Shallow lakes, saline ponds, marshes, mudflats, and flooded fields.
signatureTraits: Long upcurved bill designed for side-to-side sweeping in shallow water.
Tall legs for wading through saline ponds, marshes, and flats.
Seasonal rusty head and neck coloration during breeding.
Group feeding and defensive calls around exposed wetland nests.
interestingFacts: American Avocets often feed by sweeping the bill through water like a moving filter.
Their breeding plumage adds warm cinnamon color to the head and neck.
They may perform distraction or defense behavior near nests.
Their upturned bill gives the whole feeding motion a curved visual rhythm.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic insects, crustaceans, larvae, and tiny invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coyotes, foxes, gulls, ravens, raptors, flooding, and habitat loss threaten eggs or chicks. Grace must be paired with noisy defense and careful nest placement.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Avocets are diurnal, feeding when light and water levels make sweeping possible.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ringing recoveries show wild birds reaching about 15 years. The typical lifespan is shorter and has not been measured well.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in shallow ground nests near water, and chicks leave the nest soon after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females often have a more strongly upcurved bill than males.

american-bison.spotlight: American Bison teaches Steady Force through a massive grazer that keeps moving when weather pushes back. Heavy shoulders, snow-plowing head, herd motion, and prairie grazing make endurance physical.
american-bison.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Prairies, grasslands, river valleys, open plains, and snowy winter range.
signatureTraits: Massive head and shoulder hump for pushing through snow
Thick winter coat suited to harsh plains weather
Herd movement across grassland and prairie
Powerful grazing body that shapes the landscape
interestingFacts: American Bison are the largest land mammals in North America.
They use their heads to sweep snow aside and reach grasses.
Bison herds once numbered in the tens of millions and shaped prairie ecosystems through grazing and wallowing.
Despite their size, they can run surprisingly fast.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, herbs, and prairie plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, bears for calves, humans, harsh winters, disease, and habitat limits threaten bison. Herd protection and size help, but endurance carries them through weather.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Bison are diurnal and crepuscular, grazing, resting, and moving with conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: American Bison can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to calves that stand and follow the herd quickly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are much larger than females and compete during the rut.

american-bullfrog.spotlight: American Bullfrog teaches Amplification through a wetland body that makes sound larger than itself. Its deep boom, inflated vocal sac, pond territory, and patient water-edge posture show how a small signal can command space when the body is shaped to carry it.
american-bullfrog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, lakes, marshes, slow streams, canals, and permanent wetlands fit the bullfrog because water carries voice, hides the body, and gathers prey. The habitat turns sound into territory.
signatureTraits: Boom Call: males use deep resonant calls to claim breeding space and attract mates.
Vocal Sac Amplifier: the throat sac turns body vibration into a carrying signal.
Water-Edge Command: ponds and wetlands help the call travel across open surfaces.
interestingFacts: Male American Bullfrogs produce deep calls during breeding season.
They are large frogs that wait at water edges to catch many types of prey.
Their tadpoles can take a long time to develop compared with many smaller frogs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, fish, crayfish, frogs, small snakes, birds, and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, raccoons, snakes, turtles, large fish, otters, and humans pressure bullfrogs at different life stages. Calling is powerful but risky, so the bullfrog balances visibility of sound with the safety of water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Bullfrogs are often most active from evening into night, especially in warm weather. Darkness lets the call travel while the frog stays partly hidden at the water’s edge.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: American Bullfrogs may live several years in the wild and longer in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay large masses of eggs in water, and the young begin as aquatic tadpoles.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often recognized by larger eardrums and calling behavior.

american-dipper.spotlight: North America's only truly aquatic songbird wades, swims and dives into fast, cold streams. Under water it grips stones with its toes and rows with half-open wings to hold its place against the current. Scaly flaps close over the nostrils, and a clear third eyelid lets it see while submerged.
american-dipper.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Cold mountain streams, rocky rivers, waterfalls, and clean fast water fit dippers because their strange gift needs moving water.
signatureTraits: Plump, slate-grey body with a short tail, often cocked.
White eyelids flash each time it blinks.
Flies low and straight over the water, following the stream.
Long, pale legs and a slim dark bill.
interestingFacts: Its preen gland is reported to be about ten times the size of that of other songbirds of similar weight, and supplies the oil that waterproofs its plumage.
It replaces its wing and tail feathers all at once in late summer and is flightless for a short time, as ducks are.
Rather than migrating south, most birds move down to lower, ice-free stretches of river for the winter.
It sings through the winter, a loud run of whistles and trills that carries over the noise of the water.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic insects, larvae, small fish, and stream invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, mink, snakes, cats, and flood events can threaten dippers. Dense plumage, strong legs, and streamside nesting help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Dippers are diurnal, bobbing, diving, and singing near rushing water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most probably live only a few years. One banded bird was recaptured when more than 8 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: From early spring, females lay eggs in mossy streamside nests near rushing water. The usual clutch is four or five white eggs, incubated by the female for about 16 days. Both parents feed the nestlings, which leave at around 25 days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There is no plumage difference between the sexes. Only measurements in the hand, where males average a little larger, or behaviour at the nest will separate them.

american-marten.spotlight: American Marten teaches Agility through a long forest body that slips where bulk cannot follow. Sharp claws, snow tunnels, branch routes, and quick turns make hidden paths stronger than force.
american-marten.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Conifer forests, mixed woods, fallen logs, hollow trees, and snowy woodland.
signatureTraits: Long flexible body for trunks, branches, logs, and snow gaps
Sharp claws for climbing and gripping forest structure
Winter movement through subnivean spaces and conifer cover
Quick hunting style that turns small routes into advantage
interestingFacts: American Martens are members of the weasel family.
They are strongly associated with mature or structurally complex forests.
They hunt small mammals but also eat fruit, birds, eggs, and carrion.
Deep snow can create hidden travel spaces that suit their light bodies.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Voles, mice, squirrels, birds, eggs, insects, berries, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, hawks, foxes, coyotes, bobcats, fishers, humans, and habitat fragmentation threaten martens. Dense structure and quick climbing keep agility useful under pressure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Martens are often crepuscular or nocturnal, but activity shifts with prey and season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild martens live fewer than 4 years, with winter food shortages a main cause of death. Animals aged from their teeth have occasionally reached 12 or more, and captive martens about 15.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise kits in tree cavities, logs, or sheltered dens.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger than females. The size difference affects range and competition, while both sexes share the same agile woodland design.

american-paddlefish.spotlight: A relative of the sturgeons with a skeleton mostly of cartilage, living in the Mississippi river system. Its flat snout, about a third of the body length, carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that pick up the weak electric fields given off by swimming water fleas. With these it finds plankton swarms in muddy water and in darkness.
american-paddlefish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Large turbid rivers, reservoirs, and backwaters fit because ordinary sight is weak and hidden signals matter.
signatureTraits: Smooth, scaleless skin, grey above and pale below
Deeply forked tail with a longer upper lobe
Long, pointed gill cover reaching back past the pectoral fins
Tiny eyes set just behind the base of the snout
interestingFacts: Its only recent relative, the Chinese paddlefish of the Yangtze, was declared extinct in 2022, with no confirmed sighting since 2003.
Fossil paddlefish are known from rocks more than 100 million years old.
Its eggs are sold as caviar, and fish are farmed for this as a substitute for sturgeon roe.
Because it ignores bait, anglers catch it by snagging, dragging a bare weighted hook through the water.
Larvae hatch without the paddle, which begins to grow within a few weeks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton and tiny drifting organisms.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large fish threaten young, while humans, dams, harvest, and river changes threaten adults by breaking the flows they need.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: American Paddlefish keep swimming and filtering through river rhythms, with rest expressed more as reduced movement than a human-like sleep.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for decades, especially females, making long river continuity important for slow maturity and spawning success.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females spawn many eggs over gravel in flowing rivers, so the next generation depends on current, timing, and open migration routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females usually grow larger and mature later, while males mature earlier; both rely on the paddle-shaped sensory rostrum.

amur-leopard.spotlight: Amur Leopard teaches Frost Stealth through a rare cat whose coat turns cold into cover. Its pale winter fur, rosettes, solitary ambush, and rocky forest movement show that the right covering can make harsh weather part of the hunt.
amur-leopard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Temperate forests, snowy slopes, rocky ridges, river valleys, and Korean pine-broadleaf forests fit Amur Leopards because frost stealth needs cover and prey routes.
signatureTraits: Pale thick winter coat with widely spaced rosettes
Solitary stealth hunter of cold forests
Powerful climbing and leaping ability
Extreme rarity in the Russian Far East and nearby regions
interestingFacts: Amur Leopards are among the rarest big cats.
Their winter coats grow longer and paler than in warmer leopard populations.
They can drag prey into trees or cover.
Camera traps are important for monitoring the remaining wild population.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Roe deer, sika deer, hares, badgers, wild boar young, and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult Amur Leopards have few natural predators, but tigers, humans, and prey loss can threaten them. Camouflage and solitary range use reduce conflict.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, moving when cover improves. Their rhythm lets the pale coat work with snow, shadow, and silence.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild Amur leopards usually live about 10 to 15 years; in zoos they have reached about 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters in dens or sheltered places. Cubs stay hidden and depend on the mother’s hunting and protection for many months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and hold broader ranges, while females raise cubs. Both carry the frost coat, but their survival roles differ by range and care.

andean-cock-of-the-rock.spotlight: Andean Cock-of-the-rock teaches Lek Display through flame-orange males, loud calls, and repeated courtship stages in cloud forest. Visibility works best when the right audience gathers in the right place.
andean-cock-of-the-rock.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Andean cloud forest, ravines, rocky cliffs, stream valleys, and dense mountain trees.
signatureTraits: Brilliant orange male crest and body used in display.
Lek gatherings where males call and perform for females.
Cloud-forest and rocky ravine habitat tied to nesting and fruit.
Strong sexual dimorphism between vivid males and duller females.
interestingFacts: Andean cock-of-the-rock is the national bird of Peru.
Males gather in leks to display and call for females.
Females build nests on rocky walls or ledges and handle nesting duties.
They feed heavily on fruit and help disperse seeds.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit is central, with insects and small items also taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, monkeys, carnivores, and habitat loss can threaten eggs, chicks, or adults. Leks make males visible, while nesting cliffs and female camouflage protect reproduction.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, feeding and displaying by day, especially around active lek periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive scarlet lek birds have been reported beyond ten years; cloud-forest ages at Andean display courts remain unpublished.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build mud-and-plant nests on cliffs or rock faces and raise the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are vivid orange with large crests, while females are duller brownish-orange.

andean-condor.spotlight: Andean Condor turns huge wings into Mountain Lift. It does not flap against the Andes when the air itself can carry it; it reads rising currents and lets the cliffs share the work.
andean-condor.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Andean Condors live along the Andes, cliffs, high mountains, open grasslands, and coastal regions in parts of South America.
signatureTraits: Huge wingspan for soaring over mountains
Use of thermals and cliff winds to save energy
Scavenging role across Andean landscapes
Long-lived slow-breeding life history
interestingFacts: Andean Condors have one of the largest wingspans of any flying bird.
They often soar for long periods with very little flapping.
They are scavengers, helping clean carcasses from mountain landscapes.
They breed slowly and invest heavily in each chick.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed mainly on carrion from large mammals, including wild and domestic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but eggs and chicks can be vulnerable, and humans, poisoning, and habitat conflict are major threats. Their defense is height, size, and choosing air routes that waste little energy.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, often waiting for warming air before long soaring. The rhythm is central: the condor rises when the mountain begins to lift it.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for many decades, sometimes over 50 years. The lifespan why is that energy efficiency and slow breeding belong together: the bird survives by not wasting motion.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay a single egg, and both parents invest for a long time.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and have more pronounced combs or neck features; females are slightly smaller. Both sexes depend on the same lift-reading intelligence of wing and cliff.

andean-goose.spotlight: Andean Goose teaches Altitude Fit through a white mountain grazer accepting cold air as home. High wetlands, strong pair bonds, grazing bodies, and thin-air movement make hardship livable because the body is built for it.
andean-goose.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. High Andean lakes, bogs, wet meadows, puna grassland, and cold mountain wetlands.
signatureTraits: High-elevation goose body adapted to Andean wetlands and grasslands.
Mostly white plumage that stands out against mountain water and ground.
Strong pair bonding in exposed open landscapes.
Grazing lifestyle shaped by cold, wind, and sparse highland plants.
interestingFacts: Andean Geese live high in the Andes, often around lakes and wetlands.
They are strongly associated with open highland grazing areas.
Pairs are often seen together, making partnership part of the species image.
Their white plumage makes them visually striking in mountain settings.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, aquatic plants, and highland vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, raptors, dogs, humans, harsh weather, and nest disturbance can threaten them. Pair vigilance and open sightlines help make exposed altitude safer.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Andean Geese are diurnal, grazing and moving through high wetlands by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Andean Geese can live for years across demanding mountain seasons. Altitude Fit becomes a long lesson in conserving effort, holding bonds, and treating thin air as normal.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in ground nests near wetland cover, while the pair defends the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often mostly white while females can show darker or more patterned plumage. The sex difference adds contrast, but both sexes share the highland-fit principle.

andean-lapwing.spotlight: Andean Lapwing teaches Highland Agility through a bird made for thin air, open wet meadows, and mountain wind. Broad wings, alert calls, quick turns, and high-altitude footing make movement lighter because the body knows the place.
andean-lapwing.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. High-altitude wetlands, puna grasslands, Andean meadows, marsh edges, and lakeshores fit Andean Lapwings because open wind, water, and visibility shape every movement.
signatureTraits: Lives in high Andean wetlands and grasslands where air and weather are demanding.
Broad wings and agile flight help it move across open mountain ground.
Alert calls make open nesting and feeding safer.
Ground-foraging lifestyle links light movement with constant awareness.
interestingFacts: Andean Lapwings are associated with high elevations in South America.
Their open habitats require strong vigilance because cover is limited.
They feed by walking and picking small prey from wet ground.
Lapwings often rely on calls and display flights to defend space.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, small invertebrates, larvae, and wetland prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, raptors, gulls, dogs, snakes, weather, and trampling can threaten eggs or chicks. Alarm calls and agile flight help defend exposed open nests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Andean Lapwings are diurnal, feeding, calling, and flying in daylight. Their rhythm lets them read wind and ground when visibility is highest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lapwings can live multiple breeding seasons when nests and wetlands survive. The principle gains meaning through repeated returns to high, exposed places that demand agility every day.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on the ground in open habitat, where camouflage and parental alarm are crucial. Chicks must walk and feed early, so highland fit begins almost immediately.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar.

anhinga.spotlight: Anhinga teaches Submersion through a bird that enters depth like a spear and returns to dry its wings. Snake-like neck, submerged body, sharp bill, underwater pursuit, and wing-spread recovery show clean action after going deep.
anhinga.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Swamps, lakes, rivers, marshes, mangroves, ponds, and wooded wetlands fit Anhingas because they need fish-filled water and branches for drying.
signatureTraits: Snake-neck profile: the long neck becomes a spear above a submerged body.
Underwater stalking: fish are pursued below the surface before the strike.
Wing drying: the return to air is part of the method.
interestingFacts: Anhingas are sometimes called snakebirds because of the way the neck shows above water.
They spear fish with a sharp bill rather than scooping them.
They often perch with wings spread after swimming.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish are the main food, with aquatic insects, amphibians, and crustaceans also taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Alligators, large fish, raptors, snakes, raccoons, and nest predators threaten Anhingas or young. Trees over water provide escape and nesting safety.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Anhingas are diurnal, diving and then perching with wings spread.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly known. Banded birds have lived beyond 10 years, and most probably die younger.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick nests over or near water, usually in colonies or loose groups. Chicks depend on adults turning underwater strikes into repeated food deliveries.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often darker with more striking plumage, while females have a browner neck and chest. Both sexes share the snake-neck fishing body, but the visual difference is noticeable.

arabian-sand-boa.spotlight: Seldom longer than about 40 centimetres, this small, stout boa of the Arabian Peninsula and south-western Iran strikes sideways at a passing lizard with great speed and then wraps it in its coils.
arabian-sand-boa.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Arabian Sand Boas live in loose desert sand, dunes, and sandy flats of Arabia.
signatureTraits: Blunt sand-burrowing head
Eyes set high on head
Ambush under loose sand
Short sturdy boa body
interestingFacts: It can wait with only its eyes exposed.
Its body is adapted for moving through sand.
It is a small boa, with adults usually under about 40 centimetres long.
It relies on concealment more than speed, and its pale, finely speckled scales closely match the loose desert sand it hides in.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small lizards are the main prey, chiefly geckos that come out onto the sand after dark, and worm lizards are also reported. Prey is swallowed whole, head first.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Records of predation are scarce. Owls, foxes, monitor lizards and larger snakes probably take some, most likely when a snake is caught crossing the surface at night.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal. It passes the heat of the day buried deeper in the sand, where it is cooler, and moves up to lie just under the surface around dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individuals kept in captivity are reported to reach 10 years or more; no figure has been published for wild snakes.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Unlike most boas, which bear live young, this species lays eggs. Clutches are small, and eggs kept in captivity have hatched after about two months. No care of the eggs or young is known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are broadly similar, though females may be heavier. As in most snakes, males usually have a relatively longer tail that is thicker at the base, a difference seen only in the hand.

arapaima.spotlight: Bony, toothed plates on the tongue press prey against the roof of the mouth, the feature behind the family's common name, bonytongues. Adults commonly reach two metres and occasionally approach three. When one rises to breathe, roughly every 5 to 15 minutes, the gulp can be heard as a cough across still water.
arapaima.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Arapaima usually lives in Amazon rivers, floodplains, lakes, and low-oxygen backwaters.
signatureTraits: Modified swim bladder used for breathing air
Huge armored body suited to warm low-oxygen water
Obligate surfacing rhythm that breaks the water ceiling
Parental guarding uncommon among many large fish
interestingFacts: Arapaimas must surface to breathe air, and an adult kept from reaching the surface can drown.
Their scales have a hard mineralised outer layer over flexible collagen, which helps resist the bites of piranhas.
They can thrive in waters that would suffocate many fish.
Traditional fishers harpoon arapaima as they rise to breathe, and counts of surfacing fish are now used to manage community fisheries.
