fieldGuide.dietSummary: Arapaima feeds on fish and other aquatic animals captured with sudden lunges.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few animals can tackle an adult; caimans and jaguars are thought to take some, while other fish and birds eat unguarded young. Overfishing is the main threat. The fish are taken with harpoons and gill nets, and large adults have become scarce in heavily fished waters.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Surfaces regularly to breathe, even while resting in quiet water, making rhythm itself the key to staying alive.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: May live 15 to 20 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Parents guard nests and young, with males often protecting fry near the surface where breathing and vulnerability meet.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, though breeding adults can show color and size differences; the main identity is not display but the repeated claim to air.

archerfish.spotlight: Archerfish teaches Projection through a fish whose aim extends beyond its body. Water jets, refraction correction, surface watching, and insect shots make intelligence reach into the air.
archerfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, coral_triangle, southeast_asia_coastal, australia_coastal. Mangroves, estuaries, brackish creeks, slow rivers, and overhanging vegetation.
signatureTraits: Precise water jets used to knock prey from overhanging plants
Upward-looking surface position that reads air from water
Ability to compensate for refraction when aiming
Quick strike after prey falls to the surface
interestingFacts: Archerfish can shoot jets of water at insects above the surface.
They must account for the way light bends between air and water.
They live in brackish and freshwater habitats in parts of Asia and Australia.
Their accuracy can improve with experience, and young fish learn partly by watching skilled shooters.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, spiders, small crustaceans, and tiny aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large fish, birds, snakes, humans, and habitat loss threaten archerfish. Surface hunting gives opportunity but also exposure, so accuracy must be fast.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Archerfish are diurnal, often watching the surface and overhanging branches by day. Their rhythm is hold position, calculate angle, shoot, and seize.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Archerfish can live for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs in water during spawning, and young must survive as tiny surface-oriented fish before mastering the famous shot.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; males and females cannot be separated by colour, shape or size in the field.

arctic-tern.spotlight: The Arctic Tern is the lesson of great passage: a light seabird that does not conquer distance with bulk, but with direction. Its pole-to-pole migration makes the principle feel literal — smallness becomes enormous when it keeps following the light season after season.
arctic-tern.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic, north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean, southern_ocean, arctic_ocean. Arctic Terns breed on tundra, gravel shores, islands, and coastal flats, then spend much of the nonbreeding season over open oceans.
signatureTraits: Long pointed wings built for efficient migration
Small ocean bird with a vast yearly route
Sharp plunge-diver over cold coastal waters
Fierce nest defender despite its light body
interestingFacts: Arctic Terns travel between northern breeding grounds and southern ocean feeding areas, making one of the longest regular migrations on Earth.
Their red bill and forked tail give them a clean, arrow-like look in flight.
They feed mostly by dipping and plunging for small fish and marine invertebrates.
Pairs defend nesting areas boldly, proving that a tiny traveler can still guard a home fiercely.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat small fish, crustaceans, and other marine prey taken from the surface or with shallow dives.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks may be taken by gulls, skuas, foxes, and other coastal predators, while adults face storms and exhaustion during migration. Their defense is movement, colony vigilance, and fierce aerial attacks, showing that endurance is not passive — it protects the next generation while still answering the road.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Arctic Terns are active by day, especially in the long daylight of polar summers, and rest on water, shores, or safe open ground between flights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They often live for decades, with many individuals reaching 20 years or more. A long life makes the migration meaningful: one small bird may stitch the planet together again and again through repeated journeys.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay one to three eggs in a shallow ground scrape, and both parents incubate and defend the chicks. Offspring begin life on exposed ground.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, so the story is less about visible sex difference and more about shared travel and shared parental defense. Both sexes carry the same clean migratory design.

argentine-black-and-white-tegu.spotlight: This heavy, ground-living South American lizard eats almost anything it can find or dig up. In the breeding season it does something very few lizards are known to do: it generates its own heat, holding its body several degrees above the surrounding air through the cool of the night.
argentine-black-and-white-tegu.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Forests, savannas, grasslands, edges, burrows, and disturbed habitats fit tegus because flexibility is their advantage.
signatureTraits: Black and white bands and blotches cross the back and tail.
Small, glossy, bead-like scales cover a thick-set body.
Forked pinkish tongue flicks out constantly as it walks.
Hatchlings have green heads and shoulders that fade within months.
Thick, muscular tail is longer than the head and body.
interestingFacts: It is among the largest of the tegus: big males can exceed 1.2 metres from snout to tail tip and weigh several kilograms.
Studies have found that seeds of the fruit it eats can pass through the gut intact, so tegus spread some of the plants they feed on.
Tegus released from the pet trade have established wild populations in Florida, where they eat the eggs of ground-nesting reptiles and birds.
Tegu skins have long been traded for leather, and international trade in the species is regulated under CITES.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, eggs, insects, small animals, carrion, and plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, big cats, snakes, dogs, and humans may threaten tegus, especially young. Burrows, size, and strong jaws help defense.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tegus are diurnal and seasonal, basking when warm and entering dormancy in cooler periods. Their rhythm changes with conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 15 to 20 years in captivity. How long wild tegus live has not been well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In spring, females lay eggs in protected nests and may guard them. A clutch usually holds about 20 to 35 eggs, laid in a burrow chamber packed with damp vegetation, and hatches after roughly two months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger than females and develop broad heads with heavy, swollen jowls. Females stay slimmer in the head and neck.

argus-monitor.spotlight: Argus Monitor teaches Scanning Readiness through a lizard ready to stand, scan, dig, swim, and strike. Its tripod posture, restless foraging, claws, tongue-flicking, and water-edge movement show that opportunity favors a body prepared for many doors.
argus-monitor.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Savannas, floodplains, woodland, river edges, and open ground.
signatureTraits: Tripod stance used to lift the body and scan surroundings
Strong claws for digging, climbing, and tearing into food sources
Forked tongue used to sample scent trails and locate opportunity
Comfort across floodplains, open ground, water edges, and burrows
interestingFacts: Argus Monitors can rear up on the hind legs and tail to look around like a living periscope.
They are active hunters rather than simple sit-and-wait lizards.
Their broad diet lets them turn many habitats into feeding ground.
Young monitors are more vulnerable and must use speed, hiding, and climbing before size becomes protection.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, eggs, reptiles, birds, mammals, carrion, and aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large snakes, raptors, crocodiles, dingoes, and humans can threaten monitors. These pressures make scanning practical: the same awareness that finds food also spots danger early enough to choose a response.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Argus Monitors are diurnal, basking first and then actively foraging when heat powers movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive animals commonly live 10 to 15 years and some reach about 20. Wild lifespan is not well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nest burrows for their eggs, and some in northern Australia have been recorded at depths of about three to four metres. Incubation lasts several months, and the hatchlings dig their own way out and receive no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and more powerfully built than females, especially in mature animals. That difference can sharpen contests.

armadillo-girdled-lizard.spotlight: Unusually for a lizard, it lives in lasting groups. Several animals, and occasionally dozens, share a single rock crevice in the dry country along South Africa's west coast. Rows of thick, keeled, sharply pointed scales cover the body, and it is a slow mover that seldom strays far from its shelter.
armadillo-girdled-lizard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Armadillo Girdled Lizards usually live in rocky arid scrub and crevice-filled South African outcrops.
signatureTraits: Tail-biting ring defense and spiny armor
Adapted to rocky arid scrub and crevice-filled South African outcrops
Broad, flattened, triangular head
Rings of large spiny scales encircling the tail
Straw to yellowish-brown back above a paler yellowish belly
interestingFacts: Armadillo Girdled Lizards are closely tied to rocky arid scrub and crevice-filled South African outcrops.
Their food is mainly small insects and other tiny invertebrates.
Major pressures include birds, snakes, mongooses, and humans.
Termites, especially harvester termites, make up much of what it eats, and groups are often found within reach of termite nests.
In 2011 it was given a genus of its own, Ouroborus, named after the mythical serpent that swallows its own tail.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on small insects and other tiny invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds of prey, snakes and mongooses hunt it, and illegal collecting for the pet trade has emptied some colonies. Its first response to danger is a dash back to the crevice, where the spines help to jam it in place.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mornings are spent basking at the mouth of the crevice, with short trips out to feed. It shelters deep inside at night, and activity is reported to drop in the hottest, driest months.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to live 10 years or more in the wild; captive animals can live considerably longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female bears live young instead of laying eggs, normally one and sometimes two, and may not breed every year. The young lizard grows up in the group's crevice alongside the adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often slightly larger with broader heads.

asian-elephant.spotlight: Asian Elephant is known for family bonds, quiet strength, trunk skill, and long memory.
asian-elephant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Forests, grasslands, scrub, and wetland edges across South and Southeast Asia.
signatureTraits: Twin-domed head with a dip along the middle
Single finger-like lobe at the tip of the trunk
Rounded back, with the top of the head the highest point
Pale pink freckling on the ears, face and trunk of older animals
Usually five toenails on each front foot and four on each hind
interestingFacts: Asian elephants have smaller ears than African bush elephants.
They use low rumbles, trumpets, chirps and touch to communicate, often reaching out with their trunks to family members.
Their trunks can lift heavy objects or pick up small items.
The IUCN lists the Asian Elephant as Endangered, mainly because of habitat loss and conflict with people.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Herbivorous, eating grasses, leaves, bark, fruit, palms, and cultivated plants near human edges.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, while calves may be vulnerable to tigers in some regions.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sleeps in short periods, often with alternating rest and feeding through the day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for many decades, often around 60 years under favorable conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to single calves after long gestation and raise them within social groups.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger; tusk size varies by sex and population.

atlantic-puffin.spotlight: Atlantic Puffin teaches Three-World Fit through a bird belonging to air, sea, and cliff at once. Colorful bill, burrow nesting, wing-powered diving, and fish-carrying return show that identity can be layered without being confused.
atlantic-puffin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, arctic_ocean. North Atlantic sea cliffs, grassy island slopes, burrows, cold feeding waters, and offshore winter seas.
signatureTraits: Colorful breeding bill that signals seasonal cliff life.
Wing-propelled underwater swimming for chasing fish.
Burrow and cliff nesting that ties land to ocean work.
Ability to carry multiple small fish crosswise in the bill.
interestingFacts: Atlantic Puffins are excellent underwater swimmers as well as flyers.
They nest in burrows or crevices on coastal cliffs and islands.
Their bill becomes brighter in the breeding season.
They can hold several fish at once while returning to feed a chick.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly small shoaling fish such as sand eels, sprats, herring and capelin, chased underwater, usually within a few tens of metres of the surface. Some crustaceans and marine worms are also taken, probably more so in winter at sea.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Gulls, skuas, foxes, rats, storms, fish shortages, and marine change threaten adults, eggs, or chicks. Burrows, colonies, and diving skill help, but each world brings its own risks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Atlantic Puffins are active by day at colonies and feeding waters, spending nonbreeding months at sea.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Atlantic Puffins can live for decades, often returning to breeding sites across many seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single egg in a burrow or crevice, and both parents bring fish to the puffling.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be slightly larger.

atlantic-sailfish.spotlight: Atlantic Sailfish teaches Sail Velocity through speed shaped into strategy. Sail fin, bill, schooling prey tactics, and ocean bursts show that dramatic design matters when it cuts through confusion.
atlantic-sailfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic. Warm Atlantic offshore waters, reefs, blue-water edges, and pelagic hunting zones.
signatureTraits: Tall dorsal sail can be raised or lowered during movement and hunting.
Long bill helps slash, stun, or pressure schooling fish.
Streamlined body supports rapid acceleration in open water.
Color changes and fin displays can coordinate hunting pressure.
interestingFacts: Sailfish are famous for exceptional speed among ocean fish.
They often target schooling fish where confusion creates openings.
The sail may help maneuver and make the fish appear larger during hunting.
Their dramatic shape is tied to function, not just spectacle.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish, squid, and schooling prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks, orcas, billfish predators when young, humans, and fishing pressure threaten them. Speed helps, but open-ocean life is never risk-free.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and in low light depending on prey movement, often following temperature edges and bait concentrations.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth is fast, and many probably live only a few years. Tag recoveries suggest that a few survive for a decade or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release large numbers of eggs into open water, where larvae must survive a vast ocean with little protection.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger than males, giving them greater egg production; both sexes share the sail-and-speed hunting form.

atlantic-tarpon.spotlight: Atlantic Tarpon teaches Silver Release through air-gulping endurance, shining scales, and explosive leaps. Stored energy changes the whole moment when a fish built for low oxygen and hard runs finally breaks the surface.
atlantic-tarpon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic. Coastal waters, estuaries, mangroves, lagoons, river mouths, and warm shallows.
signatureTraits: Large silver scales that flash during leaps.
Modified swim bladder allowing air breathing in low-oxygen water.
Powerful jumps and runs when hooked or pursuing prey.
Use of coastal, estuary, and river-edge habitats.
interestingFacts: Atlantic tarpon can gulp air using a modified swim bladder.
They are famous for dramatic leaps above the water.
Their larvae are ribbon-like leptocephalus forms before transforming.
They live in coastal waters, bays, estuaries, and sometimes rivers.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, shrimp, crabs, and other aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sharks, dolphins, large predatory fish, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Air-gulping and powerful movement help in challenging water, but not against every pressure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Atlantic Tarpon are active across day and night depending on tides, prey, and temperature.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females are thought to live 50 years or more and males more than 30, going by growth rings counted in their ear bones.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place offshore, where a large female can release millions of eggs and gives no parental care. The larvae drift on currents for weeks to a few months before settling in shallow, often oxygen-poor lagoons and marshes that serve as nurseries.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger than males in many tarpon populations. Both sexes share the air-breathing, leaping design.

atlantic-yellow-nosed-albatross.spotlight: Atlantic Yellow-nosed Albatross teaches Fine-Line Navigation through a life stretched across enormous open water. Long wings save energy over the South Atlantic, a slim yellow bill stripe gives the bird its clear identity, and ocean soaring turns scattered winds into a path. Its lesson is that a small guiding mark can matter when the world feels too wide to cross all at once.
atlantic-yellow-nosed-albatross.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_atlantic, indian_ocean, southern_ocean. Atlantic Yellow-nosed Albatross usually lives in South Atlantic open ocean and remote island breeding colonies.
signatureTraits: Long wings for efficient South Atlantic soaring
Yellow stripe along the bill that gives the face a guiding mark
Remote island breeding tied to exact return routes
Ocean-foraging life built on wind, memory, and subtle cues
interestingFacts: The yellow line on the bill is a key visual feature.
They breed on remote South Atlantic islands, mainly in the Tristan da Cunha group and on Gough Island.
Like other albatrosses, they can use wind to travel far with low energy.
It is one of the smallest albatrosses, and the IUCN lists it as Endangered.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Atlantic Yellow-nosed Albatross feeds on squid, fish, crustaceans, and offal found during long foraging flights.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: At the colonies skuas take eggs and small chicks, and introduced house mice on Gough Island have been recorded attacking chicks. Adults face few natural enemies at sea. Many drown on longline hooks off southern Africa and South America, the main cause of the species' decline.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rests at sea and on nesting islands between long soaring trips, following wind and food rather than fixed borders.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to reach 30 years or more, judging from ringed birds. The maximum age is not well established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs lay one egg and invest heavily in chick growth over a long season, turning a remote island into a precise return point.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, with the fine yellow bill line serving as shared identity rather than a male-only signal.

atlas-beetle.spotlight: Atlas Beetle teaches Armored Readiness through a horned rainforest beetle that enters conflict already wearing preparation. Three-horn male contests, heavy exoskeleton, larval wood growth, and pushing battles make protection visible before pressure arrives.
atlas-beetle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Tropical forests, rotting logs, humid leaf litter, and decaying wood.
signatureTraits: Males carry large horns used for pushing and wrestling rivals.
A hard exoskeleton works as visible protection in rough encounters.
Larvae grow in decaying organic material before adult contests begin.
The body is built more for leverage and defense than for speed.
interestingFacts: Atlas Beetle males are named for their impressive horned appearance.
The larval stage does the hidden growth that funds the armored adult form.
Females do not carry the same huge horns as males.
Their armor prepares them for conflict, but it does not make them invulnerable to predators or habitat loss.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Larvae feed on decaying wood and organic matter, while adults use fruit, sap, and plant fluids.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, reptiles, mammals, ants, parasitoids, collectors, and habitat loss can threaten Atlas Beetles.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, moving in humid forest conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Larval growth in rotting wood takes roughly a year or more, while adults usually live only a few months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in decaying wood or rich organic substrate where larvae can feed. Offspring survival depends on the right hidden nursery, not on immediate armor.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have large contest horns, while females lack the same dramatic weapons and are shaped more around egg production.

atlas-moth.spotlight: Atlas Moth teaches Final Splendor through a giant silk moth that spends stored larval energy in one brief adult window. Huge patterned wings, snake-head-like tips, nonfeeding adulthood, and short reproductive flight make preparation feel magnificent because the chance does not last.
atlas-moth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia. Tropical and subtropical forests, plantations, wooded gardens, and host plants across South and Southeast Asia fit Atlas Moths because the caterpillar stage needs leafy abundance before the adult can spend its stored energy.
signatureTraits: One of the largest moths by wing area, with immense reddish-brown patterned wings.
Adult mouthparts are reduced, so the adult stage does not feed.
Wing tips can resemble snake heads, adding a visual startle defense.
The adult life is brief and focused on mating and egg-laying.
interestingFacts: Atlas Moth adults live on energy stored while they were caterpillars.
Females release pheromones that males can detect from long distances.
The huge wings are beautiful but also costly, making timing essential.
Its cocoon silk has been used locally in parts of Asia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars feed on leaves of many trees and shrubs, while adults do not feed.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, lizards, spiders, parasitoids, and habitat loss threaten Atlas Moths. Camouflage, large wing markings, and brief nighttime activity help protect a body built for one short opportunity.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are mostly nocturnal, emerging and seeking mates after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Atlas Moths often live weeks as adults at most, after a longer larval and cocoon stage. The short adult life sharpens the lesson: preparation matters because the final opening is brief.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clusters of eggs on suitable host plants, placing the next generation where leaves can fuel the long preparation stage. The future begins as stored growth, not instant display.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger and heavier-bodied for egg production, while males often have broader feathery antennae for detecting female scent. The difference reinforces the split between signal, search, and stored reproduction.

australian-green-tree-frog.spotlight: Australian Green Tree Frog is known for moisture awareness, still waiting, nocturnal calling, and sudden climbing movement.
australian-green-tree-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Woodlands, wetlands, gardens, buildings, and humid refuges across northern and eastern Australia.
signatureTraits: Sticky toe pads for climbing
Bright rounded body
Nocturnal calling after rain
Thick fold of skin above the eardrum
Large eyes with horizontal pupils
interestingFacts: It often shelters in cool damp places during dry heat.
Its toe pads help it climb smooth surfaces.
It is one of Australia's most recognizable frogs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates caught by sudden strikes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include snakes, birds, larger frogs, mammals, dehydration, and habitat loss.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, resting by day and becoming active at night or after rain.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live many years, with long lives especially recorded in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in water after rain, and tadpoles develop in ponds or temporary pools.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger, while males call to attract mates.

axolotl.spotlight: Axolotl turns Regeneration into a philosophy of staying aquatic: it keeps feathery gills, repairs damage, and masters the water before chasing transformation.
axolotl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Axolotls belong to cool, still, plant-rich freshwater such as the historic lakes and canals of Xochimilco. The habitat matters because regeneration works best in the calm aquatic world they are built to master.
signatureTraits: External feathery gills
Aquatic adult form
Famous limb regeneration
Broad smiling head
interestingFacts: Axolotls can regenerate limbs and parts of organs.
They usually remain aquatic and juvenile-looking as adults.
Wild axolotls are native to the lake and canal systems around Mexico City.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat worms, insect larvae, small crustaceans, small fish, and other aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, larger fish, pollution, invasive species, and habitat loss threaten them. Their healing power is extraordinary, but it cannot repair a destroyed lake.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often crepuscular or nocturnal, resting in cover and feeding in lower light. Their rhythm favors calm movement and repair over frantic activity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Axolotls commonly live 10 to 15 years in care and can survive for years in suitable water. The lifespan gives repeated chances to recover, grow, and remain what they are.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay many eggs attached to aquatic plants or surfaces, and larvae develop in water with external gills. The next generation begins already committed to the aquatic path.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often have a more swollen cloaca and longer tail, while females are rounder when carrying eggs. The differences support breeding, but both sexes share the regenerative aquatic design.

aye-aye.spotlight: The largest nocturnal primate, a dark, shaggy lemur found only in Madagascar, with front teeth that grow throughout life like a rodent's. It taps along a branch with a thin middle finger, up to about eight times a second, gnaws into the hollow it detects and hooks out the larva inside.
aye-aye.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Madagascar forest, tree cavities, and night canopy fit because finger percussion needs hollow wood and listening darkness.
signatureTraits: Coarse dark coat tipped with white guard hairs
Large, bare, leathery ears
Bushy tail longer than the head and body
Large, round, yellow-orange eyes
interestingFacts: The tapping finger has a ball-and-socket joint at its base, giving it an unusually wide range of movement.
It was first classified as a rodent, and is now the only living member of its own lemur family.
A small extra digit of bone and cartilage, a pseudothumb, was described on its wrist in 2019.
Females have two nipples set low on the abdomen, an unusual position for a primate.
It bites through the shells of coconuts and hard forest nuts and scoops out the contents with a finger.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Wood-boring larvae, fruit, seeds, nectar, and fungi.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fossas, raptors, snakes, humans, superstition, and forest loss threaten Aye-ayes, making night secrecy and odd tools important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Aye-ayes are nocturnal, nesting in tree shelters by day and tapping, listening, and extracting food after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live many years, giving the strange finger, learned routes, and night-foraging skill time to become mastery.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually raise a single infant with long care in nests, letting young slowly learn the tapping and listening method.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, so the elongated finger, large ears, and percussive foraging carry the main identity for both.

babirusa.spotlight: Found only on mainland Sulawesi and nearby Lembeh Island in Indonesia, this wild pig is known for the male's upper tusks. They are brittle and easily broken, and they keep growing throughout life; in some old males they curve round until the tips touch the forehead.
babirusa.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Sulawesi forests, river edges, and swampy cover fit because strange growth survives in a place that hides and reveals it.
signatureTraits: Grey-brown, wrinkled skin with very sparse hair
Long, slim legs beneath a rounded, barrel-shaped body
In males, lower tusks projecting upward from the sides of the mouth
Small ears and a narrow, tapering snout
interestingFacts: Rival males rear up on their hind legs and box each other with the forefeet.
It roots less than other pigs because the snout lacks the stiffening bone they have, and digs mainly in soft mud and sand.
Groups visit mineral springs and salt licks to drink the water and eat the soil.
A painting of a babirusa in a Sulawesi cave has been dated to at least 35,000 years ago.
The name comes from the Malay words for pig and deer.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, leaves, roots, fungi, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pythons, crocodiles, humans, hunting, and habitat loss threaten Babirusas, making cover, speed, and group awareness important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Babirusas are mainly day-active, feeding and resting in forest cover where the strange tusks can be hidden until close.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live over 10 years, repeating the strange-growth story through seasons of tusk development, feeding, and forest movement.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually have small litters for pigs, investing more care into fewer young than many familiar domestic relatives.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow the dramatic upper tusks that curve upward, while females have smaller or absent tusks; this difference defines the display.

bactrian-camel.spotlight: Bactrian Camel is known for fat-storing humps, tough feet, dryland endurance, and steady movement.
bactrian-camel.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia, domestic_global. Cold deserts, dry steppes, rocky basins, and arid travel corridors of Central Asia.
signatureTraits: Two fat-storing humps
Broad feet for soft ground
Thick coat for temperature extremes
Split upper lip that moves each half separately
Hard callused pads on the chest and knees
interestingFacts: Its two humps store fat rather than water, and they can shrink and lean over when the camel is poorly fed.
It can tolerate wide temperature swings, from hot desert summers to winters far below freezing.
It has nostrils and eyelashes suited to dusty conditions.
Wild Bactrian camels are now treated as a separate species, Camelus ferus, which is critically endangered in China and Mongolia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Herbivorous, feeding on dry grasses, shrubs, thorny plants, and sparse desert vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young may be threatened by wolves or large predators; adults rely on size, herd awareness, and human protection in domestic settings.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal to flexible, resting and feeding according to heat, travel, and herd rhythm.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for several decades under managed or favorable wild conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf after long gestation and nurse it for many months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are typically larger and may show stronger breeding-season behavior.

bairds-tapir.spotlight: No native land mammal in Central America is larger: adults weigh roughly 150 to 300 kilograms. It ranges from southern Mexico to north-western Colombia, from lowland swamp to cloud forest above 3,000 metres. It can sink and walk along a river bed, and often defecates in water.
bairds-tapir.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest, riverbanks, swamps, and trails fit because dual passage needs a body fluent on land and in water.
signatureTraits: Cheeks and throat are cream against a dark brown body
Ears are edged with white
A short, stiff mane runs along the neck
Tracks show four toes in front and three behind
interestingFacts: It calls with shrill whistles that sound more like a bird than a large mammal.
It is the national animal of Belize, where it is known as the mountain cow.
Pregnancy lasts about 13 months, and a female usually bears young no more than every second year.
Seeds of many fruits pass through its gut unharmed and are dropped far from the parent tree.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, fruit, shoots, and aquatic vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas, crocodilians for young, humans, and habitat fragmentation threaten tapirs, making water escape and forest cover valuable.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Baird’s Tapirs are often nocturnal or crepuscular, moving through forest and water when cover, coolness, and quiet improve safety.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live around 20 to 30 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear a single striped calf that hides early, then follows the mother through forest and water routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same colouring and markings. Females are often slightly larger and heavier, but the difference is too small to judge reliably in the field.

bald-eagle.spotlight: Bald Eagle teaches High Vision through a hunter that simplifies wide water from above. Its high perch, sharp eyes, massive nest, and fish-grabbing talons show that perspective turns scattered motion into one clear next move.
bald-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Large lakes, rivers, coasts, reservoirs, cliffs, and tall trees.
signatureTraits: Sharp distance vision for reading water from above
Powerful talons built for seizing fish and carrion
Huge stick nests reused and enlarged across years
High perches that turn landscape into strategy
interestingFacts: Bald Eagles often reuse the same nest site, adding material until the nest can become enormous.
They hunt fish but also scavenge, steal prey, and use whatever the water edge offers.
Females are usually larger than males, a common pattern in many raptors.
Their white head and tail appear only after young birds mature.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, waterbirds, carrion, and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult Bald Eagles face few predators, but eggs and young can be threatened by owls, raccoons, ravens, and disturbance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bald Eagles are diurnal, scanning and hunting in daylight when water movement and prey are easiest to read.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Bald Eagles can live for decades in good conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay one to three eggs in a large nest, and both parents feed and guard the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males, giving the species a useful division of strength while both birds share hunting, guarding, and parenting.

bald-uakari.spotlight: A monkey of the flooded forests of the western Amazon, with a long shaggy coat and a hairless crimson head. The colour comes from blood: the facial skin is thin, almost without pigment and densely supplied with capillaries. Groups can be large, sometimes more than 50, and break into smaller parties to forage.
bald-uakari.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Bald Uakari usually lives in Amazon flooded forests, river islands, and seasonally inundated canopy.
signatureTraits: Striking bald red face linked to health and social recognition
Strong jaws for hard seeds and tough forest foods
Group movement through flooded Amazon canopy
Short tail and unusual body profile that make it instantly memorable
interestingFacts: A brighter red face can signal better health in uakaris.
They live in forests that flood seasonally, forcing movement through changing canopy routes.
They can crack tough seeds many animals avoid.
Their most memorable feature is also socially meaningful.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bald Uakari feeds on seeds, fruits, flowers, and tough forest foods cracked with strong jaws.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harpy eagles and other large raptors, big cats and large snakes are the presumed natural predators, though few attacks have been documented. Troops keep high in the canopy and call loudly when alarmed. Hunting for meat and logging of flooded forest are the threats that matter most.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, moving and resting in social groups high in trees where the red face can signal through a flooded green world.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live around 20 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually have one infant that clings and develops within the group, learning recognition in a world where faces and calls matter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger; both sexes share the red facial signal, making health and presence visible across the group.

bali-myna.spotlight: Bali Myna teaches Protected Beauty through a white island bird whose brightness must be guarded. Its snowy crest, blue facial skin, clear calls, and tiny native range show that rare beauty becomes sacred when it could vanish.
bali-myna.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: bali, southeast_asia. Dry forest, savanna woodland, Bali island scrub, protected reserves, and tree cavities fit Bali Mynas because protected beauty needs both habitat and guarded nesting space.
signatureTraits: Snowy white plumage with elegant crest
Bright blue bare skin around the eyes
Island endemic with extremely small wild range
Cavity-nesting songbird dependent on protection
interestingFacts: Bali Mynas are native only to the Indonesian island of Bali, where wild birds are largely confined to protected areas.
They are also known as Bali Starlings or Rothschild's Mynas, reflecting their place in the starling family.
Conservation breeding and release programs are essential to their survival.
Illegal trapping for the bird trade has been a major threat.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, seeds, insects, larvae, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, monitor lizards, cats, rats, raptors, and humans can threaten birds, eggs, or chicks. Nest protection and anti-poaching work are central defenses.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bali Mynas are diurnal, calling, feeding, and displaying by day, then roosting in trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years, often over a decade in protected care.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree cavities, and both parents help feed chicks. Young begin life hidden in holes before becoming visible white jewels.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look very similar, with males sometimes slightly larger or more robust. The shared beauty makes protection a species-wide need.

banded-linsang.spotlight: Long grouped with the civets, linsangs are now placed by genetic studies as the closest living relatives of the cat family. This species weighs well under a kilogram and has claws that retract fully into sheaths.
banded-linsang.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Banded Linsangs live in Southeast Asian forests and wooded hills.
signatureTraits: Long banded body
Very long balancing tail
Nocturnal branch movement
Small carnivore agility
interestingFacts: Linsangs were long grouped with civets but are now placed in their own family, which is closer to cats.
Their long banded tails, nearly as long as the body, help them balance in trees.
They are rarely seen because they are nocturnal.
Their bands break up the body in branches.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small animals make up nearly all of the diet: rodents, birds, lizards, frogs, snakes and large insects. It hunts in trees and on the forest floor, and its sharp, blade-like cheek teeth are suited to slicing meat.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Forest clearance and snares set for other animals are the recorded threats. Large snakes, owls and wild cats probably take some, though no attack has been documented. It depends on staying hidden and on a fast climb to escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly nocturnal as far as camera-trap records show. It sleeps by day in a nest of leaves and twigs inside a hollow trunk or among tree roots.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Unknown in the wild. Captive animals have reached about 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: So far as records show, females give birth to small litters in sheltered places. Two or three young are usual. Little else about breeding has been recorded in the wild.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar; agility and night movement define both. No difference in coat markings is known, which leaves nothing to go on in a brief sighting by torchlight.

banded-palm-civet.spotlight: Banded Palm Civet teaches Striped Nightwork through a forest-floor civet following scent under darkness. Bands, long body, low vegetation routes, fruit and prey foraging, and quiet movement make hunger a nocturnal craft.
banded-palm-civet.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Lowland rainforest, swamp forest, dense understory, fallen logs, and forest edges.
signatureTraits: Bold body bands that break up shape in forest shadow
Nocturnal scent-led foraging on ground and low vegetation
Long civet body suited to slipping through dense understory
Mixed diet of fruit, insects, and small animals
interestingFacts: Banded Palm Civets are nocturnal and rarely seen well in daylight.
Their stripes and bands help break their outline in dense forest.
They forage close to the ground more than some other palm civets.
They can eat both fruit and animal prey, making them flexible night workers.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly invertebrates taken on or near the ground, including earthworms, ants, beetles, crickets and spiders, with occasional small frogs and lizards. Fruit appears to form a small part of the diet. It forages by nosing through leaf litter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Clouded leopards, large snakes, raptors, civet hunters, and habitat loss threaten them. Stripes, darkness, scent awareness, and cover are defenses for an animal whose strength is not being noticed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Banded Palm Civets are nocturnal, resting hidden by day and foraging after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About eighteen years has been recorded for captive animals. How long free-ranging banded palm civets live in Southeast Asian understorey remains unstudied.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters in sheltered dens or hidden cover.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females have the same coat pattern and are close in size, so they cannot reliably be told apart by sight.

barbary-macaque.spotlight: A stocky, sandy-brown monkey of Morocco and Algeria, living at up to about 2,600 metres where snow lies for weeks in winter. Fossils show that macaques of this kind once ranged across much of Europe, as far north as England. Troops of a dozen to more than 50 contain several adult males and females, and food is carried in cheek pouches.
barbary-macaque.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Barbary Macaque usually lives in Atlas mountain cedar forests, oak woods, cliffs, and rocky slopes.
signatureTraits: Thick fur suited to cool mountain forests
Group huddling and grooming that turn warmth into social care
Tailless macaque profile adapted to rocky forest life
Male infant-handling that strengthens group bonds
interestingFacts: Barbary Macaques are the only macaques living naturally outside Asia.
They live in North African mountains and also on Gibraltar through introduced history.
Males often interact closely with infants, carrying and grooming them and using them in social exchanges with other males.
Although often called Barbary apes, they are monkeys with a tiny vestigial tail hidden in their fur.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Barbary Macaque feeds on leaves, fruit, seeds, roots, bark, and seasonal plant foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Feral and herding dogs are now the main predators, and golden eagles may take infants; leopards and lions once hunted them. Troops give sharp alarm barks and climb trees or cliffs. Capture of infants for the pet trade, logging and overgrazing of cedar forest are greater threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, sleeping in trees or cliffs and huddling in cold weather, making warmth something the group builds together.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly about 20 to 25 years; females tend to outlive males, and a few have reached around 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually have one infant, cared for within a social group where males may also handle young, spreading warmth beyond the mother alone.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger; both sexes use grooming, closeness, and group contact to turn cold survival into social structure.

bare-throated-bellbird.spotlight: Bare-throated Bellbird teaches Forest Volume through explosive bell call. Exposed perches, courtship pressure, territorial signaling, and a metallic voice show that sound can become a force when it carries clearly.
bare-throated-bellbird.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Bare-throated Bellbird usually lives in Atlantic Forest canopy, forest edges, and exposed singing perches.
signatureTraits: Extremely loud metallic call that carries through forest
Bare throat and pale male plumage used in display
Exposed singing perches that turn canopy into a sound stage
Fruit-eating life that links voice to seed-moving forest work
interestingFacts: Bellbirds are known for some of the loudest bird calls.
The male call can sound metallic or bell-like.
Males and females look very different: males are mostly white with a bare blue-green throat, while females are olive-green.
The Bare-throated Bellbird is the national bird of Paraguay, where it is called pájaro campana.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bare-throated Bellbird feeds on fruit and berries, with some insects, supporting forest seed movement.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Natural predators are poorly documented; hawks are the likely hunters of adults, and toucans, monkeys and snakes the likely nest robbers. Clearance of Atlantic Forest and trapping for the cage-bird trade are the larger threats, and a calling male is easy for trappers to find.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, resting in forest cover outside calling and feeding times, saving force for calls that cut through leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild bellbirds of this species have not been aged, so their natural lifespan is unknown.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build nests and raise chicks while males advertise from loud perches, separating the public voice from hidden care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are pale with bare throats and famous calls; females are greener and quieter, showing the split between display volume and nesting concealment.

barn-owl.spotlight: Barn Owl teaches Acoustic Precision through a heart-shaped face designed to hear the hidden. Silent wings, facial disc, asymmetrical ears, pale ghostlike flight, and talons show darkness becoming readable through sound.
barn-owl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, north_africa_middle_east, sub_saharan_africa, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. Barns, grasslands, marsh edges, farms, cliffs, old buildings, and open hunting fields fit Barn Owls because small mammals rustle where sound can guide the strike.
signatureTraits: Heart-shaped facial disc: sound is funneled toward the ears.
Asymmetrical ears: uneven placement helps locate hidden prey precisely.
Silent flight: soft feathers reduce noise during the final approach.
interestingFacts: Barn Owls can hunt by sound in very low light.
They are valuable natural rodent hunters around farms and grasslands.
Their call is more of a harsh screech than a classic hoot.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Voles, mice, rats, shrews, small birds, and insects support Acoustic Precision because prey is often located by hearing before sight.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Great horned owls, raccoons, foxes, snakes, cats, and human disturbance can threaten Barn Owls or nests. Hidden cavities and quiet flight help protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Barn Owls are nocturnal, hunting when their hearing gives them a strong advantage. Their rhythm turns night into a map of sound.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Barn Owls often live only a few years in the wild, though some survive much longer. Every hunting season depends on sharp hearing, safe cavities, and enough small mammals nearby.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in cavities, barns, cliffs, or nest boxes, and chicks may hatch at different times. Offspring depend on repeated prey deliveries, making listening directly support the nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often slightly larger and may show more spotting, while males can be paler. Both sexes share the acoustic hunting design that defines the principle.

barn-swallow.spotlight: Barn Swallow teaches Continuity through a bird that feeds while staying in motion. Forked tail, pointed wings, open-air turns, mud nests, and insect-catching flight show how work becomes easier when the streak stays alive.
barn-swallow.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, central_asia, east_asia, europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Open fields, farms, wetlands, barns, bridges, and village edges fit Barn Swallows because they need both flying insects and nesting surfaces. The habitat lets motion and home stay connected.
signatureTraits: Aerial Feeding: the swallow catches insects while flying instead of stopping to search.
Forked-Tail Control: tail shape helps fine steering during fast turns.
Mud-Nest Return: repeated building and migration tie motion back to a chosen place.
interestingFacts: Barn Swallows catch flying insects on the wing.
They build cup-shaped mud nests on cliffs, barns, bridges, and buildings.
They migrate long distances between breeding and wintering areas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flies, mosquitoes, beetles, moths, and other airborne insects support Continuity because the swallow’s food is gathered mid-flight. The diet rewards staying in the air and adjusting constantly.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, falcons, owls, snakes, cats, raccoons, and nest parasites threaten swallows or nests. Fast flight, colony awareness, and nesting near structures help reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Barn Swallows are diurnal, feeding when insects fly and light supports agile movement. Their day is a chain of small flights that turn constant motion into survival.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Barn Swallows often live several years if they survive migration and predation. The lesson deepens because continuity is not one flight; it is returning, rebuilding, and migrating again.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in mud nests, and both parents feed the young with captured insects. Reproduction supports the lesson because constant flight becomes direct provision for the nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often have longer outer tail streamers than females in many populations. The difference connects movement to display: even courtship is shaped by flight quality.

barramundi.spotlight: A large silver fish of northern Australia and southern Asia, the barramundi grows to well over a metre. It waits beside snags, rock bars and creek mouths, then opens its wide mouth so fast that water and prey are sucked in together. At the surface the strike makes a loud pop that Australian anglers call a boof.
barramundi.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, coral_triangle, southeast_asia_coastal, australia_coastal. Estuaries, rivers, mangroves, coastal shallows, and turbid channels fit barramundi because ambush works where water hides movement.
signatureTraits: Head profile is concave, dipping above the eyes.
Tail fin is rounded, not forked.
Large silver scales cover the flanks below an olive-grey back.
Eyes shine pink-red in torchlight.
Mouth is large, with the jaw reaching behind the eye.
interestingFacts: The name is usually said to come from an Aboriginal language of central Queensland and to mean a large-scaled river fish.
Young fish move upstream at the end of the wet season and may spend several years in fresh water before returning to the coast to breed.
Outside Australia it is generally known as Asian sea bass, and it is farmed widely in South-east Asia.
Spawning is timed to the large tides around the new and full moon.
Fish stocked in dams and lakes cannot breed there, because the eggs and larvae need salt water.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, prawns, crabs and other crustaceans, and smaller aquatic animals. It lies in wait near cover and takes prey in sudden suction strikes, often at dawn, dusk or night near snags and creek mouths.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crocodiles, sharks, larger fish, birds, and humans can threaten barramundi. Size, cover, and timing help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Barramundi often feed in low light, tidal change, or active prey windows. Their rhythm waits for the clean opening.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 20 years in the wild, judging by growth rings in the ear bones; most fish caught are much younger.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Most fish first breed as males, because many barramundi change sex from male to female as they grow. Spawning takes place in estuaries early in the wet season, and a large female can release millions of eggs. The larvae are carried by the tide into mangroves and coastal swamps.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No outward feature separates the sexes; the largest fish are females.

barreleye.spotlight: Barreleye teaches Vertical Vision through a transparent-headed fish that sees opportunity above the ordinary line of sight. Its clear dome, tubular eyes, deep-sea hovering, and upward prey detection show that strange perspective can find hidden food.
barreleye.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_pacific. Deep ocean twilight zones, midwater darkness, and areas below drifting prey fit Barreleyes because their vision is shaped for faint light filtering down from above.
signatureTraits: Transparent fluid-filled head dome
Tubular eyes adapted for upward viewing
Deep-sea hovering below faint silhouettes
Small mouth suited to careful prey capture
interestingFacts: The green-looking structures inside the head are the eyes, not nostrils.
The transparent, fluid-filled dome protects sensitive upward-looking eyes while the fish hovers in midwater.
Barreleyes live in the twilight zone of the ocean.
Their eyes can rotate, helping them look forward as well as upward.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Jellies, small crustaceans, siphonophore prey, and drifting animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger deep-sea fish, squid, and midwater predators can threaten Barreleyes. Transparency, darkness, and hovering stillness help reduce detection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Barreleyes live beyond ordinary daylight rhythms, so their activity follows prey movement and faint light patterns rather than day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long it lives is unknown. The few brought to the surface alive are not known to have survived for long in aquaria, so there is no captive figure either.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Reproduction is poorly observed, but like many marine fishes they likely release eggs that develop as drifting young. Offspring begin in the vast open water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are not obvious from ordinary observation. The species is defined more by shared visual design than by dramatic male-female contrast.

basking-shark.spotlight: Once thought to lie dormant on the seabed through winter, this plankton-eating shark is now known from satellite tags to keep moving, often several hundred metres down. One tagged off the Isle of Man was tracked across the Atlantic to Newfoundland. Adults are commonly 6 to 8 metres long, with gill slits that almost encircle the head.
basking-shark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, north_pacific. Basking Sharks live in temperate coastal and open waters rich in plankton.
signatureTraits: Huge open filter-feeding mouth
Gill rakers for plankton
Slow surface cruising
Second-largest living fish
interestingFacts: Basking sharks are harmless to people despite their size.
They feed on tiny plankton, filtering it from water that flows through their wide-open mouths.
They often appear near the surface in summer, where plankton concentrates.
They can be mistaken for sea monsters when decayed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Zooplankton, above all copepods, along with fish eggs and larvae. It swims forward at walking pace so that water flows in through the gape and out past the gills, and it gathers along tidal fronts where plankton is dense.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural enemies, though killer whales have been recorded killing them. People did far more damage, harpooning the species for its liver oil and later its fins. Boat strikes and entanglement in fishing gear still kill some.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No resting period is known. In some areas it rises and sinks daily, following the plankton it feeds on.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to be around 50 years, but the species is hard to age and the figure is an estimate, not a measured record.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: So far as is known, females give birth to live young after long development. Gestation is thought to last more than a year, and embryos are thought to feed on unfertilised eggs in the womb, as in related sharks. The one well-documented litter held six pups, each about 1.5 to 2 metres long.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar, though females may grow large and carry pups internally. Mature males are told by the two claspers trailing from the pelvic fins, and they mature at a shorter body length than females.

bat-eared-fox.spotlight: Bat-eared Fox teaches Acute Listening through a small canid whose ears feed its life. Oversized ears, termite hearing, heat release, open-country trotting, and insect focus make listening practical down to the ground.
bat-eared-fox.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Short-grass savannas, dry plains, scrub, open grassland, and termite-rich areas.
signatureTraits: Oversized ears for hearing insects and releasing heat
Insect-heavy diet unusual for a fox-like canid
Open-country movement through dry grasslands and savanna
Family groups using dens and alertness for safety
interestingFacts: Bat-eared Foxes eat huge numbers of insects, especially termites where available.
Their ears help both with hearing prey and regulating heat.
They often forage with the head low, listening for small ground sounds.
They are more insect-specialized than many other fox-like canids.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Termites, beetles, grasshoppers, larvae, scorpions, small reptiles, fruit, and eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, jackals, hyenas, lions, leopards, snakes, and humans threaten foxes or pups. Large ears improve early detection, while burrows give listening a safe place to retreat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bat-eared Foxes are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, shifting with heat and insect activity. Their rhythm follows the sounds of the ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Bat-eared Foxes can live for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in dens, and pups are protected by family attention and burrow safety.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar and may both contribute to family life.

bateleur.spotlight: A stocky eagle of African savanna, so short in the tail that its feet reach beyond the tip in flight. It spends much of the day on the wing, gliding low with hardly a wingbeat, and is estimated to cover 300 kilometres or more in a day while searching for carcasses and small prey.
bateleur.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Bateleur usually lives in savannas, open woodland, scrub, and dry country across Africa.
signatureTraits: rocking flight
short tail
broad wings
colorful face
interestingFacts: Bateleur is French for a street performer or tumbler, a name given for the way the bird tips from side to side as it glides.
Young birds are brown all over and take about seven or eight years to gain full adult plumage, their tails shortening with successive moults.
The bare skin of the face and the feet can flush from pale orange to deep red when the bird is excited.
Perched birds often sunbathe standing upright with the wings spread wide and tilted towards the sun.
It is listed as Endangered, having disappeared from much of its former range outside large protected areas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bateleur feeds on carrion, reptiles, birds, small mammals, and insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have little to fear from other animals, but eggs and chicks are lost to other raptors and to climbing predators, and pairs readily desert a disturbed nest. Poisoned carcasses set out for jackals and other carnivores are the main killer, since bateleurs often find them first.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bateleur is diurnal, spending long hours soaring and scanning.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Bateleur may live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nesting in the canopy of a large tree, pairs usually raise one chick with slow parental care. The single egg is incubated for about 55 days, mainly by the female, and the chick stays in the nest for a further three to four months. It is fed by its parents for some months after fledging.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: As adults the sexes differ slightly in plumage and size. Females, the larger sex, have grey secondary feathers that show as a pale panel on the closed wing and leave only a narrow black trailing edge in flight. In males the secondaries are black and the trailing band is broad.

bawean-deer.spotlight: Bawean Deer teaches Island Rarity through a small deer whose whole world fits on one island. Its compact body, quiet forest movement, limited range, and habitat dependence show that small places can hold lives found nowhere else.
bawean-deer.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Bawean Island forest, scrub, plantations edges, grassy clearings, and dense cover fit Bawean Deer because the species survives inside one small island landscape.
signatureTraits: Compact deer restricted to Bawean Island
Quiet movement through forest and scrub
Rare island range with strong habitat dependence
Small antlers in males compared with larger deer
interestingFacts: Bawean Deer are found naturally only on Bawean Island in Indonesia.
They are also called Kuhl's deer, after the German naturalist Heinrich Kuhl.
They are generally shy and active in cover.
The IUCN lists the Bawean Deer as Critically Endangered, with only a few hundred left in the wild.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, grasses, herbs, fruits, and shoots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dogs, humans, habitat loss, and possibly large reptiles or raptors for fawns can threaten them. Dense cover and nocturnal caution are key protections.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bawean Deer are often nocturnal or crepuscular, feeding in quiet hours and sheltering by day. Their rhythm protects rarity by staying unseen.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live for more than a decade in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single fawn that hides in vegetation while it grows. Offspring survival depends on quiet cover.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow antlers and are usually larger, while females lack antlers and carry fawns. The difference is clear but restrained by the island deer’s secretive life.

bay-duiker.spotlight: About 20 kilograms and roughly half a metre at the shoulder, this stocky forest antelope has a broad black stripe running along the spine from neck to tail. Short spike horns sit partly hidden in a tuft of hair on the crown, and glands in front of the eyes leave scent on twigs and stems.
bay-duiker.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Bay Duiker usually lives in West and Central African rainforests, dense understory, and swampy forest floor.
signatureTraits: Reddish coat that melts into leaf litter and dim understory
Secretive movement through dense rainforest floor
Small antelope body suited to narrow forest paths
Fruit-fall feeding that keeps it close to hidden ground resources
interestingFacts: Bay Duikers are more secretive than many open-country antelopes.
They often use dense forest where visibility is low.
Fallen fruit can link them to the rhythms of canopy trees.
Their best defense is often not being seen at all.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bay Duiker feeds on fallen fruit, leaves, seeds, fungi, and occasional small animal matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards are the chief natural predator, with African golden cats, crowned eagles and rock pythons also taking them. An alarmed animal freezes, then plunges into thick undergrowth, the habit behind the Afrikaans name duiker, meaning diver. Snares and bushmeat hunting are the heaviest pressure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mainly nocturnal or crepuscular, resting hidden in dense cover, so its rust coat belongs to shadow before it belongs to sight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented in the wild, where about 10 years is a common estimate. Captive animals have lived into their mid to late teens.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually hide a single calf in forest cover until it can follow, giving secrecy to the young before speed.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar; in this forest antelope, survival depends more on disappearing into the floor than on standing apart.

bearded-reedling.spotlight: A small, tawny songbird that lives in reedbeds all year and has no close relatives: it is the only species in its family. It travels through the reeds by gripping upright stems, often with one foot on each of two stems, and sidles up to the seed heads or down to the mud at their base.
bearded-reedling.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Reedbeds, marshes, wetlands, and tall waterside vegetation fit Bearded Reedlings because every movement depends on flexible vertical stems.
signatureTraits: The long, graduated tail makes up about half the bird's length.
Bill is small and orange-yellow.
Wings show black, white and rufous stripes.
Flight is weak and whirring, low over the reed tops.
Call is a ringing, metallic 'ping'.
interestingFacts: In autumn the walls of its stomach thicken and it swallows grit, which lets it grind hard seeds.
Older books call it the bearded tit, though it is not a tit; genetic studies place it closest to the larks.
Pairs often form in flocks of juveniles during their first autumn and then stay together.
In some autumns flocks tower high above the reedbed, calling, before leaving for new sites.
Hard winters can cut numbers sharply, but populations usually recover within a few years.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects in summer and reed seeds in winter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harriers, owls, mustelids, snakes, and nest predators threaten reedlings. Dense reeds hide movement and nests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, climbing and feeding in daylight. Their rhythm is light contact, tail balance, and seasonal adjustment.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically two to three years. Ringed birds have lived to about seven.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both sexes build a deep cup of dead reed leaves low among the stems. Clutches of four to eight eggs hatch after about 11 to 13 days, the young leave the nest at around 12 days, and a pair may raise two to four broods in a season.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a blue-grey head, a drooping black moustache from the eye down each side of the throat, and black feathers under the tail. Females have a plain tawny-brown head, no moustache, and buff under the tail.

bearded-seal.spotlight: Bearded Seal teaches Whisker Tactility through long sensitive whiskers searching cold seafloors where sight fades. The body feels for hidden value beneath ice, mud, and dim water.
bearded-seal.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, north_pacific, arctic_ocean, arctic_antarctic. Arctic and subarctic seas, pack ice, shallow shelves, and seafloor feeding areas.
signatureTraits: Long sensitive whiskers used to detect bottom-dwelling prey.
Large body adapted to cold Arctic and subarctic waters.
Seafloor foraging under ice and low visibility.
Ice-associated breeding and resting habits.
interestingFacts: Bearded seals are named for their long whiskers.
They feed heavily on bottom-dwelling animals such as clams, shrimp, crabs, and fish.
Pups are born on ice and can enter water soon after birth.
Males produce underwater calls during the breeding season.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Clams, shrimp, crabs, worms, snails, and bottom fish.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Polar bears, orcas, sharks, humans, and climate-driven ice loss threaten them. Ice and water provide refuge, but changing habitat makes sensing alone insufficient.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Bearded Seals rest on ice and forage in water across day and night depending on season. Their rhythm is haul out, dive, feel the bottom, feed, and return to ice.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Bearded Seals can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single pup on sea ice, and the pup grows quickly on rich milk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males vocalize strongly during breeding. Both sexes rely on whisker-based foraging.

bee-hummingbird.spotlight: Males measure about 5.5 centimetres from bill tip to tail and weigh under two grams; females are slightly larger. Its heart has been reported to beat more than a thousand times a minute during activity.
bee-hummingbird.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Bee Hummingbird usually lives in Cuban woodland edges, gardens, scrub, and flowering habitats.
signatureTraits: World’s smallest bird body carrying extreme flight control
Rapid wingbeats that hold the body still in air
Tiny bill and tongue matched to small flowers
Night torpor that protects a miniature energy budget
interestingFacts: Bee Hummingbirds are native only to Cuba, including the nearby Isla de la Juventud.
They are small enough to be mistaken for large insects near flowers.
The IUCN lists the Bee Hummingbird as Near Threatened, mainly because of loss and fragmentation of its native forest.
Its genus name Mellisuga comes from Latin words meaning honey-sucker, referring to its nectar-feeding habits.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bee Hummingbird feeds on nectar from tiny flowers plus minute insects and spiders for protein.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Its size exposes it to hunters that ignore larger birds: big spiders and their webs, lizards and frogs are thought to take some, alongside small hawks and kestrels. Speed and agility are its only defence. Clearance of forest and flowering scrub has fragmented its range.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active and may enter torpor at night, lowering energy costs so the smallest bird can afford its impossible daytime control.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Small hummingbirds can live several years if they survive early danger; Tiny Precision becomes thousands of exact hovers, not one cute moment.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build tiny cup nests and raise two pea-sized eggs without male care, turning miniature architecture into the start of precision.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are brighter with iridescent head and throat colors; females are plainer, carrying the hidden precision of nesting and care.

beira.spotlight: Thick, rubbery pads under the hooves let this antelope grip bare rock. It stands a little under 60 centimetres at the shoulder, weighs around 10 kilograms, and is known only from stony hill ranges in northern Somalia, Djibouti and neighbouring eastern Ethiopia.
beira.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry rocky hills, scrubby slopes, and arid outcrops.
signatureTraits: Reddish-grey back with a dark band along each flank
White underparts, with fawn-yellow head and legs
White ring around each eye
Very large ears, about 15 centimetres long, white inside
Short, bushy tail
interestingFacts: It lives in small family groups, most often of about four to seven animals.
It is reported to go without drinking, getting its water from the plants it browses.
The only captive breeding group known was kept at Al Wabra Wildlife Preservation in Qatar.
It is listed as Vulnerable, with drought, overgrazing by livestock and hunting as the main pressures.
When alarmed it bounds uphill over loose stones, then stands still where its coat matches the rock.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, shrubs, herbs, and dry browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, hyenas, jackals, raptors for young, and humans threaten them. Rock and alertness are defense, turning terrain into shelter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are most active in cooler hours and rest in shade or cover during heat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is poorly documented: no figures appear to have been published, either for wild animals or for the one captive group.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A female bears a single calf after a gestation thought to be about six months. The calf lies hidden among rocks and scrub for its first weeks while the mother feeds nearby.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry horns while females usually do not; both depend on nimble feet and alert senses.

belted-kingfisher.spotlight: Belted Kingfisher teaches Rattle Signature through a bird whose method is impossible to mistake. Shaggy crest, heavy bill, rattling call, waterside perch, and plunge-dive show confidence sharpened into a recognizable pattern.
belted-kingfisher.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Rivers, lakes, streams, estuaries, shorelines, gravel banks, and wooded waterways fit Belted Kingfishers because they need clear fishing water and earthen banks for nesting.
signatureTraits: Rattling call: the voice announces the bird before the dive.
Shaggy crest: the head gives the silhouette a rough signature.
Riverbank burrows: nesting is dug into earthen banks near fishing water.
interestingFacts: Belted Kingfisher females are often more brightly belted than males, which is unusual among many birds.
They nest at the end of tunnels dug into earthen banks, and some tunnels are more than a metre long.
Their loud rattle is one of the easiest ways to notice them along waterways.
They hunt by diving headfirst into water, often after hovering briefly above a fish they have spotted.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crayfish, tadpoles, aquatic insects, and small amphibians.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, snakes, raccoons, foxes, cats, and burrow predators can threaten kingfishers or nests. Steep nesting banks and loud territorial behavior protect the route.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Belted Kingfishers are diurnal, patrolling waterways and calling as they move.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Belted Kingfishers can live several years in the wild, with some reaching well over a decade. Repeated seasons sharpen knowledge of perches, banks, and fishing angles.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in long burrows excavated into banks, and both parents help feed the young. The next generation begins inside the same waterside method the adults depend on.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females have an extra rusty belly band, while males usually lack it.

beluga-sturgeon.spotlight: Beluga Sturgeon teaches Ancient Magnitude through an armored fish that carries deep time between sea and river. Its huge body, scutes, long lifespan, and spawning migration show that some old designs become immense by crossing ages and waters.
beluga-sturgeon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Large rivers, estuaries, connected seas, deep channels, and spawning grounds fit Beluga Sturgeons because ancient magnitude depends on free movement between waters.
signatureTraits: Huge ancient sturgeon with armored scutes
Migrates between sea and rivers to spawn
Long-lived slow-maturing fish
Bottom-oriented feeding with a large mouth
interestingFacts: Beluga Sturgeons are among the largest freshwater-associated fishes.
They can live for many decades and mature slowly.
They migrate from the Caspian and Black Seas into rivers such as the Volga to spawn.
Overfishing and dams have made them critically threatened.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and other aquatic animals.
