interestingFacts: It feeds by sucking up sediment and sorting it inside the mouth, spitting back what it does not want — which is what makes the water turbid.
The barbels are taste and touch organs, so a carp locates food in water far too murky to see through.
It is one of the most widely introduced fish in the world and is listed among the most damaging invasive species in several countries it was stocked into.
Carp learn quickly to avoid baited hooks, and heavily fished waters produce individuals that are very hard to catch a second time.
It tolerates warm, low-oxygen and polluted water that would kill most other large freshwater fish.
Koi are not this species — they are domesticated Cyprinus rubrofuscus, the Amur carp.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: An omnivorous bottom feeder taking insect larvae, molluscs, crustaceans, seeds and plant matter, sifted from sediment rather than hunted. That feeding method is the principle in action: the food is won by disturbing the bed, and disturbing the bed is what reshapes the water above it.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pike, catfish, otters, herons and cormorants take small carp; a full-grown one has very few predators beyond people. Size, a thick scaled hide and the murk it creates all work in its favour as it grows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mostly around dawn and dusk in the shallows, and quiet through the coldest months, when it groups in deeper water and feeds very little.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 15 to 20 years, and individuals well over 40 are recorded in ponds.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A large female broadcasts hundreds of thousands of sticky eggs over flooded vegetation in spring, with no parental care at all. Survival is a numbers game, which suits a fish that can occupy water almost nothing else tolerates.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike outside the breeding season. Spawning males develop small white tubercles on the head and gill covers; females are deeper-bodied when carrying eggs.

cattle-egret.spotlight: Cattle Egret teaches Opportunity by following the movement that reveals hidden prey. Its white body beside hooves, short stalking steps, and quick strikes show how attention can turn another animal’s disturbance into your opening.
cattle-egret.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, sub_saharan_africa, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. Pastures, fields, wetlands, roadsides, farms, and short-grass areas fit Cattle Egrets because movement through grass exposes insects. The habitat is useful when something else is stirring it.
signatureTraits: Hoof-following foraging: it catches prey flushed by livestock or wild grazers.
Quick ground strike: opportunity is taken before disturbed insects vanish.
Human-edge success: it adapts well to farms, fields, roadsides, and pastures.
interestingFacts: Cattle Egrets often feed near cattle, horses, buffalo, or tractors.
They expanded widely beyond their original range.
They are less tied to deep water than many herons and egrets.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasshoppers, flies, beetles, ticks, small frogs, lizards, and other small prey support the Opportunity lesson. The egret eats what motion uncovers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, eagles, mammals, snakes, and nest predators create pressure, especially around colonies. Group nesting and alert feeding help reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Cattle Egrets are diurnal, feeding when grazing animals and insects are active. Their timing follows movement in the field, not just the clock.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years if they survive early risks. The lesson is repeated across seasons by tracking the best openings in changing landscapes.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in colony nests, often in trees or shrubs near water or feeding areas. The colony setting gives the next generation safety through numbers.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar, though breeding plumage can intensify with buff tones. Display and nesting behavior matter more than dramatic sex differences.

cayenne-caecilian.spotlight: Unlike most caecilians, which burrow in soil, this limbless amphibian of the Amazon basin and the Guianas lives almost entirely in water. The rear of the body is flattened from side to side and carries a low fin along the back, and it swims with eel-like waves. It has lungs and rises to the surface for air.
cayenne-caecilian.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Cayenne Caecilians live in slow freshwater, flooded areas, mud, and hidden tropical wetlands.
signatureTraits: Limbless amphibian body
Smooth swimming movement
Hidden wetland life
Sensory tentacles near the head
interestingFacts: Caecilians are amphibians, not snakes or worms, and are related to frogs and salamanders.
This species is aquatic, living in rivers, swamps, and flooded forests of northern South America.
Females give birth to live young, which scrape nourishment from the lining of the mother's oviduct before birth.
Its body is flattened side to side toward the tail, forming a fin-like keel that helps it swim.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, aquatic insect larvae, shrimps and small fish, along with dead fish it scavenges. It searches the bottom and the mud mainly by smell and touch, and seizes food with backward-curving teeth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators have been recorded; large fish, snakes, wading birds and caimans are the likely ones. The skin gives off a slimy secretion that is reported to be toxic to some fish and makes the animal hard to grip.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are secretive, spending much time hidden in water or mud. Activity is mainly at night, when they leave their burrows in the bank or bottom to forage; the day is passed inside burrows or under sunken debris.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No published age table exists for Typhlonectes compressicauda; this aquatic caecilian of Amazonian wetlands gives birth to live young after months of internal development.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Fertilisation is internal, and females give birth to live young after internal development. Pregnancy lasts about six to seven months. The unborn young scrape nourishment from the oviduct wall with special teeth and carry broad sac-like gills that are lost around birth. Litters are small, usually under ten.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: There is no difference in colour or body form that can be seen in the water. The vent region differs slightly in shape between males and females, so they can be sexed only by close examination in the hand.

cecropia-moth.spotlight: Cecropia Moth teaches Brief Splendor through a giant silk moth whose adult life is short but unforgettable. Huge patterned wings, eye-like markings, feathery antennae, and no adult feeding make the appearance feel like a lantern with one purpose.
cecropia-moth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Deciduous forests, orchards, parks, gardens, woodland edges, and host trees like maple, cherry, birch, and willow.
signatureTraits: Huge patterned wings that create a dramatic night presence
Adult stage with no feeding, focused on reproduction
Feathery antennae, especially in males, for sensing mates
Silken cocoon that holds transformation before emergence
interestingFacts: Cecropia Moths are among the largest native moths in North America.
Adults do not eat because their mouthparts are not functional for feeding.
Males use large feathery antennae to detect female pheromones.
The adult’s beautiful stage is brief because energy was stored during the caterpillar stage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars feed on leaves, while adults do not eat.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, spiders, parasitoid wasps, ants, and mammals threaten eggs, caterpillars, and adults. Wing patterns, cocoons, and night timing help protect a creature whose adult beauty cannot last long.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are nocturnal, flying and seeking mates at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult Cecropia Moths may live only about one or two weeks, though the full life cycle is longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release pheromones, mate, and lay eggs on host plants for the next caterpillars.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males usually have larger, more feathered antennae than females.

chambered-nautilus.spotlight: Chambered Nautilus turns inner adjustment into movement. Its shell chambers balance gas and fluid, showing that small hidden changes can decide whether a life rises, sinks, or holds depth.
chambered-nautilus.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, australia_coastal. Steep outer reef slopes and drop-offs in the tropical Indo-West Pacific, where it lives close to the sea floor, mostly at about 150 to 400 metres. The shell implodes at around 800 metres, which sets its lower limit.
signatureTraits: Coiled chambered shell used for buoyancy control
Jet propulsion for slow backward movement
Many tentacles without suction cups
Deep reef slope and vertical migration habits
interestingFacts: Nautiluses are shelled cephalopods whose nautiloid relatives date back roughly 500 million years.
They regulate buoyancy by changing gas and fluid inside shell chambers.
Unlike octopuses and squids, their tentacles do not have suction cups.
They often move vertically between deeper and shallower water.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They scavenge and eat crustaceans, fish, molts, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include triggerfish, sharks, octopuses, and humans. Their defense is the hard shell, retreat, depth change, and the ability to regulate position in the water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Often more active at night, moving shallower to feed and deeper during the day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for many years, possibly over 15 to 20 years, longer than many cephalopods. The lifespan why is that slow adjustment can be more durable than frantic brilliance.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay relatively large eggs attached to hard surfaces, and development is slow.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually slightly larger, with a broader shell. A male carries the spadix, a cluster of modified tentacles used to pass sperm, and is reported to have fewer tentacles overall than a female.

chamois.spotlight: Chamois teaches Surefooting through a mountain body whose feet understand hard ground. Specialized hooves, strong legs, steep-slope agility, and alpine alertness show confidence created by contact with the rock.
chamois.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east. Alpine meadows, rocky slopes, cliffs, forests near mountains, and high pastures fit Chamois because safety and food both depend on steep terrain.
signatureTraits: Specialized hooves: flexible edges grip steep alpine ground.
Slope agility: escape routes run through terrain that challenges predators.
Seasonal coat: mountain weather changes the body’s covering.
interestingFacts: Chamois are goat-antelopes in the subfamily Caprinae, related to goats but not members of the true goat genus.
They can move across very steep terrain with speed and control.
Their hooves are adapted for grip on rock and snow.
Their coat turns dark brown to nearly black in winter, contrasting with the paler, reddish-brown summer coat.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, herbs, leaves, shoots, bark, lichens, and alpine plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, lynx, golden eagles for young, bears, and humans pressure Chamois. Steep escape routes and group alertness turn harsh slopes into protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chamois are diurnal, often feeding in morning and evening while resting during harsher periods. Their rhythm follows slope, weather, and safety.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild chamois can live to about 15 to 20 years, females generally outliving males; age can be read from the yearly growth rings on the horns.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to kids on safer mountain terrain, where young must learn footing quickly. Offspring turn the slope from danger into nursery and training ground.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes have short hooked horns, though males are often heavier and more solitary outside the rut.

cheetah.spotlight: Cheetah teaches Cheetah Acceleration through a body prepared for a sprint before the chase begins. Flexible spine, long legs, enlarged breathing, semi-retractable claws, and tail balance make speed an architecture.
cheetah.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east. Open savanna, grassland, semi-desert, and lightly wooded plains fit Cheetahs because Cheetah Acceleration needs visibility, space, and enough cover for the approach. The habitat turns prepared design into a short decisive chase.
signatureTraits: Flexible spine that lengthens each stride during pursuit
Semi-retractable claws that grip the ground like running spikes
Long tail for balance during high-speed turns
Tear marks and sharp vision for daytime hunting focus
interestingFacts: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals over short distances.
They must rest after intense sprints because acceleration costs enormous energy.
Their claws do not retract fully, helping with traction while running.
Cubs have a mantle of longer fur that may help with camouflage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly small and medium antelopes, such as Thomson's gazelle in East Africa and impala and springbok in southern Africa, with hares and the young of larger antelopes. It stalks close before sprinting, trips the prey with a forepaw and kills with a suffocating throat bite.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, hyenas, leopards, wild dogs, eagles on cubs, and humans threaten cheetahs or steal kills. Speed helps in pursuit, but vulnerability after the sprint shows why acceleration must be used wisely.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Cheetahs are mainly diurnal or crepuscular, hunting when visibility favors precision and larger predators may be less active. Their rhythm is rest deeply, sprint completely.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Cheetahs often live around 10 to 12 years in the wild when they survive cubhood.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Gestation lasts about three months and litters are usually three to five cubs, born blind in a lair in long grass or thicket. The mother shifts them to a new lair every few days. Cubs follow her from around six weeks and stay for about 18 months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are slightly larger and may form coalitions, while females are usually solitary with cubs. The sex difference adds social strategy, but both sexes share the sprint-built body.

chimpanzee.spotlight: Great apes of equatorial Africa, chimpanzees are, with bonobos, our closest living relatives. They make and use tools: stripped stems to fish termites from mounds, stone and wooden hammers to crack nuts, chewed leaves to sponge up water. Which tools a community uses differs from one forest to the next, and the young learn by watching their mothers.
chimpanzee.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. African forests and woodland mosaics fit because tool culture needs materials, problems, and social learning close together.
signatureTraits: Black hair with bare face, ears, palms and soles
Arms longer than the legs
Walks on all fours on its knuckles
No tail, as in all apes
Large, rounded ears standing out from the head
interestingFacts: Humans and chimpanzees share roughly 98 to 99 per cent of their DNA sequence.
A community of 20 to more than 100 chimpanzees is rarely all together, splitting into small parties whose size and membership change through the day.
The pant-hoot, a loud call that builds to a scream, carries a kilometre or more through forest, and each animal's version is recognisably its own.
At Fongoli in Senegal, chimpanzees sharpen sticks with their teeth and jab them into tree hollows to catch bushbabies.
Parties of males patrol the borders of their community's territory and sometimes kill chimpanzees from neighbouring groups.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, leaves, seeds, termites, ants, meat, and nuts.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, humans, disease, habitat loss, and conflict threaten chimpanzees, making group knowledge and social warning systems important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chimpanzees are diurnal, feeding and traveling by day before building tree nests each night with learned forest skill.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Chimpanzees can live for several decades, giving tool habits, social bonds, and local traditions time to pass between generations.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about eight months, a female bears a single infant that clings to her belly and later rides on her back. Nursing lasts four to five years, so births are usually five or more years apart. Many young females leave to join a neighbouring community.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and often more involved in dominance politics, while females carry long teaching roles through infant care and foraging.

chinese-alligator.spotlight: Chinese Alligator teaches Ancient Belonging through old armor that still fits muddy wetlands. Its small size, burrow use, pond life, and seasonal patience show that an ancient design can belong by hiding, waiting, and returning.
chinese-alligator.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Ponds, wetlands, slow streams, marshes, rice-field edges, and burrowed banks fit Chinese Alligators because ancient belonging now depends on small protected waters.
signatureTraits: Small alligator with broad armored body
Burrows used for refuge and winter dormancy
Freshwater wetland and pond dependence
Ancient crocodilian design surviving in altered landscapes
interestingFacts: Chinese Alligators are much smaller than American Alligators.
They dig or use burrows for shelter and winter dormancy.
They are among the most endangered crocodilians, and wild numbers now depend heavily on releases of captive-bred alligators.
They are native to the lower Yangtze River region of China.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, snails, crustaceans, insects, frogs, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and young face birds, snakes, mammals, and larger predators, while adults are mostly threatened by people and habitat loss. Burrows protect all seasons.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They bask and feed in warm months and may become inactive in burrows during colder periods. Their rhythm is seasonal return from hidden armor.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Chinese Alligators can live for several decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build mound nests and guard eggs and hatchlings. Young begin life near water and shelter, relying on both warmth and protection.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females, while females take the nesting role. Both sexes carry the same ancient armor, but size and care divide the work.

chinese-cobra.spotlight: Chinese Cobra is known for hood display, fast warning, venom defense, and ridge-like body movement.
chinese-cobra.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Woodlands, shrublands, agricultural edges, rocky areas, and warm lowland habitats in southern China and nearby regions.
signatureTraits: Expandable hood
Venomous defensive bite
Agile ground movement
Dark brown to black body with narrow pale crossbands
Pale spectacle-like marking on the back of the hood
interestingFacts: It often raises the front body when threatened.
Its hood makes its warning easy to read.
It can live near farms, forests, and edges where prey is available.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on rodents, frogs, lizards, snakes, and other small vertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include raptors, mongooses, larger snakes, and humans.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Often active at dusk or night in warm seasons, with activity shifting by temperature.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan varies, but cobras can survive many years when not persecuted.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected warm places; young are independent after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are modest, though males may be larger in some populations.

chinese-crocodile-lizard.spotlight: Chinese Crocodile Lizard teaches Stream Stillness through a small dragon that waits exactly where water, shade, and patience meet. Its armored scales, strong tail, cool-stream perches, and long pauses show that presence can be serious without constant motion.
chinese-crocodile-lizard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia, southeast_asia. Cool forest streams, shaded pools, wet rocks, overhanging branches, and subtropical valleys fit Chinese Crocodile Lizards because stillness needs a precise waterside perch.
signatureTraits: Armored crocodile-like tail and rough scales
Semi-aquatic life along cool forest streams
Long motionless basking or waiting periods
Small predator of wet forest edges
interestingFacts: Chinese Crocodile Lizards are sometimes called living fossils because they represent a very distinctive lineage.
They can remain still for long periods on branches or rocks near water.
They are associated with cool, shaded streams in southern China and northern Vietnam.
They give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, small fish, tadpoles, snails, and aquatic invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, snakes, mammals, larger lizards, and humans can threaten them. Water retreat, stillness, and armored texture help reduce danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal to crepuscular, often basking or waiting quietly near streams. Their rhythm is slow warming, long stillness, and short movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years in protected care, often over a decade.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young, usually a small number at a time. Young begin life already shaped for the same stream-edge hiding and waiting.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may show brighter breeding color and broader heads, while females are generally less vivid. The difference makes display secondary to the shared stream strategy.

chinese-giant-salamander.spotlight: Chinese Giant Salamander teaches River Hidden Magnitude through a huge body that disappears into cold water. Its wrinkled skin, flattened shape, rock shelter, and ambush feeding show that great size can survive by becoming the river’s shadow.
chinese-giant-salamander.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Cold mountain streams, rocky rivers, underwater crevices, caves, and oxygen-rich freshwater fit Chinese Giant Salamanders because magnitude must hide in flowing structure.
signatureTraits: Enormous aquatic salamander with flattened body
Wrinkled skin that helps exchange oxygen in water
Rock-crevice ambush life in cold streams
Ancient amphibian lineage with hidden power
interestingFacts: Chinese Giant Salamanders are among the largest amphibians in the world.
They breathe partly through their skin, so clean oxygen-rich water matters.
They often shelter under rocks or in underwater cavities.
Their populations have been heavily reduced by habitat loss and overharvest.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, frogs, crustaceans, insects, worms, and small aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large fish, mammals, birds, other salamanders, and humans can threaten eggs or young, while adults mainly face human pressure. Rock shelter is the main refuge.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, hiding by day and feeding in dark water. Their rhythm lets a giant body move like a secret.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many decades, especially in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay strings of eggs in underwater dens, and males may guard the nest site. Young begin as aquatic larvae dependent on clean cold water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may guard breeding dens and can have swollen cloacal areas in breeding season, while females carry eggs. Most visual differences are subtle outside breeding.

chinese-softshell-turtle.spotlight: Chinese Softshell Turtle teaches Mud Concealment through a flat turtle needing only a snorkel of self exposed. Soft shell, long nose, buried body, and sudden bite make quiet advantage a matter of revealing less.
chinese-softshell-turtle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia, southeast_asia. Slow rivers, ponds, lakes, canals, muddy bottoms, sandy banks, and freshwater wetlands.
signatureTraits: Flat soft shell suited to burying in mud or sand
Long snorkel-like snout for breathing with little exposure
Aquatic ambush style from soft freshwater bottoms
Fast defensive bite when danger comes too close
interestingFacts: Softshell turtles have leathery shells instead of hard domed shells.
Their long snouts help them breathe while staying mostly hidden.
They can bury themselves in soft mud or sand.
They are quicker and more flexible than many people expect from a turtle.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crustaceans, insects, molluscs, worms, frogs and carrion. It often lies buried in soft mud or sand with only its snorkel-like snout showing, darting its long neck out to snap passing prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large fish, birds, mammals, snakes, humans, and egg predators threaten softshells. Burial reduces visibility, while a fast bite defends close range.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chinese Softshell Turtles may be active by day or night depending on temperature, basking or burying as needed. Their rhythm is exposure when useful, concealment when wise.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Chinese Softshell Turtles can live for decades in suitable conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in nests dug on banks or sandy ground.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences can include size and tail shape in mature turtles.

chinese-water-dragon.spotlight: Chinese Water Dragon teaches Escape Timing through a riverbank lizard that turns one clean leap into endurance. Arboreal perches, long tail balance, water dives, swimming, and submerged hiding make refuge a timed decision.
chinese-water-dragon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, east_asia. Tropical riverbanks, forest streams, humid vegetation, overhanging branches, and ponds.
signatureTraits: Riverbank climbing keeps the lizard close to both height and water refuge.
A long tail supports balance on branches and steering in water.
Diving and swimming create a rapid escape route from land predators.
Green coloration blends with humid vegetation near streams.
interestingFacts: A pale, light-sensitive parietal eye sits on top of the head between the true eyes.
It is reported to stay submerged for up to about 25 minutes when hiding from danger.
A captive female has been shown to produce young without mating, by parthenogenesis.
The tail makes up roughly two-thirds of the total length, which reaches about 90 centimetres in large males.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, small fish, frogs, fruit, flowers, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, larger lizards, fish for young, humans, and habitat loss can threaten Chinese Water Dragons. Their defense is layered: alertness, climbing, diving, swimming, and hiding.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chinese Water Dragons are diurnal, basking and foraging by day when body heat supports quick movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Kept water dragons commonly reach 10 to 15 years, a few about 20; how long they last in the wild has not been studied.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil or suitable nesting substrate near humid habitat, and hatchlings must quickly rely on small size, cover, and escape reflexes. Offspring survival begins with choosing a place close enough to moisture and shelter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger with more pronounced crests, jowls, and territorial display features, while females are smaller and built around egg production.

chiru.spotlight: An antelope-like relative of sheep and goats that lives on the open steppe of the Tibetan Plateau, at heights of roughly 3,300 to 5,500 metres. Its underwool, traded as shahtoosh, is made of fibres finer than cashmere, and demand for it drove heavy poaching in the late twentieth century.
chiru.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Tibetan Plateau steppe and cold open plains fit because weatherproofing turns harsh altitude into road.
signatureTraits: Swollen, rounded muzzle with wide nostrils
Pale fawn to reddish-brown coat, whitish below
Black face and black leg stripes on breeding males
About 80 centimetres at the shoulder, on slim legs
interestingFacts: The swollen muzzle holds enlarged nasal passages, thought to help warm and moisten thin, cold air.
International trade in its wool has been banned under CITES since 1979.
The Qinghai-Tibet railway was built with underpasses so that migrating herds could cross beneath the line.
The rut falls in early winter, when males gather small groups of females and fight rivals with their horns.
It scrapes shallow hollows in the ground and lies in them out of the wind.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, and herbs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, lynx, snow leopards, humans, and harsh weather threaten Chiru, making speed, herding, and insulating wool important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Chiru are day-active, feeding and resting in open visibility where wind, altitude, and herd alertness shape the daily rhythm.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live around 8 to 10 years, if migration routes, cold grasslands, and protection from hunting remain available.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females migrate to calving grounds and usually bear one calf, linking reproduction to route memory and weather-ready movement.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have long slender horns, while females are hornless; both depend on fine underwool and high-plateau endurance.

cicada.spotlight: Stout, broad-headed, sap-feeding insects, usually with clear wings, whose males produce some of the loudest sounds made by any insect. Almost the whole life is spent out of sight as a nymph in the soil; the winged adults singing from the trees are in their last few weeks.
cicada.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, central_asia, east_asia, europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Woodland, forest, savanna, scrub, parks and gardens with trees or shrubs, mostly in warm temperate and tropical regions. Adults live on trunks and branches; nymphs live in soil burrows among the roots of the same plants.
signatureTraits: Stout body with a broad, blunt head
Large eyes set wide apart
Wings usually clear and strongly veined, held like a roof
Loud buzzing or rattling song from trees
Very short, bristle-like antennae
interestingFacts: A male's abdomen is largely hollow and works as a resonating chamber, amplifying the clicks of the buckling tymbals.
Songs of some species exceed 100 decibels at close range, and each species has its own pattern that females recognise.
A fungus, Massospora, infects some cicadas and replaces the rear of the abdomen with a plug of spores while the insect stays active.
Species called annual cicadas still take several years to develop; adults appear every summer because the generations overlap.
Three small simple eyes sit in a triangle on the top of the head between the two large compound eyes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Watery sap from the xylem vessels of plants, drawn through a piercing beak. Nymphs tap roots underground and adults tap twigs and branches. Because the sap is so dilute they drink large volumes and excrete the excess as fine droplets.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, squirrels, lizards, spiders, mantises and cicada-killer wasps take adults, and moles eat nymphs. Camouflage, a loud squawk on being seized and rapid flight help individuals; periodical cicadas emerge in such numbers that predators cannot eat them all.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most species sing and fly in the heat of the day, some mainly at dusk, and a few call after dark. Adults rest on branches at night. Nymphs usually leave the soil after sunset to moult on a trunk or stem.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Two to five years in many species, almost all spent underground as a nymph, and 13 or 17 years in the periodical cicadas of eastern North America. Adults live about two to six weeks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female cuts slits in twigs with her ovipositor and lays batches of eggs, up to several hundred in total. Eggs hatch after several weeks to several months, depending on species; the nymphs drop to the ground and burrow to the roots.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Only males sing, using a pair of ribbed, drum-like membranes called tymbals at the base of the abdomen. Females lack tymbals and have a pointed ovipositor at the abdomen tip; otherwise the sexes look alike.

cicada-killer-wasp.spotlight: Cicada Killer Wasp teaches Provision through heavy work placed underground for a future larva. The female’s burrow, cicada hunt, paralyzing sting, and food-stocked chamber make devotion practical, muscular, and hidden.
cicada-killer-wasp.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Sandy soil, lawns, open ground, garden edges, and sunny banks fit Cicada Killer Wasps because burrows must be dug where cicadas can be carried and stored.
signatureTraits: Females dig underground burrows with separate brood cells.
Paralyzed cicadas are stored as fresh food for larvae.
Adults drink nectar while larvae depend on prey provisioned by the mother.
interestingFacts: Female cicada killers can carry prey nearly as large as themselves.
Males may patrol and defend territories near nest burrows, but they cannot sting because only females have stingers.
Nesting females often gather in loose aggregations, digging many burrows in the same patch of sunny, well-drained soil.
They are among the largest wasps in eastern North America, with females reaching roughly four centimetres long.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar, while larvae feed on paralyzed cicadas stored by the mother.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, parasites, ants, and rival insects can threaten adults, larvae, or burrows. Underground chambers protect the future from the exposed surface.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Cicada Killer Wasps are active by day in warm summer, when cicadas are available and digging conditions work. Their rhythm follows the short season of provision.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults live only a few weeks in mid to late summer, and males die earlier than females. Most of the one-year life cycle is spent underground, where the full-grown larva overwinters in a silk cocoon and pupates the next summer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females do almost the famous work: digging burrows, hunting cicadas, stinging them, and laying eggs on the stored prey. Offspring are the whole reason the heavy carry exists.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex difference is important: females are larger and can sting, while males guard areas but lack a sting.

cinereous-vulture.spotlight: Among the largest birds of prey in the world, this dark brown vulture has a wingspan of about 2.5 to 3 metres. Its deep, heavy bill can tear hide, sinew and dried muscle that smaller scavengers cannot manage, and at a carcass it usually displaces griffon vultures. It mostly searches alone or in pairs.
cinereous-vulture.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Cinereous Vulture usually lives in open mountains, steppe, woodland edges, and wide dry country.
signatureTraits: vast wings
dark plumage
hooked bill
carrion patrol
interestingFacts: The species name monachus means monk, a reference to the ruff of feathers around the neck, which resembles a cowl.
Many birds from Mongolia and northern China move south for the winter, and young ones regularly reach the Korean peninsula.
Spain holds the largest European population, which has grown from roughly 200 pairs in the 1970s to more than 2,000.
Reintroduction projects have returned breeding birds to southern France and, more recently, to Bulgaria.
Young birds are almost black; adults fade to dark brown, with paler down on the head.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Cinereous Vulture feeds on carrion, especially large carcasses and tough scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Nothing regularly preys on the adults, and nests are seldom raided. Poisoned baits laid for wolves and other carnivores are the chief cause of death, followed by collisions with overhead cables, disturbance near nests and a shortage of carcasses where livestock remains are cleared away.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Cinereous Vulture is diurnal, soaring for hours on thermals.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild birds often live 20 years or more; captive individuals have reached nearly 40 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding from late winter, pairs usually raise one chick slowly in a large nest. The stick platform, built on a treetop or less often a cliff ledge, is reused and can grow to two metres across. The egg hatches after about 50 to 55 days, and the chick fledges at roughly three and a half to four months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is the same in both sexes. Females average slightly heavier, but the sexes cannot reliably be told apart in the field.

clouded-leopard.spotlight: Clouded Leopard embodies Canopy Range through a body that can hunt both above and below. Its rotating ankles, long tail, large paws, and clouded coat turn forest layers into connected paths instead of separate worlds.
clouded-leopard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Clouded Leopards live in tropical and subtropical forests, including dense canopy, hill forest, and forest edges.
signatureTraits: Rotating ankles that help it descend and maneuver in trees
Long balancing tail for branch movement
Cloud-like blotches that break its shape in forest light
Powerful bite and climbing body for layered hunting
interestingFacts: Clouded Leopards can climb down trees headfirst, a rare skill among cats.
Their canine teeth are proportionally very long for their skull size.
They use both arboreal and ground routes in dense Asian forests.
The cloud pattern helps dissolve their outline among leaves and shadows.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Takes prey both on the ground and in trees: macaques, langurs and other primates, squirrels, birds, muntjac and other small deer, and young wild pigs. It hunts by stalking and ambush.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults face humans more than natural predators, while cubs may be vulnerable to larger carnivores or snakes. Their real defense is secrecy, vertical escape, and a body able to leave danger by routes most animals cannot use.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, they rest hidden in dense vegetation or trees and move when cover is strongest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 10 to 15 years in the wild, longer in care. The lesson is not constant speed but repeated access: a life lasts by having more routes than danger can easily close.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters in secluded dens, where cubs must grow into climbing bodies before the canopy becomes safe. The offspring why is that range begins as hidden development.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar in pattern, though males are often larger.

clown-loach.spotlight: The Clown Loach turns playful cohesion into a field-guide principle. Its bright stripes, social movement, and bottom-searching barbels show that joy can stay useful when the group keeps searching together.
clown-loach.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra, borneo. Clown Loaches live in freshwater rivers, floodplains, and connected forest waters of Southeast Asia.
signatureTraits: Bright orange-and-black banding
Social group behavior
Barbels for bottom foraging
Active river-bottom movement
interestingFacts: Clown Loaches are social fish that often do best in groups.
They use barbels to explore the substrate for food.
They can make clicking sounds, especially during feeding or social activity.
In the wild they come from river systems in Southeast Asia and may move with seasonal floods.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat worms, small crustaceans, insects, snails, plant matter, and detritus.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger predatory fish, birds, and habitat changes can threaten them. Their defense is schooling, cover, and spines near the eyes, showing that playfulness can travel with hidden protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active in pulses through the day and twilight, often resting in cover and emerging to forage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Clown Loaches can live a long time for aquarium fish, sometimes decades in good conditions; wild longevity varies. Their long life makes cohesion important: a social fish is built for repeated group rhythms, not brief display.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females scatter eggs during breeding rather than providing parental care, and young develop in watery seasonal habitats. Offspring begin in the same moving river system where group life later becomes valuable.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females may become fuller-bodied when mature, but sexes are otherwise similar. The most visible identity is not sex difference but the shared striped social design.

clown-triggerfish.spotlight: Clown Triggerfish teaches Locked Boundary through a reef fish whose defense can physically click into place. Bold pattern, strong jaws, territorial reef behavior, and locking trigger spine make boundaries visible, memorable, and hard to move.
clown-triggerfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea. Coral reefs, lagoons, reef slopes, caves, and crevices fit Clown Triggerfish because a locked boundary only works where structure can hold the body.
signatureTraits: Large round white spots on the dark lower half of the body
Yellow net-like pattern over the dark back
Bright yellow-orange ring around the small mouth
Swims by rippling the dorsal and anal fins with a stiff body
interestingFacts: Triggerfish get their name from the locking spine mechanism on the back.
The clown triggerfish is one of the most visually striking reef fishes.
They can use powerful jaws to crush hard prey.
Their bold appearance pairs with assertive reef behavior.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sea urchins, crustaceans, mollusks, worms, coral rubble prey, and hard-shelled animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large reef predators, sharks, groupers, eels, and humans can threaten triggerfish. Reef crevices, warning colors, and the trigger spine help prevent easy removal.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Clown Triggerfish are diurnal, foraging and defending reef space by day before sheltering at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity it commonly passes 10 years, with ages near 20 occasionally reported. Wild lifespan appears not to have been studied.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in prepared reef or sandy nesting areas and may defend the site aggressively. Offspring begin as tiny drifting young, so adult boundary strength protects only the earliest vulnerable stage.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are not dramatically different to casual view.

clownfish.spotlight: Clownfish teaches Symbiosis through a small fish that makes danger into home. Its protective mucus, anemone shelter, bright bands, and close pair or group life show that survival can come from learning the rules of a sting.
clownfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: coral_triangle, indian_ocean, south_pacific. Coral reefs, lagoon edges, shallow tropical waters, and host anemones fit Clownfish because their safety depends on a living shelter that most predators cannot enter.
signatureTraits: Protective mucus helps clownfish avoid being stung by their host anemone.
Bright bands make the small fish recognizable around its living shelter.
Group hierarchy and host loyalty keep life centered on one dangerous refuge.
interestingFacts: Clownfish can change sex within their social group when the breeding female is lost.
They live closely with sea anemones that deter many predators.
The fish may help clean or defend the anemone while gaining shelter.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Algae, plankton, small crustaceans, leftover prey, and anemone-associated food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, eels, and reef predators threaten clownfish outside the anemone. The sting-filled shelter changes the danger map and makes closeness protective.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Clownfish are diurnal, active around the anemone by day and sheltering among tentacles at night. Their rhythm stays tied to the home that protects them.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aquarium fish commonly live 10 years or more, with reports beyond 20. Wild lifespans are poorly measured, though the closely related orange clownfish, Amphiprion percula, is estimated to reach 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on hard surfaces near the anemone, and males commonly guard and fan the eggs. Offspring make the shelter relationship practical because the next generation begins beside the same sting-filled home.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Clownfish are sequential hermaphrodites: the dominant breeding individual is female, with a breeding male below her. Sex roles are directly tied to hierarchy and the anemone home.

cockroach.spotlight: Flattened, fast-running insects with a shield-like plate over the head, cockroaches number roughly 4,500 described species. Only about 30 are regular pests of buildings; most live in leaf litter, rotting logs, caves and burrows, where they help break down dead plant matter.
cockroach.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, central_asia, east_asia, europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Most species live in warm, humid tropical and subtropical forest, in leaf litter, under bark, in rotting wood, caves and burrows. Fewer live in temperate woodland, desert or scrub, and a handful live in buildings and sewers.
signatureTraits: Flattened, oval body able to squeeze into narrow cracks
Broad plate covering most of the head from above
Long, whip-like antennae, often as long as the body
Spiny legs built for fast running
Pair of short cerci at the tip of the abdomen
Leathery forewings folded flat over the back, reduced or absent in some species
interestingFacts: Females of many species enclose their eggs in a hard, purse-shaped case called an ootheca, which is dropped, glued to a surface or carried until hatching.
Some species give birth to live young, and the Pacific beetle cockroach nourishes its embryos with a protein-rich, milk-like fluid inside a brood sac.
Wood-eating cockroaches of the genus Cryptocercus live in family groups and pass gut microbes to their young, like their close relatives the termites.
Fine hairs on the cerci sense tiny puffs of air, so a cockroach can begin its escape run within a few hundredths of a second of an attack.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Decaying organic matter, crumbs, starches, grease, and almost any edible waste support the principle because flexibility keeps survival open.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, centipedes, birds, lizards, rodents, pesticides, and drying conditions threaten them. Speed and hiding make persistence possible.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal, resting in cracks by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They often live around a year, enough for rapid reproduction and repeated escape.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females produce egg cases with many young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes are winged; males may have slightly longer wings. The lesson sits in whole-body resilience.

coconut-crab.spotlight: No land-living arthropod grows larger: big males weigh about 4 kilograms and span close to a metre across the legs. This relative of the hermit crabs strips the husk from a coconut and works the shell open, a task that can take hours or days. In one study its pinch was the strongest measured in any crustacean.
coconut-crab.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific. Coconut Crab usually lives in tropical islands, coastal forests, burrows, and palm areas.
signatureTraits: huge claws
land life
climbing strength
hard-food cracking
interestingFacts: Young crabs shelter the soft abdomen in a snail shell as hermit crabs do, then give up shells as the abdomen hardens.
Adults breathe air through a lung-like chamber and drown if kept under water.
Food is found largely by smell, and the antennae work in air much as an insect's do.
To moult it seals itself in a burrow for several weeks, and afterwards it eats the shed shell.
Colour varies between individuals, from orange-red to purplish blue.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Coconut Crab feeds on fruit, nuts, coconuts, carrion, and varied plant or animal matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: At sea the drifting larvae are eaten by fish. On land small crabs fall to rats, pigs and larger coconut crabs, and hide in crevices and burrows. Full-grown adults have little to fear except people, who have hunted them out of many inhabited islands.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Coconut Crab is mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, sheltering by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth is very slow. Estimates of maximum age commonly run to 40 years or more and sometimes to about 60, but the ages of wild crabs are hard to verify.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place on land, and females release larvae into the sea after carrying eggs. The egg mass is held under the abdomen for a few months and shed at the shoreline. Larvae drift for about a month before settling on the sea bed and later moving ashore.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are often larger with stronger claws. Females have three feathery limbs on the underside of the abdomen for holding eggs, which males lack.

coelacanth.spotlight: Coelacanth teaches Living Relic through a deep fish that never stopped moving through ancient time. Its lobed fins, slow drift, cave use, and unexpected rediscovery show that some bodies carry old stories by surviving quietly.
coelacanth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, indian_ocean. Deep volcanic slopes, submarine caves, twilight depths, and steep reef walls fit Coelacanths because living relics survive in dark stable refuges.
signatureTraits: Fleshy lobed fins that move in a limb-like rhythm
Deep cave and slope habitat
Ancient lineage once known mainly from fossils
Slow drifting movement in dark water
interestingFacts: Coelacanths were once thought extinct until a living one was found in 1938.
They are lobe-finned fishes, related to the lineage that led toward land vertebrates.
They often rest in deep caves during the day.
They give birth to live young rather than laying small eggs externally.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, squid, cuttlefish, and deep-water animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks and deep predators may threaten them, while humans and accidental capture are major risks. Depth and caves protect the old design.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Coelacanths often shelter in caves by day and drift out at night to feed. Their rhythm is deep rest and ancient movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Coelacanths are very long-lived and may live many decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry large developing young internally and give birth to live pups after a long reproductive cycle. Offspring begin life already large for fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger than males and carry developing young. The difference reinforces slow, heavy investment in survival.

collared-falconet.spotlight: The Collared Falconet proves small boldness. It is tiny for a raptor, but the strike knows itself; size stops mattering when focus, speed, and courage line up.
collared-falconet.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Collared Falconets live in open woodland, forest edges, groves, and clearings across parts of South and Southeast Asia.
signatureTraits: Tiny raptor body
Fast perch-to-prey attacks
Bold hunting of insects and small birds
Sharp falcon-like posture
interestingFacts: Collared Falconets are among the smallest birds of prey.
They often hunt from exposed perches, dashing out after prey.
They eat mostly large insects such as butterflies and dragonflies, along with occasional small birds.
Unlike most falcons, they nest in old barbet or woodpecker holes in trees.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat insects, small birds, and other small prey taken in quick attacks.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger raptors, snakes, and nest predators may threaten them. Their defense is flight, alert perching, and nesting choices, showing that boldness still works with awareness.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, hunting in daylight from lookout perches.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Small raptors can live several years in the wild, though exact longevity varies. The lifespan supports repeated proof: small boldness is a daily pattern, not one lucky strike.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in cavities or old holes, and both parents may help raise the young depending on nesting conditions. Offspring begin protected in small spaces before learning open-air courage.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females may be slightly larger in many raptors, but visible differences are subtle. The main guide signal is the shared miniature predator shape.

comet-moth.spotlight: The caterpillar spins a silvery cocoon pierced by many small holes, thought to let rainwater drain away so that the pupa inside does not drown in Madagascar's wet forests. With a wingspan of about 20 centimetres, the adult is among the largest of the silk moths.
comet-moth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Comet Moths live in Madagascar forests where larval host plants grow.
signatureTraits: Long comet-like tails
Large yellow silk-moth wings
No adult feeding
Madagascar endemic
interestingFacts: Adults live only about a week and spend that time finding mates and laying eggs.
The long tails may confuse bat attacks, as shown in related tailed silk moths.
Males use large feathery antennae to detect scent signals released by females.
It is often ranked among the world's largest moths, with a wingspan commonly reported at around 14 centimetres.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults have no working mouthparts and live on reserves laid down as caterpillars. The caterpillars eat the leaves of forest trees; recorded food plants include Weinmannia and Eugenia, and captive stock is reared on substitutes such as sumac and eucalyptus.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, lizards and spiders take adults, and parasitic wasps and flies attack caterpillars and pupae. The eyespot on each wing may startle or misdirect an attacking bird. Forest clearance is the main wider threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly at night and hang motionless among foliage through the day. Males do most of the flying, while females tend to stay near the cocoon they emerged from until mated.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult moths live about 4 to 8 days. The caterpillar feeds for about two months and the pupa stays in its cocoon for two to six months, so a generation takes under a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Newly emerged females release scent to attract males and lay eggs on host plants. Each lays roughly 120 to 170 eggs over the few nights available to her.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males usually have especially long tails and feathery antennae for sensing females. Their tails reach about 15 centimetres. Females are heavier-bodied, with broader, rounder wings, tails roughly half as long and narrower antennae.

common-basilisk.spotlight: Common Basilisk teaches Impossible Timing through a lizard running on water only while the moment holds. Long toes, rapid hind-leg slaps, river-edge escape, and tree refuge make the impossible a timed window.
common-basilisk.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical riverbanks, forest streams, ponds, wet lowlands, and vegetation over water.
signatureTraits: Long toes and fringed feet for brief water running
Explosive escape from riverbanks and low branches
Tree and water-edge lifestyle that keeps escape routes close
Crests and agile body used in display and movement
interestingFacts: Common Basilisks can run short distances across water when escaping.
Their long toes help slap and push against the water surface.
Young and lighter individuals are especially capable of water running.
They often live near streams and rivers where this escape makes sense.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, flowers, fruit, small fish, frogs, and tiny vertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, snakes, fish, larger lizards, mammals, and humans threaten basilisks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Basilisks are diurnal, basking and foraging by day so body heat can power sudden escape.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Basilisks can live for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil or hidden nesting sites near suitable habitat. Offspring fit the principle because young basilisks must quickly rely on speed, cover, and water-edge timing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger with more obvious crests, while females are less ornamented. The difference adds display, but both sexes rely on the same timed escape logic.

common-genet.spotlight: A slender, short-legged carnivore about the size of a small cat, pale grey-buff with rows of dark spots and a crest of black hair along the spine that it raises when alarmed. Its claws can be partly drawn back, which keeps them sharp for climbing. Droppings are left at regular latrines on prominent rocks, walls and branches.
common-genet.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, europe. Woodland, scrub, rocky areas, farms, tree cover, and forest edges fit Common Genets because they need routes above and below ground.
signatureTraits: Spotted coat breaks the outline in branches and rocks.
Long tail gives balance during climbing and leaps.
Night hunting turns darkness into cover.
interestingFacts: Common Genets are agile relatives of civets, not cats.
They can climb well and often move through trees or rocky cover.
Their ringed tails help balance the spotted body.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, birds, reptiles, insects, fruit, and eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, leopards, large snakes, dogs, and humans can threaten genets. Climbing, concealment, and night movement help keep them safe.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Genets are mostly nocturnal, resting by day in sheltered sites and hunting after dark. Their rhythm belongs to quiet attention.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Genets may live for many years, often longer in safe or captive settings. Experience helps a night hunter learn routes, den sites, and prey timing.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in hidden nests or sheltered cavities, and young stay concealed until mobile. Offspring survival depends on secrecy before agility arrives.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger than females, but both share the same spotted, long-tailed night design.

common-gundi.spotlight: Common Gundi teaches Sun Readiness through a desert rodent using warm rock as preparation, not laziness. Ledge basking, crevice retreat, gripping feet, group alarms, and quick dashes make rest a readiness system.
common-gundi.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Rocky deserts, cliffs, boulder fields, dry slopes, and sunlit crevices fit Common Gundis because warmth and shelter must sit almost beside each other.
signatureTraits: Basks on sunlit rocks to warm the body for activity.
Uses crevices as fast shelter in rocky desert habitats.
Flattened, agile body helps it move across ledges and cracks.
Often lives socially, with alert calls and shared rock space.
interestingFacts: Gundis are small North African rodents adapted to rocky dry places.
They rely on sun and shade to manage body temperature.
Their quick retreat into cracks is a major defense.
They feed on dry plant material in sparse desert habitats.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, grasses, seeds, stems, flowers, and dry desert plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, foxes, snakes, wild cats, dogs, and humans can threaten gundis. Alarm calls and immediate crevice retreat turn rest into preparation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Gundis are diurnal, warming in the sun before feeding and retreating during heat or danger.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Gundis can live multiple years when rock shelter and food remain stable. The principle depends on repeated cycles of warming, feeding, and retreating safely.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to well-developed young that can fit into rocky refuge early. Offspring survival depends on safe ledges and the group's readiness signals.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar.

common-kingfisher.spotlight: Common Kingfisher teaches Moment Reading through a flash that only comes after water is understood. Its still perch, sharp eyes, blue-orange body, and sudden dive show that clean action begins with patient observation.
common-kingfisher.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia. Rivers, streams, canals, lakes, and wooded banks.
signatureTraits: Still perching above water before sudden dives
Sharp pointed bill for catching fish below the surface
Brilliant blue-orange body that flashes during flight
Burrow nesting in riverbanks and soft banks
interestingFacts: Common Kingfishers often nest in tunnels dug into riverbanks.
They must judge refraction because prey appears shifted under water.
A successful dive depends on both patience and precise timing.
Their bright color can look like a sudden spark over dark water.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish, aquatic insects, tadpoles, and crustaceans.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Sparrowhawks, cats, rats, snakes, flooding, and hard winters can threaten kingfishers or nests. These pressures make precision important because wasted dives cost energy and exposed banks can fail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Kingfishers are diurnal, perching and diving in daylight when water can be read.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Kingfishers may live for several years, though many young birds face harsh early survival.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in a tunnel nest dug into a bank, and both parents may feed the chicks with small fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The female usually has an orange-red base to the lower half of the bill, while the male's bill is all black. Plumage and size are otherwise alike.

common-loon.spotlight: Common Loon teaches Deep Focus through a lake bird whose mastery lives below and above the surface. Spear bill, rear-set legs, deep dives, and haunting calls make focus both silent and echoing.
common-loon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe. Northern lakes, clear ponds, coastal winter waters, and fish-rich freshwater.
signatureTraits: Powerful underwater diving with legs set far back
Haunting calls that carry across northern lakes
Dagger-like bill for catching fish
Striking black-and-white breeding plumage tied to lake presence
interestingFacts: Common Loons are excellent swimmers but awkward on land because their legs sit far back.
Their calls include wails, yodels, tremolos, and hoots.
They need long stretches of water to take off.
Chicks often ride on a parent’s back during their first weeks, which keeps them warm and safe.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish dominate, with crustaceans, insects, amphibians, and aquatic prey also taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, gulls, raccoons, mink, snapping turtles, large fish for chicks, lead tackle, and shoreline disturbance threaten loons. Deep skill cannot replace clean habitat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Loons are diurnal, diving and calling by day, with rest on water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Loons can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs near the water’s edge, and chicks enter the lake soon after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be larger and yodel in territory defense.

common-murre.spotlight: Common Murre teaches Two-World Discipline through a seabird that stands packed on cliffs and flies underwater with the same wings. Dense ledges, pointed eggs, cold dives, and fish pursuit make discipline necessary in both worlds.
common-murre.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, north_pacific. Cold northern seas, rocky islands, cliff ledges, offshore feeding grounds, and productive currents.
signatureTraits: Wing-propelled diving lets the bird pursue fish below the sea surface.
Dense cliff colonies demand balance, spacing, and social tolerance.
Pear-shaped eggs help reduce rolling on bare ledges.
The same wings must serve air travel and underwater swimming.
interestingFacts: Common Murres often lay eggs directly on narrow cliff ledges rather than in built nests.
Their eggs vary in color and pattern, helping parents recognize them in dense colonies.
Chicks leave cliffs before they can fly well, reaching the sea with a parent.
They are alcids, birds that look penguin-like but can still fly.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mainly small schooling fish such as sand lance, capelin, herring and sprat, with some squid and crustaceans. Prey is chased underwater, and pursuit dives have been recorded well beyond 100 metres.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Gulls, ravens, eagles, foxes, rats, large fish, storms, oil spills, and food shortages can threaten murres, eggs, or chicks. Colony density protects and endangers at once, so discipline keeps chaos manageable.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Murres are active by day around colonies and feeding waters, with rhythms shaped by fish availability, weather, and breeding stage. Their schedule shifts between ledge duty and sea work.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Murres can live for decades if they survive early risks and changing ocean conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single large egg on a cliff ledge, and both parents incubate and feed the chick.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and size, so the sexes cannot be told apart in the field. Only the male escorts the fledgling at sea, feeding it there for several weeks.

common-potoo.spotlight: Common Potoo teaches Still Disguise by becoming a broken branch until night returns. Bark plumage, upright posture, slit-eyed watching, and nocturnal hunting make stillness a survival tool.
common-potoo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical and subtropical forests, woodland edges, plantations, and branch-rich clearings.
signatureTraits: Bark-like plumage matches dead branches and stumps.
Rigid upright posture completes the broken-branch illusion.
Tiny eyelid slits let it watch while appearing asleep.
Huge mouth opens at night to catch flying insects.
interestingFacts: Common potoos often perch on exposed branch tips where their disguise is strongest.
They do not build elaborate nests, often using a simple branch depression.
Their haunting calls are more noticeable than their daytime bodies.
Pairs usually lay a single egg, and the chick soon adopts its own frozen, branch-like pose.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Moths, beetles, flying insects, and night prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Monkeys, snakes, raptors, arboreal mammals, and habitat loss threaten adults, eggs, and young. The branch illusion reduces discovery before flight is needed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly nocturnal. The day is spent asleep in the open on a stump or broken branch, often the same perch day after day. Hunting starts at dusk with short flights after passing insects, and calling is most frequent on moonlit nights.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often several years in the wild, with exact lifespan poorly known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single egg on a branch or stump, so the chick's safety depends heavily on the parent's still disguise and the perch choice.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike and cannot be told apart in the field. Individuals vary from greyer to browner, but the variation is not linked to sex.

common-raven.spotlight: Common Raven teaches Foresight through a mind that stores value before hunger arrives. Its food caches, watchful intelligence, social awareness, and flexible problem-solving turn the future into something prepared for, hidden, remembered, and recovered.
common-raven.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic. Mountains, forests, tundra, coasts, deserts, cliffs, farms, and towns fit the raven because its real habitat advantage is mental flexibility. It reads openings wherever resources appear.
signatureTraits: Food caching: ravens hide surplus meals for later use.
Memory and observation: they track both their own stores and the attention of others.
Flexible intelligence: they solve problems across wild, mountain, coastal, and human-edge habitats.
interestingFacts: Common Ravens are among the most intelligent birds.
They can cache food and remember stored locations.
They use varied calls, play behavior, and social learning.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carrion, insects, eggs, small animals, grains, fruit, and human scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, owls, larger carnivores, nest predators, and rival ravens create pressure around food and nesting. Caching only works when memory and secrecy stay ahead of thieves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Ravens are active by day, often traveling, calling, caching, and investigating.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild ravens commonly live 10 to 15 years, and ringed birds have passed 20; captive birds have reached 40 or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs often nest on cliffs, trees, or structures and care for young together. Reproduction is supported by stored knowledge of safe nest sites and seasonal food.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may average larger. The key difference is not color but partnership, territory, and shared intelligence around nesting and food.

common-snapping-turtle.spotlight: Common Snapping Turtle teaches Snap Timing through a bottom-dwelling body that waits until readiness matters. Mud stillness, algae-dark shell, long neck, and powerful jaws show that victory does not always begin with movement.
common-snapping-turtle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, marshes, lakes, slow rivers, muddy bottoms, and vegetated wetlands.
signatureTraits: Powerful jaws and long neck used for sudden defensive or feeding snaps.
Bottom-dwelling aquatic life in ponds, lakes, marshes, and slow rivers.
Rugged shell and tail that give a prehistoric, armored profile.
Patient ambush and scavenging behavior in muddy water.
interestingFacts: Common Snapping Turtles are much more defensive on land than in water, where they can retreat.
Females often travel over land to lay eggs in suitable soil.
Their long neck lets the snap reach farther than the shell suggests.
Females can store sperm and lay fertile eggs for more than one season after a single mating.
Nest temperature sets hatchling sex: cool and very warm nests produce females, intermediate temperatures mostly males.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, frogs, insects, carrion, aquatic plants, birds, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and hatchlings face raccoons, skunks, foxes, herons, fish, and crows, while adults mostly face humans, roads, and habitat loss. The famous snap is strongest after the vulnerable early stages.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Common Snapping Turtles are active by day or night depending on conditions, often resting hidden underwater. Their rhythm is wait in mud, sense movement, snap when needed, and conserve energy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Snapping Turtles can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in dug nests on land, often far from water, and provide no parental care after laying.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often grow larger with longer tails, while females invest heavily in egg laying and nesting journeys. Both sexes carry the same patient aquatic design.

common-warthog.spotlight: Common Warthog teaches Pragmatism through a rough body that finds the angle that works. Kneeling on calloused wrists, grazing short grass, tusks, burrow backing, and raised-tail running show clever usefulness without elegance.
common-warthog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, grasslands, open woodland, scrub, burrows, and water edges fit Warthogs because they need short grass, cover, and abandoned burrows for shelter.
signatureTraits: Kneeling wrists: calloused front legs let the animal graze short grass efficiently.
Burrow backing: warthogs often reverse into holes so tusks face danger.
Raised-tail run: the tail acts like a signal flag during escape.
interestingFacts: Warthogs often shelter overnight in abandoned aardvark burrows rather than digging their own from scratch.
They commonly kneel while feeding on short grass.
Their tusks are used in defense and male contests.
The wart-like bumps on the face are pads of thickened skin thought to cushion blows during fights.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Short grasses, roots, bulbs, tubers, bark, fruit, and occasional carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, leopards, hyenas, wild dogs, crocodiles, and humans pressure Warthogs. Tusks, burrows, speed, and practical escape protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Warthogs are diurnal, grazing and digging by day before retreating to burrows at night. Their rhythm favors practical work in visible hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Common Warthogs often live around a decade in the wild, with predation and drought shaping survival. A practical animal survives by remembering burrows, water, and usable feeding patches.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in burrows, where piglets are protected before following the mother into open feeding grounds. Offspring make the burrow strategy essential, not optional.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger with more prominent warts and tusks, while females invest heavily in nursing and protecting piglets. Pragmatism appears in both feeding posture and family shelter.

coquerels-sifaka.spotlight: Groups of about three to ten of these large lemurs live in the dry deciduous forests of north-western Madagascar. The animal clings upright to a vertical trunk, pushes off with its long hind legs and turns in the air to land feet first on the next trunk, several metres away.
coquerels-sifaka.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Madagascar dry forest and canopy gaps fit because sideways grace needs vertical trunks and awkward ground crossings.
signatureTraits: White coat with maroon patches on chest, arms and thighs
Face is black and bare, with white fur along the nose
Eyes are yellow
Tail is about as long as the body
interestingFacts: The word sifaka imitates the shi-fak alarm call the animals give.
In studied populations births are reported mostly in June and July, in the dry season, after a pregnancy of about five and a half months.
Ankarafantsika National Park holds one of the main protected populations.
Its forests are being cleared and burned, and it is now rated Critically Endangered.
It was long treated as a subspecies of Verreaux's sifaka before being recognised as a species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, flowers, fruit, and bark.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fossas, raptors on young, humans, and habitat loss threaten sifakas, making vertical leaps and group awareness important defenses.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Coquerel’s Sifakas are diurnal, resting in trees and moving by day when their sideways ground dance and vertical leaps are visible.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to reach 18 to 20 years in the wild. Captive animals have lived to about 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear a single infant that clings to the belly and back, learning leap timing through the mother’s movement.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, though females are often socially assertive.

corn-snake.spotlight: Corn Snake teaches Tracking through a tongue that reads invisible trails. Its slender body, patterned camouflage, climbing ability, and Jacobson’s-organ scent work show that the hidden path opens to the one who samples the world carefully.
corn-snake.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Fields, pine woods, barns, forest edges, abandoned buildings, and brush fit Corn Snakes because rodents leave chemical stories there. The habitat is full of signs that eyes alone might miss.
signatureTraits: Tongue Sampling: chemical particles are gathered and read through the Jacobson’s organ.
Rodent Tracking: scent trails guide the snake through barns, fields, brush, and edges.
Quiet Constriction: once found, prey is held by controlled pressure rather than noise.
interestingFacts: Corn Snakes are nonvenomous constrictors native to the southeastern United States.
They are strong climbers and often hunt rodents.
Their belly pattern is one possible source of the common name.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mice, rats, small birds, eggs, and lizards.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, foxes, raccoons, larger snakes, and humans threaten Corn Snakes. Camouflage, climbing, freezing, and quiet escape help protect the tracker while it follows prey.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Corn Snakes are often crepuscular or nocturnal, especially in warm weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 6 to 8 years is typical in the wild. Captive corn snakes commonly reach 15 to 20 years, and a few have passed 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches of eggs in warm, sheltered, humid places such as rotting logs or hidden cavities. The young hatch already carrying the tracking body plan: tongue, scent organ, and stealth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though females may be heavier and males may have longer tails.

corsac-fox.spotlight: The Corsac Fox is steppe fit in pale fur. It survives open wind by matching the land, using burrows and flexible food choices to make exposure feel less hostile.
corsac-fox.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia. Corsac Foxes live in open steppes, semi-deserts, grasslands, and dry plains.
signatureTraits: Pale open-country coat
Steppe and semi-desert life
Burrow use for shelter
Flexible small-prey foraging
interestingFacts: Corsac Foxes live across Central Asian steppes and semi-deserts.
They use burrows but often take over or modify existing dens.
Their pale coat helps them blend with dry open ground.
