They feed on rodents, insects, birds, carrion, and plant matter when needed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat rodents, pikas, birds, insects, reptiles, carrion, and occasional plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, eagles, larger carnivores, humans, and harsh winters can threaten them. Their defense is burrows, speed, pale camouflage, and flexible movement, showing that environmental fit is a survival tool.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often nocturnal or crepuscular, resting in dens during severe weather or daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Corsac Foxes may live several years in the wild and longer in care. Their lifespan depends on prey cycles and weather, making fit a season-by-season practice.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in dens to litters of several pups, often with family support around shelter. Offspring begin life in the burrow, the fox's answer to open exposure.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, with males sometimes larger. The main guide feature is the shared pale steppe-adapted body.

coscoroba-swan.spotlight: Coscoroba Swan teaches Simple Elegance through a white waterbird whose clean form and strong call make quiet wetlands ceremonial. White body, red bill, pair presence, and lake movement show that simplicity can still carry a room.
coscoroba-swan.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Lakes, marshes, lagoons, slow rivers, flooded grasslands, and southern South American wetlands fit Coscoroba Swans because open water lets clean form and voice carry clearly.
signatureTraits: Clean white plumage with a contrasting reddish bill and feet.
Strong vocal presence compared with many swan-like waterbirds.
Graceful swimming links visual calm with audible territory.
Often seen in pairs or family groups on open wetlands.
interestingFacts: Coscoroba Swans are often considered swan-like but taxonomically unusual among waterfowl.
Their white body makes them highly visible across open water.
They occur in southern South American wetlands and may move with seasonal water.
Both parents are involved in protecting and raising young.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic plants, grasses, seeds, roots, and small aquatic invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, dogs, gulls, raptors, snakes, humans, and wetland disturbance can threaten eggs or young. Open water gives visibility, but nesting still needs guarded edges.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Coscoroba Swans are mostly diurnal, feeding, calling, and moving across wetlands by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly documented in the wild. Birds kept in waterfowl collections have lived for about 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in a nest built near water, and both parents help defend and guide the cygnets. Offspring survival depends on calm water, cover, and watchful adult presence.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be slightly larger.

cotton-top-tamarin.spotlight: Cotton-top Tamarin teaches Shared Carrying through a tiny primate family that keeps energy alive by sharing babies. Its white crest, group calls, cooperative infant carrying, and fast branch movement show that liveliness lasts longer when care is distributed.
cotton-top-tamarin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Tropical dry forest, humid forest edges, secondary growth, and Colombian canopy routes fit Cotton-top Tamarins because group foraging and infant carrying need connected branches.
signatureTraits: Explosive white crest around a small expressive face
Family groups with cooperative infant care
Quick branch movement through tropical forest
Calls and social contact that keep the group coordinated
interestingFacts: Cotton-top Tamarins usually give birth to twins, making shared carrying especially important.
Fathers and other group members often carry infants between nursing.
They are found naturally only in a limited region of northwestern Colombia.
Their crest makes them one of the most visually recognizable tamarins.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, insects, nectar, tree sap, small animals, and gums.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, cats, and humans can threaten tamarins. Group alarm calls, fast movement, and many watchful eyes help protect infants.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Cotton-top Tamarins are diurnal, traveling, feeding, and calling by day, then sleeping in sheltered trees at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive cotton-top tamarins often live into their mid-teens, and some have been recorded past 20 years. Wild animals live shorter lives, though good field figures are few.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females often give birth to twins, and the group helps carry them while the mother nurses. Offspring survival depends on teamwork rather than one exhausted parent.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though females carry pregnancy and nurse. The strongest difference is social role during infant care, where several helpers can matter as much as display.

cougar.spotlight: Cougar teaches Range Stealth through a solitary cat whose silence and flexibility open an enormous map. Wide habitat tolerance, quiet paws, ambush leap, and adaptable prey make broad life possible without noisy dominance.
cougar.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Mountains, forests, deserts, wetlands, scrub, grassland edges, and suburban wild margins.
signatureTraits: One of the widest habitat ranges of any large cat in the Americas.
Powerful hind legs support long leaps and sudden ambushes.
Solitary hunting style relies on cover, patience, and silence.
Plain coat helps the body blend across many landscapes.
interestingFacts: Cougars are also known as pumas, mountain lions, or panthers in different regions.
They can live from sea level forests to mountains and deserts.
They usually avoid humans and depend on stealth more than confrontation.
Their long tail helps balance during leaps and tight movement.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Deer are central prey in many regions, with rabbits, rodents, birds, livestock, and other mammals also taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Bears, wolves, jaguars in some regions, humans, roads, and territorial conflict can threaten cougars. Stealth, range, and avoidance are often safer than direct contest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Cougars are mostly crepuscular and nocturnal, moving and hunting when cover is stronger. Their rhythm gives silence more power.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild cougars often live around a decade or more if they avoid conflict, disease, and human pressure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After about three months of gestation, usually 2 or 3 spotted kittens, occasionally up to 6, are born in a den among rocks or dense cover. They stay with the mother for about 12 to 24 months, learning to hunt with her before dispersing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger and hold wider ranges, while females carry the main burden of raising kittens.

coyote.spotlight: Coyote teaches Elasticity through a canid that bends into almost every edge. Broad diet, alert ears, family packs, urban travel, and wild-land movement show survival that keeps changing shape without breaking.
coyote.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Deserts, prairies, forests, farms, suburbs, city edges, mountains, and scrub fit Coyotes because their real habitat is the boundary between opportunity and caution.
signatureTraits: Broad omnivory allows coyotes to switch food as conditions change.
Edge travel lets them use wild, rural, and urban spaces.
Family groups and pair bonds can support pup raising and territory use.
interestingFacts: Coyotes expanded into many regions after wolves declined in some areas.
They can be active by night near people and by day in quieter places.
Their yips and howls help maintain contact and territory.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, rabbits, fruit, insects, carrion, birds, reptiles, and human scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, cougars, bears, eagles, dogs, humans, and cars create pressure. Coyotes persist by shifting time, route, diet, and group behavior.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Coyotes are often crepuscular or nocturnal near people, but flexible in quieter places.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Few wild coyotes live beyond 6 to 8 years, although some reach 10 to 14; captive animals have lived about 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females den to give birth to pups, and both parents may help feed and protect them. Offspring make adaptability urgent because pups need stable care inside unstable edge landscapes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often slightly larger, but both sexes share the flexible canid body and broad diet.

crab-eating-fox.spotlight: Crabs are only part of what this grey-brown South American canid eats. It hunts them along muddy floodplain edges, but its menu shifts through the year as flooding, insect numbers and fruit crops change what is easiest to find.
crab-eating-fox.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Savannas, wetlands, forests, grasslands, mangroves, and human edges fit Crab-eating Foxes because they can use many worlds.
signatureTraits: Grizzled grey-brown coat, paler on the throat and belly.
Dark line runs along the spine onto the tail.
Ears and tail are tipped with black.
Reddish tinge on the face and legs.
Short, strong legs and a bushy tail.
interestingFacts: Pairs are monogamous and often forage together at night, and both parents bring food to the growing pups.
Litters usually hold three to six pups, born in a burrow taken over from another animal or hidden in dense vegetation.
Despite its name it is not a true fox of the genus Vulpes, but belongs to a separate South American lineage of canids.
By dropping the seeds of fruits it swallows, it helps disperse many plants across farmland and forest edges.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, fruit, insects, rodents, birds, reptiles, carrion, and eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas, dogs, large snakes, and humans can threaten them. Flexibility and nocturnal movement reduce exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, foraging when cover improves. Their rhythm bends around opportunity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured. In captivity animals have lived for about 11 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Three to six pups are born after a gestation of about eight weeks; females raise pups in dens with pair or family support. The young are weaned at roughly three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are alike in colour and close in size; nothing in their appearance separates them at a distance.

crested-oropendola.spotlight: Crested Oropendola teaches Weaving through a bird that braids shelter into the air. Long hanging nests, colony trees, woven fibers, and loud display show beauty becoming useful when patience makes it protective.
crested-oropendola.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Tropical forest edges, tall trees, plantations, river edges, and canopy colonies fit Crested Oropendolas because their nests need height, hanging space, and group protection.
signatureTraits: Hanging woven nests: shelter is suspended away from many ground threats.
Colony trees: many nests turn one canopy into a village.
Loud display: construction and courtship are matched with sound and motion.
interestingFacts: Crested Oropendolas build long pouch-like nests that hang from trees.
They often nest in colonies, with many woven nests hanging together from a single tall tree.
Their displays can include bowing movements and distinctive calls.
Their tail is largely bright yellow, which flashes conspicuously when they fly between trees.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, nectar, insects, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Toucans, monkeys, snakes, raptors, and nest parasites can threaten eggs or chicks. Hanging nests and colony placement make access harder.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Crested Oropendolas are diurnal, foraging and displaying in canopy groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Crested Oropendolas can live several years, with adult success tied to repeated use of colony trees, feeding routes, and woven nest sites. Weaving becomes stronger through practice and place memory.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females do most or all nest weaving and raise the young in hanging nests. Offspring make the craft practical: beauty must hold eggs, chicks, wind, and distance from predators.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are much larger and more display-focused, while females build and care for the nest. This species’ sex difference is central because courtship display and actual shelter-making are not the same job.

crested-pigeon.spotlight: Crested Pigeon teaches Alarm through wings that turn takeoff into a warning. Its tall crest, ground feeding, flock life, and whistling wing feathers show a body designed to move the group before danger lands.
crested-pigeon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Open woodland, grassland, parks, farms, roadsides, towns, and dry scrub fit Crested Pigeons because they feed on open ground where early warning matters.
signatureTraits: Special wing feathers create a loud whistle during takeoff.
A pointed crest makes the bird instantly recognizable on open ground.
Flock feeding keeps many heads close to exposure, so early alarm matters.
interestingFacts: The wing whistle can communicate alarm to nearby pigeons.
Crested Pigeons are common in many open and urban Australian habitats.
They feed mostly on seeds gathered from the ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grains, grasses, and small plant matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, falcons, cats, foxes, snakes, and nest predators create pressure that rewards fast group response. The whistle spreads danger before every bird has seen it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Crested Pigeons are diurnal, feeding and moving in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Crested Pigeons can live for several years when food, water, and nesting sites are stable. Alarm works through repetition because birds learn the difference between ordinary takeoff and urgent wing sound.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in simple stick nests, and both parents feed young with crop milk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike, both with the tall black crest, pinkish-red eye-ring and glossy green and purple wing bars. In courtship the male bows repeatedly with his tail raised and fanned and his wings partly spread.

crested-porcupine.spotlight: This large, heavily built rodent answers a threat in stages. First it raises its quills into a fan that makes it look far bigger, then it stamps its feet and shakes a cluster of hollow, open-ended tail quills that rattle loudly. Quills detach easily on contact but cannot be thrown.
crested-porcupine.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, europe. Rocky hills, scrub, forests, savannas, burrows, and farmland edges fit Crested Porcupines because they need shelter near roots and plant food.
signatureTraits: Quills banded in black and white cover the back and flanks.
Crest of long, coarse bristles runs from crown to shoulders.
Blunt, rounded muzzle with small eyes and ears.
Dark, bristly fur on the head, neck, legs and underside.
Heavy, shuffling walk on short legs.
interestingFacts: Quills are modified hairs made of keratin, and the longest can reach about 35 centimetres.
Gnawed bones often litter the ground around dens; porcupines chew them, probably for minerals and to wear down their ever-growing incisors.
Burrow systems may be used for many years, and it also shelters in caves and rock crevices.
In Europe it lives only in Italy, where it has spread northwards in recent decades; whether people brought it there in ancient times is still debated.
Shed quills lying on a path are often the first sign that a porcupine is living nearby.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Roots, bulbs, bark, fruit, crops, and tubers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, lions, hyenas, wolves, dogs, and humans can threaten it. Raised quills and backward defense make pursuit painful.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Crested Porcupines are nocturnal, feeding by night and sheltering by day. Their rhythm protects slow confidence.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 10 to 15 years is often quoted for wild animals, though field data are thin. In zoos, individuals have lived beyond 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about 16 weeks, one or two young are born with softer quills that harden after birth. They arrive with their eyes open in a grass-lined chamber of the burrow, and both parents stay close to them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: No reliable outward difference separates the sexes. Males and females are similar in size and carry the same quills and crest.

crested-serpent-eagle.spotlight: Crested Serpent Eagle teaches Serpent Focus through a forest raptor whose eye knows exactly what work it is hunting. Crested head, broad wings, perch watching, and reptile specialization turn mastery into narrowed search.
crested-serpent-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Forests, wooded hills, plantations, forest edges, and tropical canopy openings.
signatureTraits: Crested head and bright facial skin with strong visual presence
Perch-based watching for snakes and reptiles
Broad wings for forest-edge soaring and maneuvering
Talons and focus suited to dangerous prey
interestingFacts: Crested Serpent Eagles specialize heavily in reptiles, especially snakes.
They often hunt from perches rather than constant high-speed pursuit.
Their loud calls are a familiar sound in many Asian forests.
Hunting snakes requires careful timing because prey can also be dangerous.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Snakes, lizards, frogs, small mammals, birds, and reptiles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger raptors, human persecution, nest disturbance, and habitat loss threaten them. Hunting snakes also brings prey risk, making focus a disciplined form of courage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Crested Serpent Eagles are diurnal, watching from perches and soaring in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: lifespan schedules stay unpublished; snake-hunting raptors calling from South and Southeast Asian forest canopies are rarely recovered with rings.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree nests, where chicks depend on adults bringing difficult prey safely.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often slightly larger than males, as in many raptors. The difference may support nesting and defense, while both sexes share the same focused hunting design.

crocodile-monitor.spotlight: A slender black monitor speckled with yellow, living in the lowland rainforests of New Guinea. Adults commonly exceed two metres. It hunts in the canopy as readily as on the ground and seizes birds and mammals with teeth that are unusually long and straight for a monitor.
crocodile-monitor.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, australia_oceania. Crocodile Monitor usually lives in New Guinea rainforest trees, trunks, canopy, and forest edges.
signatureTraits: Very long tail that balances a large body in trees
Sharp claws and strong limbs for climbing rainforest trunks
Large monitor intelligence applied to vertical hunting routes
Powerful bite and alert head held high above the forest floor
interestingFacts: Crocodile Monitors are among the longest lizards in the world.
Their tail can make up much of their total length.
They are strongly associated with New Guinea forests.
Their size is surprising because much of their life is arboreal.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crocodile Monitor feeds on birds, eggs, small mammals, reptiles, insects, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few animals threaten a grown adult. Pythons and birds of prey probably take the young, though this is poorly recorded. People hunt it for meat and for skin used on drumheads, and logging removes its forest. Cornered, it lashes with the tail and bites.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, basking and climbing before sheltering in trees or cavities, turning heat into upward force.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live over 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in secure sites such as termite mounds or cavities, placing young where structure protects what the body cannot yet defend.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and more robust, but both sexes share claws, tail, and the ability to make the canopy a route.

crowned-eagle.spotlight: Crowned Eagle is Forest Grip: a predator whose power is concentrated in talons strong enough to finish the chase inside dense canopy.
crowned-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Crowned Eagles live in African forests, woodland, and dense riverine habitats.
signatureTraits: Massive talons for forest prey
Crested head and powerful raptor build
Canopy hunting of monkeys and small antelope
Ambush and short powerful flight through forest
interestingFacts: Crowned Eagles are among Africa's most powerful forest eagles.
They can take monkeys and small antelope as prey.
Pairs may use large nests over multiple years.
Their hunting style depends on strength in enclosed forest rather than open soaring alone.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat monkeys, small antelope, hyraxes, birds, and other forest animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, while eggs and chicks may face nest threats; humans and habitat loss are major dangers. Their defense is height, nest placement, territoriality, and formidable grip.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Hunting happens by day, mostly after long spells sitting still on a hidden perch below the canopy, watching and listening for prey. At night it roosts in tall trees within its territory, often close to the nest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for decades. The lifespan why is that a powerful grip becomes a long strategy when paired with territory, mate bonds, and repeated nest success.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches, usually raising one chick with long parental care. Offspring develop slowly because forest power takes time to grow into usable grip.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger than males, as in many raptors.

cuban-crocodile.spotlight: Few crocodilians have a range as small as this one: Zapata Swamp in south-western Cuba, plus a reintroduced population in Lanier Swamp on the Isla de la Juventud. It spends more time on land than most of its relatives and walks with the belly held well clear of the ground, on strong legs whose feet have little webbing.
cuban-crocodile.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Cuban swamps, marshes, lagoons, and firm wetland edges.
signatureTraits: Black and yellow speckling over the back and flanks
Raised bony ridge behind each eye
Short, broad snout for a crocodile
Large, strongly keeled scales on the hind legs
Adults mostly 2 to 2.5 metres, smaller than American crocodiles
interestingFacts: It interbreeds with the American crocodile where the two meet in Zapata Swamp, and hybridisation is a threat to the pure species.
The blunt teeth at the back of the jaw are suited to crushing the shells of turtles.
Fossils show that it once lived on the Cayman Islands and in the Bahamas as well as Cuba.
Captive groups have been seen hunting together, but coordinated hunting has not been confirmed in the wild.
Only a few thousand are thought to remain in the wild, and the IUCN lists the species as Critically Endangered.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, turtles, birds, mammals, and wetland prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but eggs and young face birds, mammals, and other reptiles; humans and habitat limits are major threats. Surprise works only if nesting space survives.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They bask and rest by day but may hunt at night or in active bursts.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Crocodilians can live for decades, making explosive action a rare moment inside a long patient life.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build nests and guard eggs and hatchlings.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males grow larger than females, while both sexes share the agile crocodile body plan.

cuban-rock-iguana.spotlight: Big males grow well over a metre from snout to tail tip and weigh several kilograms, making this one of the largest lizards in the Caribbean. Adults are grey to olive, while young animals are marked with darker crossbands that fade with age.
cuban-rock-iguana.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Cuban Rock Iguana usually lives in rocky Cuban coasts, limestone areas, scrub, and dry forest edges.
signatureTraits: Heavy island-lizard body built for rock, heat, and territory
Strong limbs and claws for climbing limestone and scrub
Sun-basking rhythm that turns stillness into usable energy
Plant-heavy diet that ties authority to the local island vegetation
interestingFacts: Cuban Rock Iguanas are part of the Cyclura group of rock iguanas.
They use burrows and crevices as shelter from heat and danger.
Their plant feeding can help move seeds through dry island habitats.
Territorial displays make a sunny rock into a claimed stage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Cuban Rock Iguana feeds on leaves, flowers, fruits, cactus pads, and occasional animal matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Feral pigs dig up nests, while cats and dogs kill young and sometimes adults. Native snakes and birds of prey take mainly hatchlings. A threatened iguana sprints for cover, and a cornered adult bites and lashes with its tail.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, warming on rocks before feeding and sheltering in crevices or burrows when heat or danger rises.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at 20 to 40 years, and possibly more; long-term records from the wild are lacking.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nest chambers in soil or sand and leave eggs to develop with sun heat, making the ground itself part of parental strategy.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males tend to be larger with bigger jowls and stronger territorial displays, while females carry the authority of nest placement and egg investment.

de-brazzas-monkey.spotlight: De Brazza's Monkey teaches Quiet Distinction through a white beard, orange brow, river forest stillness, and secretive movement. It is distinct enough to be remembered, yet quiet enough to avoid unnecessary attention.
de-brazzas-monkey.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Riverine forest, swamp forest, dense tropical woodland, and wet forest edges.
signatureTraits: White beard and facial markings that create unmistakable identity.
Quiet concealed behavior near forested rivers and swamps.
Arboreal and ground movement shaped by cover and water edges.
Small-group life with watchful stillness.
interestingFacts: De Brazza’s monkeys are among the more secretive guenons.
They often freeze when threatened instead of fleeing loudly.
Their white beard and orange brow make them visually distinctive.
They live near rivers, swamps, and dense African forests.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, seeds, leaves, flowers, insects, and fungi.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, eagles, snakes, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Freezing, hiding, and staying near dense cover turn quietness into protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: De Brazza's Monkeys are diurnal, feeding and resting by day in trees and cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 20 to 22 years in the wild is the usual estimate. Zoo animals have lived to about 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to single infants that cling and learn hidden forest routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and more visually pronounced, while females are smaller.

deaths-head-hawkmoth.spotlight: Death's-head Hawkmoth teaches Unmistakable Mark through a night moth owning the strange sign on its body. Skull-like thorax mark, strong flight, squeak, hive entry, and honey theft make identity powerful because it cannot be mistaken for ordinary.
deaths-head-hawkmoth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, europe, north_africa_middle_east. Gardens, fields, farmland, woodland edges, warm open areas, and beehive-rich landscapes fit Death's-head Hawkmoths because host plants, night flight, and risky sweetness meet there.
signatureTraits: Skull-like marking on the thorax creates an unmistakable visual identity.
Strong body and wings allow powerful night flight and migration.
Can produce squeaking sounds when disturbed.
Known for entering honeybee hives and feeding on honey.
interestingFacts: The moth's skull-like pattern has made it famous in folklore and popular culture.
It can raid beehives using scent and sound-related adaptations that reduce bee attacks.
Adults are strong fliers capable of long-distance movement.
Caterpillars feed on plants such as potato-family hosts and other suitable plants.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults feed on honey, nectar, and sweet liquids, while caterpillars feed on host plant leaves.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, bats, spiders, parasitoids, honeybees, humans, and pesticides threaten them. Squeaking, strong flight, and hive adaptations help but do not remove the risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are nocturnal, flying and feeding at night. The skull-marked presence belongs to darkness, where identity, risk, and sweetness overlap.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults usually live only weeks, while the full life cycle includes egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult stages. The brief adult span makes the unmistakable mark feel urgent.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on suitable host plants so larvae can feed heavily before pupation. Offspring success depends less on adult care and more on placing the next appetite correctly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar in the famous skull-marked body, though size and reproductive anatomy differ.

degu.spotlight: Degu teaches Daylight Trust through a dryland rodent whose safety has tunnels and voices. Diurnal activity, colony burrows, vocal calls, shared care, and social digging show trust built from repeated small signals.
degu.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Dry Chilean scrub, rocky slopes, grasslands, burrow networks, and open feeding areas fit Degus because they need daylight for foraging and tunnels for safety.
signatureTraits: Day-active rodent: unlike many small mammals, it works in sunlight.
Burrow colonies: tunnels make dry open ground safer.
Vocal communication: calls coordinate warning and contact.
interestingFacts: Degus are native to Chile and are not found in the wild anywhere else.
They are highly social and communicate with many vocal sounds.
They are diurnal, which makes them unusual among many pet rodents.
Like some lizards, degus can shed the skin of their tail to escape when a predator grabs it.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, leaves, seeds, bark, herbs, and dry vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, owls, hawks, snakes, cats, and dogs pressure Degus. Alarm calls, burrows, and group awareness turn trust into protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Degus are diurnal, active by day unlike many rodents.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Degus can live several years in the wild and longer under careful care. Their lifespan supports repeated social bonds, learned burrow systems, and daylight routines.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to relatively developed young, and social groups may provide warmth or support around pups. Offspring make trust practical because young animals need both tunnels and group tolerance.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, with no dramatic visual split. The key differences appear in social role, reproduction, and how individuals contribute to colony stability.

demoiselle-crane.spotlight: Demoiselle Crane teaches Light Strength through a migrant whose elegance survives distance. Slim body, long flights, precise steps, and courtship dances show that lightness can carry real endurance.
demoiselle-crane.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Open steppe, grassland, semi-desert, wetlands, agricultural fields, and migration corridors.
signatureTraits: Slender crane body with elegant neck and plumes
Long migration across open landscapes and high passes
Precise walking and courtship display movements
Flock travel that makes light bodies resilient
interestingFacts: Demoiselle Cranes are the smallest crane species, standing roughly 90 centimetres tall.
They make long migrations between breeding and wintering grounds.
Some populations cross very high mountain regions during migration.
Their courtship includes graceful dances with bowing, leaping, and calling, performed by pairs and groups.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grains, grasses, insects, small animals, and plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, foxes, dogs, humans, storms, power lines, and habitat loss threaten adults, eggs, or chicks. Migration makes grace useful but costly.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Demoiselle Cranes are diurnal, feeding, walking, and migrating by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive birds have lived for several decades; wild lifespan is less well known, and around 20 years is a commonly cited estimate.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on open ground nests, and both parents help guard chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be slightly larger.

desert-horned-viper.spotlight: Desert Horned Viper teaches Concealment through power buried under sand. Horns, sidewinding, sand-colored scales, and ambush patience make the desert itself part of the strike.
desert-horned-viper.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Sandy deserts, dunes, gravel plains, wadis, and arid scrub.
signatureTraits: Sand-colored body disappears against dunes and gravel.
Burying behavior leaves only eyes or head exposed for ambush.
Sidewinding reduces contact with hot sand and improves movement on loose ground.
Horn-like scales break the outline above the eyes.
interestingFacts: Desert horned vipers can move with a distinctive sidewinding track.
They often ambush rodents and lizards that cross their hidden position.
The horns may help protect or shade the eyes in sandy habitats, though their exact function is debated.
Their power depends on not being noticed too early.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, lizards, small birds, and desert animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, foxes, mongooses, larger snakes, humans, and vehicles threaten them. Concealment protects until human disturbance breaks the pattern.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, avoiding extreme heat by sheltering beneath sand or in cover during the day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 10 to 15 years in care and variable in the wild; survival depends on many nights of waiting without spending water or energy carelessly.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected sandy or sheltered sites, and hatchlings begin life already patterned for concealment.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, though females may be heavier.

desert-rain-frog.spotlight: Desert Rain Frog teaches Tiny Defiance through squeaking sand burrow. Moist sand, coastal desert life, burrowing, small size, and a sharp defensive squeak make refusal audible even from a tiny body.
desert-rain-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Desert Rain Frog usually lives in coastal dunes and sandy desert where fog keeps sand moist.
signatureTraits: Round tiny body that burrows into moist coastal sand
High defensive squeak that makes smallness audible
Dependence on fog-moistened dunes in an arid landscape
Short limbs suited to digging rather than leaping far
interestingFacts: Development is direct: the eggs hatch as tiny froglets, with no free-swimming tadpole stage.
The name macrops means large-eyed, after the big, bulging eyes on the rounded head.
In rain frogs of this genus the male's short arms cannot clasp the rounded female, so during mating he sticks to her back with a glue-like skin secretion.
It is found only in a narrow coastal strip of dunes along the border region of South Africa and Namibia.
Adults are only about 4 to 6 centimetres long.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Desert Rain Frog feeds on termites, beetles, ants, and small invertebrates found in sand.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on this frog is scarcely documented; snakes, birds and small carnivores of the dune belt are the presumed predators. A frog that is dug up or cornered puffs its body up. The better-known threat is loss of dune habitat to coastal diamond mining and development.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, burrowing in cool moist sand by day so a soft tiny body survives a severe landscape.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: There are no records of how long this frog lives, either in its dunes or in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in moist underground chambers after rain or fog-supported periods, beginning life hidden inside the desert’s brief softness.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, with the tiny defensive voice more important than visual difference.

devils-flower-mantis.spotlight: Hanging head-down in shrubs, it takes flying insects out of the air with its spined forelegs when they come within reach. Adults are pale green and white, with broad flaps on the legs and behind the head, and females reach about 13 centimetres, among the largest of the flower-like mantises.
devils-flower-mantis.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Devil's Flower Mantis usually lives in dry bush, shrubs, and flowering vegetation in eastern Africa.
signatureTraits: flower-like body
threat display
ambush arms
cryptic colors
interestingFacts: It is the only species in the genus Idolomantis, within the mantis family Empusidae.
Newly hatched nymphs are shiny black and look more like ants than mantises.
Older nymphs are brown and resemble withered leaves; the green and white colours appear only with the final moult.
Like many mantises it rocks gently from side to side, as foliage does in a light wind.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Devil's Flower Mantis feeds on flies, moths, bees, and other insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders and larger insects all hunt it. Hanging still among foliage is its first defence. When that fails it rears up and spreads its forelegs, showing red, white, blue and black patches on their inner faces and on the underside of the thorax.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Devil's Flower Mantis is mostly still by day, hunting when prey comes near.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity a Devil's Flower Mantis usually lives months rather than years. Nymphs take several months to mature and adults survive a few months more, females outlasting males, so hatching to death usually takes under about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Some weeks after mating, females lay eggs in foamy ootheca cases. The froth hardens on a twig, and a case commonly releases 10 to 50 nymphs after roughly six weeks. Several cases may be laid, and none is guarded.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult females are larger and heavier than males. Males are slimmer, with longer, feathery antennae, and fly readily. From below, a male shows eight abdominal segments and a female six.

dhole.spotlight: Dhole turns sound into pack movement. Whistles, calls, speed, and shared pursuit make dense forest and grassland easier to cross as a coordinated team.
dhole.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, central_asia. Dholes live in forests, grasslands, scrub, and mountain foothills across parts of Asia.
signatureTraits: Whistling calls used in pack communication
Cooperative hunting and pursuit
Red coat and agile canid body
Strong social bonds around pups and food sharing
interestingFacts: Dholes are known for whistle-like calls that help coordinate group movement.
They hunt cooperatively and can pursue prey over distance.
Pack members often feed pups and nursing females at dens.
They live across parts of Asia but are threatened in many regions.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: In India, chital and sambar make up most kills, with muntjac, wild pig, hares and rodents; in mountains wild goats such as ibex and serow are taken. A pack runs prey down, often driving deer into water, and starts feeding as soon as the animal is pulled down.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include tigers, leopards, disease from domestic dogs, humans, and habitat fragmentation. Their defense is pack awareness, speed, vocal contact, and group response.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Often active by day or twilight, resting between hunts and den duties. The rhythm shows coordination as energy management: the pack must know when to move and when to recover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 8 to 10 years in the wild. The lifespan why is that survival depends on keeping communication clear across seasons of hunting, breeding, and conflict.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females den and raise pups with help from the pack, including food brought by adults. Offspring learn the whistle-world early: survival means answering the group signal.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look broadly similar, with roles shaped more by pack structure than ornament. The principle lives in shared calls, not visual display.

diamondback-terrapin.spotlight: No other North American turtle spends its whole life in the brackish water of coastal marshes. Glands near the eyes shed excess salt, and after rain it drinks the thin layer of fresh water lying on the surface. Its range follows the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Cape Cod to Texas.
diamondback-terrapin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Diamondback Terrapins usually live in salt marshes, tidal creeks, and brackish estuaries.
signatureTraits: Patterned shell and brackish-water tolerance
Adapted to salt marshes
Raised concentric rings on each plate of the shell
Pale grey skin flecked with dark spots
Large, strongly webbed hind feet
interestingFacts: Diamondback Terrapins are closely tied to salt marshes, tidal creeks, and brackish estuaries.
Their food is mainly snails, clams, crabs, worms, and marsh prey.
In the late 1800s and early 1900s it was caught in great numbers for terrapin soup, and many populations collapsed.
Hatchlings from late nests may stay underground through the winter and come out the following spring.
A small rigid frame fitted to the entrance of a crab pot keeps most terrapins out while still letting crabs in.
It is the state reptile of Maryland and the mascot of the University of Maryland.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on snails, clams, crabs, worms, and marsh prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons dig up a large share of nests, and foxes, crows and gulls take eggs and hatchlings. Adults drown in crab pots, and nesting females are killed on coastal roads. An alarmed terrapin dives and buries itself in mud.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Activity follows both the sun and the tide: it feeds by day as rising water floods the marsh and basks on mud banks at low water. In the colder parts of its range it lies dormant in creek-bottom mud through winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at 25 to 40 years in the wild, though few animals of known age have been followed that long.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females come ashore in early summer to dig nests in sand above the high-tide line, laying about 4 to 20 eggs and often two or three clutches a season. Eggs hatch in roughly two to three months, and nest temperature decides the sex of the hatchlings.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are much larger than males.

dibatag.spotlight: Dibatag teaches High Browsing through a desert antelope stretched toward scarce leaves. Long neck, long legs, narrow face, and dry-country alertness make its body a solution to food that sits above the ordinary reach of the ground.
dibatag.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry shrubland, semi-desert, thornbush, and arid plains.
signatureTraits: Long neck and legs for reaching elevated desert browse
Light antelope build suited to arid shrubland
Secretive movement through sparse cover
Scarcity-shaped feeding rather than open grass dependence
interestingFacts: Dibatags are sometimes called Clarke’s gazelles, though they are not typical open-plains grazers.
They live in dry parts of the Horn of Africa.
Their long neck helps them browse shrubs in arid landscapes.
They are rare and strongly tied to specific dry habitats.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, buds, and dry shrub browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include cheetahs, leopards, hyenas, wild dogs, jackals, and humans. Alertness and light-footed escape protect the browser, showing that reach must be paired with readiness in open dry country.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Dibatags are active mainly in cooler hours and rest when heat makes movement costly.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Dibatags likely live several years in the wild when predation and drought are avoided.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear one calf hidden in cover while it is small.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry slender horns while females usually do not.

discus-fish.spotlight: Discus Fish teaches Hovering Calm through a round river body that holds shape in soft water. Controlled fins, social groups, parental mucus feeding, and quiet Amazonian habitats make composure both beautiful and useful.
discus-fish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Warm Amazon floodplain waters, slow channels, submerged roots, fallen branches, and calm forest pools.
signatureTraits: Tall round laterally compressed body built for controlled hovering.
Social behavior in warm slow freshwater habitats.
Subtle fin movements that hold position without frantic motion.
Unusual parental care where fry feed on mucus from parents' skin.
interestingFacts: Discus fish are famous for their round shape and calm hovering posture.
Parents produce skin mucus that young fry feed on after hatching.
They live in warm slow waters of the Amazon basin.
Their body shape helps them maneuver among roots, branches, and quiet cover.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small invertebrates, insect larvae, detritus, plant matter, and tiny aquatic foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, birds, snakes, habitat change, poor water quality, and egg predators threaten discus. Social grouping, cover, and parental care help calm become protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Discus Fish are diurnal, feeding and socializing through daylight while sheltering among cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Aquarium discus commonly reach about ten years and sometimes fifteen; wild Amazon floodplain ages remain little measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on cleaned surfaces, and both parents guard the young; fry feed from parental skin mucus.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are hard to tell apart visually in many cases.

dobsonfly.spotlight: Dobsonfly teaches Hidden Power through an adult body that began as a fierce river larva. Hellgrammite jaws, aquatic predation, long larval life, dramatic wings, and male mandibles show power built beneath before it is seen above.
dobsonfly.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Clean streams, rivers, rocky bottoms, riffles, banks, and waterside vegetation fit Dobsonflies because larvae need oxygen-rich water and adults emerge near it.
signatureTraits: Hellgrammite larva: the hidden juvenile is a fierce aquatic predator.
Large veined wings: the adult form looks dramatic but is brief.
Male mandibles: huge jaws are mostly for display and mating, not powerful biting.
interestingFacts: Dobsonfly larvae are called hellgrammites and are popular with anglers as fishing bait.
Larvae can live in clean streams for years before becoming adults.
Male adults have huge mandibles that look more dangerous than they are.
Because hellgrammites need well-oxygenated water, their presence is used as a sign of good stream quality.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic larvae eat insects, small fish, and other stream animals, while adults often feed little or not at all.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, birds, bats, spiders, frogs, and aquatic predators threaten dobsonflies. Larval strength and underwater cover protect the long hidden phase.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are often nocturnal and attracted to lights, while larvae live underwater for years. Their rhythm is long hidden power followed by short emergence.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The larval stage usually lasts about 2 to 3 years, followed by one to two weeks as a pupa in a chamber under a stone or log on the bank. Adults live only about a week.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in masses near water so hatchlings can reach streams. Offspring begin as underwater predators, not as the dramatic winged adults people usually notice.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have extremely long mandibles, while females have shorter, stronger-looking jaws that can bite more effectively. The sex difference is one of the species’ clearest traits.

domestic-chicken.spotlight: With more than 20 billion alive, the chicken is the most numerous bird on Earth, a domestic form of the red junglefowl of South and Southeast Asia. A junglefowl hen lays perhaps a dozen eggs a year, whereas hens of modern laying breeds produce around 300. Stout legs and blunt claws suit a bird that finds nearly all its food on the ground.
domestic-chicken.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: domestic_global. Kept worldwide in farmyards, gardens, orchards and poultry houses, from sea level to high mountain villages. Free-ranging birds use bare or grassy ground for foraging, dry dust for bathing and raised perches or trees for roosting. The wild ancestor lives in forest edge and bamboo scrub in tropical Asia.
signatureTraits: Fleshy red comb on the crown
Paired wattles hanging below the beak
Short, rounded wings and brief, low flight
Scaly legs with three toes forward and one behind
Head bobs forward with each step
interestingFacts: Like all birds, chickens descend from theropod dinosaurs, the group that included Tyrannosaurus.
Researchers have described more than 20 distinct chicken calls, including separate alarms for danger from the air and danger on the ground.
A rooster that finds food often calls hens over while picking the item up and dropping it, a display known as tidbitting.
In experiments, chicks only a few days old kept track of small numbers of objects hidden behind screens.
The term pecking order comes from a Norwegian study of hens published in the 1920s.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous. Chickens eat grain, seeds, grass and other greens, insects, worms, snails and sometimes small lizards or mice. Having no teeth, they swallow grit, which lodges in the muscular gizzard and grinds the food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, dogs, raccoons, snakes, raptors, and humans threaten it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active from first light to dusk. As the light fades the flock goes to roost on perches or branches off the ground and sleeps through the night, and roosters begin crowing shortly before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically 5 to 10 years for a well-kept backyard bird, with occasional individuals reaching their teens. Commercial birds are slaughtered far younger.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A broody hen gathers a clutch of about 8 to 12 eggs, laid roughly one a day, then sits on them for 21 days. Chicks hatch covered in down and feed themselves within a day, staying close to the hen for several weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Roosters have larger combs, wattles, spurs, and stronger display. They also grow long, pointed neck and saddle feathers and arched tail plumes, and they crow. Hens are smaller, with rounded feathers and a shorter tail.

double-crested-cormorant.spotlight: Double-crested Cormorant teaches Reset through a diver that must return to air after deep work. Strong feet, hooked bill, underwater pursuit, dark body, and spread-wing drying show recovery as part of the hunt, not a failure after it.
double-crested-cormorant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Lakes, rivers, coasts, estuaries, islands, reservoirs, and fishing waters fit Double-crested Cormorants because they need fish-rich depths and perches for drying.
signatureTraits: Underwater pursuit: strong feet drive repeated fish-chasing dives.
Spread-wing reset: drying posture marks the return from deep work.
Hooked bill: the tool fits slippery aquatic prey.
interestingFacts: Double-crested Cormorants often perch with wings spread after diving.
They nest in colonies near productive water, and large colonies can hold hundreds or even thousands of pairs.
Their dark body and low swimming posture can make them look almost reptilian on the surface.
The paired head crests that give the species its name appear only briefly on breeding adults and are often hard to see.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish are the main food, with some amphibians, crustaceans, and aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, gulls, raccoons, foxes, owls, and humans can threaten adults, eggs, or colonies. Group nesting and water access help reduce danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Double-crested Cormorants are diurnal, diving repeatedly and then perching to dry or rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild birds live about 6 years on average. The oldest banded bird on record was at least 22.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick nests, usually in colonies on trees, islands, cliffs, or human structures near water. Chicks depend on adults returning from repeated fishing trips.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be slightly larger.

dragonfly.spotlight: Four wings, each driven by its own flight muscles, can be angled and beaten independently, letting a dragonfly hover, turn sharply and fly backwards. The muscles pull directly on the wing bases, whereas most other insects flap by flexing the thorax. Dragonflies are stout-bodied predatory insects, with about 3,000 known species.
dragonfly.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, central_asia, east_asia, europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Ponds, lakes, marshes, bogs, ditches, streams and rivers, since the larvae live underwater. Adults hunt over water and along sunny hedges, woodland rides and meadows, sometimes several kilometres from where they emerged. Different species need still, flowing, acidic or temporary water.
signatureTraits: Huge eyes covering most of the head
Wings held flat and open when perched
Hindwings broader at the base than the forewings
Long, slender abdomen
Very short, bristle-like antennae
interestingFacts: In the larger species each compound eye can hold up to about 30,000 facets, giving vision in almost every direction.
The largest griffinflies, extinct relatives such as Meganeura from about 300 million years ago, had wingspans near 70 centimetres.
The globe skimmer crosses the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa, the round trip spread over several generations.
Larvae breathe through gills inside the rectum and can squirt water out of it to jet forward.
Pairs mate in a wheel shape, the male gripping the female behind the head while she curls her abdomen forward to collect sperm.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults eat flying insects, mainly midges, mosquitoes, flies and mayflies, with larger species taking butterflies and smaller dragonflies. Larvae ambush tadpoles, small fish and aquatic insects by shooting out a hinged lower lip tipped with hooks.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Small falcons, bee-eaters, swallows, frogs, spiders and larger dragonflies catch adults, while fish, newts and water beetles eat larvae. Adults are most exposed while soft and pale just after emerging, which many species do at night or dawn.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most fly by day and need warmth, so they are busiest in sunshine. At night and in cold or wet weather they hang motionless from stems, twigs or leaves. A few, including some hawkers, hunt at dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Larvae live underwater for a few months to about five years, depending on species and climate. Winged adults usually survive only a few weeks, though some last several months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay hundreds to thousands of eggs, either dipped or dropped onto the water or inserted into plant stems, mud or wet wood. Larvae moult roughly ten to fifteen times as they grow, then climb out of the water for the adult to emerge.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In many species males are brightly coloured, often blue or red, while females are yellow, brown or green. Mature males of some develop a powdery blue bloom. Males carry secondary genitalia under the second abdominal segment.

drill.spotlight: Drill carries Troop Force through a powerful body and social ground movement. In dense rainforest, strength goes farther when it is organized through the group.
drill.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Drills live in lowland rainforest, forest floor, swamp forest, and dense cover.
signatureTraits: Powerful ground-moving monkey body
Dense rainforest and forest-floor troop life
Strong social groups with male display features
Foraging across fruit, seeds, and ground foods
interestingFacts: Drills are close relatives of mandrills but less brightly facially colored.
They live in social groups in parts of West and Central Africa.
They are among the more endangered African primates.
Adult males are much larger and more visually striking than females.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fruits, seeds, leaves, roots, insects, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include leopards, crowned eagles on young, pythons, and humans. Their defense is group vigilance, size, alarm signals, and the difficulty of challenging an organized troop.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, foraging and traveling in groups, then sleeping in safer trees or cover. The rhythm shows force as daily coordination: move together, feed together, withdraw together.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live into the 20s or longer where protected. The lifespan why is that social strength must be maintained over years of hierarchy, care, and forest pressure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to single infants that develop within the troop's social world. Offspring inherit more than food; they inherit rank, warning systems, and group protection.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and more visually impressive, while females anchor infant care and group continuity.

dromedary-camel.spotlight: Dromedary Camel teaches Fortitude through a body built to cross heat without wasting what matters. Fat-storing hump, wide feet, long lashes, closing nostrils, and dehydration tolerance show endurance as conservation before toughness.
dromedary-camel.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east. Deserts, dry scrub, arid plains, caravan routes, and hot open country fit Dromedary Camels because their design turns scarcity and heat into a survivable road.
signatureTraits: One fat-storing hump supports long travel through scarce landscapes.
Wide feet spread weight over sand and loose ground.
Long lashes and closable nostrils protect against wind and dust.
interestingFacts: The dromedary's single hump stores fat, not water, and that fat can be drawn on for energy when food is scarce.
Dromedaries have been essential transport animals in many desert cultures.
They can tolerate dehydration and heat swings that would overwhelm many mammals.
After going without water, a thirsty dromedary can reportedly drink around 100 litres in roughly ten minutes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Thorny shrubs, dry grasses, saltbush, leaves, dates, and tough desert plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Historically, large predators such as lions, wolves, and humans were threats, especially to young camels. Herding, size, and endurance reduce vulnerability in open land.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeds by day, mostly in the cooler morning and late afternoon, and rests through the midday heat, lying down in the open or in whatever shade there is. At night it kneels down onto the hard pad on its chest and sleeps in short spells.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually about 20 to 30 years, and up to about 40; wild dromedaries no longer exist, so figures come from domestic and feral animals.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf after a long gestation, and the calf depends on milk, shade, and herd or human protection. Offspring make conservation practical because reproduction is slow and costly in dry country.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger and may develop stronger rut behaviors, including display and aggression.

dugong.spotlight: The only living member of its family, and the only plant-eating mammal that lives wholly in the sea. Its closest relative, Steller's sea cow, was hunted to extinction within three decades of its discovery in 1741. Adults reach about 3 metres and 250 to 400 kilograms, with dense, heavy bones that act as ballast on the bottom.
dugong.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, coral_triangle, australia_coastal. Dugongs live in warm shallow coastal seagrass meadows.
signatureTraits: Downturned grazing mouth
Paddle-shaped tail
Seagrass specialist
Gentle marine mammal body
interestingFacts: Dugongs are close relatives of manatees, and their group also included the extinct Steller's sea cow.
They can leave feeding trails in seagrass beds.
Calves nurse for more than a year and stay close to their mothers throughout.
Healthy seagrass meadows are vital for them, since seagrass makes up nearly all of their diet.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seagrass is almost the whole diet, above all soft, fast-growing kinds such as Halophila and Halodule. The animal digs out entire plants, roots included, with its bristly upper lip. Algae are eaten when seagrass is scarce.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tiger sharks, killer whales and saltwater crocodiles take some animals, chiefly calves; far more die in fishing nets, from boat strikes or by hunting. In Shark Bay, Western Australia, dugongs leave the richest shallow meadows for deeper water when tiger sharks are most numerous.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and night, with no fixed sleeping time. Where meadows are shallow, feeding follows the tide, because the plants can be reached only at high water. Resting animals hang near the surface or lie on the bottom, rising to breathe every few minutes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many decades, sometimes over 60 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Roughly every three to seven years, females give birth to one calf after a long pregnancy and nurse it for many months. Gestation lasts about 13 to 15 months and suckling up to 18, though calves start eating seagrass within weeks of birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males may develop tusks more visibly; females carry long calf care. The tusks are short upper incisors that break through the gum at puberty in males and only in some old females. In colour and build the sexes are alike.

dung-beetle.spotlight: Dung Beetle teaches Renewal by turning waste into movement, food, soil, and future. Rolling, burying, tunneling, and brooding around dung show that value is not always found in clean places; sometimes it is made by returning what others abandon.
dung-beetle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, central_asia, east_asia, europe, north_africa_middle_east, north_america, south_america, south_asia, southeast_asia, sub_saharan_africa. Grasslands, savannas, pastures, forests, and places with large mammals fit dung beetles because their resource appears where animals leave waste.
signatureTraits: Dung rolling: waste becomes a movable resource.
Burial work: nutrients are returned into soil instead of staying exposed.
Brood provisioning: dung can feed and protect the next generation.
interestingFacts: Dung beetles recycle nutrients and improve soil health.
Some species navigate using celestial cues, including the Milky Way.
They can reduce parasites and flies by removing dung quickly.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Dung is the center of the diet and reproduction strategy.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, reptiles, ants, mites, and parasitic flies can threaten dung beetles or their brood. Burial and speed reduce the time spent exposed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Many dung beetles are active at night or during cooler parts of the day, depending on species and climate. Their schedule follows dung freshness, heat, and competition.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many adults live weeks to months, though timing varies by species. The short life still leaves a large ecological effect through repeated burial work.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in dung balls or buried dung masses so larvae hatch into food. Reproduction is literally built from transformed waste.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males in some species have horns or fight over dung and mates, while females focus heavily on brood provisioning. Sex differences often reflect competition and nest work.

dusky-dolphin.spotlight: Dusky Dolphin teaches Acrobatic Joy through a cold-water dolphin turning play into mastery. Twisting leaps, fast groups, coordinated feeding, and social motion make joy skilled rather than careless.
dusky-dolphin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_pacific, south_atlantic. Cold temperate coastal waters, continental shelves, bays, and productive upwelling zones.
signatureTraits: Acrobatic leaps and twists above cold coastal water
Social groups with coordinated movement and feeding
Fast streamlined body for agile swimming
Playful behavior tied to communication and group life
interestingFacts: Dusky Dolphins are known for energetic aerial behavior.
They often live in productive cold or temperate coastal waters.
Their groups can coordinate to herd schooling fish such as anchovies into tight balls near the surface.
Their play-like movement may also support social bonding and communication.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small schooling fish, squid, and crustaceans.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Orcas, large sharks, entanglement, boat disturbance, and prey decline threaten them. Social groups and agility help, making joy a connected survival behavior rather than decoration.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Dusky Dolphins are active by day and night, with feeding and socializing shifting by prey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Dusky Dolphins can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to calves that learn swimming, social signals, and feeding behavior within the group.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar in appearance, with size differences possible.

dusky-gopher-frog.spotlight: Dusky Gopher Frog teaches Dual Refuge through a life split between buried shelter and temporary breeding ponds. Its burrow dependence, rainy migration, explosive breeding, and upland-longleaf habitat show that survival sometimes needs two homes.
dusky-gopher-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Longleaf pine uplands, sandy burrows, wet pine savannas, temporary ponds, and forested seasonal pools fit Dusky Gopher Frogs because one refuge is not enough.
signatureTraits: Stocky dusky frog tied to upland burrows
Breeding migration to temporary fishless ponds
Dependence on longleaf pine ecosystem structure
Seasonal life split between shelter and water
interestingFacts: Dusky Gopher Frogs often use burrows made by gopher tortoises or other animals.
They breed in temporary ponds that usually lack fish predators.
The species is critically rare and tied to a small remaining range.
Their call has been described as deep and snoring.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, spiders, worms, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, fish in unsuitable ponds, and habitat loss threaten adults, eggs, or tadpoles. Burrows and fishless ponds are the two shields.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They spend much time hidden in burrows and move to breeding ponds during rains.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A reliable figure in years has not been published. Most adults are thought to survive only a few breeding seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in temporary ponds, where tadpoles develop before water dries. Offspring survival depends on ponds lasting long enough but staying fish-free.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males call from breeding ponds, while females arrive to lay eggs. Outside breeding, males and females are hard to separate without close examination.

dusky-leaf-monkey.spotlight: A slender, long-tailed langur of the Malay Peninsula and neighbouring parts of Thailand and Myanmar. Its large, chambered stomach holds bacteria that ferment leaves, letting it live on foliage that most monkeys could not digest.
dusky-leaf-monkey.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Lowland and hill rainforest, both old-growth and regrowth, where it keeps mainly to the middle and upper canopy. It also uses coastal forest, old plantations and wooded parks on the Malay Peninsula, in southern Thailand and southern Myanmar, and on islands such as Penang and Langkawi.
signatureTraits: White rings of bare skin circle the eyes, giving the name spectacled langur.
A pale patch of bare skin surrounds the mouth.
The coat is dark grey to blackish, often paler on hind legs and tail.
The tail is longer than the head and body and hangs straight down.
interestingFacts: Groups usually number about 5 to 20 animals, typically one or a few adult males with several females and their young.
The IUCN Red List classes it as Endangered, following an assessment in 2020 that found numbers falling across its range.
In Penang, Malaysia, conservationists have hung canopy bridges over roads so that these monkeys can cross without coming down to the traffic.
Travelling groups move by running along branches and leaping between tree crowns, and they rarely come down to the ground.
Several subspecies are recognised, some of them confined to single islands off the Malay Peninsula.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Young leaves form most of the diet, with shoots, flowers and fruit, much of it unripe, and some seeds. Feeding animals sit in the crown and pull twigs in by hand.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few kills have been recorded. Clouded leopards, large pythons and big raptors are the likely natural predators, and dogs kill monkeys at forest edges. Forest clearance, road traffic and capture for the pet trade are the greater dangers. Alarmed groups call loudly and climb higher.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Groups feed mainly in the early morning and late afternoon, rest and groom through the middle of the day, and sleep at night high in tall trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive animals have lived about 25 to 30 years. How long they survive in the wild has not been measured, though it is probably less.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females bear a single infant after a gestation of roughly five months. The newborn's coat is bright yellow-orange and turns to the adult grey within about six months. Other females in the group often carry and handle the infant.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes share the same colouring and markings. Males are slightly larger and heavier than females, a difference that is hard to judge in the field.

dusky-pademelon.spotlight: Dusky Pademelon teaches Edge Discretion through a shy forest-edge hopper moving where attention is expensive. Dusk activity, cover use, springing legs, and quiet browsing show that low profile can still build momentum.
dusky-pademelon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, australia_oceania. Forest edges, dense understory, secondary growth, thickets, clearings, and New Guinea lowland forests.
signatureTraits: Small macropod body suited to hopping through dense edge cover.
Shy dusk and night activity that reduces exposure.
Forest-edge browsing on leaves, shoots, and fallen plant matter.
Quick retreat into cover instead of open confrontation.
interestingFacts: Pademelons are smaller relatives of wallabies and kangaroos.
Dusky Pademelons are associated with New Guinea and nearby forest habitats.
They rely on dense cover and cautious movement.
Like other marsupials, young develop in the mother’s pouch.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, grasses, fallen fruit, herbs, and forest-edge plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dogs, pythons, raptors, humans, hunting, and habitat loss threaten pademelons. Quiet movement and fast retreat protect them, making discretion a survival tool.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Dusky Pademelons are mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, resting in cover by day and feeding when attention drops.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been documented for the dusky pademelon, either for wild animals or for animals kept in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry joeys in the pouch, where young develop before gradually exploring outside.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger than females, but both sexes share the same shy hopping design.

dwarf-caiman.spotlight: Dwarf Caiman teaches Armored Patience through a small crocodilian that lets armor hold the line. Heavy scutes, creek stillness, forest water, and quiet ambush make patience protective.
dwarf-caiman.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Forest creeks, rivers, flooded forests, wetlands, rocky streams, and dark pools.
signatureTraits: Heavily armored body for a small crocodilian
Still-water ambush behavior in forest creeks
Compact size suited to narrow streams and wetlands
Night hunting from cover and shadow
interestingFacts: Dwarf Caimans are among the smallest crocodilians, with adults usually under about 1.6 metres long.
They have strong bony armor compared with many crocodilians.
They live in South American forest streams, wetlands, and rivers.
They hunt fish, crustaceans, amphibians, and small animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crabs, shrimp, frogs, insects, small mammals, and aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, large snakes, birds for young, larger caimans, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Armor helps, but cover and stillness complete the defense.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Dwarf Caimans are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, resting hidden by day and hunting in low light.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Dwarf Caimans can live for decades in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build nests and guard eggs or young in many crocodilian patterns. Offspring fit the principle because tiny armored bodies begin vulnerable and need guarded water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger than females. The difference affects territory and breeding, while both sexes share the armored creek strategy.

dwarf-cassowary.spotlight: Dwarf Cassowary teaches Hidden Seedwork through a mountain forest bird quietly carrying future trees. Helmeted head, strong legs, fruit diet, and montane wandering make forest renewal happen behind the leaves.
dwarf-cassowary.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. New Guinea montane rainforest, cloud forest, dense understory, fruiting slopes, and cool highland valleys.
signatureTraits: Smaller cassowary body adapted to montane forest movement
Fruit-heavy diet that disperses seeds through droppings
Strong legs for moving through dense slopes and vegetation
Secretive solitary behavior in highland forest cover
interestingFacts: Dwarf Cassowaries are the smallest of the living cassowary species.
They live in New Guinea’s montane forests rather than lowland rainforest alone.
By eating fruit, they can move seeds away from parent trees.
Like other cassowaries, males play a major role in incubating and raising chicks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fallen fruit, berries, fungi, insects, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large pythons, dogs, humans, habitat loss, and threats to eggs or chicks challenge Dwarf Cassowaries. Strong legs and secrecy defend the bird that quietly performs forest service.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Dwarf Cassowaries are mostly diurnal, moving through cover by day and resting in dense forest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: published lifespan data for Casuarius bennetti are scarce; highland forest fruit and long chick care by males shape a life paced by montane seasons in New Guinea.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay large eggs, and males incubate and guard the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger or more dominant, while males handle incubation and chick care.

earless-monitor-lizard.spotlight: Earless Monitor Lizard teaches Hidden Relic through a secretive streamside body that survives by not announcing itself. Its smooth ancient look, semi-aquatic movement, damp forest habits, and rare presence show mystery as a survival strategy.
earless-monitor-lizard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Bornean rainforest, stream banks, damp leaf litter, seepages, and muddy shelters fit Earless Monitor Lizards because mystery survives near hidden water routes.
signatureTraits: Rare earless lizard from Borneo
Semi-aquatic movement near streams and damp forest
Secretive nocturnal or low-light habits
Ancient-looking body with bead-like scales
interestingFacts: Earless Monitor Lizards are not true monitor lizards, despite the name.
They are the only living species in their family.
They spend much time hidden near water and damp soil.
Their rarity and secrecy make them vulnerable to illegal collection.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Wild diet is known mainly from a few observations: it is thought to take earthworms, crustaceans, small fish and tadpoles from stream beds and wet soil. Captive animals feed readily on earthworms, fish and shrimp.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, larger reptiles, and humans can threaten them. Secrecy, water retreat, and hidden crevices are the main protections.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly secretive and often active at night or in dim conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Exact lifespan is not well documented, but rare reptiles of similar size can live for many years. The lesson is mystery extended through slow survival.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs, likely in protected humid sites. Young begin life as miniature secret streamside hunters.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle, though males may have broader heads or tail-base differences. The species’ defining feature is hidden lineage rather than display.

eastern-glass-lizard.spotlight: Eastern Glass Lizard teaches Category Escape through a legless lizard slipping past the wrong label. Eyelids, ear openings, breakable tail, and grass-gliding movement show that not fitting the box can become the escape route.
eastern-glass-lizard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america.
