A black stripe runs down the outer side of each leg
Scent glands form dark slits in front of the eyes
Muzzle is dark, with black marks behind the ears
interestingFacts: In India it is known as the chousingha, from Hindi words meaning four horns.
It is the only member of its genus, and its closest living relative is the nilgai.
Animals return to the same spots to defecate, building up piles of droppings.
It usually stays within reach of water and drinks regularly.
Clearance of dry forest for farming is the main reason it is rated Vulnerable.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, herbs, leaves, fruit, and shoots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, dholes, wolves, pythons, humans, and habitat loss threaten this secretive antelope, making alertness and cover important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Four-horned Antelope are often crepuscular, feeding near cooler hours and resting in cover where the rare signature is less exposed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They likely live around 8 to 10 years, carrying the rare four-horned male identity through cautious woodland seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually hide single or twin fawns in cover, giving the young safety before they can follow through scrub.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the unusual four horns, while females lack horns.

francois-langur.spotlight: Francois' Langur carries Cliff Steadiness through black fur, pale cheek lines, and a body built for limestone edges. It turns dramatic terrain into routine by trusting grip, group, and exact movement.
francois-langur.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia, southeast_asia. Francois' Langurs live in limestone karst forests, cliffs, caves, and steep wooded slopes.
signatureTraits: Strong climbing limbs for limestone cliffs and forest
Dark coat with pale cheek whiskers
Leaf-heavy diet suited to karst forest life
Social groups that move through steep terrain together
interestingFacts: Infants are born bright orange, contrasting sharply with the darker adults.
Francois' Langurs are strongly associated with limestone karst landscapes.
They eat many leaves and rely on specialized digestion for fibrous food.
Groups use cliffs and caves as safer resting places.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed mostly on leaves, plus shoots, fruits, flowers, and buds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators can include clouded leopards, large raptors, snakes, and humans. Their defense is steep terrain, group vigilance, and sleeping sites where exact climbing becomes protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, they feed and travel in groups, then rest on cliffs, caves, or trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 15 to 20 years or more where protected. The lifespan why is that steadiness compounds: every safe ledge, careful route, and group warning keeps the body in the cliff world longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one orange infant, which receives attention from group members. The bright baby makes care visible in a dark-cliff species, reminding that steadiness also protects the vulnerable.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, though males are usually larger.

freshwater-butterflyfish.spotlight: Freshwater Butterflyfish teaches Surface Composure through a still fish holding the thin line between air and water. Wing-like fins, upward mouth, surface insects, and sudden strikes show calm is not weakness; it is loaded readiness.
freshwater-butterflyfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Slow streams, quiet pools, swampy waters, floating plants, and shaded freshwater margins.
signatureTraits: Wing-like pectoral fins spread at the water surface.
Upward-facing mouth built for surface insects and sudden strikes.
Still hovering posture beneath floating cover and calm water.
Ability to jump or strike at prey near the air-water boundary.
interestingFacts: Freshwater Butterflyfish are surface specialists from African freshwater habitats.
Their pectoral fins create a butterfly-like outline from above.
They watch the air-water boundary for insects and small prey.
Their calm surface posture hides explosive feeding readiness.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects, surface insects, small fish, and tiny aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, birds, snakes, and habitat changes can threaten them. Stillness and surface camouflage help, but the same surface that feeds them also exposes them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Spends long periods day and night hanging almost motionless just beneath the surface, often under floating plants. Feeding is reported to increase around dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Freshwater Butterflyfish can live several years in stable waters.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Fertilisation is thought to be internal. The female releases small batches of eggs over several days; the eggs float at the surface and are reported to hatch within a few days, and there is no parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar, though fin details may help distinguish them in close observation.

frilled-lizard.spotlight: Frilled Lizard teaches Startle Display through a reptile that suddenly becomes bigger than the threat expected. Neck frill, open mouth, upright posture, sprinting, and tree retreat turn surprise into the space needed to live.
frilled-lizard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, australia_coastal. Tropical savanna woodland, dry forest, tree trunks, and open ground near trees.
signatureTraits: A large neck frill can be flared suddenly to startle or intimidate threats.
Open-mouth display and upright posture make the body seem larger.
Fast retreat to trees turns the display into a bridge toward escape.
Ground and tree use combine warning, sprinting, and refuge.
interestingFacts: The frill is supported by cartilage rods and can fold back when not displayed.
Frilled Lizards are capable climbers and often flee toward trees after a display.
The display is a deterrent, not a guarantee; the escape route still matters.
Their famous upright running makes them look dramatic, but the goal is practical distance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, spiders, ants, termites, small lizards, and other arthropods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, snakes, monitor lizards, cats, and mammals threaten Frilled Lizards. The frill, mouth display, sprinting, camouflage, and climbing work together: surprise creates hesitation, and hesitation creates distance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Frilled Lizards are diurnal, basking and foraging when heat gives the body speed. Their rhythm matters because a display without enough body warmth would not convert quickly into escape.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Frilled Lizards can live for several years, with protected individuals living longer. Across that life, survival depends on repeating the same sequence: notice danger, enlarge the signal, then move before the bluff is tested.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil, where warmth and moisture shape development. Young hatch without parental care and must rely early on camouflage, small size, climbing, and the same startle logic in miniature.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and may have more developed display features, while females invest in egg production.

gaboon-viper.spotlight: The Gaboon Viper was designed to show the secret power of Hidden Magnitude. The main rule for this creature is that giant, explosive power should look completely invisible. Instead of making a snake that slithers around chasing things, the design compressed a heavy body, the longest fangs in the world, and super-strong venom into a living rug that sits perfectly still on the forest floor, waiting to surprise its dinner.
gaboon-viper.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. The floor of the rainforest was chosen because it is covered in piles of old, messy leaves—the perfect hiding place to mask a giant snake's heavy body and reward it for staying completely still.
signatureTraits: Leaf-litter camouflage
Very long fangs
Heavy ambush body
Potent venom
interestingFacts: Its bold geometric pattern of buff, brown, and purple can look like fallen leaves on the forest floor.
It is famous for extremely long fangs, which can reach about 5 centimetres, the longest of any venomous snake.
It usually waits motionless for long periods and strikes when prey passes within reach.
It gives birth to live young, and a single litter can number several dozen snakes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A diet of mice and birds that walk right up to the snake proves the design works; the viper never goes looking for food, because its invisibility makes food come straight to it.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Scary animals like mongooses or hawks are defeated simply because they walk right past the viper without ever realizing a giant weapon is sitting right under their feet.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It acts at night or at twilight to let the darkness help its camouflage, making its secret surprise attack even easier to pull off.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Living for 15 to 20 years shows that sitting perfectly still and saving your energy is one of the smartest and most successful ways to live.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Giving birth to live babies instead of laying eggs means the young snakes don't have to wait in a defenseless nest; they start life ready to hide and hunt instantly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes share the same pattern. Females grow heavier and thicker-bodied, while males have relatively longer tails; the sexes are hard to tell apart without handling.

gargoyle-gecko.spotlight: Gargoyle Gecko teaches Odd Advantage through a night climber whose strange ridges and gripping toes become perfect on bark. Bumpy head, sticky pads, arboreal movement, and quiet New Caledonian forest life turn oddness into fit.
gargoyle-gecko.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. New Caledonian forest, scrub, tree trunks, branches, and humid night cover.
signatureTraits: Cranial ridges that give the gecko a gargoyle-like face.
Gripping toe pads for climbing bark, branches, and leaves.
Nocturnal arboreal movement through forest structure.
Tail use for balance, with ability to lose and regrow a tail.
interestingFacts: Gargoyle Geckos are native to New Caledonia, where they live only on the southern part of Grande Terre.
Their bumpy head ridges inspire the gargoyle name.
They can climb using toe pads and claws.
Like many geckos, they may drop the tail under stress and later regenerate it.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, fruit, nectar, soft plant material, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, snakes, larger lizards, rats, cats, and habitat loss can threaten them. Camouflage, climbing, biting, and tail loss help turn odd design into survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Gargoyle Geckos are nocturnal, hiding by day and climbing after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 15 to 20 years in captivity with good care. How long wild animals survive in New Caledonia has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected humid sites, and hatchlings begin life as tiny climbers already needing grip and cover.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adults are similar in size and pattern. Mature males show a pair of bulges at the base of the tail and a row of enlarged pores in front of the vent; females lack both.

gelada.spotlight: Gelada teaches Routine through a whole community sitting down to graze. Highland cliffs, grass-plucking fingers, vocal social life, and daily bands show that repetition can nourish more than one body.
gelada.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Ethiopian highland grasslands, cliffs, plateaus, and alpine meadows.
signatureTraits: Specialized grazing habits are unusual among primates.
Dexterous fingers pluck grass with steady precision.
Large social bands make routine a shared structure.
Cliff sleeping sites add safety to open highland feeding.
interestingFacts: Geladas are sometimes called bleeding-heart monkeys because of the chest patch.
They spend much of the day seated and grazing like primate grass-eaters.
Their social communication is rich, with many vocal sounds and facial signals.
They are native only to the highlands of Ethiopia, mostly above about 1,800 metres.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grass blades, seeds, roots, and herbs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, hyenas, jackals, dogs, raptors for infants, and habitat pressure threaten them. Cliff sleeping and group vigilance turn routine into protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding and socializing by day, then retreating to cliffs or safer sleeping places at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 15 to 20 years; routine becomes meaningful because a whole life is built from thousands of small shared grazing sessions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear one infant and remain inside close social units where care, grooming, and status shape the young's early world.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and display the chest patch strongly, while females' social bonds hold the daily structure; both matter to the routine.

gemsbok.spotlight: Gemsbok teaches Desert Poise through an antelope that keeps grace under heat, thirst, and predator pressure. Long straight horns, pale heat-reflecting markings, water discipline, and steady movement make protection elegant.
gemsbok.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Desert, semi-desert, dry savanna, dunes, salt pans, and open scrub.
signatureTraits: Long straight horns carried by both males and females.
Heat-tolerant desert body able to conserve water and endure dry country.
Bold face markings that sharpen presence in open light.
Powerful running and defensive horn use against predators.
interestingFacts: Gemsbok can survive long periods without drinking by drawing moisture from food and conserving water.
Both sexes carry long, straight horns, and females' horns are often longer and thinner than males'.
They live in some of southern Africa’s driest open habitats.
Their horns can be dangerous defensive weapons when cornered.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Dry grasses, desert herbs, roots, tubers, pods, and moisture-rich plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, hyenas, wild dogs, leopards, cheetahs for calves, humans, and drought threaten gemsbok. Horns, herd alertness, and heat endurance protect them, making poise active rather than passive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Gemsbok are active in cooler parts of the day and may rest during harsh heat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 18 years in the wild and around 20 in captivity, though predation and drought kill many well before that.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to calves that hide early before joining stronger herd movement.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes have horns, though males are usually heavier and females may have longer, slimmer horns.

gentoo-penguin.spotlight: Gentoo Penguin teaches Context Shift through a bird that looks awkward on land but becomes brilliant in water. Waddling colonies, white head stripe, strong flippers, fast swimming, and krill-fish pursuit show that fit changes everything.
gentoo-penguin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_atlantic, south_pacific, southern_ocean, arctic_antarctic. Subantarctic islands, rocky beaches, ice-free colony sites, cold coastal waters, and nesting slopes.
signatureTraits: Strong flippers turn the penguin into a fast underwater swimmer.
A white head stripe and orange bill make the species easy to recognize.
Pebble nests tie courtship and breeding to small repeated building acts.
Land awkwardness contrasts with smooth underwater pursuit.
interestingFacts: Gentoo Penguins are among the fastest swimming penguins.
They build nests from stones and may add pebbles throughout the breeding season.
Their bright orange-red bills and white head markings help distinguish them.
The same body that waddles on land becomes streamlined once the context changes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Krill, fish, squid, and crustaceans.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopard seals, orcas, skuas, giant petrels, eggs predators, storms, and human-driven ocean change threaten Gentoo Penguins. Colonies protect on land, while swimming skill protects at sea.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Gentoo Penguins are active by day and variable around breeding and foraging trips.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Breeding adults are thought to live around 10 years on average, and a minority reach 15 to 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay two eggs in pebble nests, and both parents incubate and feed the chicks. Offspring survival depends on both land care and the parents’ ability to shift into ocean hunters.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, though males are often slightly larger.

geometric-tortoise.spotlight: Geometric Tortoise teaches Geometric Armor through a shell that protects while looking like careful art. Its high dome, yellow-black pattern, fynbos camouflage, and slow ground life show that precision can be both shield and signature.
geometric-tortoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Fynbos, renosterveld, lowland shrubland, seasonal grasses, and sandy South African soils fit Geometric Tortoises because the shell pattern belongs to broken dry vegetation.
signatureTraits: High-domed shell marked with crisp geometric lines
Camouflage among grasses and fynbos shadows
Small rare tortoise of South African lowlands
Slow protected movement through seasonal scrub
interestingFacts: Geometric Tortoises are among the most threatened tortoises in the world.
Their shell pattern helps break up the outline in dry vegetation.
They are native to a small region of South Africa.
Fire, farming, and habitat loss are major pressures on their habitat.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, herbs, flowers, succulents, and seasonal plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Mongooses, birds, rodents, snakes, fire, and humans can threaten eggs, young, or adults. Shell pattern, stillness, and vegetation cover help defense.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active in suitable warm conditions and retreat during heat, cold, or dryness. Their rhythm follows season, moisture, and safe grazing windows.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: A reliable lifespan estimate for Psammobates geometricus is still unpublished; this Critically Endangered Cape tortoise fares poorly in captivity and is tied to renosterveld shrubland.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches of eggs in soil, and hatchlings emerge with tiny patterned shells. Young are vulnerable until armor and size improve.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually smaller with longer tails and a more concave underside, while females are larger for egg carrying. The differences stay tucked beneath the shared pattern.

gerenuk.spotlight: The Gerenuk was engineered to rule the rule of Standing Reach. The blueprint solves the problem of living in dry places with no grass by changing how the animal stands. By stretching its neck and modifying its hips so it can stand balance-beams style on its back legs, the design allows this antelope to reach a private buffet of high-up leaves that other ground animals can't touch.
gerenuk.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry, crispy bushlands were chosen instead of green fields. In these hot deserts, there is no grass on the ground, forcing the design to look upward to the high tree leaves for survival.
signatureTraits: Long slender neck
Hind-leg browsing posture
Dry-country browsing
Large eyes and ears
interestingFacts: Gerenuks often stand upright on their hind legs to reach leaves up to about two metres high.
They can get much of their moisture from browse and may rarely or never need to drink.
Only males have horns, which are thick and curve backward and then forward near the tips.
Their name is often associated with a giraffe-like neck.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A selective diet of high-up, juicy leaves provides both food and water, meaning the Gerenuk never has to walk to scary, predator-filled rivers for a drink.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions and cheetahs are avoided because the Gerenuk eats with its head held high in the air, giving it a perfect lookout tower to spot sneaking predators early.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It does its grocery shopping during the day when it can clearly see the juiciest leaves, taking long naps in the deep shade when the sun gets too hot.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Living 8 to 13 years shows that standing on two legs is a tough, durable, and brilliant alternative to walking on all fours like a normal animal.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Tucking a single baby safely away in the bushes allows the adults to focus on stretching high into the trees without worrying about a little one wandering off.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Only the dads get heavy, curved horns for territory games, leaving the moms unburdened, lightweight, and perfectly shaped to stretch for food.

giant-african-millipede.spotlight: Giant African Millipede teaches Decomposition through a slow body returning the forest to itself. Many legs, coiled defense, leaf-litter feeding, and patient digestion show that decay can become renewal through tiny repeated steps.
giant-african-millipede.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Tropical forest floors, leaf litter, rotting wood, moist soil, and shaded understory fit Giant African Millipedes because their work happens where fallen plant matter gathers.
signatureTraits: Many-legged movement: slow progress happens through repeated tiny steps.
Coiled defense: the body protects itself by turning inward.
Leaf-litter diet: decay becomes fuel and forest renewal.
interestingFacts: Giant African Millipedes are among the largest millipedes in the world.
They release irritating defensive secretions from glands along the body and curl into a tight coil when threatened.
They help recycle nutrients by breaking down dead plant material.
Despite the name millipede, they have only a few hundred legs, with two pairs on most body segments.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Decaying leaves, rotting wood, soft fruit, and organic debris.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, reptiles, ants, mites, and parasitic organisms can threaten millipedes. Coiling and defensive secretions make slow movement safer.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant African Millipedes are mostly nocturnal or active in moist conditions, avoiding drying heat. Their rhythm follows humidity and the hidden schedule of decay.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Giant African Millipedes can live several years, especially in stable moist conditions. Their lifespan supports a slow service role: night after night of returning fallen matter to soil.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in soil or protected organic material, where young hatch into smaller many-legged recyclers. Offspring continue the forest-floor work at a smaller scale.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males have modified legs used in mating.

giant-anteater.spotlight: The largest of the anteaters, around two metres from nose to tail tip and weighing up to about 40 kilograms. It walks on its knuckles with the long front claws folded inwards, which keeps them sharp. Its body temperature, near 33°C, is among the lowest of any placental mammal.
giant-anteater.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Giant Anteaters live in grasslands, savannas, wetlands, and forest edges.
signatureTraits: Long tubular snout
Sticky extendable tongue
Huge digging claws
No teeth
interestingFacts: The tongue can flick in and out very quickly.
It opens ant and termite nests with powerful foreclaws, feeding briefly at each before moving on.
Young ride on the mother’s back for months, their stripes lining up with hers.
It is specialized for insects rather than chewing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ants and termites, by some estimates up to about 30,000 in a day. It feeds at each nest for only a minute or so before the soldiers' bites and sprays drive it off, so many nests are visited and none is emptied.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars and pumas are the main natural predators. A cornered anteater rears up on its hind legs, braced by its tail, and slashes with the front claws. Road traffic, grassland fires, large dogs and hunting by people kill many more.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day or by night depending on heat and disturbance, turning more nocturnal in hot weather and near people. It sleeps for up to about 16 hours in a shallow scrape or thicket, with the bushy tail folded over its body.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably around 14 to 16 years in the wild, though field data are thin. In zoos, individuals have lived past 25.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Gestation lasts about six months, and females carry a single youngster on the back after birth. The pup's shoulder stripe lines up with the mother's, which makes it hard to pick out. This continues for six to nine months, and the young becomes independent at about two years.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look similar, though males may be larger. Coat pattern is the same in both, and the male's reproductive organs are internal, so sex is hard to judge in the field unless a female is carrying young.

giant-armadillo.spotlight: About 1.5 metres from nose to tail tip, this is the largest living armadillo, with wild adults usually weighing 20 to 30 kilograms or more. It often digs a new burrow after only a night or two. Camera traps in the Brazilian Pantanal have recorded more than 20 other species sheltering or feeding at the abandoned holes.
giant-armadillo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Savanna, forest edges, grassland, and termite-rich soils fit because excavation needs both protection and buried work.
signatureTraits: Shell is dark brown with a pale band along the lower edge
Eleven to thirteen movable bands cross the back
Long, tapering tail is covered in small scales
Can rear up on its hind legs, propped on the tail
interestingFacts: It can have up to about 100 small, peg-like teeth, an unusually high number for a land mammal.
Tracked animals in the Pantanal used home ranges of roughly 25 square kilometres.
The middle claw on each forefoot is huge, reported at up to about 20 centimetres along its curve.
Hunting for meat and loss of habitat have left it Vulnerable.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Termites, ants, larvae, worms, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas, humans, and threats to young make armor, burrows, nocturnal timing, and digging skill important defenses.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Armadillos are nocturnal, resting in burrows by day and emerging at night to dig into insect nests and soil.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They likely live 12 to 15 years or more, repeating slow underground work across many nights and burrow systems.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually raise one young after long investment, making each offspring dependent on secure burrows and protected digging territories.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, though males may be larger.

giant-clam.spotlight: Giant Clam teaches Solar Partnership through a massive still animal hosting light inside living tissue. Open mantle, symbiotic algae, reef water, and patient filtering show that abundance can come from cooperation with the sun.
giant-clam.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, south_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea, australia_coastal. Shallow coral reefs, clear lagoons, reef flats, and sunlit tropical waters fit Giant Clams because Solar Partnership needs light strong enough for algae and water rich enough for filtering. The habitat makes stillness productive.
signatureTraits: Large shell anchored in shallow sunlit reef habitat
Bright mantle tissue hosting photosynthetic symbiotic algae
Filter feeding combined with solar energy partnership
Long-lived reef presence that becomes microhabitat for others
interestingFacts: Giant Clams host algae that provide energy through photosynthesis.
Their colorful mantles help expose symbionts to sunlight.
They also filter feed from seawater, adding plankton to the sugars supplied by their algae.
They are among the largest living bivalves, with shells that can exceed a metre across.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Photosynthetic sugars from symbiotic algae plus plankton and dissolved nutrients from filter feeding.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predatory snails, fishes, rays, octopuses, humans, and reef degradation threaten Giant Clams. Shell closure, size, and reef placement protect the partnership that must stay open to light yet safe from harm.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Clams remain mostly stationary, opening by day to light and closing when disturbed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Giant Clams can live for many decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning clams release sperm first and eggs afterwards, a large adult shedding hundreds of millions of eggs, often after sensing spawn from neighbours. Larvae drift for about one to two weeks before settling, and each young clam takes up its algae from the surrounding water rather than inheriting them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Giant Clams are functional hermaphrodites, producing eggs and sperm at different phases.

giant-eland.spotlight: The word giant in its name refers to the horns, which are tightly spiralled, set in a V and can exceed a metre in bulls. In body size it roughly matches the common eland, the two being the largest of all antelopes, and big bulls are reported to approach 900 kilograms. Herds are shy and range widely.
giant-eland.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Giant Eland usually lives in savanna woodland, open forest, and forest-edge mosaics.
signatureTraits: massive body
spiral horns
long legs
calm browsing
interestingFacts: The reddish-brown coat carries roughly 8 to 15 thin white vertical stripes on each flank.
Despite its weight it is reported to clear obstacles about 1.5 metres high.
Of the two subspecies, the western one survives mainly in Niokolo-Koba National Park in Senegal and numbers only a few hundred at most.
It is also called Lord Derby's eland, after the thirteenth Earl of Derby, for whom the first specimens were collected.
It breaks branches with its horns to bring leaves within reach.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Giant Eland feeds on leaves, shoots, grasses, fruit, and browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions and spotted hyenas can kill adults, and leopards and African wild dogs take calves. Herds are alert and flee at a fast trot they can keep up for long distances. Hunting for meat and the spread of farming and livestock have done most to shrink the range.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Eland is mostly active in cooler parts of day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In the wild the Giant Eland may live into the teens or longer. Published maximum figures are around 20 to 25 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about nine months, females bear a single calf hidden at first. Within a few weeks the calf joins other young in the herd, and it is suckled for roughly four to six months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes carry horns, but males are much larger with heavier necks and horns. Mature bulls develop a black neck and a large hanging dewlap, and their coats darken with age. Cows stay more reddish-brown.

giant-forest-scorpion.spotlight: The Giant Forest Scorpion is calm grip in dark armor. Its huge pincers and slow confidence show that strength does not have to rush to be convincing; sometimes control comes claw-first.
giant-forest-scorpion.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Giant Forest Scorpions live in humid tropical forests, leaf litter, burrows, and sheltered ground spaces in South and Southeast Asia. This habitat fits Calm Grip because dark, close, cluttered forest rewards slow sensing, firm holding, and armored patience.
signatureTraits: Large powerful pincers
Dark armored exoskeleton
Nocturnal forest-floor life
Defensive posture before stinging
interestingFacts: Giant forest scorpions rely heavily on their pincers for grabbing prey and defense.
They are nocturnal and often hide under logs, bark, or burrows by day.
Their venom is generally not their only defense; size and claws matter greatly.
Like other scorpions, mothers carry young on their backs after birth.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat insects, spiders, and other small animals captured with pincers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators may include birds, mammals, reptiles, and larger arthropods. Their defense is armor, claws, posture, and sting, showing that calm strength can layer protection instead of relying on one dramatic weapon.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal, sheltering by day and emerging at night to forage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Large scorpions can live several years, and some may survive a decade or more in stable care. Their lifespan supports a slow-strength identity built from repeated nights of control.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young and carry them on the back until they molt and disperse. This care makes the armored animal unexpectedly tender, linking protection to patience.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females can differ in body proportions, with males often showing relatively longer or slimmer structures depending on species. In casual viewing, the shared pincers and armor are the clearer signal.

giant-freshwater-stingray.spotlight: A thin, almost circular ray of large rivers and estuaries in Southeast Asia, and one of the largest freshwater fish known. A female caught in the Mekong in Cambodia in 2022 weighed about 300 kilograms and measured nearly four metres from snout to tail tip.
giant-freshwater-stingray.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Large muddy rivers and deep channels fit because riverbed power is strongest when it becomes almost part of the bottom.
signatureTraits: Broad, thin disc that can exceed two metres across
Small pointed tip projecting from the front of the snout
Plain brown to grey above; white below with dark margins
Long whip-like tail without fin folds
Serrated tail spine, up to about 38 centimetres long
interestingFacts: The record fish from the Mekong was fitted with an acoustic tag and released alive so its movements could be followed.
Sensory pores on the snout detect the weak electrical fields of prey hidden in sand or mud.
Anglers report that a hooked ray can tow a boat or clamp itself to the bottom for hours.
It was long known as Himantura chaophraya, after the Chao Phraya river in Thailand, before the older name polylepis was restored.
It also enters brackish estuaries, and whether individuals move between river systems by sea is not well understood.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crustaceans, shellfish, and bottom prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large crocodiles may threaten young, while humans, fishing, habitat changes, and river disturbance are major pressures on adults.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Freshwater Stingrays rest buried or low on the riverbed, blending power into mud until feeding or movement is needed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They are likely long-lived, with slow growth and large size making stable river systems important across many years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live pups, placing young directly into the same muddy bottom world where low, wide power matters.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females often grow larger, while males have claspers.

giant-grouper.spotlight: Adults reach about 2.5 metres in length, and the heaviest weigh around 400 kilograms. Young fish are boldly blotched yellow and black, a pattern that breaks up into mottled grey-brown as they grow. Large adults are often curious and may approach divers closely.
giant-grouper.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea, australia_coastal. Giant Grouper usually lives in reefs, rocky ledges, wrecks, and deep coastal caves.
signatureTraits: Massive mouth that turns a short lunge into suction power
Cave and ledge presence that makes territory feel occupied
Slow patrol style that saves energy for decisive feeding
Heavy reef body built for authority more than speed
interestingFacts: Giant Groupers can grow into some of the largest bony reef fish.
Their suction feeding makes prey disappear in one sudden mouth expansion.
Wrecks and caves can become stations of quiet dominance.
Their size gives adults fewer natural enemies, but it also makes them targets for humans.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Giant Grouper feeds on fish, crustaceans, rays, and other reef animals swallowed by suction.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Only large sharks regularly threaten an adult, though bigger fish eat the juveniles that shelter in estuaries and mangroves. Fishing is the serious danger: the species grows slowly, matures late and is easily speared or hooked at sites it is known to occupy.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rests in caves and moves slowly between feeding bouts, spending energy only when a close strike is worth it.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for several decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs into open water during spawning events, sending future giants into the currents before any cave can belong to them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Like many groupers, sex can change across life; size and age become part of authority rather than simple male-female display.

giant-ibis.spotlight: At a little over a metre long, this is the largest of all ibises. It lives in dry deciduous forest, feeding at the pools and muddy clearings that dwindle through the dry season, and pairs nest high in tall trees well away from settlements. Only a few hundred birds survive, nearly all in northern and eastern Cambodia.
giant-ibis.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Seasonal wetlands, forest pools, muddy clearings, grassland ponds, and open marsh edges.
signatureTraits: Bare grey head and neck with dark bars across the nape
Dark grey-brown body with silvery-grey wing panels
Dull red legs and dark red eyes
Usually seen in pairs or small family parties
interestingFacts: It is the official national bird of Cambodia.
Loud, ringing calls carry a long way through open forest, mostly at dawn and dusk.
Many of the pools it uses in the dry season are thought to be kept open by the wallowing of buffalo and other large animals.
In the wet season it has been recorded feeding inside the forest on earthworms and mole crickets.
Conservation teams pay local people to guard nests and fit the trunks of nest trees with belts that stop climbing predators.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic insects, frogs, small fish, crustaceans, worms, snails, and other wetland prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and young can be threatened by snakes, raptors, mammals, and human disturbance. Large presence helps, but the real protection is quiet wetland space where nesting and feeding are not interrupted.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, spending much of the daylight feeding on the ground. At night it roosts off the ground in trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan data for Thaumatibis gigantea have not been published; Cambodia's largest ibis probes flooded forest pools with a long, down-curved bill.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a small clutch in platform nests, with young depending on protected wetlands and parental feeding. Offspring show why habitat matters: without quiet pools, the whole search-based life breaks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage and cannot reliably be separated in the field. Any difference in size or bill length has not been well documented.

giant-isopod.spotlight: Giant Isopod teaches Deep Endurance through abyssal scavenging armor. Deep pressure, scarce food, armored plates, slow movement, and scavenging make patience a survival system for the deep.
giant-isopod.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, north_pacific. Soft mud and clay bottoms of the continental slope in the western Atlantic, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean, mostly between about 300 and 2,100 metres deep, in cold, dark water.
signatureTraits: Armored segmented body suited to pressure, darkness, and defense
Scavenging lifestyle that waits for rare deep-sea food falls
Low-energy movement that conserves strength between meals
Large eggs and heavy investment in a sparse world
interestingFacts: Giant Isopods are related to familiar pill bugs and woodlice.
They can go long periods without food in captivity, matching the deep sea’s scarcity.
Their large eyes are adapted to low light.
Their armor makes endurance look ancient and mechanical.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Giant Isopod feeds on carrion, dead fish, whale falls, and occasional slow prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators have been documented; deep-water sharks and large bottom-dwelling fish are thought to take them, smaller individuals especially. A disturbed animal is reported to curl its body to shield the softer underside. Some are caught incidentally in deep-water trawls and traps.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Slow deep-sea rhythms involve long inactive periods between meals, so conservation becomes as important as feeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Likely long-lived compared with shallow-water crustaceans; Deep Endurance means surviving scarcity without panic.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females brood relatively large eggs, investing heavily in fewer deep-sea young where every beginning is expensive.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle; survival is centered on armor, patience, and endurance rather than display.

giant-leaf-tailed-gecko.spotlight: One of the largest geckos in the world, reaching about 30 centimetres including the tail. Its mottled skin can lighten or darken to suit the trunk it rests on, and the huge lidless eyes have pupils that close to thin vertical slits in daylight. A cornered animal gapes to show a bright red mouth.
giant-leaf-tailed-gecko.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Giant Leaf-tailed Geckos live in Madagascar rainforests, tree trunks, bark, and lichen-covered surfaces.
signatureTraits: Fringed skin edges
Leaf-like tail
Flattened bark-matching body
Nocturnal insect hunting
interestingFacts: It can press flat to erase its shadow.
Its fringed skin flaps along the jaw and body edges help break up its outline against bark.
It is endemic to Madagascar, where it lives in eastern rainforests.
It is one of the largest leaf-tailed geckos, reaching roughly 30 centimetres in total length.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crickets, moths, cockroaches, spiders and other invertebrates are taken after dark. It hunts mostly by waiting on a trunk or branch and lunging at prey that moves within reach.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds of prey and carnivorous mammals take geckos in Madagascar's forests, and larger reptiles eat the young. A gecko that has been found out may give a loud distress call and can shed its tail. Clearing of rainforest is the most serious long-term threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. The day is spent motionless on a tree trunk, head pointing down, often a metre or more above the ground; after dusk it climbs into the branches to hunt.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured. Captive animals commonly live about 5 to 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In the wet season females lay eggs in hidden forest sites. A clutch is usually two round, hard-shelled eggs placed in leaf litter or under loose bark, and several clutches may follow. Hatching takes roughly two to three months, and the young get no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In colour and size the sexes are similar, though males may have broader tail bases. The swelling houses the hemipenes and shows only in adults, so young animals cannot be sexed by eye.

giant-pacific-octopus.spotlight: Giant Pacific Octopus teaches Fluid Intelligence through a soft giant that solves by changing shape. Eight arms, suckers, camouflage, dens, and escape skill turn tight places open.
giant-pacific-octopus.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_pacific. Cold North Pacific reefs, rocky dens, kelp edges, seafloor crevices, and coastal waters.
signatureTraits: Eight flexible arms lined with sensitive suckers
Rapid color and texture change for camouflage
Den use and problem-solving around shelter and prey
Soft body able to squeeze through tight spaces
interestingFacts: Giant Pacific Octopuses are among the largest octopus species.
They are intelligent problem-solvers, and captive individuals have learned to open jars and to recognize particular keepers.
They use dens and may pile shells or debris near entrances.
Females guard eggs intensely and usually die after brooding.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, shrimp, clams, fish, and other seafloor animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Seals, sea lions, large fish, sharks, humans, and habitat disturbance threaten them. Ink, camouflage, dens, and squeezing escape make flexibility defensive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Pacific Octopuses are often nocturnal or crepuscular, though activity varies.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Giant Pacific Octopuses usually live only a few years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay large strings of eggs and guard them without leaving to feed much, often dying after they hatch.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have a specialized arm for reproduction, while females invest heavily in egg guarding.

giant-panda.spotlight: Bamboo makes up almost all the diet of this bear of the mountain forests of central China, yet it keeps the short, simple gut of a carnivore. It digests only about a fifth of what it swallows, so an adult must eat heavily, commonly 10 kilograms or more a day.
giant-panda.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Giant Pandas live in mountain bamboo forests in China.
signatureTraits: Pseudo-thumb wrist bone
Powerful bamboo-crushing jaws
Black-and-white coat
Low-energy specialist lifestyle
interestingFacts: Pandas are bears, but bamboo makes up more than 99 percent of their diet.
Their pseudo-thumb, an enlarged wrist bone, helps them grip bamboo stems.
Cubs are tiny at birth, weighing only about 100 to 200 grams.
They spend many hours feeding each day, often around 10 to 16 hours.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tender shoots are eaten when they sprout in spring and summer, leaves and stems at other times, from whichever bamboo species grow at that altitude. It occasionally eats other plants, carrion or small animals. It feeds sitting upright, peeling each stem with its teeth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators. Cubs may be taken by leopards, dholes and yellow-throated martens, and older cubs climb trees when threatened. The division of forest into small, isolated blocks by roads and farmland is the greater danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active in bouts through both day and night, most of all around dawn and dusk. Between feeds it rests for a few hours at a time, lying on the ground among bamboo or against a tree. It does not hibernate.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 15 to 20 years in the wild. In captivity they often live into their twenties, and a few have passed 35.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females are fertile for only two or three days each spring. Cubs are born in late summer in a hollow tree or rock den, and in the wild females usually raise one cub even when twins are born. The cub stays with her for eighteen months or more.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are larger; females carry the demanding cub-rearing work. Males weigh roughly 10 to 20 per cent more, but the coat pattern is identical and the sexes are hard to tell apart at a distance. Adult males sometimes scent-mark trees from a handstand, placing the mark higher.

giant-trevally.spotlight: Giant Trevally teaches Explosive Power through a reef predator that holds force until a school opens. Deep body, hard turns, lagoon patrols, and sudden attacks make power valuable because it is released at the exact opening.
giant-trevally.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, south_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea. Reefs, lagoons, channels, reef flats, drop-offs, and coastal waters.
signatureTraits: Deep muscular body built for sudden reef attacks
Fast pursuit of schooling fish around reefs and lagoons
Bold predatory presence across reef edges and open water
Stored energy released in short decisive bursts
interestingFacts: Giant Trevally are among the most powerful reef-associated predators.
They hunt alone or in groups depending on prey and place.
They can move between lagoons, reefs, channels, and open water.
Their attacks often depend on a brief opening in a moving school.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crustaceans, cephalopods, and other reef prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks, larger predatory fish, humans, and reef habitat change threaten them. Young fish face more predators, so growing into power takes survival through many smaller risks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Trevally are active by day and night depending on prey, tides, and reef conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ear-bone ageing of Hawaiian fish has suggested a maximum of about 25 years, though few populations have been aged.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs into open water during spawning, producing drifting larvae that must survive before joining reef and coastal systems.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are generally alike in shape and colour, and no reliable outward way of separating them is known.

giant-water-bug.spotlight: Giant Water Bug teaches Ambush Grip through an underwater hunter whose forelegs are ready before prey arrives. Raptorial arms, air-siphon breathing, still pond cover, and sudden piercing strike turn patience into a grip from below.
giant-water-bug.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, marshes, slow streams, ditches, weedy shallows, and still freshwater fit Giant Water Bugs because ambush grip works best in cover where prey passes close.
signatureTraits: Powerful raptorial forelegs seize prey in aquatic ambushes.
Piercing-sucking mouthparts inject digestive saliva into captured prey.
Can take surprisingly large prey such as tadpoles, small fish, and frogs.
Uses air-breathing adaptations while living as an underwater predator.
interestingFacts: Giant water bugs are sometimes called toe-biters because of their painful bite.
Some related water bugs show male egg-carrying behavior, though habits vary by species.
They can fly between ponds, especially when searching for new water.
They are important predators in small freshwater ecosystems.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic insects, tadpoles, small fish, frogs, snails, and other pond animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, birds, turtles, frogs, larger insects, and drying pools can threaten giant water bugs. Concealment, flight, and a painful defensive bite help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often active at night or in low light, waiting in aquatic cover. Their rhythm is stillness first, sudden grip second.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Nymphs pass through five moults over roughly one to two summer months, and adults can survive the winter, so an individual commonly lives about a year.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females glue a cluster of dozens of eggs to a plant stem or stick just above the waterline. The male is reported to guard the clutch and wet it with water, and nymphs hatch after roughly one to two weeks and drop into the pond.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in the field. They are separated by the shape of the plates at the tip of the abdomen.

giant-waxy-monkey-frog.spotlight: A big tree frog of the Amazon basin, about 9 to 12 centimetres long, it climbs hand over hand along branches with grasping fingers and toes and seldom leaps. Like other monkey frogs, it makes its waxy coating in glands in its own skin.
giant-waxy-monkey-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Giant Waxy Monkey Frog usually lives in Amazonian forest edges and warm vegetation near water.
signatureTraits: waxy skin coating
slow climbing
large body
leaf resting
interestingFacts: Several Indigenous peoples of the western Amazon, among them the Matses, apply the dried skin secretion to small burns in a ritual known as kambo or sapo.
The secretion contains peptides such as dermorphin and deltorphin, which act on the same receptors as opioid drugs and have been studied by pharmacologists.
The scientific name bicolor refers to the contrast between the green back and the pale, spotted belly and flanks.
Adults spend most of their time high in trees and come down to lower vegetation mainly to breed over pools.
It is listed as Least Concern because it is widespread across the Amazon basin.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Giant Waxy Monkey Frog feeds on insects and other small invertebrates caught at night.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tree snakes, birds and mammals are possible predators of adults, and eggs and tadpoles are eaten by a wider range of animals. Its skin secretion carries a mix of potent peptides thought to make it distasteful, and by day it sits still, green against the leaves.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giant Waxy Monkey Frog is nocturnal, resting through hot daylight on leaves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive Phyllomedusa that seal skin with waxy lipids have lived about ten years; Amazon canopy ages stay unmeasured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In the rainy season females lay eggs on leaves above water, where tadpoles later drop. The clutch, often several hundred eggs in a mass of jelly, is wrapped inside a folded leaf, and hatching comes after roughly one to two weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: At full size females are usually larger than males. Only males call, giving low notes from perches in the trees above breeding pools.

gidgee-skink.spotlight: Gidgee Skink teaches Crevice Kinship through spiny lizards sharing hard cracks in hot rock. Rough scales, spiny tail, group shelter, and crevice wedging make resilience communal.
gidgee-skink.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Arid rocky outcrops, crevices, gidgee woodland, dry scrub, and stone piles.
signatureTraits: Rough spiny scales and tail used for defense
Rock-crevice sheltering in dry Australian habitats
Social group living unusual for many lizards
Wedging defense that turns cracks into protection
interestingFacts: Gidgee Skinks often live in family or social groups.
Their spiny tails help block predators from entering crevices.
They shelter in rocky cracks where heat and danger can be managed.
They are omnivorous, eating both plant matter and small animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds, insects, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, raptors, monitor lizards, cats, foxes, and humans threaten them. Wedging into cracks and presenting a spiny tail creates a boundary that works best when the shelter is known and shared.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Gidgee Skinks are diurnal, basking before foraging and retreating to rock shelter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Long-lived for a lizard of its size: ages of up to about 25 years are reported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young, which can remain close to the group and shelter system.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, though mature males may be more robust.

gila-monster.spotlight: The largest lizard native to the United States, a heavy-bodied reptile up to about 55 centimetres long from the deserts of the south-western USA and north-western Mexico. It can eat a third of its body weight at one sitting, and a few such meals may supply most of its energy for a year.
gila-monster.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Gila Monsters usually live in desert scrub, rocky slopes, washes, and burrows.
signatureTraits: Beaded skin, fat tail, venomous bite
Adapted to desert scrub
Black blotches or bands on pink, orange or yellow
Blunt, broad head with a black snout
Slow, low walk on short, sturdy legs
interestingFacts: Gila Monsters are closely tied to desert scrub, rocky slopes, washes, and burrows.
Their food is mainly eggs, nestlings, small mammals, reptiles, and carrion.
Major pressures include coyotes, raptors, snakes, and humans.
Venom glands lie in the lower jaw, and venom seeps along grooved teeth as the lizard chews.
A compound found in its saliva led to exenatide, a diabetes drug approved in 2005.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on eggs, nestlings, small mammals, reptiles, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coyotes, badgers, hawks and some snakes are reported or thought to take Gila monsters, mainly the young. The black and pink or orange pattern advertises a painful bite, and a threatened lizard backs away hissing with its mouth open. Road traffic, illegal collecting and housing development are the main human threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: More than nine-tenths of its life is thought to be spent underground in burrows, rock shelters and packrat nests. It surfaces on spring mornings, shifts to dusk and night in summer heat, and lies dormant below ground through winter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 20 years or more in the wild; captive animals have passed 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place in late spring, and in midsummer the female buries a clutch of about 2 to 12 eggs in damp soil. The eggs pass the winter underground and the young emerge the following spring, some ten months after laying. Parents give no care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may be bulkier, but sexes are similar.

giraffe.spotlight: Giraffe teaches High Reach through perspective made physical. Long neck, high browsing, wide scanning, long legs, and calm savanna movement open food and sightlines hidden to shorter animals. Its lesson is that a different height can reveal a different opportunity.
giraffe.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savanna woodland, acacia scrub, open bush, and grassy tree edges.
signatureTraits: Coat of brown patches divided by pale lines, patterned differently by population
Back slopes steeply down from high shoulders to the rump
Tufted black tail flicked against flies
Walks by moving both legs on one side together
interestingFacts: Its neck holds seven vertebrae, the same number as most mammals, each up to about 25 cm long.
A dark tongue up to about 45 cm long and tough lips let it strip leaves from thorny acacia branches.
Its blood pressure is roughly twice that of a human, enough to push blood up the long neck to the brain.
To drink, it must splay its front legs wide or bend them before lowering its head to the water.
Genetic studies suggest there may be four giraffe species rather than one, though many authorities still recognise a single species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Acacia leaves, shoots, flowers, pods, and other high browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions threaten calves and sometimes adults; hyenas and leopards may threaten young. Height helps watch danger before it arrives.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giraffes feed and ruminate through day and night with short sleep.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live around 20 to 25 years or more, making perspective a long advantage.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth standing to a single calf that must stand quickly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with heavier ossicones and use necking fights; females are smaller and central to calf care.

giraffe-weevil.spotlight: A leaf-rolling weevil found only in Madagascar, about 2 to 2.5 centimetres long, with a black body and red wing covers. The neck is a long, jointed extension of the head and thorax. Males nod and wrestle with it, pushing rivals away from a leaf where a female is at work.
giraffe-weevil.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Giraffe Weevil usually lives in Madagascar forest vegetation, especially host plants used for nesting.
signatureTraits: long neck
red body
leaf rolling
tiny body
interestingFacts: Each female rolls a leaf of her host tree into a tight tube and seals a single egg inside it.
The larva hatches inside the rolled leaf and feeds on its tissue, completing its growth within that shelter.
Its main recorded host plant is Dichaetanthera cordifolia, a small tree of the melastome family.
Females also have a lengthened neck, but it is much shorter than the male's, so pairs are easy to tell apart.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Giraffe Weevil feeds on leaves and plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of this weevil are poorly documented; insect-eating birds, chameleons and spiders are the likely ones. A disturbed adult may drop from its leaf or fly off. Clearing of forest, which removes the host trees, is the clearest threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Giraffe Weevil is diurnal or daylight-active around foliage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adult Trachelophorus giraffa that roll Dichaetanthera leaves in Madagascar live only a short season; year-scale ages are unpublished.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, females roll leaves into cradles for single eggs. The finished tube is cut free from the rest of the leaf, and the larva that hatches feeds on the rolled leaf around it. No care is given after laying.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In this species males have much longer necks than females. A male's neck is two to three times the length of a female's; hers is shorter but still long. Colour is the same in both sexes.

glasswing-butterfly.spotlight: Glasswing Butterfly teaches Wing Transparency through clear wings that let the world pass through without breaking the body. Transparent panels, soft flight, humid forest light, and chemical defense make softness a strategy, not weakness.
glasswing-butterfly.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Humid forests, cloud forest edges, shaded clearings, stream corridors, and tropical understory fit Glasswing Butterflies because shifting light makes transparency useful.
signatureTraits: Transparent wing panels reduce visibility in shifting forest light.
Dark wing edges give shape without destroying the clear effect.
Soft floating flight makes the butterfly difficult to track.
Chemical compounds from host plants can add defensive value.
interestingFacts: Glasswing transparency comes from wing structure that reduces reflected light.
Greta oto is found in Central and parts of South America.
Adults may visit flowers for nectar and also seek mineral sources.
Transparent wings are camouflage, not absence of design.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar, mineral-rich fluids, and caterpillar host plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, spiders, wasps, ants, and habitat loss threaten glasswings. Transparency, chemical defense, and gentle broken movement reduce visibility and pursuit.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Glasswing Butterflies are diurnal, moving when forest light creates the disappearing effect. Their rhythm turns daylight into camouflage rather than exposure.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults are reported to live from a few weeks to several months; exact figures for wild butterflies are not known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on host plants that will feed the caterpillars. Offspring protection begins through plant choice, where chemistry and future transparency start indirectly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar in transparent design, though reproductive roles differ.

glossy-ibis.spotlight: Glossy Ibis teaches Flock Passage through a curved-billed bird crossing wet places with company. Iridescent plumage, marsh probing, flock flight, and seasonal movement show that a wide wet world becomes easier together.
glossy-ibis.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, southeast_asia, australia_oceania. Marshes, flooded fields, rice paddies, lagoons, wetlands, and mudflats fit Glossy Ibises because they need shallow probing sites and flock-safe feeding areas.
signatureTraits: Curved probing bill: hidden wetland food is reached below the surface.
Iridescent body: bronze and green gloss appear as light changes.
Flock travel: movement follows water levels and group safety.
interestingFacts: Glossy Ibises can travel widely between wetlands, and they are the most widespread ibis species in the world.
Their curved bills probe mud rather than spear visible prey.
Their dark feathers can flash bronze, green, or purple in sunlight.
They often breed in mixed colonies alongside herons, egrets, spoonbills, and cormorants in well-vegetated wetlands.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic insects, worms, crustaceans, small fish, frogs, and larvae support Flock Passage because food is hidden in mud and reached by repeated probing.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, foxes, raccoons, snakes, gulls, and nest predators pressure ibises, especially at colonies. Flocks spread awareness across the marsh.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Glossy Ibises are diurnal, feeding and traveling in groups by day. Their rhythm follows water levels, seasonal wetlands, and flock movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ringing records show some wild birds living beyond 15 years, although average survival is considerably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in colony nests built in reeds, shrubs, or trees near water. Offspring depend on wetland timing because food and safety rise and fall with water levels.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be somewhat larger. Flock Passage is not built on bright sex difference; it is built on shared movement and timing.

goblin-shark.spotlight: Scattered records along continental slopes, mostly from about 250 to 1,000 metres down, are nearly all that is known of this shark, the only living species of an old family. Its body is soft and flabby with small fins, so it is thought to be a slow swimmer. Pores on the long snout detect the weak electric fields of nearby animals.
goblin-shark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Deep slopes, submarine canyons, and dark offshore water fit because extension matters where prey is sensed before clearly seen.
signatureTraits: A long, flat, blade-shaped snout overhangs the mouth
Skin is pink to pinkish-grey in life
Long, thin, nail-like front teeth show even with the mouth closed
Fins are small and rounded; the tail has no lower lobe
interestingFacts: It was described in 1898 from a specimen caught off Japan.
Many specimens have come from deep nets off Japan, and one event off north-eastern Taiwan in 2003 is reported to have produced about 100.
Its large, oily liver is thought to help it hang in the water near neutral buoyancy.
The few brought alive to aquariums in Japan have survived only days.
Its conservation status is Least Concern, because most of its range lies deeper than fisheries operate.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Deep-sea fish, squid, and crustaceans.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger sharks and human bycatch threaten Goblin Sharks, though deep offshore habitat keeps much of their life rarely observed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Goblin Sharks likely move slowly through deep water rather than following a clear sleep pattern, conserving energy until prey is detected.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is poorly known, but deep-sea sharks are often long-lived enough for slow growth and rare encounters to matter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females likely give birth to live young as related mackerel sharks do, sending pups into the same deep, dim hunting world.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, though females may grow larger.

goitered-gazelle.spotlight: A pale, sandy gazelle of steppe and semi-desert from the Middle East to Mongolia and northern China. Where many gazelles bounce stiff-legged when alarmed, this one simply runs flat out and can reach about 60 kilometres an hour. Northern herds make long seasonal movements between summer and winter pastures.
goitered-gazelle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Goitered Gazelle usually lives in dry steppes, semi-deserts, and open plains.
signatureTraits: Long legs and light build for rapid escape across exposed ground
Alert head-up grazing that treats distance as protection
Dry-country movement tuned to open horizons and sparse cover
Seasonal breeding that follows brief windows of better forage
interestingFacts: The swollen throat of breeding males gives the goitered gazelle its common name.
Its open-country safety depends on seeing danger early, not on hiding late.
Fawns are vulnerable, so timing births with greener seasons matters.
Its grace is practical: beauty and sprinting are both survival tools.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Goitered Gazelle feeds on grasses, herbs, shoots, and desert shrubs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves are the main predator over much of the range, leopards take some adults, and eagles and foxes kill fawns. An alarmed animal raises its black tail as it bolts, alerting the rest of the herd. Poaching and fences across migration routes are the main human pressures.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly active in cooler daylight and twilight, saving the hottest hours for rest so speed is available when the open land gives no cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Roughly 8 to 12 years in the wild; captive animals have reached about 16.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear a single calf after spring or early-summer rains, hiding new life when forage and cover are briefly kinder.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with heavier horns and a swollen throat region during the rut, while females carry the quieter survival work of calf concealment.

golden-eagle.spotlight: Golden Eagle teaches High Descent through a mountain hunter whose strike begins long before it drops. Soaring height, sharp vision, cliff nesting, thermal riding, and talons make power clean because perspective chooses the moment.
golden-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Mountains, cliffs, open moorland, steppe, tundra, and wide valleys.
signatureTraits: Powerful wings and soaring flight give the eagle a wide hunting view.
Sharp vision lets prey be selected before any costly descent begins.
Strong talons turn the final drop into a committed strike.
Cliff and open-country nesting keep height built into the life strategy.
interestingFacts: Golden Eagles can hunt across huge territories where distance and patience matter.
They use both active hunting and carrion depending on season and opportunity.
Pairs may reuse and add to large nests over multiple years.
Their power is not constant attack; much of the work is scanning, waiting, and choosing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Hares, rabbits, marmots, ground squirrels, birds, reptiles, young ungulates, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult Golden Eagles face few natural predators, but eggs and chicks can face ravens, owls, storms, falls, and human disturbance. Cliff nests reduce risk, yet the next generation still depends on guarded height.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Golden Eagles are diurnal, hunting when light and air currents support seeing and soaring.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Golden Eagles can live for decades, especially when they survive the risky early years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large nests on cliffs or tall trees, and both parents help feed the young. Offspring begin life high above danger, but that height also demands careful guarding and steady food delivery.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males, a common pattern in many raptors.

golden-headed-lion-tamarin.spotlight: Golden-headed Lion Tamarin turns bright energy into family work. Its golden mane, agile fingers, and cooperative infant care show that brilliance lasts longer when carried by the group.
golden-headed-lion-tamarin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Golden-headed Lion Tamarins live in Atlantic Forest canopy, secondary forest, cabruca shade-cacao systems, and dense tree networks.
signatureTraits: Golden head and mane contrasting with dark body
Cooperative infant carrying within family groups
Nimble canopy movement in Atlantic Forest
Foraging in bromeliads, bark, fruit, and small prey
interestingFacts: Golden-headed Lion Tamarins are endemic to Brazil's Atlantic Forest region.
Family members other than the mother help carry infants.
They forage for insects and small animals in tree holes and bromeliads.
Their golden mane, forearms and part of the tail contrast with an otherwise black body.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fruit, insects, spiders, small vertebrates, nectar, and gums.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include raptors, snakes, small cats, and humans through habitat loss. Their defense is alarm calling, quick canopy movement, group vigilance, and staying connected.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, traveling and foraging with the group, then sleeping in tree holes or dense cover. The rhythm makes kinship practical: the family moves, feeds, and hides as one unit.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 10 to 15 years in the wild, longer in care. The lifespan why is that small brightness survives by being socially carried through risk.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females often give birth to twins, and fathers and older siblings help carry them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, so the principle is not male display but family cooperation. Brightness belongs to the group rather than one performer.

golden-jackal.spotlight: Golden Jackal teaches Opportunism through a survivor that accepts many doors at dusk. Omnivory, scavenging, pair or small-group hunting, sharp senses, and twilight movement show that survival improves when the body can feed from more than one path.
golden-jackal.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, central_asia. Grasslands, scrub, wetlands, villages, farms, woodland edges, and semi-desert margins fit Golden Jackals because they are built for mixed opportunity. The habitat does not need to be perfect if the animal can read openings.
signatureTraits: Twilight Flexibility: dusk gives the jackal openings between day danger and night cover.
Omnivore Strategy: meat, fruit, insects, carrion, and scraps all become possible fuel.
Pair Coordination: jackals may hunt or defend with a mate, turning opportunity social.
interestingFacts: Golden Jackals range from southeastern Europe through the Middle East to South Asia and have been spreading into central Europe.
Golden Jackals eat both animal and plant foods, and in farmland they are reported to eat crops such as grapes, melons, and maize.
They can hunt, scavenge, and use human-influenced landscapes.
Mated pairs defend shared territories and often howl together in choruses that neighbouring jackals answer.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, birds, reptiles, insects, fruit, carrion, and human scraps.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, leopards, large dogs, hyenas, eagles, humans, and disease create pressure. The jackal survives by avoiding direct contests when possible and using the side path.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Golden Jackals are often crepuscular or nocturnal, moving when cover improves and human pressure may drop.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Golden Jackals can live several years in the wild and longer in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in dens, and pair bonds or family helpers may support pup raising.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often slightly larger than females, but both can share territory, care, and foraging pressure.

golden-lion-tamarin.spotlight: Golden Lion Tamarin teaches Family Fire through a bright small primate whose gold survives by shared carrying. Mane-like fur, cooperative infant care, tree-hole sleeping, and group foraging turn brilliance into family labor.
golden-lion-tamarin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Brazilian Atlantic Forest, secondary woodland, vines, bromeliads, tree holes, and dense canopy edges.
signatureTraits: Bright golden mane-like fur that gives a lionlike appearance
Cooperative infant carrying by fathers and group members
Small agile canopy movement through Atlantic Forest
Foraging with long fingers in bark, bromeliads, and crevices
interestingFacts: Golden Lion Tamarins often have twins, making shared infant care especially important.
Fathers and helpers carry infants for much of the day after birth.
They sleep in tree holes, which are valuable forest resources.
Conservation programs have helped restore populations in protected forest.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, insects, spiders, small vertebrates, nectar, gums, and prey found in crevices.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, small cats, nest predators, and habitat fragmentation threaten tamarins. Group alarm calls, shared care, and tree-hole sleeping keep the family flame protected.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Golden Lion Tamarins are diurnal, foraging by day and sleeping together in tree cavities at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 8 years on average in the wild, with some reaching around 15. Captive animals have lived past 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females often give birth to twins, and males plus older siblings help carry and feed them.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, but roles differ around infant care and breeding.

golden-mantella.spotlight: Golden Mantella turns Amber Warning into tiny honesty, wearing bright orange skin so predators read danger before the frog has to move.
golden-mantella.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Golden Mantellas live in humid forest edges, swampy areas, and seasonal pools in Madagascar. The habitat gives the tiny warning body enough moisture and breeding water to survive.
signatureTraits: Bright orange skin works as a clear warning signal
Tiny terrestrial frog body carries a bold visual message
Moist Madagascar habitats support breeding and daily activity
Toxic skin defense makes smallness harder to ignore
interestingFacts: Its color warns predators of skin toxins before attack
It is tiny but visually unmistakable on the forest floor
It is restricted to a small area of Madagascar

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat small insects, mites, ants, termites, and other tiny invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, habitat loss, collection pressure, and drying wetlands threaten them. Bright color deters some predators, but it cannot protect a vanished pool.
