fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active in warm, humid daylight or low-light conditions, especially around breeding seasons. Their rhythm lets the warning color be seen when danger is nearby.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live several years in suitable conditions, longer in protected care. A small life can still carry a repeated clear message across seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in damp places, and tadpoles develop in small pools or flooded areas. Offspring depend on moisture before they can carry the full amber signal.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar, though females may be larger and males call during breeding. The main difference is reproductive; the warning color belongs to both.

golden-pheasant.spotlight: Golden Pheasant teaches Radiance through a male body that saves impossible color for courtship. Crest, cape, scarlet body, yellow-gold crown, and long tail turn display into a timed event rather than constant noise.
golden-pheasant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Dense undergrowth in the mountain forests of central China, especially bamboo thickets and scrub on steep slopes, mostly at middle altitudes of roughly 500 to 2,500 metres. It also uses young conifer plantations and overgrown terraces where ground cover is thick.
signatureTraits: Golden crest and cape: courtship is carried by vivid ornamental plumage.
Long tail: movement extends the display beyond the body.
Forest-edge secrecy: bright males still rely on cover when not displaying.
interestingFacts: Male Golden Pheasants are far brighter than females.
The species is native to forested mountain regions of China.
It is widely kept in aviaries because of its striking plumage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, berries, leaves, shoots, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, wild cats, raptors, snakes, and humans can threaten adults, eggs, or chicks. The bright male must balance visibility with the protection of thick vegetation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Golden Pheasants are mostly active by day, foraging on the ground and roosting in trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live several years in wild or managed settings, with longer lives under care.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches in concealed ground nests and provide most direct incubation. Reproduction shows why radiance and camouflage both matter in the same species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are brilliantly colored, while females are brown and cryptic.

golden-poison-frog.spotlight: Among the most toxic animals known, this poison frog is about five centimetres long and lives in a small area of rainforest near Colombia's Pacific coast. Its skin carries batrachotoxin, which it does not make itself but accumulates from its wild diet; frogs raised in captivity on other food are harmless.
golden-poison-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Humid Colombian rainforest floor and leaf litter fit because warning color must be visible in a place full of hidden mouths.
signatureTraits: Adults are one plain colour: yellow, orange or pale green
Juveniles are dark with gold stripes along the back
Large black eyes stand out against the skin
Small round pads tip each toe, with no webbing
interestingFacts: Emberá people of western Colombia have tipped blowgun darts by wiping them across the back of a live frog.
Males hold territories with a long, rapid trilling call.
The species was described by scientists in 1978.
Batrachotoxin locks the sodium channels of nerves and muscles open, so signals cannot switch off.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ants, mites, termites, and tiny invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators attack adults because of toxins, but some snakes, habitat loss, collection, and pollution still threaten this tiny warning body.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Golden Poison Frogs are diurnal, moving in damp forest light where their bright warning color can be seen before contact.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Eggs are laid in moist places, guarded, and tadpoles may be carried to water, making parental placement part of survival.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, though males call and females may be larger; the main message remains the shared bright toxic warning.

golden-silk-orb-weaver.spotlight: A large orb-weaving spider of the warm Americas whose silk is yellow, so that the web shines gold in sunlight. A mature female's orb can be a metre or more across, hung on support lines several times longer. She usually repairs it a section at a time and may keep the same web going for weeks.
golden-silk-orb-weaver.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Forest edges, gardens, mangroves, open gaps, and branches fit this spider because large orb webs need anchor points and flying-insect traffic.
signatureTraits: The front of the female's body is covered in silvery-white hair.
Her long, cylindrical abdomen is orange-brown to olive with rows of pale spots.
Tufts of dark hair ring the first, second and fourth pairs of legs.
Legs are banded yellowish and dark brown.
She hangs head-down at the hub of the web.
interestingFacts: Small silvery spiders of the genus Argyrodes often live in the web and steal wrapped prey.
The main orb is usually flanked on one or both sides by a loose tangle of barrier threads.
Its genome, published in 2017, was found to contain more than two dozen genes for silk proteins.
In 2019 the species was moved from the genus Nephila to Trichonephila.
In the United States it is often called the banana spider, a name also given to unrelated spiders elsewhere.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects such as flies, moths, bees, and beetles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, wasps, lizards, monkeys, and larger spiders can threaten orb-weavers. Web placement, vibration sensing, and retreat lines reduce danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often active around web repair and prey capture through day or night depending on conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year. In seasonal climates spiderlings emerge in spring and mature by late summer, and adults die with the first cold weather; males die sooner than females.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In autumn the female fixes one or more egg sacs to leaves or twigs near the web, each wrapped in yellow silk and holding several hundred eggs. The spiderlings stay together in a shared tangle of silk for a short time after emerging, then disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females reach 2.5 to 4 centimetres in body length. Males are about 6 millimetres long, slender and dark brown, and weigh a small fraction of what she does. Several males often wait at the edge of one female's web.

golden-snub-nosed-monkey.spotlight: Winter in the mountain forests of central China brings deep snow and temperatures well below freezing, and this long-furred, leaf-eating monkey stays through it. One-male family units travel together in bands that can number in the hundreds, and members of a unit huddle tightly on a branch to rest and sleep.
golden-snub-nosed-monkey.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Golden Snub-nosed Monkey usually lives in cold high mountain forests and seasonal temperate woodland.
signatureTraits: golden fur
snub nose
social bands
cold tolerance
interestingFacts: Bare skin on the face is pale blue, set off by the orange-gold fur of the cheeks and forehead.
Most live between about 1,500 and 3,400 metres, moving to lower slopes in winter as the snow deepens.
Males without a family unit join all-male groups that travel on the edge of the breeding band.
Three separate populations, in Sichuan and Gansu, in the Qinling Mountains of Shaanxi and in Shennongjia in Hubei, are treated as subspecies.
The species is classed as Endangered, and parts of its range lie inside reserves set up for the giant panda.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Golden Snub-nosed Monkey feeds on lichens, leaves, buds, bark, fruit, and seeds depending on season.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, golden cats, dholes and large birds of prey such as the golden eagle and northern goshawk are the reported predators, mostly of young animals. Bands keep to the trees and give alarm calls, and adult males move towards the threat. Logging and past hunting have done more damage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Golden Snub-nosed Monkey is diurnal, feeding and resting in coordinated social groups.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: In captivity the Golden Snub-nosed Monkey can live into the twenties or longer. Wild lifespans have not been documented reliably and are probably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about six to seven months, females usually bear one infant and rely on group protection. Births fall mainly in spring. Other females in the unit often carry the infant and, in one long-studied population, commonly nurse it as well.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Among adults, males are larger, with stronger display features. A full-grown male can weigh more than one and a half times as much as a female, carries a long cape of golden guard hairs over the back, and develops fleshy swellings at the corners of the mouth.

goliath-beetle.spotlight: Goliath Beetle teaches Heavy Lift through an insect whose huge body is still built to rise. Armored mass, powerful flight muscles, larval growth, and forest strength show that big power needs structure, not apology.
goliath-beetle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Tropical African forests, sap flows, fruiting trees, decaying wood, and humid forest edges.
signatureTraits: One of the heaviest adult insects, with a massive armored body.
Strong wings hidden beneath protective wing cases.
Larval growth fueled by rich forest material and protein sources.
Male head horn used in contests and positioning.
interestingFacts: Goliath Beetles are among the largest and heaviest beetles in the world.
Adults can fly despite their bulky armored bodies.
Males have horn-like head structures used in contests.
Their larvae grow large before transforming into the famous adult form.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tree sap, fruit, and sugary liquids feed adults, while larvae use rich decaying organic matter and protein-rich foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, reptiles, ants, parasites, collectors, and habitat loss threaten Goliath Beetles. Armor helps, but the heavy body still depends on forest continuity.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are active by day, flying most in the warmest hours between tree crowns and sap flows; at night and in cool weather they are thought to rest high in the trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults typically live a few months, after a larval stage of roughly four to six months in soil or rotting wood.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in suitable substrate where larvae grow large before pupation.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have larger horns and more obvious contest structures, while females lack the same horn display.

goliath-birdeater.spotlight: Goliath Birdeater teaches Intimidation through urticating-hair defense. Huge size, threat posture, irritating hairs, large fangs, and patient ground life show that defense can begin before anyone gets close enough to touch.
goliath-birdeater.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Goliath Birdeater usually lives in Amazon and Guiana rainforest floor, burrows, and humid leaf litter.
signatureTraits: Huge tarantula body that makes approach psychologically costly
Urticating hairs that irritate attackers before contact
Large fangs and threat posture for close defense
Burrow-based rainforest floor life built around patience
interestingFacts: Goliath Birdeaters are among the largest spiders by mass.
They rarely eat birds, despite the dramatic common name.
Urticating hairs flicked from the abdomen can irritate the skin and eyes of attackers.
The birdeater name is often traced to an early 1700s engraving by Maria Sibylla Merian showing a tarantula eating a hummingbird.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Goliath Birdeater feeds on insects, worms, amphibians, small vertebrates, and opportunistic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coatis, snakes and large spider-hunting wasps are among the animals reported to attack it, and some Indigenous communities in the north of its range roast and eat it. A disturbed spider also hisses, rubbing bristles on its legs together with a sound audible from a few metres away.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, sheltering by day and emerging when the forest floor cools, so threat and feeding happen on its terms.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Females may live many years, while males are shorter-lived after maturity; Intimidation lasts longest when it is paired with patience.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay silk-wrapped egg sacs and guard spiderlings early on, making a fearsome body briefly become a nursery wall.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger and longer-lived; mature males are slimmer and roam for mates, shifting from fortress to searcher.

goliath-frog.spotlight: No living frog grows larger: the biggest recorded specimens measured about 32 cm from snout to vent and weighed more than 3 kg. It lives only in south-western Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. A study published in 2019 reported adults digging nesting pools on riverbanks and shifting stones of up to 2 kg to do so.
goliath-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Fast rocky rainforest rivers and stream edges.
signatureTraits: Greenish-brown, granular skin on the back
Yellowish to orange underside and inner legs
Hind feet webbed to the tips of the toes
Sits on spray-soaked rocks beside rapids and waterfalls
interestingFacts: Its tadpoles are no bigger than those of ordinary frogs; the great size comes from growth after metamorphosis.
Males have no vocal sac, which is unusual among frogs.
Tadpoles are reported to feed mainly on a single kind of plant that grows on rocks in rapids and waterfalls.
It is eaten locally and collected for the pet trade, and is listed as Endangered.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, crustaceans, small frogs, fish, and other river prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, large fish, monitor lizards, birds, mammals, and people threaten eggs, tadpoles, and adults. Prepared nests show that size alone is not enough; the river must be shaped for the young.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults are often active in evening and night around streams, resting near water by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live for many years if streams remain clean and protected, making preparation a repeated river habit.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in streamside nest areas that adults may clear or maintain.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger than males in many frogs, while males compete and call around breeding sites. The lesson is shared through river nesting more than ornament.

goliath-tigerfish.spotlight: Largest of the African tigerfishes, this silvery predator is reported to reach about 1.5 metres and 50 kilograms. The pointed teeth, up to about 2.5 centimetres long, interlock and show even when the mouth is shut.
goliath-tigerfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Goliath Tigerfish usually lives in large African rivers and lakes with strong currents.
signatureTraits: huge teeth
muscular body
fast pursuit
river power
interestingFacts: The genus name Hydrocynus is built from Greek words meaning water dog.
It belongs to the African tetras, family Alestidae, which places it in the same order as the South American piranhas.
Its range covers the Congo River system, including the Lualaba and Lake Upemba, and Lake Tanganyika.
A small fleshy fin with no rays sits on the back between the dorsal fin and the deeply forked tail.
Anglers travel to the Congo to fish for it, and it is regarded as one of the hardest freshwater game fish to land.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Goliath Tigerfish feeds on fish and other aquatic prey captured by force.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Little is recorded about what preys on this species. Crocodiles probably take some adults, and young tigerfish are probably eaten by larger predatory fish. People catch it for food.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: The daily pattern of activity and rest of this fish has not been documented.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Growth studies have not fixed a typical age; Congo Basin predators with interlocking dagger teeth lack a widely cited year schedule.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding of this species has not been studied, beyond the general fact that females release eggs into aquatic habitats during spawning. Spawning season, number of eggs and any care of the young are not known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: To the eye, sex differences are not strongly obvious outside size and breeding condition. No external mark is known that reliably separates males from females.

gopher-tortoise.spotlight: A land tortoise of the sandy uplands of the south-eastern United States. Its burrow typically runs four to five metres long and about two metres deep, holding a steady temperature and humidity through the year. A single tortoise usually keeps several burrows and moves between them over a season.
gopher-tortoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Gopher Tortoise usually lives in sandy pine flatwoods, scrub, dunes, and open dry uplands.
signatureTraits: Powerful front limbs shaped for digging deep sandy burrows
Burrows used by many other species during heat, fire, and danger
Slow grazing life that still reshapes a whole upland community
Long-lived presence that makes one home matter for decades
interestingFacts: Gopher Tortoises are considered a keystone species of the longleaf pine and sandhill uplands of the south-eastern United States.
Their burrows can shelter hundreds of other animal species over time.
They need open sunny uplands, often maintained by fire.
It is the only tortoise species native to the United States east of the Mississippi River.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Gopher Tortoise feeds on grasses, legumes, fruits, flowers, and low vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, skunks, foxes, armadillos, snakes and fire ants destroy most nests and many hatchlings, whose shells stay soft for several years. Adults are protected by the shell and a quick retreat underground, and die mainly under vehicles, from dog attacks or when land is developed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rests in deep burrows that buffer heat, cold, drought, and fire, turning shelter into a rhythm of survival for more than itself.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live 40 to 60 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in sandy nests near burrows, but hatchlings receive no direct care, so the habitat and soil inherit part of the parenting role.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males often have longer tails and more concave lower shells; females carry the future into sandy nests while both sexes engineer refuge.

gouldian-finch.spotlight: Gouldian Finch carries Small Brilliance as living color in grassland, proving a tiny seed-eater can become unforgettable when brightness, flocking, and movement work together.
gouldian-finch.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Gouldian Finches live in tropical savanna woodland and grasslands with seeding grasses and water nearby. The habitat turns small brilliance into flashes of color over dry seed country.
signatureTraits: Vivid rainbow plumage
Small seed-cracking beak
Grassland flocking
Multiple head color forms
interestingFacts: Gouldian Finches can have different head colors, including red, black, or yellow.
They feed heavily on grass seeds, often taking them straight from standing seed heads.
They are native to northern Australia, from the Kimberley across to Cape York Peninsula.
Nestlings have reflective blue-edged nodules at the gape that help parents feed them in dark hollows.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat grass seeds, especially from native grasses, and may take small insects during breeding.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include snakes, raptors, mammals, and nest raiders, while fire patterns and habitat change affect food. Flocking and quick movement help protect small brilliance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, feeding by day and moving with flocks between seed and water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live several years in the wild and longer in care. Even a small life can be memorable across repeated seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree hollows or nest sites, and both parents feed the chicks. Offspring begin hidden before joining the bright grassland movement.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually brighter than females, especially in chest and belly color. The difference supports display, while both sexes carry the small seed-eater design.

gray-four-eyed-opossum.spotlight: Gray Four-eyed Opossum teaches False Eyes through pale brow spots that change how the night reads its face. Nocturnal climbing, undergrowth searching, pouch-borne young, and a second-looking gaze make odd details useful instead of ornamental.
gray-four-eyed-opossum.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest, secondary growth, river edges, dense undergrowth, and tangled vegetation.
signatureTraits: Pale spots above the eyes that resemble a second gaze.
Nocturnal movement through low branches, vines, and forest floor cover.
Omnivorous searching that uses smell, touch, and opportunity after dark.
Marsupial pouch care that keeps early young carried close to the body.
interestingFacts: The pale marks above the eyes give this opossum its four-eyed name.
It is a marsupial, so very young offspring continue developing attached to the mother.
It moves both on the ground and in vegetation while foraging at night.
Its diet is broad, helping it use many small opportunities in tropical forests.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, insects, small vertebrates, eggs, carrion, and other small foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes, wild cats, raptors, and larger mammals can threaten them. The false-eye markings are not armor, but they add confusion to a life already protected by darkness, climbing, and quick retreat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Gray Four-eyed Opossums are nocturnal, resting hidden by day and searching after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Gray Four-eyed Opossums usually live only a few years in the wild, where predation and exposure are constant.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry very small young in the pouch, then later keep them close as they grow.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be larger. The false-eye facial pattern is a shared species signal rather than a display limited to one sex.

gray-fox.spotlight: Few members of the dog family climb trees, and this fox does so regularly. Forearms that rotate more freely than those of other canids let it hug a trunk while hooked claws grip the bark. It descends by backing down the trunk or running head first down a sloping one.
gray-fox.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Woodlands, brush, rocky slopes, farms, and edge habitats fit Gray Foxes because trees and cover create hidden routes.
signatureTraits: Grizzled salt-and-pepper grey coat on the back and sides.
Rusty orange fur on the neck, flanks and legs.
Black stripe runs along the top of the tail to a black tip.
White throat and cheeks, with a black patch beside the muzzle.
Shorter legs and muzzle than a red fox.
interestingFacts: Its lineage is thought to be the oldest among living canids, having separated from the ancestors of other foxes, wolves and dogs several million years ago.
Dens are sometimes made in hollow trees, and some have been found several metres above the ground.
The island fox of California's Channel Islands descends from gray foxes that reached the islands thousands of years ago and became dwarfed.
A long scent gland lies along the upper side of the tail, beneath a mane of stiff black hairs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coyotes, bobcats, dogs, eagles, and humans threaten gray foxes. Climbing adds escape routes other canids rarely use.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Gray Foxes are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, moving when cover improves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild gray foxes die within a few years, and 6 to 8 years is about the upper limit. Captive animals have reached 12 or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about 53 days, females den in hidden sites and raise kits until they follow adults. Litters usually number three to five, born in spring, and the male brings food to the den. Young begin foraging with their parents at about three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in coat colour and pattern; males average slightly larger and heavier than females.

great-argus.spotlight: Great Argus teaches Eyespot Theater through eyespot-wing courtship stage. Cleared courts, huge patterned wings, patient preparation, and forest-floor performance show that display works best when the stage is ready.
great-argus.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra, borneo. Great Argus usually lives in Southeast Asian rainforest floor and low vegetation.
signatureTraits: Male wings covered in eye-like spots for courtship display
Cleared forest-floor courts prepared like stages
Long feathers that transform hidden ground into spectacle
Female camouflage that protects nesting after the performance
interestingFacts: Male Great Argus displays can look like a wall of eyespots.
The male prepares and maintains a display area.
Females choose from performances rather than shared parental care.
The forest floor becomes theater only after careful preparation.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Great Argus feeds on fallen fruit, seeds, insects, and small animals found on the forest floor.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Clouded leopards, leopard cats, civets, pythons and hawk-eagles are the likely predators of adults and chicks, though kills are seldom recorded. Alarmed birds walk or run off through the undergrowth rather than fly, and roost up in trees at night. Snaring and lowland logging are the main threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, moving quietly in forest and displaying in cleared courts, saving the spectacle for the prepared stage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Likely many years if predation is avoided; Eyespot Theater grows through repeated clearing, calling, waiting, and display.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females nest on the ground and raise chicks alone after male display, turning the theater’s result into hidden practical care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have enormous spotted wings and tails; females are smaller and cryptic, dividing display and concealment sharply.

great-blue-heron.spotlight: Great Blue Heron teaches Poise through a long body that turns stillness into one clean strike. Spear bill, folded neck, slow step, marsh posture, and sudden lunge show decisive action born from quiet control.
great-blue-heron.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Marshes, lakes, rivers, estuaries, ponds, mangroves, and wet fields fit Great Blue Herons because shallow edges let patience become a strike.
signatureTraits: Long legs and a spear-like bill suit shallow-water hunting.
The folded neck stores speed for a sudden forward strike.
Slow stalking lets the bird approach prey without wasting motion.
interestingFacts: Great Blue Herons can hunt fish, frogs, snakes, small mammals, and even birds.
They often nest in colonies called heronries, usually building stick nests high in trees near water.
Despite their size, they can stand nearly motionless for long periods.
Patches of powder-down feathers on the chest crumble into a fine dust that herons use to clean fish slime from plumage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, frogs, crayfish, insects, snakes, small mammals, and birds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, raccoons, foxes, owls, snakes, and nest predators threaten herons, eggs, or chicks. Height, colony nesting, and water distance reduce danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Blue Herons are mostly diurnal, hunting slowly through daylight and sometimes at dusk.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: More than half are thought to die in their first year. Around 15 years is often quoted for adults, and the oldest banded wild bird was at least 24.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, often in colonies, and both parents feed chicks by regurgitation. Offspring make poise practical because every clean strike becomes fuel for tall hungry young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males are often slightly larger.

great-blue-turaco.spotlight: The largest of the turacos, about 70 to 75 centimetres from bill to tail tip and close to a kilogram in weight. Turquoise-blue above with a yellow-green breast and chestnut belly, it lacks the crimson wing feathers that most other turacos flash in flight.
great-blue-turaco.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Canopy of lowland and montane rainforest, gallery forest along rivers and tall secondary growth, from Guinea east to western Kenya and south to northern Angola. It also visits forest edge, clearings with tall fruiting trees and well-wooded farmland.
signatureTraits: A tall blue-black crest stands upright on the crown.
The bill is bright yellow with a red tip.
The long tail has a broad black band near the tip.
It runs and bounds along large branches rather than flying between them.
interestingFacts: It is the only species in its genus, Corythaeola, and is usually placed apart from the other turacos in a subfamily of its own.
Seeds pass through its gut intact, so feeding parties carry the seeds of many forest trees far from the parent plant.
Pairs and family groups hold territories, yet birds from several groups will often gather peacefully in one large fruiting tree.
In Kenya it is confined to the far west of the country, chiefly Kakamega Forest and neighbouring forests.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit forms the bulk of the diet, taken from figs, umbrella trees and many other forest trees, together with a large share of leaves, buds, shoots and flowers. Small fruits are swallowed whole.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large forest raptors such as the crowned eagle are the likely predators of adults, and the open nests are exposed to monkeys, snakes and birds of prey. People hunt it for meat and for its tail feathers. A disturbed bird runs up into dense foliage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most active and vocal soon after dawn and again in the late afternoon, with a quiet spell in the midday heat. Parties roost at night high in tall trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No standard wild lifespan is published; the largest African turaco of Central forest canopy yields few banding recoveries.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Both sexes build a flimsy platform of sticks high in a tree and share the incubation of usually two eggs for about a month. Chicks clamber about the branches near the nest before they can fly and are fed by the parents for several more weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike in plumage and are similar in size; the sexes cannot be told apart in the field.

great-cormorant.spotlight: Great Cormorant teaches Deep Work through a body built to go under and return with tools that fit the depth. Strong feet, streamlined shape, hooked bill, dark plumage, and wing drying show focus that accepts recovery as part of the task.
great-cormorant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, sub_saharan_africa, east_asia, australia_oceania, north_america. Coasts, lakes, estuaries, reservoirs, rivers, cliffs, islands, and fishing waters fit Great Cormorants because they need deep feeding zones and safe resting sites.
signatureTraits: Hooked bill: the tip grips fish after underwater pursuit.
Strong swimming feet: propulsion comes from below the surface.
Wing-drying posture: recovery is part of the fishing system.
interestingFacts: Great Cormorants are widespread across Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia.
They have long been associated with human fishing traditions in some cultures.
They often sit with wings spread after repeated dives.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Almost entirely fish: bottom-living kinds such as flatfish, eels and sculpins on coasts, and whatever species are commonest in lakes and rivers. It dives from the surface, usually for less than a minute, and brings large prey up to swallow head first.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, gulls, foxes, raccoons, snakes, and human disturbance threaten colonies, eggs, or chicks. Group nesting and water access protect the work.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Cormorants are diurnal, diving through daylight and drying wings between efforts. Their rhythm is focused descent followed by visible reset.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 10 to 12 years for birds that survive to breed; the oldest ringed birds have passed 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick or seaweed nests in colonies, and both parents feed the chicks. The young grow from repeated adult trips between depth, surface, and nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may average larger.

great-curassow.spotlight: A long-tailed gamebird of the guan family, found from eastern Mexico to western Ecuador. In the breeding season the male gives a booming call so low in pitch that it is hard to place and carries far through the trees. Birds are usually met in pairs or small family parties.
great-curassow.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Great Curassows live in tropical forest floors and forest edges in Central America.
signatureTraits: Curled crest feathers
Large ground-foraging body
Fruit-heavy diet
Tree roosting
interestingFacts: It is one of the largest cracids, with adults reaching roughly 90 centimetres long.
Males are black with a yellow knob on the bill, while females can be barred, rufous, or blackish.
By eating fallen fruit and passing some seeds intact, it can help move seeds through forests.
It walks heavily but can fly to roost.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fallen fruit and seeds make up most of the diet, with insects and other small animals taken as they are found. It feeds while walking slowly, picking items from the ground, and also takes fruit from low branches.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, ocelots, large raptors and snakes take adults, chicks or eggs, and people hunt it for meat across its range. An alarmed bird gives a sharp, high whistle, then runs or flies up into the trees.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal. Foraging starts soon after dawn, and before dark the bird flies up to roost on a branch well above the ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live well over a decade, especially in care.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After pairing, females lay eggs in tree nests and care for chicks. The clutch is two large, rough-shelled white eggs, incubated for about a month. Chicks leave the nest within a day or two of hatching and can flutter up to low perches when a few days old.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are usually black with a yellow bill knob; females are more barred or rufous. The male's belly is white. Females lack the knob, occur in barred, rufous and dark forms, and have a crest banded black and white.

great-egret.spotlight: Great Egret teaches White Elegance through a tall wader whose beauty ends in a clean strike. White plumage, long neck, spear bill, slow step, and sudden flash show stillness becoming useful without losing grace.
great-egret.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. Marshes, ponds, rivers, lakes, estuaries, rice fields, mangroves, and mudflats fit Great Egrets because shallow water gives room for poise and prey.
signatureTraits: White plume presence: breeding feathers made the species historically vulnerable to hunting.
Slow wading: stillness turns shallow water into opportunity.
Spear strike: the long bill finishes the patient approach.
interestingFacts: Great Egrets were once heavily hunted for decorative plumes.
The slaughter of egrets for plumes helped inspire bird conservation movements, including early Audubon societies in the United States.
Their S-shaped neck straightens quickly during a strike.
During breeding, adults grow long lacy plumes on the back, and the bare skin near the eyes turns bright green.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, frogs, crayfish, insects, snakes, and small mammals support White Elegance because each meal rewards patience, position, and one quick strike.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, foxes, snakes, crows, gulls, and raptors threaten nests, eggs, or chicks. Colony nesting and tall trees reduce vulnerability.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Egrets are diurnal, hunting slowly in daylight and roosting in groups. Their rhythm turns white stillness into repeated precision.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most wild birds live only a few years, but banded individuals have been recorded surviving more than 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick nests, often in mixed colonies with other wading birds. Both parents feed the chicks, making graceful hunting directly serve the nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though breeding plumes and courtship displays appear seasonally. White Elegance is shared by both sexes rather than held in one ornamental sex.

great-frigatebird.spotlight: Great Frigatebird teaches Lift through a seabird spending the air before spending itself. Huge wings, forked tail, ocean soaring, kleptoparasitic chases, and red throat display make efficiency dramatic rather than dull.
great-frigatebird.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean, coral_triangle. Tropical oceans, islands, coastal cliffs, mangroves, and open sky above warm seas fit Great Frigatebirds because Lift depends on rising air and wide space.
signatureTraits: Extremely long wings and low wing loading for efficient soaring.
Forked tail used for agile steering over tropical oceans.
Male red throat pouch inflated during courtship display.
Ocean lifestyle that relies on air mastery because feathers are not suited to long swimming rests.
interestingFacts: Great Frigatebirds can remain aloft for long periods with very little flapping.
Males inflate a red throat pouch to attract mates.
They often take food from the surface or chase other seabirds for meals.
Unlike many seabirds, frigatebirds avoid sitting on the water for long because their feathers are not highly waterproof.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying fish, squid, fish scraps, surface prey, and stolen meals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks face rats, cats, crabs, storms, and colony disturbance; adults face storms, starvation, and human impacts. Efficient soaring saves energy but does not remove ocean risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Frigatebirds are active by day and can soar for long periods, even resting partly while airborne.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Long-lived: ringing records are reported to show some birds surviving more than 30 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single egg in island or coastal colony nests, and parental care can be prolonged.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the inflatable red throat pouch, while females lack it and often have different chest patterning.

great-gray-owl.spotlight: Great Gray Owl teaches Deep Listening through a huge-faced hunter hearing life hidden under snow. Facial disc, silent wings, patient perch, plunge strike, and boreal winter make the strongest action begin with invisible information.
great-gray-owl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia. Boreal forests, bog edges, meadows, forest openings, burned areas, and snowy northern landscapes fit Great Gray Owls because hidden prey and listening perches meet there.
signatureTraits: Large facial disc funnels sound toward the ears for precise listening.
Silent flight lets it approach without warning prey.
Can locate and plunge onto prey hidden beneath snow.
Huge appearance comes mostly from feathers rather than heavy body mass.
interestingFacts: Great Gray Owls are among the tallest owls, but not the heaviest.
They rely heavily on hearing to hunt voles and other small mammals.
They often use old nests built by other large birds.
Their pale gray pattern blends with boreal forest and winter light.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Voles, mice, shrews, pocket gophers, and other small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Great horned owls, goshawks, martens, ravens, foxes, starvation, and habitat loss can threaten owls, eggs, or chicks. Listening helps hunting, but nesting still needs shelter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Gray Owls are often crepuscular but may hunt by day or night, especially in northern conditions. Their rhythm follows sound, snow, and prey movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Ringed wild birds have lived well over a decade, though most die much younger. Captive owls have lived considerably longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females incubate eggs in reused nests or platforms while males provide food. Chicks depend on adults that can hear enough prey to feed a growing family through harsh country.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males, as in many raptors. The size difference supports nesting and prey demands, while both sexes share the deep-listening design.

great-hornbill.spotlight: One of the largest hornbills, about 1 to 1.3 metres long, living in tall forest from the Western Ghats and Himalayan foothills to the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra. The yellow of its bill, casque and neck is a cosmetic: the bird wipes on tinted oil from the preen gland at the base of the tail. The casque itself is hollow and light.
great-hornbill.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Mature rainforest with huge nesting trees fits because fidelity needs cavities big enough to become a living wall.
signatureTraits: White tail crossed by a single black band
Black wings with a broad pale bar and white trailing edge
Casque concave on top, ending in two points at the front
Black face and chin against a pale neck
Loud, barking calls that carry across valleys
interestingFacts: Males fight in flight by crashing their casques together, a behaviour known as aerial casque-butting.
It tosses a fig into the air and catches it at the back of the throat, because its tongue is too short to move food along the bill.
As in other hornbills, the first two neck vertebrae are fused, which helps to carry the weight of the bill.
Outside the breeding season, dozens of birds may gather at one fruiting tree or at a shared roost.
It is the state bird of both Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh in India.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly fruit, especially figs, plus small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, snakes, martens, humans, and loss of nesting trees threaten hornbills, making secure cavities and committed provisioning essential.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Hornbills are diurnal, moving through the canopy by day and roosting in trees while the sealed nest remains guarded.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Great Hornbills can live for decades, giving long pair bonds and repeated nesting seasons time to make fidelity visible.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female seals herself inside a tree cavity with the eggs and chicks while the male feeds them through a narrow slit.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with red eyes, while females often have paler eyes, but both roles make the sealed-nest partnership work.

great-horned-owl.spotlight: Great Horned Owl teaches Dominion through a night predator that wears its crown in silence. Ear tufts, heavy talons, broad wings, deep hoot, and high perch show authority that can wait in darkness without chasing every disturbance.
great-horned-owl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Forests, deserts, wetlands, farms, cliffs, suburbs, and city parks fit Great Horned Owls because their dominion is flexible. They rule from any perch that gives cover, height, and prey.
signatureTraits: Prominent ear tufts create the horned silhouette behind the name.
Powerful talons allow it to take a wide range of prey.
High perches and nocturnal hunting turn darkness into territory.
interestingFacts: Great Horned Owls can prey on skunks because their sense of smell is limited compared with mammals.
They often reuse nests built by hawks, crows, or other large birds.
Their deep, soft hoots are important territorial signals, and mated pairs often call back and forth in duets.
The feather tufts on the head are not ears; the real ear openings sit hidden at the sides of the facial disc.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rabbits, rodents, skunks, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and even other raptors.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults face few predators, but eggs and young may be threatened by raccoons, foxes, crows, ravens, and larger raptors. Fierce nest defense protects the crown early.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Horned Owls are nocturnal, calling and hunting through darkness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many die in their first year. Survivors commonly live 10 years or more, the oldest banded wild bird was at least 28, and captive owls have lived longer still.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in reused nests, tree cavities, cliffs, or platforms, and chicks depend on fierce defense and steady prey. Offspring make dominion protective, not just intimidating.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are larger than males, while males often have lower-pitched territorial calls.

great-kiskadee.spotlight: Great Kiskadee teaches Boldness through a flycatcher that announces itself before the strike. Its loud call, yellow belly, strong bill, and visible perch-hunting show readiness becoming presence, not by hiding skill but by making the method obvious.
great-kiskadee.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Open woodland, river edges, gardens, parks, farms, towns, and watersides fit Great Kiskadees because they need exposed perches and varied prey.
signatureTraits: Loud calls announce presence across open edges and watersides.
A strong bill supports a varied diet beyond tiny flying insects.
Visible perch hunting turns readiness into quick outward action.
interestingFacts: Great Kiskadees are flycatchers but eat more than flying insects.
They are common around water, gardens, farms, and towns in much of their range.
Their bold calls make them easy to notice before they are seen.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, small fish, frogs, lizards, fruit, and other small foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, snakes, cats, nest predators, and larger birds keep pressure on adults and young. The kiskadee’s loudness and aggression help defend space before threats get comfortable.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Kiskadees are diurnal, calling and hunting when visibility is high. Their day belongs to clear signals, visible perches, and quick moves from readiness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Great Kiskadees can live across many breeding seasons when territories and food remain available. Boldness becomes useful because the same exposed stations can be reused and defended.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build bulky nests and feed chicks with insects and other small prey. Offspring make the loud perch strategy practical because bold adults must repeatedly convert visibility into food delivery.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike: both have the black-and-white striped head, rufous edges to the wings and bright yellow underparts, and both can raise a partly hidden yellow crown patch.

great-potoo.spotlight: Great Potoo teaches Branch Illusion through a huge night bird disappearing by becoming a broken log in daylight. Bark-like plumage, rigid stillness, slit-eyed watching, and nocturnal insect hunting turn fixed shape into freedom.
great-potoo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Forest edges, mature trees, tropical woodland, plantations, and open forest gaps.
signatureTraits: Bark-colored plumage that blends with dead branches and trunks.
Rigid upright daytime posture that completes the branch illusion.
Huge eyes suited to night hunting after the disguise phase ends.
Large mouth and aerial hunting style for catching nocturnal prey.
interestingFacts: Great Potoos often rest upright on broken branches during the day.
They can narrow the eyes while still monitoring movement through small eyelid slits.
Their haunting calls are part of tropical night soundscapes.
They nest with very little structure, often using a stump or branch surface.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Large moths, beetles, insects, and sometimes small vertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Monkeys, snakes, raptors, owls, and nest predators can threaten eggs or young. The branch disguise reduces daytime attention, making stillness a real defensive strategy.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Potoos are nocturnal hunters and daytime statues. Their rhythm is vanish as wood, wait out the light, then open huge eyes and mouth into the night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Field lifespan is unpublished; motionless daytime mimics frozen on broken Neotropical branches are almost never ringed.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single egg on a branch stump or bare surface rather than in a complex nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar in appearance. The shared disguise matters most because both parents and young depend on looking like part of the tree.

great-skua.spotlight: Great Skua teaches Kleptoparasitism through a storm-coast bird bold enough to turn pressure into food. Strong wings, seabird chases, fierce nest defense, and meal-raiding show that boldness can become a strategy in harsh air.
great-skua.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic. Northern islands, moorland breeding grounds, sea cliffs, open ocean, and stormy coasts.
signatureTraits: Aggressive food-stealing behavior from other seabirds.
Powerful flight in rough coastal and ocean conditions.
Fierce territorial defense around nesting sites.
Opportunistic feeding that includes fish, chicks, carrion, and stolen meals.
interestingFacts: Great Skuas are known for harassing other seabirds until they drop food.
They defend nesting territories boldly, even against larger intruders.
They breed in northern coastal and island habitats.
Their feeding strategy mixes hunting, scavenging, and stealing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, seabird eggs, chicks, carrion, offal, and stolen catches.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large gulls, eagles, humans, storms, food shortages, and nest disturbance threaten skuas or chicks. Fierce defense protects the breeding ground, but harsh seas keep the strategy risky.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great Skuas are diurnal around colonies and feeding areas, active when other seabirds are moving.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Great Skuas can live for decades. Kleptoparasitism becomes a long-learned strategy because timing, target choice, and territory knowledge improve with age.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on ground nests, and both parents defend chicks aggressively.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though size can vary.

great-white-pelican.spotlight: Great White Pelican teaches Scoop Strategy through a bird whose giant pouch turns group effort into one clean motion. Broad wings, cooperative fish herding, and a flexible bill make the right tool multiply teamwork.
great-white-pelican.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia, south_asia. Lakes, deltas, marshes, lagoons, shallow wetlands, and large rivers.
signatureTraits: Huge bill pouch used to scoop fish from shallow water
Cooperative group feeding that herds fish into reach
Broad wings for soaring between lakes and wetlands
Large colonial bird body built around shared water resources
interestingFacts: Great White Pelicans often feed cooperatively in groups.
Their bill pouch is used as a scoop, not as a permanent storage bag.
They nest colonially on islands, reedbeds, or safe wetland sites.
Their broad wings let them travel efficiently between feeding areas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish are central, with occasional amphibians or aquatic prey taken.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, gulls, jackals, foxes, monitor lizards, humans, disturbance, and wetland loss threaten eggs, chicks, or colonies. Group nesting helps, but crowded success depends on safe water.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Great White Pelicans are diurnal, feeding and traveling by day, often resting communally.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Zoo birds have passed 30 years. Wild lifespans are less well documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in colonial nests, and both parents help feed chicks with regurgitated fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be larger.

great-white-shark.spotlight: Great White Shark is known for dorsal silhouette, sensory range, ambush speed, and ocean dominance.
great-white-shark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Temperate and subtropical coastal waters, offshore routes, seal colonies, and productive marine edges worldwide.
signatureTraits: Iconic dorsal fin
Countershaded body
Burst attack speed
Broad triangular teeth with serrated edges
Crescent tail with upper and lower lobes nearly equal in size
interestingFacts: Great whites can breach when attacking prey from below.
They use electroreception through jelly-filled pores on the snout to sense the weak electric fields of animals.
Tagged individuals travel long distances, including one female that swam from South Africa to Australia and back.
Females give birth to live pups, which feed on unfertilized eggs inside the mother before birth.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on fish, rays, seals, sea lions, carrion, and other marine prey depending on age and size.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few predators, though orcas can kill them in some regions.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Does not sleep like land mammals; it alternates active swimming with lower-activity periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for several decades, with some estimates exceeding 50 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young after internal development; pups are independent at birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females often grow larger than males.

greater-adjutant.spotlight: Greater Adjutant teaches Messy Service through a giant stork willing to do valuable work that is not pretty. Its bare head, huge bill, scavenging habit, and wetland-refuse feeding show that cleanup can be ecological care.
greater-adjutant.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Wetlands, river floodplains, dumps, carcass sites, fish ponds, and nesting trees fit Greater Adjutants because messy service happens where waste and water meet.
signatureTraits: Huge scavenging stork with bare head and neck pouch
Feeds at wetlands, carcasses, and refuse sites
Massive bill suited to messy food handling
Rare colonial nester dependent on tall trees
interestingFacts: Greater Adjutants are among the largest storks, standing roughly one and a half metres tall.
Their bare head helps them feed in messy places.
Some important populations live close to human communities and waste sites.
They nest colonially in tall trees, and Assam in India holds most of the world's breeding colonies.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carrion, fish, amphibians, reptiles, refuse, and discarded food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks can face crows, raptors, snakes, and tree loss, while adults face human disturbance and habitat loss. Tall colony trees protect breeding.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Adjutants are diurnal, soaring, scavenging, and returning to colonies by day. Their rhythm follows heat, waste, wetlands, and service.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is poorly documented: no reliable figures appear to have been published for wild or captive birds of this species.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, and both parents help incubate and feed the chicks. Young depend on messy food gathered by adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be larger. The shared form matters more than ornament because the role is service.

greater-bamboo-lemur.spotlight: The largest of the bamboo lemurs, at about 2.5 kg, and one of the rarest lemurs in Madagascar. Nearly all its food comes from giant bamboo. In the dry season it rips open woody stems to reach the pith inside, and when the rains bring new shoots it switches to those.
greater-bamboo-lemur.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Humid forest with dense stands of large woody bamboo in eastern Madagascar. Groups also use degraded forest and bamboo thickets beside farmland. Well-documented sites include Ranomafana National Park, Kianjavato and the Torotorofotsy wetlands near Andasibe.
signatureTraits: White tufts on the ears
Grey-brown coat with an olive or reddish tinge
Broad, blunt muzzle on a rounded head
Clings upright to bamboo stems and leaps between them
interestingFacts: It was feared extinct for much of the twentieth century until living animals were found again in south-eastern Madagascar.
Subfossil bones show that it once lived across much of Madagascar, including the far north and the central highlands.
Groups of more than 20 animals have been recorded, larger than is usual for other bamboo lemurs.
Feeding groups leave the ground littered with shredded stems and strips of bamboo.
It is listed as Critically Endangered and has appeared repeatedly on lists of the world's 25 most endangered primates.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Bamboo shoots, pith, leaves, and tough bamboo parts.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fossas, raptors, snakes, and humans threaten lemurs, while habitat loss removes the bamboo itself. Specialization becomes risky when the one food-world shrinks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active by day and rest in forest cover. The rhythm fits Bamboo Specialization because feeding is repeated, focused, and tied to the daily search for usable bamboo.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live into the teens or beyond in protected settings, making specialization a long commitment to one difficult resource.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born around the start of the rainy season after a gestation thought to be about five months. In its first weeks the mother is reported to carry it in her mouth and leave it parked in dense vegetation while she feeds.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are alike in size and coat colour and are hard to tell apart in the field.

greater-bilby.spotlight: Greater Bilby teaches Desert Provision through a long-eared marsupial doing future-work under cool darkness. Spiral burrows, strong claws, seed digging, insect hunting, and night foraging make survival a quiet preparation.
greater-bilby.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Sandy deserts, spinifex grasslands, acacia shrublands, and arid plains.
signatureTraits: Long ears for hearing and heat release in arid country
Strong foreclaws for burrows and digging food from soil
Nocturnal foraging that avoids desert heat
Backward-opening pouch that protects young from soil while digging
interestingFacts: Greater Bilbies dig multiple burrows and may move among them.
Their digging can help turn soil and influence desert ecosystems.
They are nocturnal, avoiding the hottest parts of the day.
Their pouch opens backward so it does not fill with dirt while digging.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, bulbs, fungi, termites, ants, beetles, larvae, and other small foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, cats, dingoes, raptors, habitat change, and competition from introduced animals threaten bilbies. Burrows, night movement, and alert ears are defenses that protect the quiet provider.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Bilbies are nocturnal, resting in deep burrows by day and working through cooler darkness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Greater Bilbies often live several years, but survival depends heavily on predator pressure and habitat.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry young in a backward-facing pouch and raise them from the safety of burrows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger than females, but both sexes share the long ears, digging claws, and night-work design that carry the lesson.

greater-bird-of-paradise.spotlight: Largest of the plumed birds-of-paradise, it lives in lowland and hill forest of south-western New Guinea and the Aru Islands. Males gather in traditional trees high above the ground, calling together and competing side by side while females look on. A few males obtain most of the matings.
greater-bird-of-paradise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, australia_oceania. Greater Bird-of-paradise usually lives in New Guinea rainforest canopy and display trees.
signatureTraits: golden flank plumes
display perch
courtship dance
forest stage
interestingFacts: The name apoda means footless: early trade skins reached Europe with the legs removed, and the birds were believed to float through the air for life.
Alfred Russel Wallace watched the displays in the Aru Islands in 1857 and published one of the first accounts by a naturalist.
Several dozen birds were released on Little Tobago in the Caribbean between 1909 and 1912; the colony lasted for decades before dying out.
Two central tail feathers are reduced to long bare wires that trail behind the male.
Loud, repeated wauk calls from displaying males carry a long way through the forest.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Greater Bird-of-paradise feeds on fruit, insects, and small forest animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few attacks have been recorded. Birds of prey, tree snakes and climbing mammals are presumed to rob nests, which the female places in a tree fork. Plume hunting fed a large export trade into the early twentieth century and continues for local dress, and logging removes the trees males use.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Bird-of-paradise is diurnal, with males displaying in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long greater birds-of-paradise live in the wild has not been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female alone builds the nest, incubates and feeds the young; males take no part. Clutches are small, usually one or two eggs, and nesting in the wild is poorly documented.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are ornate with plumes; females are plainer brown. The male has a yellow crown and nape and an emerald-green throat, and is the larger bird. The female is maroon-brown all over, without barring.

greater-bulldog-bat.spotlight: Flying low over calm water at night, this large bat of the American tropics picks out the ripples and fins of fish at the surface by echolocation. It then rakes its long-clawed hind feet through the water to gaff them.
greater-bulldog-bat.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Greater Bulldog Bats usually live in tropical rivers, lagoons, mangroves, and coastal waters.
signatureTraits: Full, drooping lips and a cleft upper lip give a bulldog look.
Long legs and a long calcar stiffen a wide tail membrane.
A pale stripe runs down the middle of the back.
Pointed ears and a plain muzzle with no nose-leaf.
Roosts and the bats themselves carry a strong musky odour.
interestingFacts: Fish are chewed on the wing and stored in cheek pouches, so the bat can keep hunting before it lands to finish eating.
If it falls into the water it swims competently, using its wings as oars, and can take off again from the surface.
Together with the lesser bulldog bat it makes up the whole family Noctilionidae.
It is often called the fishing bat, one of the few bats that regularly catch fish.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on small fish plus aquatic insects and crustaceans.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators are documented. Owls and other raptors may catch bats leaving the roost, and snakes can reach roosts in hollow trees and caves. Disturbance of roost sites and pollution of the waters it fishes are the wider concerns.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal. Groups spend the day in hollow trees, sea caves and rock crevices, and leave around dusk to hunt over nearby water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is poorly documented. Marked animals have been followed for several years, and a captive bat is reported to have lived about 11 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single pup is born each year. It stays in the roost until it can fly, at roughly a month old. Females roost together in stable groups that are usually attended by one adult male.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and may differ in fur tone.

greater-flamingo.spotlight: Greater Flamingo teaches Lake Filtration through a tall pink bird turning muddy water into nourishment. Bent bill, long legs, saline lakes, and patient straining make grace practical because it knows what to filter.
greater-flamingo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east, europe, south_asia. Shallow saline lakes, alkaline wetlands, lagoons, mudflats, and coastal marshes.
signatureTraits: Specialized bent bill used upside-down for filter feeding
Long legs that open access to shallow saline water
Pink color tied to pigments in food
Large flocks that turn harsh lakes into shared feeding grounds
interestingFacts: Greater Flamingos get their pink color from carotenoid pigments in their diet.
They filter tiny organisms from water with specialized bill structures.
They often gather in very large flocks, sometimes numbering tens of thousands of birds at favored lakes.
They build mud mound nests in shallow wetland areas.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Algae, brine shrimp, small crustaceans, mollusks, and aquatic microorganisms.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, foxes, jackals, gulls, humans, water changes, and breeding-site disturbance threaten adults, eggs, or chicks. Flocks help, but filtration depends on healthy water chemistry.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Flamingos are active by day and night depending on food, disturbance, and climate.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Greater Flamingos can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single egg on a mud mound, and both parents feed the chick with crop milk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males are often larger.

greater-glider.spotlight: Greater Glider teaches Falling Flight through a quiet possum turning descent into distance. Skin sail, long tail, eucalyptus diet, hollow dependence, and night glides make falling a designed crossing rather than a failure.
greater-glider.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Tall eucalyptus forests, mature woodland, hollow-bearing trees, and connected canopy.
signatureTraits: Large gliding membrane stretched between limbs
Silent nocturnal movement between eucalyptus trees
Specialized feeding on eucalyptus leaves
Dependence on tree hollows for daytime shelter
interestingFacts: Greater Gliders can glide long distances between trees.
They feed mainly on eucalyptus leaves, a tough specialist diet.
They are nocturnal and spend days sheltering in tree hollows.
They do not flap like birds; they steer a controlled glide.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eucalyptus leaves and buds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, pythons, quolls, cats, foxes, fire, logging, and hollow loss threaten Greater Gliders. Gliding helps escape, but the true defense is a connected canopy with safe hollows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Gliders are nocturnal, resting in hollows by day and gliding to feed at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild animals are thought to live up to about 15 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise a single joey in the pouch and later in dens or hollows.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar in size and build and are hard to tell apart in the field. Coat colour ranges from sooty dark grey to pale cream, but these colour forms occur in both sexes.

greater-grison.spotlight: A long, low relative of the weasels, the greater grison hunts on the ground with its nose down, travelling in quick zigzags and stopping to stretch up its neck and sniff the air. It is seen alone, in pairs or in small groups, which may be females with nearly grown young.
greater-grison.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Forests, savannas, grasslands, scrub, river edges, and burrows fit Greater Grisons because they hunt through cover and ground routes.
signatureTraits: Grizzled grey back and crown above a black face, throat and legs.
White stripe crosses the forehead and runs down each side of the neck.
Small, rounded ears set low on a flat head.
Short, bushy grey tail.
interestingFacts: When threatened it can release a strong-smelling musk from glands beneath the tail.
Although it ranges from southern Mexico to Brazil and Bolivia, it is seldom seen, and much of what is known comes from captive animals and camera traps.
Adults weigh roughly 1.5 to 3.5 kilograms, with a head and body about half a metre long.
It has been reported sheltering in hollow logs, among tree roots and in burrows dug by other animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, and fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas, large raptors, snakes, and humans can threaten them. Boldness, speed, scent, and cover help reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Grisons are mostly diurnal to crepuscular, moving low and fast.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not documented in the wild. Captive animals have lived for around 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding in the wild is poorly studied. Litters of one to four have been recorded after a gestation of about 40 days, and females raise kits in protected burrows or cavities.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes share the same grizzled grey back, black face and white head stripe; males are somewhat larger and heavier than females.

greater-kudu.spotlight: Greater Kudu teaches Spiral Power through an antelope whose elegance never wastes itself. Twisting horns, striped camouflage, tall ears, and brush-country grace make power quiet, controlled, and difficult to catch.
greater-kudu.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Woodland, bushveld, thickets, rocky hills, riverine cover, and savanna edges.
signatureTraits: Huge spiral horns in males used for display and contests.
Vertical white stripes that break up the body in woodland cover.
Large ears for detecting danger in dense brush.
Graceful high-legged movement through thickets and woodland.
interestingFacts: Male Greater Kudus have some of the most dramatic spiral horns among antelope.
Their stripes help camouflage them in broken light and brush.
They are strong jumpers despite their large size.
They browse on leaves and shoots more than they graze open grass.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, pods, flowers, fruits, vines, and shrubs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, leopards, hyenas, wild dogs, humans, and drought threaten kudus. Camouflage, ears, jumping, and brush retreat protect them, making power subtle rather than loud.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Kudus are often active in early morning, late afternoon, and night in hot or disturbed areas.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Usually 7 to 8 years in the wild, with some reaching about 15; more than 20 years has been recorded in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to calves that hide for early protection before joining the mother more openly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and carry spiral horns, while females are hornless. This sex difference is central: the horns make power visible, while the species as a whole still depends on brush-wise grace.

greater-roadrunner.spotlight: Greater Roadrunner teaches Pursuit through a desert bird that turns harsh ground into hunting ground. Long legs, quick turns, raised crest, strong bill, and ground chase behavior show speed with purpose, not motion for show.
greater-roadrunner.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Desert scrub, chaparral, open woodland, thornbush, roadsides, and dry grasslands fit Roadrunners because prey is scattered across hot open ground.
signatureTraits: Long legs and quick turns support ground pursuit across desert and scrub.
A strong bill handles lizards, insects, snakes, and other active prey.
Morning sunning helps warm the body before high-speed hunting.
interestingFacts: Greater Roadrunners are cuckoos, despite their ground-running lifestyle.
They can prey on venomous scorpions and small snakes.
They often prefer running to flying when escaping or hunting.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Lizards, insects, snakes, scorpions, rodents, birds, eggs, and fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coyotes, hawks, raccoons, snakes, cats, and larger predators threaten adults, eggs, or young. Speed, cover, and alertness keep pursuit from becoming exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Roadrunners are diurnal, often warming themselves in the morning before hunting. Their rhythm uses sun, speed, and ground familiarity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Few figures exist for wild birds; the oldest known banded roadrunner was about 7 years old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs build nests in shrubs or low trees, and both parents help feed the young. Offspring make pursuit practical because quick hunting must become steady delivery of insects, reptiles, and small prey.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be slightly larger.

greater-siren.spotlight: Greater Siren teaches Aquatic Simplicity through an eel-like salamander keeping gills and dropping what it does not need. External gills, tiny forelimbs, no hind legs, and swamp life make simplicity adaptive, not incomplete.
greater-siren.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Shallow, warm, still or slow fresh water on the south-eastern coastal plain of the United States: swamps, ditches, ponds, marshes and canals with soft mud bottoms and dense submerged or floating vegetation.
signatureTraits: External gills retained into adulthood for aquatic breathing.
Eel-like salamander body with tiny forelimbs and no hind limbs.
Muddy wetland life built around hiding, swimming, and burrowing.
Ability to survive difficult wetland conditions by simplifying the body plan.
interestingFacts: Greater Sirens are salamanders, even though they look eel-like.
They keep external gills as adults, a trait known as paedomorphosis.
They lack hind limbs entirely, having only a pair of small front legs.
They can burrow into mud when wetlands become harsh or dry.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, snails, insects, crustaceans, algae, and aquatic plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, snakes, wading birds, turtles, mammals, and drought threaten sirens. Burrowing into mud helps survival, proving that simplicity can include hidden resilience.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Greater Sirens are mostly nocturnal and secretive, often active in muddy water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive sirens without hind limbs have lived about twenty-five years (AnAge); wild ages in coastal plain swamps stay poorly known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in aquatic or muddy protected sites, where young begin life already tied to water.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are not usually dramatic from a distance. The shared body plan matters most because the whole species lesson is about aquatic fit, not display.

green-anaconda.spotlight: Green Anaconda teaches Setting Fit through a huge body made easier by water. River buoyancy, ambush patience, eyes high on the head, and crushing coils show that great strength works best where the setting carries it.
green-anaconda.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Swamps, slow rivers, flooded forests, marshes, oxbow lakes, and wetlands.
signatureTraits: Massive semi-aquatic body supported by river and swamp buoyancy.
Eyes and nostrils positioned for low-profile water watching.
Ambush constriction strategy near edges and shallows.
Strong swimming that makes heavy strength fluid.
interestingFacts: Green Anacondas are among the heaviest snakes in the world.
They are far more comfortable and efficient in water than on open dry land.
Females are typically much larger than males, sometimes weighing several times as much.
They give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, birds, capybaras, caimans, turtles, mammals, and other wetland animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, caimans, large birds for young, humans, and habitat disturbance threaten anacondas. Water, size, concealment, and patience reduce risk, but the setting remains the real ally.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Green Anacondas are often crepuscular or nocturnal, spending long periods hidden in water or vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Green Anacondas can live for decades in suitable conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young, and newborns must immediately hide, swim, and hunt at small scale.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are dramatically larger than males, making sex difference central to the species.

green-iguana.spotlight: Green Iguana teaches Recharge through a tree-dwelling lizard that receives strength before spending it. Basking posture, green body, dewlap, claws, tail, and shade-water movement show energy returning through the warmth it was built to need.
green-iguana.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forests, riverbanks, mangroves, gardens, canopy edges, and trees over water fit Green Iguanas because sun, shade, leaves, and escape routes must stay close.
signatureTraits: Sun basking: body heat is gathered before feeding and movement.
Dewlap display: the throat fan helps signal, thermoregulate, and communicate.
Tree-water escape: climbing and dropping into water create multiple exits.
interestingFacts: Green Iguanas are mostly herbivorous as adults, feeding largely on leaves, flowers, and fruit.
They can use their tails defensively like a whip.
They often sleep on branches above water or safe drop routes.
A pale scale on top of the head, called the parietal eye, senses light and helps them notice overhead shadows.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, flowers, fruit, and tender plant material.
