It kills or drives off foxes and mongooses in its territory, which may leave more rabbits for itself.
In 2024 the IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable after the population passed 2,000 animals.
Kittens fight fiercely at around six to eight weeks old, and one is sometimes killed by a sibling.
Females often give birth in hollow cork oak trunks and move the kittens between several dens.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly European rabbits, with some birds and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Humans, dogs, disease, prey collapse, road deaths, and habitat loss threaten Iberian Lynx, making rabbit-rich scrubland essential.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Iberian Lynx are often crepuscular and nocturnal, hunting when rabbits are available and cover helps close the final distance.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live around 10 to 13 years, with survival tied closely to territory quality, prey supply, and human pressure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females den in cover and raise kittens on rabbit-rich territory.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger, adult males weighing roughly 11 to 14 kilograms against about 8 to 10 for females. Otherwise the sexes look alike, with the same coat and ear tufts.

ibisbill.spotlight: Ibisbill teaches River Precision through curved-bill stone probing. Fast mountain water, gravel bars, hidden invertebrates, and a long curved bill turn survival into exact searching between stones.
ibisbill.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Ibisbill usually lives in fast stony rivers, mountain streams, gravel bars, and cold valleys.
signatureTraits: Long downcurved red bill built for probing between stones
Gray body and dark markings that blend with river gravel
Mountain-stream specialization in fast cold water
Quiet solitary or paired feeding on narrow river edges
interestingFacts: Ibisbills are the only species in their family.
Their eggs and nests can blend with gravel bars.
They feed by probing where water hides small prey under stones.
The bird looks unusual because its whole body is tuned to a very specific river job.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ibisbill feeds on aquatic insect larvae, small invertebrates, and prey probed from stones.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators are poorly recorded; foxes, crows and birds of prey probably take eggs and chicks on open shingle. Flooding, gravel extraction, damming and the disturbance of river bars by people and livestock are the better-documented dangers to nests.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, resting on stones or banks near feeding territories, matching its life to cold water clarity and moving gravel.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long ibisbills live has not been recorded.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Pairs nest in gravel scrapes near rivers where eggs match the stones, making camouflage an extension of the riverbed itself.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, making bill shape and river precision the defining signal rather than ornament.

impala.spotlight: Impala teaches Elastic Escape through a herd body built for sudden space. Long legs, high leaps, sharp turns, alert ears, and synchronized movement show escape as rhythm, not panic.
impala.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, light woodland, bushveld, and grassland edges fit Impalas because they need grazing, browsing, cover, and open room for leaping away.
signatureTraits: Elastic leaping: high jumps and sharp turns disrupt predators.
Herd rhythm: escape works through many bodies moving together.
Mixed feeding: grazing and browsing let the animal adjust to seasonal food.
interestingFacts: Impalas can leap impressively high and far during escape.
Males hold territories or harems during the breeding season.
They switch between grazing and browsing depending on conditions.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, leaves, shoots, herbs, and shrubs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, leopards, cheetahs, wild dogs, hyenas, jackals, crocodiles, and eagles pressure impalas. Herd alertness and explosive leaping spread confusion into the chase.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Impalas feed mostly by day and around cooler periods, resting when heat rises. Their rhythm balances feeding with readiness for sudden escape.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Impalas often live around a decade in the wild, though predation keeps many lives shorter. Survival depends on turning every year of herd experience into quicker escape decisions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to calves that must stand, hide, and later join nursery groups. Offspring survival depends on timing birth with food, cover, and herd protection.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry lyre-shaped horns and compete for breeding access, while females are hornless. The herd’s escape rhythm is shared, but male display and contest shape the breeding season.

inca-tern.spotlight: The Inca Tern is signature made functional: the white moustache is memorable, but it travels with real cliff-flight skill over cold Pacific water.
inca-tern.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america, south_pacific. Inca terns live along rocky Pacific coasts, cliffs, islands, and guano ledges of Peru and Chile.
signatureTraits: White moustache-like facial plumes
Dark slate-gray body
Red bill and feet
Agile coastal flight
interestingFacts: Inca terns are strongly tied to the Humboldt Current coast.
They nest in crevices, burrows, and guano-covered ledges.
Their facial plumes are part of the adult display look.
They feed by diving or picking fish from productive cold waters.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat small fish and other marine prey from cold coastal waters.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators and threats include gulls, skuas, rats, cats, and disturbance at nesting colonies. Their cliff nesting shows that a memorable mark still needs a difficult, protected stage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active by day, flying, foraging, calling, and returning to colony ledges to rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented; a figure of around 14 years is often quoted but rests on limited data.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay one or two eggs in sheltered crevices or cavities. Chicks begin life hidden in rough coastal architecture, where the parents’ bright marks return with food.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, both carrying the moustached signature. The point is shared identity: the mark belongs to the species, not only one sex.

indian-muntjac.spotlight: Indian Muntjac teaches Forest Alarm through a small deer whose bark turns dense cover into a warning system. Short antlers, tusks in males, solitary movement, and sharp calls make voice protective.
indian-muntjac.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Dense forest, secondary woodland, bamboo, plantations, scrub, and ravines.
signatureTraits: Loud bark-like alarm calls in dense cover
Small deer body suited to forest edges and thickets
Males with short antlers and tusk-like canine teeth
Solitary or pair-based movement through vegetation
interestingFacts: Indian Muntjacs are often called barking deer because of their alarm call.
Males can have small antlers and elongated canine teeth.
Their small size helps them move through dense forest cover.
The bark can continue repeatedly when danger is suspected.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, fruit, seeds, grasses, bark, and fallen plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tigers, leopards, dholes, pythons, crocodiles, raptors for fawns, dogs, and humans threaten them. Barking warns before distance closes, making voice a boundary around a small body.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Indian Muntjacs are often crepuscular or nocturnal, though active by day in safer areas. Their rhythm follows cover, quiet, and the need to raise alarm when the forest changes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive animals have lived about 17 years. Wild muntjac face heavy predation and are thought seldom to pass 10.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small fawns that hide in cover while they grow.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry antlers and tusk-like canines, while females usually lack antlers.

indian-peafowl.spotlight: Indian Peafowl teaches Magnificence through a body that opens its gift fully in the light. The male’s train, eye-spots, fan display, shimmer, and vibration turn attraction into a visual identity that cannot be half-shown.
indian-peafowl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Open forest, scrub, farmland edges, palace grounds, villages, and parklands fit Indian Peafowl because display needs ground space, roosting trees, and nearby cover. Magnificence works best where stage and refuge meet.
signatureTraits: Male train feathers form a huge fan used in courtship display.
Eye-spots and shimmering color turn movement into visual attraction.
Tree roosting keeps a ground-displaying bird safer at night.
interestingFacts: The famous train is made of elongated upper tail coverts, not the true tail feathers.
Peafowl roost in trees despite spending much time on the ground.
Peahens choose among displaying males, which fan their trains and shake them so the feathers rattle and shimmer.
The Indian Peafowl is the national bird of India, where it is protected by law.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grains, shoots, fruit, insects, small reptiles, and other small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, dogs, jackals, pythons, mongooses, raptors, and nest predators pressure peafowl to stay alert despite their ornament. The train is magnificent, but survival still depends on roosting, alarm calls, and cover.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Indian Peafowl are active by day, foraging, calling, and displaying in light, then roosting high in trees at night. Their rhythm saves the full fan for visible hours.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild birds are usually put at around 10 to 15 years, though few have been followed for life; well-kept captive birds commonly reach 20 or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in ground nests and raise peachicks that must follow, hide, and feed soon after hatching. Offspring keep the display honest because visual glory still has to lead to survival on the ground.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex difference is central: males carry the huge train and brilliant colors, while females are more cryptic. Magnificence belongs especially to male courtship, while female camouflage protects the next generation.

indian-rhinoceros.spotlight: Indian Rhinoceros is known for armor-like skin, mass, grazing endurance, and territorial force.
indian-rhinoceros.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Tall grasslands, riverine forests, floodplains, and wetlands in South Asia.
signatureTraits: Single thick horn on the end of the snout
Rounded, wart-like bumps stud the shoulders, rump and upper legs
Pointed upper lip that curls around grass stems
Grey-brown, almost hairless skin, with hair on the ear fringes and tail tip
interestingFacts: Its skin folds give it an armor-plated appearance.
It is a strong swimmer despite its size.
Its single horn is made of keratin, the same protein found in hair and fingernails.
Kaziranga National Park in Assam holds roughly two-thirds of the world's Indian Rhinoceroses.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mostly grazes on grasses while also eating leaves, fruit, and aquatic plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, while calves may be threatened by tigers in some landscapes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active across day and night with resting periods, often using wallows to cool and protect skin.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live several decades in the wild under good protection.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf after a long gestation and protect it closely.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger and more territorial than females.

indian-rock-python.spotlight: Indian Rock Python carries Constriction Power through stillness, camouflage, and muscle. It does not win by frantic chase; it wins by holding position until one patient coil can decide the moment.
indian-rock-python.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Grasslands, rocky scrub, wetlands, forests, farms, and river edges fit this python because heavy power works best where cover and waiting places are available.
signatureTraits: Stone-like pattern breaks the body into patches of shade and ground.
Muscular coils turn patience into pressure after the strike.
Ambush hunting saves energy for the moment that matters.
Heat-sensing pits help locate warm prey in cover or darkness.
interestingFacts: Indian rock pythons are among South Asia's large constrictors.
They can swim well, which expands their ambush routes near water.
Females may coil around eggs and use muscle activity to help regulate warmth.
Their power is slow-looking until the strike and constriction begin.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mammals, birds, and reptiles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large cats, crocodiles, raptors for young, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Size helps adults, but concealment and caution matter at every age.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Often crepuscular or nocturnal in warm seasons, resting in cover by day and becoming active when temperatures and prey movement suit ambush.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 20 years or more in captivity, with individuals reported living beyond 30. Lifespan in the wild is not known and is probably shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches of eggs and may coil around them, showing that constriction is not only capture power but also protective warmth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger than males, while males may compete during breeding; both sexes share the same patient muscular design.

indian-star-tortoise.spotlight: Indian Star Tortoise carries Radiant Armor as a slow moving shell of geometry: bright star lines break the outline in dry grass while turning protection into beauty.
indian-star-tortoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia. Indian Star Tortoises live in dry scrub, grassland, and open woodland where broken light, stems, and soil match the shell’s lines. This habitat lets beauty work as camouflage.
signatureTraits: Star-patterned domed shell
Dryland tortoise body
Slow careful steps
Visual camouflage pattern
interestingFacts: Each shell pattern is individually distinctive, with yellow lines radiating from the centre of each scute.
The star pattern can disrupt the outline among grasses.
It is heavily threatened by illegal wildlife trade.
In 2019 it was moved to CITES Appendix I, banning international commercial trade in the species.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They graze on grasses, leaves, flowers, fruits, and other plant matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators of eggs and young include birds, mammals, reptiles, and people through collection pressure. The shell protects adults, while pattern and stillness help reduce notice.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly active in cooler parts of the day and may shelter during harsh heat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Indian Star Tortoises can live for many decades in suitable conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches of eggs in nests dug in soil, with young hatching as miniature shelled walkers. Offspring begin with the same need for hidden, patterned protection.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger and rounder, while males are smaller with longer tails. The difference reflects reproduction and movement rather than flashy display.

indochinese-box-turtle.spotlight: Indochinese Box Turtle teaches Wise Retreat through a shell that closes the boundary completely. Its hinged plastron, forest-floor caution, slow searching, and tight defensive seal show that retreat can be chosen strength, not defeat.
indochinese-box-turtle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, east_asia. Humid forest floors, leaf litter, stream edges, hill forest, and shaded Southeast Asian undergrowth fit Indochinese Box Turtles because retreat needs damp cover and shelter.
signatureTraits: Hinged lower shell that can close tightly
High-domed patterned shell for forest-floor life
Slow cautious movement through humid cover
Complete retreat as a defensive tool
interestingFacts: Box turtles are named for the way the shell can close like a box.
Indochinese Box Turtles live in humid forests of Southeast Asia.
They are heavily threatened by collection and trade.
Their bright shell and head pattern make them visually distinctive.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fallen fruit, mushrooms, worms, insects, snails, and plant matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Mammals, snakes, monitor lizards, birds, and humans threaten turtles and eggs. The hinged shell makes many attacks harder to finish.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often crepuscular or active in damp conditions, retreating during heat or dryness. Their rhythm protects energy through careful closure.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Published lifespan figures for Cuora galbinifrons remain sparse; the hinged-shell turtle of Indochinese hills is scarce in studies and hard to keep long-term.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches of eggs in soil or leaf litter. Hatchlings begin life with softer shells and depend heavily on hiding.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may have longer thicker tails and sometimes different eye or plastron features, while females are built for egg carrying. Differences are subtle compared with the shared shell defense.

indri.spotlight: Indri turns Songbound Motion into a living announcement: long legs launch the body through Madagascar canopy while loud calls make the route part of the forest’s memory.
indri.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Indris belong to eastern Madagascar rainforests, where tall trees create the vertical routes their leaping bodies need.
signatureTraits: Powerful vertical leaper
Loud territorial songs
Large tailless lemur body
Strong family-pair signalling
interestingFacts: Indris are the largest living lemurs, with adults weighing roughly six to nine kilograms.
Their songs can carry across forest valleys and are reportedly audible about two kilometres away.
They do not have the long tail seen in many other lemurs.
Indris are reported not to survive well in captivity, and no zoo currently keeps them.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, young shoots, flowers, fruits, and seeds feed the Indri.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fossas, large raptors, snakes, habitat loss, and human pressure threaten Indris. Their calls, height, and group awareness help turn presence into protection before danger reaches the branch.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Indris are mainly active in daylight, feeding, resting, leaping, and calling across the morning and day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Indris can live for decades in suitable conditions, with slow reproduction and long family dependence. The long lifespan makes each voice and each forest territory especially valuable.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single infant after a long gestation, and the young cling to the mother before gaining independence. Small family growth gives each new voice real weight.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though females may be socially prominent in some groups. The similarity keeps the focus on paired calls, family bonds, and shared territory rather than display alone.

indus-river-dolphin.spotlight: Indus River Dolphin teaches Sound Navigation through a river mammal that finds the path without relying on sight. Its poor vision, long beak, side-swimming style, echolocation, and turbid-water hunting show that there is more than one way to see.
indus-river-dolphin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia. The Indus River, deep channels, turbid freshwater, confluences, and slow-moving pools fit Indus River Dolphins because sound navigation works where sight fails.
signatureTraits: Very poor eyesight adapted to muddy rivers
Echolocation used for hunting and navigation
Long narrow beak for probing river prey
Restricted life in the Indus River system
interestingFacts: Indus River Dolphins are sometimes called blind dolphins because their eyes are tiny and vision is limited.
They swim in turbid rivers where sound is more useful than sight.
They often surface with a low, rolling movement.
Dams, water extraction, and fishing gear threaten their remaining range.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, prawns, catfish, carp, and bottom-dwelling aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but calves may face large fish or crocodiles, and humans create the largest risks through nets, dams, and low flows.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: River dolphins rest and surface in short cycles rather than sleeping like land mammals. Their rhythm is breathe, listen, dive, and follow the river.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live for decades, though exact wild lifespan is hard to measure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf that must surface to breathe soon after birth. The calf learns the river through the mother’s movement and sound world.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger than males in river dolphins. Both sexes share the same sound-based navigation, but mothers carry calves through the river’s hazards.

jabiru.spotlight: Jabiru teaches Measured Strike through a towering wetland stork that lets the moment sharpen before the bill lands. Slow walking, huge spear bill, shallow-water hunting, and nest height make calm decisive.
jabiru.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Marshes, floodplains, wetlands, river edges, ponds, and seasonally flooded savannas.
signatureTraits: Towering stork body with a massive black bill.
Slow deliberate walking through shallow wetlands.
Powerful strike at fish, amphibians, reptiles, and aquatic prey.
Large nest building high in trees near wetland feeding grounds.
interestingFacts: Jabirus are among the tallest flying birds in the Americas.
They hunt by walking through shallows and striking prey with the bill.
They build large nests, often reused or maintained across seasons.
Their black head and red neck band make the white body especially striking.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, frogs, snakes, small reptiles, crustaceans, insects, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, caimans, large raptors for young, snakes, nest predators, humans, and wetland loss can threaten jabirus. Height and size help, but nesting success depends on stable wetlands.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Jabirus are diurnal, walking and feeding by day while resting or nesting near wetlands.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often given as about 30 years or more, with captive birds reported in their mid-thirties. Survival of wild birds has been little studied.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, and both parents help incubate and feed the chicks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger with heavier bills, while females share the same shape at smaller scale.

jackdaw.spotlight: Jackdaw teaches Adaptation through a social corvid that sees a home where others see only a gap. Tree holes, chimneys, cliffs, ruins, and buildings all become openings when a clever bird is willing to use the available door.
jackdaw.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Cliffs, old trees, farmland, towns, church towers, chimneys, ruins, and woodland edges fit Jackdaws because the species thrives wherever cavities and social feeding opportunities appear.
signatureTraits: Pale eyes and corvid intelligence support social reading and flexible choices.
Cavity nesting lets cliffs, tree holes, chimneys, and buildings become homes.
Group roosting and flock movement turn information into shared advantage.
interestingFacts: Jackdaws belong to the corvid family, a group known for intelligence.
They often nest close to people in chimneys, towers, and old buildings.
Pairs can maintain strong social bonds across seasons.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, insects, fruit, scraps, carrion, eggs, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, owls, cats, foxes, martens, and nest competitors pressure Jackdaws to choose protected cavities and stay socially alert. The safe opening matters because the outside world keeps testing it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Jackdaws are diurnal, feeding and socializing by day and gathering to roost in groups. Their daily rhythm supports adaptation through shared information and repeated return to safe sites.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 5 years for birds that reach breeding age; the oldest ringed jackdaws have lived 18 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs inside cavities where the narrow entrance protects chicks from weather and many predators. Offspring turn the gap into more than shelter; it becomes a guarded future.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the grey shawl on the nape and the pale eye and cannot reliably be told apart in the field; males average slightly larger and heavier.

jaguar.spotlight: Where most big cats throttle their prey, the largest cat of the Americas often kills with a single bite through the skull or the back of the neck. Its canines can pierce the shells of river turtles, and along rivers it drags caimans from the water's edge.
jaguar.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Jaguar usually lives in rainforest, wetlands, river edges, savanna, and dense cover.
signatureTraits: rosette camouflage
crushing bite
swimming strength
ambush patience
interestingFacts: Each rosette usually encloses one or more small dark spots, which a leopard's rosettes lack.
Black jaguars are the same species, and their rosettes remain visible in strong light.
Jaguars of the Pantanal and Llanos can weigh more than 100 kilograms, roughly twice the weight of those in Central American forests.
The historic range reached the south-western United States, and lone males still occasionally cross into Arizona from Mexico.
Its roar is a series of deep, hoarse coughs, often compared to the sound of sawing wood.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Jaguar feeds on deer, peccaries, capybaras, caimans, turtles, and many prey animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have no regular natural predators. Cubs may be killed by adult male jaguars and other large predators. People cause most deaths, through shooting after cattle losses, poaching for skins, teeth and bones, and forest clearance that breaks up their range.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Jaguar is mostly crepuscular and nocturnal, resting in cover by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Jaguar often lives around a decade or more in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Following roughly 14 weeks of pregnancy, females raise one to four cubs in hidden dens. Two is the usual litter. Cubs open their eyes at around two weeks and stay with the mother for up to two years.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The coat is the same in both sexes, but males are larger and range more widely. Males are typically 10 to 20 per cent heavier, and one male's range overlaps those of several females.

jaguarundi.spotlight: The Jaguarundi is streamlining in cat form: long, low, plain, and efficient. It shows that power does not always need ornament — sometimes the strongest design is the one that wastes no shape.
jaguarundi.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Jaguarundis live in scrub, grassland edges, forests, wetlands, and dense cover across parts of the Americas.
signatureTraits: Long low body and short legs
Sleek unspotted coat
Flexible edge-habitat hunter
Often more daytime-active than many small cats
interestingFacts: Jaguarundis look more weasel-like than many spotted wild cats.
They can occur in gray, brown, or reddish coat colors.
They hunt small mammals, birds, reptiles, and other small prey.
Their low body helps them move through grass, brush, and tangled edges.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat rodents, birds, reptiles, frogs, and other small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large cats, canids, humans, and habitat loss can threaten them. Their defense is secrecy, speed through cover, and broad habitat tolerance, showing that efficiency can also be resilience.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Jaguarundis are often active during the day and twilight, though timing can vary.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live around 10 years in the wild and longer in human care. A streamlined life is not about dramatic bursts but about years of moving without waste.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters, often in dense shelter such as hollow logs or thick vegetation. Kittens begin life hidden in the same edge-world their parents navigate.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females, but both sexes share the sleek low shape.

japanese-macaque.spotlight: Japanese Macaque is known for troop structure, seasonal adaptation, alert faces, and social learning.
japanese-macaque.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Forests, mountains, snowy regions, and island landscapes across Japan.
signatureTraits: Expressive face and troop signals
Cold-tolerant primate behavior
Agile movement through forest and rock
Bare red face and rump in adults
Short tail and thick grey-brown coat
interestingFacts: Japanese macaques are among the northernmost wild non-human primates.
Some groups are famous for bathing in hot springs.
They learn food-handling behaviors socially, as when young monkeys on Koshima island took up washing sweet potatoes in water.
Japanese macaques are native only to Japan, ranging from Yakushima in the south to the northern tip of Honshu.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Omnivorous, eating fruits, leaves, seeds, bark, insects, and seasonal foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include large raptors, carnivores, harsh winters, habitat conflict, and human pressure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, moving and feeding by day while resting in groups at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Can live for two decades or more in the wild, with longer lives under protection.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually raise single infants with strong mother-infant bonds and troop social learning.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger, while females remain central to troop continuity and kin groups.

japanese-serow.spotlight: Japan's only wild bovid, a stocky goat-antelope about the size of a large goat, lives in mountain forest on Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu. Each adult holds a territory on steep slopes all year round, following regular paths through it and marking twigs and rocks with scent.
japanese-serow.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Deciduous broadleaf and mixed conifer forest on steep mountain slopes, with rocky outcrops and dense undergrowth, from the foothills up to around the tree line. It is commonest in northern and central Honshu and more thinly spread in Shikoku and Kyushu.
signatureTraits: Short black horns curve backwards from the top of the head.
The coat is shaggy and grey-brown to blackish, sometimes nearly white.
A scent gland opens as a dark slit below each eye.
The body is stocky, with short sturdy legs and a small tail.
It often stands motionless for minutes, watching an observer.
interestingFacts: Japan declared it a Special Natural Monument in 1955, after hunting had made it scarce, and numbers have since recovered strongly.
Age can be read from the growth rings that form on the horns each year, since the horns are never shed.
Its Japanese name is kamoshika, and although it is often described as a deer it is more closely related to goats and sheep.
Most adults live alone; the commonest groups are a female with her kid or a male and female together.
As numbers recovered, browsing damaged young conifer plantations, and licensed culling began in some prefectures in the late 1970s.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A browser. Leaves, shoots and buds of deciduous trees and shrubs are taken in the growing season and acorns in autumn; in winter it turns to evergreen and conifer foliage, twigs and dwarf bamboo. It feeds alone or as a pair, nipping growth within reach.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: The Japanese wolf, once its main predator, is extinct. Asiatic black bears are known to take serows on occasion, and deep snow and disease kill others, especially the young. An alarmed animal gives a whistling snort and bounds away to steep, rocky ground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Feeding peaks come in the early morning and late afternoon, with some movement after dark. Between bouts it lies up to chew the cud under a rock overhang, in a small cave or on a ledge with a wide view.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 20 to 25 years. Many die much younger, particularly in their first winters.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating is in autumn, mostly October and November. A single kid is born in late spring or early summer after about seven months' gestation and stays with its mother for roughly a year. Females first breed at about two and a half to three years.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are nearly identical in size, coat and horns, and cannot reliably be told apart at a distance.

java-mouse-deer.spotlight: Among the smallest of all hoofed mammals, it stands about 30 centimetres at the shoulder and weighs roughly 1 to 2 kilograms. Legs little thicker than a pencil carry it through gaps in thickets that are too tight for larger animals. It is known with certainty only from the Indonesian island of Java.
java-mouse-deer.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, java. Lowland rainforest, secondary forest and dense thickets on Java, where it keeps to the ground beneath thick cover, often near streams.
signatureTraits: Tiny hooves and secretive forest movement
Adapted to dense tropical forest and tangled undergrowth
Hunched back, higher at the rump than at the shoulder
No horns or antlers in either sex
Reddish-brown coat with white underparts and white throat stripes
interestingFacts: Java Mouse-deers are closely tied to dense tropical forest and tangled undergrowth.
Their food is mainly fallen fruit, leaves, shoots, and fungi.
Major pressures include snakes, civets, wild cats, raptors, and humans.
Although it looks like a miniature deer, it is a chevrotain, part of an old family of ruminants separate from the true deer.
In Indonesian and Malay folk tales the mouse-deer, called kancil, is a small trickster that outwits crocodiles, tigers and other large animals.
Mouse-deer across South-east Asia were long treated as one species until a revision in 2004 split them into several.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on fallen fruit, leaves, shoots, and fungi.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Likely predators on Java include pythons, leopard cats, Javan leopards, civets, eagles and village dogs, though few kills have been recorded. People snare it for meat and the pet trade. It freezes first, then bolts into thick cover; alarmed animals have been recorded drumming their hooves rapidly on the ground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Most movement comes around dawn and dusk and during parts of the night, though daytime activity has also been recorded. Between feeding bouts it lies up in dense thicket.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not measured in the wild. Captive mouse-deer have lived about 12 years, with a few reports of 14 to 16, but older records often did not separate this species from its mainland relatives.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single fawn, rarely twins, is born after a gestation of about four and a half months. It can stand within about half an hour and lies hidden in cover between nursing visits. Females are able to conceive again very soon after giving birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have small tusk-like canines.

javan-rhinoceros.spotlight: Head and body reach about 3 metres, and this rhinoceros feeds by force: it leans on saplings until they bend or snap, then browses leaves from the fallen crown. Well over a hundred plant species have been recorded in its diet. The whole known population, only in the tens, lives in Ujung Kulon National Park at the western tip of Java.
javan-rhinoceros.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, west_java, java. Dense lowland rainforest, riverine thickets, wallows, and tropical forest paths.
signatureTraits: Single horn, short, usually under 25 cm
Loose skin folds give the look of armour plates
Skin surface patterned like a mosaic of small scales
Broad three-toed footprints on muddy forest trails
interestingFacts: It once ranged widely across mainland South-east Asia as well as Sumatra and Java.
The last known animal on the mainland was found dead in Vietnam in 2010, killed by poachers.
Mud wallows are visited regularly, and the coating of mud helps protect the skin from heat and biting insects.
Researchers tell individuals apart in camera-trap footage by horn shape, skin folds and scars.
It is slightly smaller than the Indian rhinoceros, its closest living relative.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, twigs, fallen fruit, and young plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but calves may face big cats and the species is most threatened by habitat limits, disease, and human pressure. Quiet forest survival depends on keeping safe room.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often crepuscular or nocturnal, using forest cover, wallows, and shade.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been measured directly. It is usually estimated at roughly 30 to 40 years, and none are held in captivity to check against.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear a single calf after a long gestation and keep it close in dense cover. Offspring show why softness matters: a giant mother must protect without exposing the calf.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have larger horns or more visible horn development, while females are usually less horned.

javan-slow-loris.spotlight: Venom sets this small primate apart: it licks a gland on the inside of its arm, and the secretion, mixed with saliva, is delivered by the front teeth when it bites. Weighing under a kilogram and found only on Java, it climbs hand over hand without leaping and can clamp onto a branch for hours without tiring.
javan-slow-loris.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, west_java, east_java, java. Javan forest, bamboo, plantations, and connected canopy edges.
signatureTraits: Dark forked stripes run from crown to eyes
Pale diamond on the forehead between the dark stripes
Dark stripe down the middle of the back
No visible tail; small ears half hidden in fur
Eyes shine orange in torchlight
interestingFacts: It gouges holes in bark with its comb of lower front teeth and licks up the gum that flows out.
The second finger is much reduced, giving the hand a wide pincer grip around branches.
Until the 2000s it was usually treated as a form of the Sunda slow loris, not as a species of its own.
Traders often clip out the teeth of lorises sold as pets, which leads to infection and frequently death.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tree gum, nectar, fruit, insects, and small prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, raptors, civets, and humans threaten lorises. Slow movement works because grip, toxin, and night cover replace speed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are nocturnal, resting hidden by day and moving deliberately at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years, especially when protected from capture and habitat loss, turning careful movement into a long-term strategy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually bear one young that clings and is sometimes parked safely while the mother forages.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle to casual viewers.

jerboa.spotlight: Jerboa teaches Desert Lightness through long hind legs, bouncing travel, and a body that crosses sand without becoming heavy. Hard ground becomes passable when movement stays light, efficient, and nocturnal.
jerboa.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east, central_asia. Deserts, sandy plains, dry scrub, and burrowable soils.
signatureTraits: Elongated hind legs for efficient hopping across desert ground.
Long tail used for balance during leaps and turns.
Nocturnal habits that avoid daytime heat.
Burrowing shelter that protects a light body from exposure.
interestingFacts: Jerboas are desert rodents known for kangaroo-like hopping.
Their long tails, tipped with a tuft, help them balance during jumps and change direction mid-leap.
They spend hot days in burrows and emerge mostly at night.
Many species gain moisture from food and conserve water carefully.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, grasses, roots, shoots, and insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, foxes, snakes, cats, and raptors threaten them. Long leaps, night activity, and burrows keep lightness from becoming vulnerability.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Jerboas are nocturnal, resting underground by day and foraging after dark. Their rhythm is hide from heat, emerge, bounce, feed, and return before dawn.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive animals have been reported to live up to about 6 years. Most wild jerboas probably live only a year or two, though some survive several seasons.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in burrows, where young begin protected from heat and predators.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Both sexes are the same size and colour; nothing visible separates them in the field.

joro-spider.spotlight: This large orb-weaver of East Asia spins silk with a yellow tint that shows gold in sunlight. The main orb, often a metre or so across, hangs between two looser tangles of barrier threads, one in front and one behind, and its anchor lines can span several metres between trees or wires.
joro-spider.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia, north_america. Forest edges, gardens, power lines, porches, shrubs, and open gaps fit Joro Spiders because large webs need anchor points and insect traffic.
signatureTraits: Female's abdomen is yellow crossed by blue-grey bands.
A red patch marks the underside of the abdomen.
The spider hangs head-down at the centre of the web.
Webs often hang above head height between trees or wires.
Several webs are often built close together, sharing support lines.
interestingFacts: The name comes from jorōgumo, a spider of Japanese folklore said to take the form of a woman.
It was first recorded in North America in northern Georgia around 2014 and has since spread into neighbouring states.
In laboratory tests it survived a brief freeze better than the related golden silk spider, which suggests it can live in colder regions.
Its bite is not considered dangerous to people, and the spider rarely bites even when handled.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flies, moths, beetles, mosquitoes, and other flying insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, wasps, lizards, mantises, and larger spiders can threaten them. Strong silk and retreat behavior help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Joro Spiders repair and use webs through warm active periods, often waiting for vibration. Their rhythm is build, sense, and reset.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About one year: adults mature in late summer and die with the first hard frosts of late autumn, and the next generation overwinters inside the egg sac.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Of the two sexes, females are much larger and make egg sacs. In autumn the female spins a dense silk sac on bark, a leaf or a wall and lays several hundred eggs in it, then dies within weeks. Spiderlings emerge the following spring, and many drift away on wind-borne strands of silk.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are the large, brightly coloured spiders seen at the centre of webs, with a body about 17 to 25 millimetres long. Males reach only about 7 to 10 millimetres, are plain brown, and wait near the edge of a female's web.

jumping-spider.spotlight: Jumping Spider teaches Courage through a leap that is never blind. Forward-facing eyes, distance judgment, stalking pauses, and silk draglines show bravery with aim and a lifeline, not reckless motion.
jumping-spider.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america, europe, north_africa_middle_east, sub_saharan_africa, central_asia, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania. Leaves, walls, bark, grass, gardens, rocks, and sunny surfaces fit jumping spiders because they need visual hunting stages with small hiding places and clear launch points.
signatureTraits: Forward vision: large front eyes judge prey and distance.
Silk safety line: many jumps are backed by a dragline.
Stalking pounce: it approaches, measures, then commits.
interestingFacts: Jumping spiders have some of the best vision among spiders.
They hunt actively instead of relying only on webs.
Many species perform visual courtship displays, with males waving their legs and showing colourful body parts to females.
The jumping spider family, Salticidae, is the largest spider family, with more than 6,000 described species worldwide.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flies, mosquitoes, small insects, and other tiny arthropods support the Courage lesson because the spider must close distance and leap at moving prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, wasps, lizards, frogs, ants, and larger spiders make measured courage important. The dragline gives the leap a way back.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Jumping spiders are mostly active by day because vision drives their hunting and courtship. Light is part of their courage system.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many live months to a year or more depending on species and conditions. Their lesson is built from many small stalks, not one giant jump.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in silk retreats and often guard egg sacs. Reproduction turns silk from safety line into nursery wall.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may be more colorful, smaller, or display with leg and body movements, while females are often larger. The differences support visual courtship and egg production.

kagu.spotlight: Kagu carries Crested Display as quiet drama on the forest floor, raising crest and wings to transform a pale walker into a sudden message when the moment asks.
kagu.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Kagus live in humid New Caledonian forests where the ground, not the sky, is their main stage. The habitat makes a quiet walker’s sudden display feel theatrical.
signatureTraits: Pale gray plumage gives the forest walker a ghostlike presence
Raised crest and wing displays create sudden visual drama
Flightless ground movement makes the forest floor its stage
Powder-down feathers help keep the plumage clean
interestingFacts: Kagus are endemic to New Caledonia and depend on forest protection
Their wing displays reveal striking patterns during threat or courtship
Both sexes can display, making presence a shared behavior

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat insects, worms, snails, lizards, and other small ground prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dogs, cats, rats, pigs, and habitat disturbance threaten them, especially nests and chicks. A striking display helps, but island ground birds need predator control.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, walking the forest floor, probing for prey, calling, and displaying. Their rhythm mixes quiet search with sudden ceremony.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild birds have been recorded living beyond 20 years, and captive birds have reportedly reached about 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay usually one egg in a simple ground nest, and both parents help guard and raise the chick. Ground nesting makes protection central.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look very similar, and both can display.

kakapo.spotlight: The heaviest living parrot and the only living parrot that cannot fly, with large males weighing up to about 4 kilograms. Its breastbone lacks the deep keel that anchors flight muscles in other parrots, and its short wings serve for balance and for parachuting down from trees.
kakapo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. New Zealand forest floor, shrubs, low branches, and predator-managed islands.
signatureTraits: Owl-like disc of fine, bristly feathers around the face
Large pale grey bill and heavy, scaly grey feet
Walks or jogs with a rolling gait
Freezes when disturbed instead of running
Strong sweet, musty scent noticeable at close range
interestingFacts: Breeding is tied to the heavy fruiting of rimu trees, which happens only every two to four years.
Males dig shallow bowls in the ground, linked by cleared tracks, and call from them nightly for two to three months.
By 1995 only 51 birds were known; intensive management has since raised the number about fivefold.
The name comes from Māori and means night parrot.
Eggs are incubated for about 30 days, and chicks stay in the nest for around ten weeks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, fruits, seeds, roots, and native plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Introduced cats, rats, stoats, and habitat loss threaten them. Flightlessness becomes survivable only when the ground is made safe again.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal movement and daytime hiding fit because the kakapo’s true rhythm belongs to darkness, scent, and slow climbing.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Kakapos can live for many decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise chicks alone, often breeding only when food conditions are good.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and boom at leks; females choose and raise young. The difference shows uniqueness through both display and quiet care.

kea.spotlight: A large olive-green parrot of the mountains of New Zealand's South Island, living around and above the tree line. Young birds in particular investigate any unfamiliar object, and groups at car parks and ski fields strip rubber from vehicles and open packs. In experiments Keas have solved puzzles that require several steps in order.
kea.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Kea usually lives in New Zealand alpine forest, mountains, valleys, and human-edge habitats.
signatureTraits: curved bill
object testing
alpine curiosity
social learning
interestingFacts: A government bounty led to an estimated 150,000 Keas being killed before it ended around 1970; full protection followed in 1986.
A few Keas learn to land on sheep and dig through the skin of the back to feed on fat.
The underwings are bright orange-red, hidden until the bird flies.
The name is Māori and imitates the loud, drawn-out flight call.
In one study, playing recordings of the warbling play call set wild Keas playing with each other and alone.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Kea feeds on fruit, seeds, roots, insects, carrion, and many opportunistic foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Stoats do the most damage, killing sitting females and chicks; cats and brushtail possums also raid nests. Lead from old roofing and nails poisons birds that chew it, and traffic and pest-control baits kill others. Predator trapping around nests improves breeding success.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Kea is diurnal and highly active when exploring or foraging.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild birds are thought to reach about 20 years at most, and many die much younger. Captive Keas have lived to around 50.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Under boulders, logs and tree roots, females nest in cavities and males help feed them. Two to four eggs are usual, incubated by the female for about three to four weeks. Chicks leave the nest at roughly three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Plumage is alike in both sexes. Males are larger and heavier, with a noticeably longer, more strongly curved upper bill, which lets experienced observers sex many birds.

keel-billed-toucan.spotlight: Green, orange, blue and red meet on the bill of this toucan, found in forests from southern Mexico to northern Colombia and Venezuela, and the bill makes up about a third of the bird's length. Fruit is plucked and swallowed whole, and the larger seeds are later coughed up, often far from the parent tree.
keel-billed-toucan.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forests, canopy edges, fruiting trees, and humid woodlands fit Keel-billed Toucans because reach and display happen above ground.
signatureTraits: Plumage is black with a bright yellow face, throat and chest.
Red feathers show under the tail and white ones above it.
Feet are blue, with two toes forward and two back.
Flight is a burst of quick flaps followed by a glide.
The call is a croaking, frog-like note repeated many times.
interestingFacts: It is the national bird of Belize, where it is often called the bill bird.
Small flocks roost together in tree holes, each bird folding its tail over its back and tucking its bill under a wing to fit.
Pairs and flock-mates fence with their bills and toss fruit to one another.
The tongue is long and narrow, with frayed edges that give it the look of a feather.
It spends more time hopping from branch to branch than flying.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit is central, with insects, eggs, lizards, and small prey added.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, monkeys, coatis, and nest predators threaten toucans. Cavity nesting and group movement reduce danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Keel-billed Toucans are diurnal, feeding and calling in daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been measured. Captive birds commonly live beyond 15 years, and some have reached about 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In the breeding season, females lay eggs in tree cavities and both parents feed chicks. The 2 to 4 white eggs are incubated by both parents in turn for about 16 to 20 days. Chicks hatch naked and blind and stay in the hole for about six to eight weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same colours. Males average slightly larger, with a somewhat longer bill, but the difference is hard to judge unless a pair sits side by side.

kiang.spotlight: The Kiang is open freedom on the high plateau. Its long legs, herd movement, and cold-air grazing show that freedom can be the body simply continuing forward through thin air.
kiang.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Kiang live on the Tibetan Plateau and surrounding high-altitude grasslands, steppes, and open valleys.
signatureTraits: Large wild ass of Tibetan Plateau
Long-distance open-country movement
Cold high-altitude coat
Herd grazing behavior
interestingFacts: Kiang are the largest wild asses, with adults standing roughly 1.4 metres at the shoulder.
They live on high, cold plateaus and open alpine grasslands.
Their herds move widely to graze and find water.
They are strong runners in open landscapes where hiding is limited.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They graze on grasses, sedges, and hardy alpine plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves and snow leopards may threaten them, especially young animals, while humans and habitat pressure can also affect populations. Their defense is herd awareness, speed, and open sightlines, showing that freedom works best with vigilance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active by day, grazing, traveling, and resting in open country.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild equids can live into their teens or beyond, depending on conditions. A long life on the plateau makes freedom feel like endurance, not escape.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one foal, which must stand and follow quickly in open terrain. Offspring learn from the beginning that movement is safety.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger and may compete for access to females, while females and young form groups. Both sexes share the long-legged highland design.

king-cobra.spotlight: King Cobra is known for height, hood display, nest defense, and snake-hunting specialization.
king-cobra.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia. Forests, wetlands, bamboo thickets, and edge habitats across South and Southeast Asia.
signatureTraits: Tall defensive hood display
Rare nest-building behavior among snakes
Long venomous body with regal posture
Two large scales on the crown behind the usual head shields
Low, growling hiss, deeper than that of most snakes
interestingFacts: Its genus name, Ophiophagus, means snake-eater, and other snakes make up most of its diet.
Females build and guard nests for their eggs.
It is the world's longest venomous snake, with some individuals exceeding five metres.
Despite its name, it is not a true cobra of the genus Naja but sits in its own genus.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Specializes in eating other snakes, including venomous species, while also taking lizards when available.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but eggs and young may be taken by monitor lizards, mongooses, and birds of prey.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly diurnal, moving and hunting during daylight or warm active periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is often estimated around two decades, with longer survival possible under protection.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females gather vegetation into a nest mound and guard eggs with unusual intensity for a snake.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females and may compete during breeding season.

king-eider.spotlight: King Eider carries Arctic Style through color that does not soften the cold. Its crowned male head, dense body, sea diving, and tundra breeding show toughness can arrive beautifully dressed.
king-eider.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic, north_atlantic, north_pacific, arctic_ocean. Arctic tundra, coastal lagoons, sea ice edges, cold marine waters, and rocky winter coasts.
signatureTraits: Male head shield and colors create a royal breeding signal.
Dense body and waterproof plumage suit cold northern seas.
Diving ability turns icy water into feeding ground.
Seasonal movement links style to endurance, not comfort.
interestingFacts: King eiders breed in Arctic tundra and winter in cold marine waters.
Males are far more colorful than females during breeding plumage.
They dive for mollusks, crustaceans, and other benthic prey.
Their elegance is built on a life of cold-water work.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mollusks, crustaceans, aquatic insects, and other seafloor prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Arctic foxes, gulls, jaegers, raptors, polar bears near nests, hunters, oil, and climate change threaten them. Camouflage matters especially for nesting females.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal in Arctic summer light and flexible at sea, with feeding shaped by tides, ice, and prey access.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 15 to 20 years or more; arctic style becomes a long cycle of molt, migration, breeding, and diving.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tundra nests and incubate them with cryptic plumage, proving that quiet endurance supports the male's visible style.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are colorful with a crown-like head pattern, while females are mottled brown for nesting camouflage.

king-penguin.spotlight: King Penguin teaches Underwater Focus through a royal-looking bird whose real power is below the surface. Dense colonies, deep pursuit dives, fish, squid, and cold endurance make quiet grace practical.
king-penguin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_atlantic, south_pacific, indian_ocean, southern_ocean, arctic_antarctic. Subantarctic islands, cold seas, beaches, and colony plains.
signatureTraits: Tall upright body with golden-orange neck markings.
Powerful underwater pursuit diving for fish and squid.
Dense colony life in harsh subantarctic conditions.
Chick-rearing strategy that demands long parental endurance.
interestingFacts: King Penguins are the second-largest penguin species after Emperor Penguins.
They do not build a typical nest; the egg is held on the feet under a brood patch.
Their chicks can take many months to grow before fledging.
Their elegant land posture hides how powerful they are underwater.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Lanternfish, other fish, and squid.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopard seals, orcas, giant petrels, skuas, harsh weather, and food shifts threaten adults, chicks, or eggs. Colony life and diving answer different risks, so focus must change by setting.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: King Penguins rest and move according to colony demands and long foraging trips. Their rhythm is stand, guard, dive, return, and endure the cold between meals.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimates for wild birds run from about 15 to 25 years. Birds in zoos have lived beyond 30.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay a single egg, and both parents take turns carrying it on their feet and feeding the chick.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be slightly larger.

king-vulture.spotlight: The King Vulture makes scavenging regal. Its bright head and powerful bill show that necessary cleanup can carry dignity, color, and leadership even when the work touches decay.
king-vulture.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. King Vultures live in tropical forests, savannas, and open woodland edges across Central and South America.
signatureTraits: Bright multicolored bare head
Powerful carcass-opening bill
Large tropical scavenger wings
Cleanup role that supports other scavengers
interestingFacts: King Vultures can open tough carcass skin that smaller scavengers struggle with.
Their bare head helps keep feeding cleaner when working inside carcasses.
They often soar over tropical forests and open areas searching for food.
Their vivid head makes them one of the most visually striking vultures.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed mainly on carrion, using a strong bill to tear into carcasses.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but eggs and chicks can be vulnerable at nest sites, and poisoning or habitat loss are human threats. Their protection is size, flight, and ecological usefulness, showing how service can place an animal within a wider system.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, soaring in daylight when warm air helps lift them over large areas.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: King Vultures can live for decades, especially in captivity, and many large vultures are long-lived.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay a single egg in a hollow, stump, or sheltered site rather than building a classic twig nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, so the regal color is shared rather than reserved for one sex. The species' dignity belongs to the whole design.

kinkajou.spotlight: Kinkajou teaches Curiosity through a night canopy explorer turning sweetness into opportunity. Prehensile tail, rotating ankles, long tongue, fruit feeding, and nectar visits make exploration gentle and upward.
kinkajou.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical rainforest canopy, fruiting trees, forest edges, vines, and flowering night trees.
signatureTraits: Prehensile tail used like an extra climbing hand
Nocturnal canopy exploration through tropical forest
Long tongue for nectar, fruit, and sweet food sources
Rotating ankles that help climbing down and around branches
interestingFacts: Kinkajous are relatives of raccoons in the family Procyonidae, not monkeys, though they are often mistaken for primates.
Their prehensile tails help them grip branches while climbing.
They often feed on fruit and nectar and can help with pollination.
They are mostly nocturnal and rest in tree hollows by day.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, nectar, flowers, honey, insects, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ocelots, jaguars, harpy eagles, snakes, humans, and habitat loss threaten kinkajous. Night movement and canopy routes protect them, making curiosity safest when paired with climbing skill.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Kinkajous are nocturnal, resting in tree hollows by day and exploring after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Zoo animals often live 20 to 25 years, and one reached about 40. Wild kinkajous are thought to have shorter lives.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to young in tree hollows or sheltered canopy spaces, caring for them until they can climb and explore.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be larger.

kipunji.spotlight: Kipunji turns Group Voice into montane cohesion, using honking calls, social movement, and mist-forest life to keep the group together when visibility fades.
kipunji.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Kipunji live in Tanzanian montane forests where fog, slopes, and dense vegetation make contact difficult. The habitat makes a traveling voice more than noise: it is group safety.
signatureTraits: Distinctive honking call
Crested head hair
Montane forest monkey
Group-living social movement
interestingFacts: The Kipunji was formally described only in the 2000s.
Its loud honk-bark call is distinctive and helped researchers recognise it as a new species.
It lives only in two small, isolated montane forest areas of southern Tanzania: Mount Rungwe with Kitulo, and the Udzungwa Mountains.
Genetic study led scientists to place it in its own genus, Rungwecebus, separate from the mangabeys.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat leaves, shoots, fruits, flowers, bark, and small forest foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, eagles, snakes, habitat loss, and small population size threaten them. Group calls and vigilance help, but they need connected forest to remain whole.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, moving and feeding in groups through the day while calling to maintain contact.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live for many years like related monkeys, though exact wild lifespan is not fully known. Long social life gives calls and group knowledge time to matter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to single infants that cling and learn group movement over time. Offspring survive by being carried inside the social voice of the troop.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, with males often larger in many monkeys. The key difference is less visual than social: all members rely on contact.

kiwi.spotlight: Kiwi turns flightlessness into Ground Trust. Its nostril-tipped beak, strong legs, whisker-like feathers, and night foraging show that the forest floor can be a complete world when the senses read it well.
kiwi.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Kiwis live in forests, scrub, and damp ground habitats of New Zealand.
signatureTraits: Nostrils near the tip of the long bill
Flightless body with strong walking legs
Nocturnal ground foraging by scent and touch
Large egg compared with adult body size
interestingFacts: Kiwis are unusual birds because their nostrils sit near the tip of the bill.
They lay very large eggs relative to body size.
Their feathers are hair-like compared with many flying birds.
They probe soil and leaf litter for hidden invertebrates.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat worms, insects, larvae, spiders, berries, seeds, and small invertebrates found by probing.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators and threats include stoats, dogs, cats, ferrets, pigs, and habitat loss, with eggs and chicks especially vulnerable. Their defense is nocturnal secrecy, burrows, and the ability to read cover before danger closes.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Forages through the night and spends the day asleep in a burrow it has dug, a hollow log or a dense clump of vegetation, moving between several such shelters within its territory.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often several decades where protected. The lifespan why is that a grounded strategy can be long-lived when the habitat and predator pressure allow slow, sensory work to continue.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay very large eggs, and in many kiwi species males do much of the incubation. Offspring begin as a huge investment.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger, partly linked to egg production. The difference makes the reproductive cost visible: a ground bird's future is carried in one enormous hidden promise.

klipspringer.spotlight: Klipspringer teaches Hoof Surefooting through a tiny antelope that treats steep rock as normal ground. Rubber-like hoof edges, compact body, high lookout posture, and pair vigilance make danger ordinary through exact contact.
klipspringer.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Rocky kopjes, cliffs, boulder fields, escarpments, dry hills, and sparse shrubland.
signatureTraits: Specialized narrow hooves create secure contact on steep rock.
A compact body keeps balance tight on small ledges.
Pairs often stay alert together in rocky territories.
Large ears and lookout behavior turn stone refuge into an observation post.
interestingFacts: Klipspringers can stand on the tips of their hooves, giving them precise footing.
Their name means rock jumper in Afrikaans, reflecting how they bound between boulders.
They are often seen in pairs, using rocky slopes as both home and defense.
Their coarse, hollow hair insulates them and is thought to help cushion bumps against rocks.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, flowers, fruit, herbs, and tough browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, eagles, hyenas, jackals, caracals, pythons, humans, and dogs can threaten Klipspringers. Their defense is not size; it is sure-footed retreat into rock that larger predators cannot use as easily.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Klipspringers are mainly active by day and around cooler periods, resting in shade and watching from stone.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Klipspringers can live around a decade in the wild, with longer lives possible under protection. Their survival is built from thousands of precise steps across the same hard territory.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single calf hidden in cover until it can follow. Offspring survival begins with stillness, concealment, and eventually learning the stone-footed route of the adults.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have short straight horns, while females usually lack horns and may be similar in size.

koala.spotlight: Koala teaches Eucalyptus Selectivity by refusing most of the forest. Specialized digestion, long rest, climbing claws, and careful leaf choice show that focus can be a survival strategy, not laziness.
koala.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Eucalyptus forests and woodlands of eastern and southern Australia.
signatureTraits: Specialized gut microbes help process tough eucalyptus leaves.
Long sleep and rest conserve energy on a low-nutrient diet.
Strong claws and gripping limbs keep the body anchored in trees.
Selective feeding avoids leaves that are too toxic, old, or poor in moisture.
interestingFacts: Koalas are marsupials, not bears, and their closest living relatives are wombats.
Young joeys develop in the pouch before riding on the mother's back.
Different regions and individuals may prefer different eucalyptus species.
Koalas have fingerprints that closely resemble human fingerprints, even under a microscope.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Eucalyptus leaves make up nearly all of the diet, with occasional foliage from related trees such as Corymbia and Angophora. An adult eats roughly 200 to 500 grams a day, sniffing leaves before picking them, and takes most of its water from the foliage.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Dingoes, large pythons in some areas, dogs, cars, disease, heat, fire, and habitat loss threaten them. Tree dependence protects and exposes them at the same time.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, resting many hours by day and feeding during cooler periods to conserve water and energy.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 10 to 15 years in the wild, sometimes longer; its life shows selectivity repeated leaf by leaf, tree by tree, season by season.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a tiny joey that grows in the pouch, then transitions by eating pap to gain the gut microbes needed for eucalyptus life.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger, with scent glands and louder bellows; females carry the pouch-based care that passes the specialized leaf life to the next generation.

komodo-dragon.spotlight: Komodo Dragon is known for ambush hunting, immense size, serrated teeth, and island dominance.
komodo-dragon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Dry tropical islands, savanna, scrubland, and monsoon forest in parts of eastern Indonesia.
signatureTraits: Massive monitor lizard body
Serrated teeth and powerful bite
Camouflage-based ambush movement
Long, yellow, deeply forked tongue flicks out constantly
Muscular tail is about as long as the body
interestingFacts: It is the largest living lizard, with big males reported to reach about three metres long.
Adults can take large prey such as deer and pigs.
Young Komodo dragons may climb trees to avoid cannibalistic adults.
Females can reproduce by parthenogenesis, producing offspring from unfertilised eggs when no male is present.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carnivorous, feeding on carrion and live prey including deer, pigs, birds, and smaller dragons.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults are apex predators, while juveniles face danger from birds, snakes, and larger Komodo dragons.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly diurnal, using daylight warmth for activity and sheltering during cooler or harsher periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often estimated at several decades in the wild, with maturity taking many years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in nesting burrows or mound nests, and hatchlings survive independently.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger and heavier than females.

korean-rat-snake.spotlight: Korean Rat Snake is known for climbing, constriction, habitat variety, and quiet movement.
korean-rat-snake.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Grasslands, dry scrub, rocky areas, forest edges, and river or lake margins in Korea and nearby regions.
signatureTraits: Non-venomous constrictor strategy
Semi-arboreal movement
Olive-grey to brown body with dark crossbands towards the tail
Young boldly blotched, adults much plainer
Large adults reach about 1.5 to 1.8 metres
interestingFacts: It is known from Korea and parts of China.
It can use rocky, scrubby, and waterside habitats.
Its long body makes it a strong real-species anchor for Korean dragon forms.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Feeds on small mammals, birds, eggs, and other small vertebrates using constriction.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Threats include birds of prey, carnivorous mammals, larger snakes, and human persecution.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly diurnal to crepuscular depending on weather and temperature.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Large rat snakes can live for many years in the wild when habitat and prey remain stable.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected warm sites where the young hatch independently.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle, though mature males may be longer-tailed and more active in breeding periods.

kori-bustard.spotlight: Kori Bustard teaches Ground Presence through weight, stride, and display. As one of the heaviest flying birds, it carries power slowly across open land instead of trying to look quick.
kori-bustard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Open savannas, grasslands, scrublands, and semi-arid plains.
signatureTraits: Massive body creates presence before any display begins.
Long legs support slow, watchful walking across open country.
Males inflate and display to turn size into ceremony.
Ground feeding makes patience more useful than restless flight.
interestingFacts: Kori bustards are often cited among the heaviest birds capable of flight.
They usually prefer walking and running to flying unless necessary.
Males are much larger than females, making display size especially dramatic.
Their broad diet lets them use dry open habitats flexibly.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, seeds, berries, reptiles, small mammals, and plant matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, jackals, caracals, mongooses, snakes, humans, and grassland disturbance threaten eggs or young. Adults rely on watchfulness, size, and distance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, foraging and striding by day, often using cooler periods for more active movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well known in the wild. Captive birds have lived into their twenties, with about 26 to 28 years reported for the oldest.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females nest on the ground and raise chicks with little cover, so careful site choice and early chick mobility matter enormously.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are far larger and more display-heavy, while females carry the quiet burden of nesting; the species teaches both visible and hidden forms of ground presence.

kowari.spotlight: Kowari turns Desert Boldness into a tiny night charge: a tuft-tailed marsupial hunter races across stony country where courage must fit inside a small body.
kowari.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Kowaris live in arid gibber plains, stony deserts, and sparse dry country with burrows for shelter. The open hard ground makes boldness necessary because there is little cover for hesitation.
signatureTraits: Black brush-tipped tail
Tiny carnivorous marsupial build
Fast nocturnal hunting
Arid stony habitat specialist
interestingFacts: Kowaris are carnivorous marsupials, not rodents, belonging to the same family as quolls and dunnarts.
The black tail tuft makes them visually distinctive.
They shelter in burrows in harsh dry country.
Its species name byrnei honours P. M. Byrne, who collected specimens near Charlotte Waters in central Australia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat insects, spiders, small lizards, and other small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, snakes, foxes, cats, and habitat change threaten them. Speed, burrow use, and night activity help a tiny body avoid being turned into prey.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Kowaris are mainly nocturnal, resting underground by day and hunting when desert heat drops. Their schedule makes the night belong to quick feet and sharp appetite.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live several years in good conditions, though wild life is risky. The lesson is sharpened by a short, active life that has to spend courage carefully.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise small litters in pouch and nest shelter, relying on hidden burrows for safety.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males may be larger. The important mark is not sex display but the shared tuft-tail hunter form.

lace-monitor.spotlight: Lace Monitor is known for climbing, scavenging, forked-tongue investigation, and forest-edge alertness.
