Many breeders from the Russian Far East and north-east China move south for the winter, reaching southern China and Japan.
Pairs of mandarins are a traditional wedding emblem of faithful marriage in China and Korea, although pair bonds are generally thought to last only one season.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, acorns, aquatic plants, insects, snails, and small invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, raccoons, snakes, raptors, crows, and nest predators threaten ducks, eggs, or ducklings. Tree cavities and water escape help protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mandarin Ducks are mostly diurnal, feeding and displaying around water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly measured and probably averages only a few years; birds in captivity commonly live around 10 years, sometimes more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In spring, females nest in tree cavities and ducklings leap down to water. The clutch of about 9 to 12 eggs is incubated by the female alone for roughly four weeks, and the ducklings jump from the hole within a day of hatching. They fly at around six weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are grey-brown with a white ring around the eye that trails back as a thin line, and pale spots along the flanks. Males in summer moult look similar but keep a reddish bill, where the female's is grey.

mandarinfish.spotlight: Mandarinfish teaches Reef Radiance through a small fish glowing in rubble rather than open stage. Psychedelic colors, mucus-coated skin, slow hovering, and tiny prey picking make a niche feel bright.
mandarinfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, north_pacific, coral_triangle, southeast_asia_coastal, australia_coastal. Coral rubble, sheltered lagoons, reef flats, broken coral, and shallow Indo-Pacific reefs.
signatureTraits: Brilliant blue, orange, and green reef coloration
Small hovering movement through coral rubble
Mucus-coated skin instead of heavy scales
Patient feeding on tiny prey in sheltered reef niches
interestingFacts: Mandarinfish are famous for their unusually bright colors.
They live close to reef rubble and sheltered coral spaces.
Their skin lacks scales and has a thick, foul-smelling protective mucus coating that may deter predators.
Courtship often happens near dusk with paired rising movements.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tiny crustaceans, copepods, amphipods, worms, and microfauna.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger reef fish, eels, scorpionfish, habitat damage, and collection pressure can threaten Mandarinfish. Mucus, hiding, and small-space movement protect it, showing that radiance still needs refuge.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mandarinfish are often active in sheltered reef periods, with courtship commonly associated with dusk. Their rhythm is hover, pick, hide, and glow when timing is right.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Mandarinfish can live for several years in suitable reef conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Each spawning produces a small batch of eggs, reported as up to about 200, fertilised in open water above the reef. The buoyant eggs hatch within about a day, the larvae drift for some weeks, and neither parent gives care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger and may have a longer dorsal fin spine than females.

mandrill.spotlight: An adult male's face works as a signal of rank in this, the largest of the monkeys. The red stripe down his nose brightens as his testosterone and status rise and fades if he is deposed. In a long-studied colony in Gabon, males tended to avoid contests with redder rivals.
mandrill.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Mandrills usually live in Central African rainforests and forest-savanna edges.
signatureTraits: Bright face, canines, and social rank
Adapted to Central African rainforests and forest-savanna edges
Swollen, grooved ridges run along each side of the long muzzle.
Olive-brown fur is set off by a yellow-orange beard.
The tail is a short stub, only a few centimetres long.
interestingFacts: Mandrills are closely tied to Central African rainforests and forest-savanna edges.
Their food is mainly fruit, seeds, roots, insects, and small animals.
Major pressures include leopards, large snakes, raptors for young, and humans.
Groups, called hordes, commonly number several hundred, and one filmed in Lopé National Park in Gabon held about 1,300 animals.
Adult males rub a scent gland on the chest against tree trunks, leaving marks that other mandrills sniff.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on fruit, seeds, roots, insects, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards are the main natural predator, and crowned eagles and pythons can take the young. A group answers with alarm calls and flight, often up into trees, while adult males may face the danger with canines bared. Hunting for bushmeat kills many more.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Groups forage through the day, mostly on the ground. Before dusk they climb into trees to sleep, usually at a different site each night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 20 years in the wild is the usual estimate. Captive mandrills commonly reach 30, and a few have lived to around 40.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One infant is born after a gestation of about six months, at intervals of one to two years. It clings to its mother's belly for the first weeks. Daughters stay in the group for life, while sons leave as they approach maturity.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are much larger and far more brightly colored.

maned-wolf.spotlight: Neither a wolf nor a fox, this is the only member of its genus and the tallest wild canid, standing about 90 centimetres at the shoulder. It hunts alone, stepping slowly through tall grass with its large ears turned towards rustling prey, then pounces with stiff forelegs as a fox does.
maned-wolf.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Maned Wolf usually lives in South American savannas, cerrado, grasslands, and scrub.
signatureTraits: long legs
red coat
black mane
grassland scanning
interestingFacts: Its urine has a strong smell often compared to cannabis or skunk, and scent marks left along paths advertise an occupied territory.
The main call is a deep, single roar-bark, given at dusk and at night and audible over long distances.
A pair shares a territory, measured at roughly 25 to 30 square kilometres in some studies, but the two animals mostly travel and hunt apart.
Wolf apple seeds pass through the gut intact, and droppings are often left on the nest mounds of leafcutter ants, where seedlings later sprout.
It walks with a pacing gait, moving both legs on the same side of the body together.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Maned Wolf feeds on small mammals, birds, insects, fruit, and especially wolf apples.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Pumas and jaguars are the only natural predators, and attacks appear to be uncommon. Domestic dogs chase maned wolves and pass on diseases, road traffic kills many, and farmland has replaced much of the cerrado. A threatened animal raises its mane and turns side-on to look bigger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Maned Wolf is mostly crepuscular and nocturnal, resting by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Maned Wolf often lives around a decade in the wild.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Two or three pups make up a typical litter, born after about 65 days of gestation with blackish fur and a white-tipped tail. In the wild, females raise small litters in hidden dens. Weaning comes at around four months, and captive males have been seen bringing food to the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In coat and build the sexes look similar, with males often slightly larger. They cannot reliably be told apart in the field by appearance alone.

mangrove-monitor.spotlight: Mangrove Monitor teaches Edge Versatility through a lizard fluent in mud, water, roots, and bark. Swimming, climbing, claws, long tail, and broad prey use make many paths open.
mangrove-monitor.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, australia_oceania, coral_triangle, southeast_asia_coastal, australia_coastal. Mangroves, coastal forests, river mouths, tidal roots, beaches, and swamp edges.
signatureTraits: Semi-aquatic monitor body comfortable near tidal edges
Strong claws for climbing, digging, and gripping roots
Long tail useful for swimming and balance
Broad diet across mangrove layers and shoreline habitats
interestingFacts: Mangrove Monitors can swim well and often use coastal or island habitats.
They climb trees and move through mangrove roots as well as ground.
Their diet is highly flexible compared with many more specialized predators.
They belong to the intelligent and active monitor lizard group.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, fish, insects, eggs, birds, reptiles, carrion, and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large birds, snakes, crocodilians, bigger monitors, dogs, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Swimming, climbing, biting, and hiding offer multiple responses, making versatility defensive as well as opportunistic.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mangrove Monitors are diurnal, basking before foraging through roots, water, and trees. Their rhythm is warm up, explore the edge, and switch methods as the ground changes.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Coastal monitors that swim among mangroves and island shorelines across Wallacea leave few wild lifespan records; a typical figure stays unpublished.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected sites such as soil, decaying vegetation, or hidden cavities depending on conditions.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and more robust than females. The difference may matter in competition, but both sexes share the same swim-climb-hunt versatility.

mangrove-snake.spotlight: The Mangrove Snake is controlled pattern in motion: bold black and yellow bands carried through branches at night without becoming noisy. Its lesson is that strong visual identity can still move with restraint.
mangrove-snake.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Mangrove Snakes live in mangroves, swamp forests, river edges, and lowland tropical woodland. This habitat fits Controlled Pattern because the snake must move through tangled, reflective, broken spaces where a bold body only works if movement stays exact.
signatureTraits: Bold black-and-yellow banding
Nocturnal tree and mangrove movement
Slender climbing body
Rear-fanged venomous hunting strategy
interestingFacts: Mangrove Snakes are often active at night in trees and wet forest edges.
Their dramatic banding makes them visually memorable even though they often hunt quietly.
They feed on birds, lizards, frogs, small mammals, and other vertebrates.
They are associated with mangroves, swamp forest, and lowland tropical habitats in Southeast Asia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat birds, eggs, lizards, frogs, and small mammals, often hunting from branches or dense cover. The diet fits the lesson because the pattern is not decoration alone — it rides on a body built to climb, wait, and take the right opening.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large birds, monitor lizards, larger snakes, and humans can threaten them. Their defense is a mix of concealment, intimidating pattern, musk, bite, and night timing, showing how control turns danger into distance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mainly nocturnal, resting hidden by day and moving after dark. The night rhythm matters because the bright bands become part of a controlled shadow system rather than a loud invitation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years, with captive individuals often reaching well over a decade. That lifespan supports the principle: a strong pattern is useful only when carried through many careful nights.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches of eggs in protected humid sites, with young emerging already patterned and independent. The offspring note fits the lesson because the signal is inherited early — even small snakes begin life carrying the visual code.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same black body and narrow yellow bands. Males have a relatively longer tail that is thicker at its base; otherwise the sexes are hard to tell apart.

mangshan-pit-viper.spotlight: Adults reach about two metres and can weigh several kilograms, making this one of the largest pit vipers in Asia. The species is known only from the Mangshan mountains on the Hunan–Guangdong border in southern China. It hunts from ambush and finds warm-blooded prey in the dark with heat-sensing pits on the face.
mangshan-pit-viper.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Humid mountain forest, mossy rocks, leaf litter, and streamside vegetation.
signatureTraits: Lichen-green body crossed by irregular dark brown bands
Tail tip pale and whitish, contrasting with the body
Broad triangular head, clearly wider than the neck
Vertical pupils, like a cat's
Thick, heavy body, often resting in a tight coil
interestingFacts: Science formally described it only in 1990, from snakes collected on Mount Mang in Hunan Province.
Surveys have put the wild population at only a few hundred animals.
The snake has been seen wriggling its pale tail tip, which may work as a lure for frogs or birds.
Illegal collection for the reptile trade is one of the main threats, made worse by the very small area it occupies.
It has been moved between genera several times, from Trimeresurus to Zhaoermia and now Protobothrops.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, birds, frogs, and small vertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, mammals, other snakes, and humans threaten vipers. Venom helps, but camouflage reduces the need to spend danger loudly.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often crepuscular or nocturnal and spend long periods still.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years in protected habitat, making stillness a durable strategy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young, already patterned for concealment. Offspring fit the lesson because survival begins by matching the forest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females may be heavier; males may roam more during breeding. Both sexes depend on the moss-like body.

manta-ray.spotlight: The largest ray in the world, with a disc commonly 4 to 5 metres across and close to 7 in the biggest animals. It has the largest brain recorded in any fish. Each animal carries its own pattern of dark spots on the belly, which researchers use to identify individuals from photographs.
manta-ray.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: indian_ocean, south_pacific, north_pacific. Open ocean and coastal waters of tropical, subtropical and warm temperate seas, often around offshore islands, seamounts and headlands where upwelling brings plankton to the surface. It spends much time near the surface but has been recorded diving several hundred metres.
signatureTraits: Huge wing-like pectoral fins that turn size into grace
Cephalic lobes that guide plankton-rich water into the mouth
Cleaning-station visits that show trust and patience
Open-water intelligence expressed through smooth movement
interestingFacts: Manta Rays are filter feeders despite their huge size.
Their cephalic lobes can unfurl near the mouth during feeding.
They may visit cleaning stations where small fish remove parasites.
Their width looks powerful because it moves gently, not because it crashes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Manta Ray feeds on plankton and small drifting animals guided into the mouth with cephalic lobes.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large sharks and killer whales attack them, and some adults carry healed bite scars. Fishing kills far more: mantas are targeted for their gill plates, sold as a tonic, and drown as bycatch in nets and on lines. Escape is by speed and by diving.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day and night, gliding continuously through open water, conserving force by making motion smooth instead of frantic.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at about 40 years or more; few wild animals have been followed for long enough to be sure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to usually one large live pup after a long reproductive cycle, making each new life a major investment rather than a swarm.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger; males have claspers used in mating, while both sexes share the winged calm that defines the lesson.

mantidfly.spotlight: Neither wasp nor mantis, but a relative of the lacewings. Its front legs are folded, spined grasping limbs like those of a praying mantis, while its colours and wing markings copy paper wasps. The pattern varies from region to region, apparently matching whichever paper wasps are common locally.
mantidfly.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Woodland edges, meadows, gardens, shrubs, and insect-rich vegetation fit Mantidflies because they need prey and places to wait.
signatureTraits: A long, neck-like front segment carries the forelegs just behind the head.
Wings are clear with a dark brown band along the leading edge.
Abdomen is banded reddish-brown and yellow.
Large bulging eyes sit on a small triangular head.
Body length is about 2 to 3 centimetres.
interestingFacts: A larva that boards a male spider has been shown to cross to a female when the spiders mate.
While it waits on the spider, the larva is reported to feed on its host's blood.
Despite its looks the adult has no sting.
The larva changes form as it grows: the active first stage that boards a spider is followed by fat, short-legged grub stages, a pattern called hypermetamorphosis.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults ambush flies, small bees and other small insects, seizing them with a fast strike of the spined front legs. Larvae develop inside spider egg sacs, where they feed on the eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, mantises, wasps, and larger insects can threaten them. Mimicry, agility, and grabbing tools help reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mantidflies are generally active in warm periods, hunting from vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The whole life cycle takes about a year. Adults are on the wing for only a few weeks in summer, and most of the year is spent as a larva.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females glue many hundreds of tiny stalked eggs to the undersides of leaves. Each hatchling waits for a passing spider, climbs aboard, and slips into the egg sac as the female spider spins it. It feeds and pupates inside the sac, and the adult cuts its way out.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes share the same wasp-like colours and banding and cannot easily be told apart in the field; size differences between them are not well documented.

mantled-howler-monkey.spotlight: Mantled Howler Monkey teaches Distant Presence through a canopy voice that travels where the body does not. Enlarged throat structures, prehensile tail, leaf diet, and dawn calls make presence efficient across forest space.
mantled-howler-monkey.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical forest canopy, riverine forest, secondary growth, and fruiting or leafy trees.
signatureTraits: Enlarged hyoid structure that helps produce loud howling calls.
Prehensile tail used for secure canopy movement and feeding.
Leaf-heavy diet that favors energy conservation over constant speed.
Group spacing maintained partly through long-distance sound.
interestingFacts: Howler monkeys are among the loudest land animals relative to body size.
Mantled Howler Monkeys use a prehensile tail like a fifth limb in the canopy.
Their calls can reduce the need for direct confrontation between groups.
They eat many leaves, so conserving energy is central to their lifestyle.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, fruit, flowers, and tender shoots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, harpy eagles, large snakes, disease, humans, and habitat fragmentation threaten them. Canopy height, group living, and sound help manage distance and danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mantled Howlers are diurnal, often calling around dawn and resting through heat.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults often live into their teens in the wild, and about 20 years is thought to be near the upper limit. Howlers fare poorly in captivity, so zoo records are few.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to single infants that cling to the mother before gaining independence.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are often larger and may have stronger throat structures linked to loud calling.

marabou-stork.spotlight: Marabou Stork teaches Acceptance through a giant bird willing to do the work beauty avoids. Its bare head, massive bill, scavenging habit, and cleanup role show that useful service may begin at carrion, waste, and endings.
marabou-stork.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, wetlands, river edges, rubbish sites, slaughter areas, grasslands, and human-influenced landscapes fit Marabou Storks because their role begins where remains and scraps gather.
signatureTraits: Bare head and neck help keep scavenging work cleaner around carrion.
Huge bill and tall body let it handle scraps, carrion, fish, and small animals.
Soaring on thermals saves energy while searching wide open landscapes.
interestingFacts: Marabou Storks are among the largest flying birds by wingspan.
They often gather around carcasses, rubbish sites, wetlands, and human edges.
Their scavenging helps remove remains that could otherwise linger in the environment.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carrion, fish, insects, small vertebrates, scraps, and nestling birds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large carnivores, hyenas, crocodiles, raptors, and human disturbance can challenge Marabou Storks, especially around food or nesting sites. Size and social feeding help them hold space around ugly work.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Marabou Storks are diurnal, often soaring on thermals, scavenging, or standing near food sources by day. Their rhythm follows heat, visibility, and where cleanup is needed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented, but it is a long-lived bird: captive marabous have reportedly lived beyond 40 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, often in colonies, and both parents feed the young. Offspring make the cleanup role concrete because ugly food sources become energy carried back to a nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger and may have more developed throat features, but both sexes share the bare-headed scavenger design.

marbled-godwit.spotlight: Marbled Godwit teaches Deep Probing through a shorebird whose long upturned bill reaches beneath surfaces others only touch. Mudflat steps, migration, and hidden invertebrates make reach a discipline rather than a single action.
marbled-godwit.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Mudflats, beaches, estuaries, prairie wetlands, and tidal flats.
signatureTraits: Long slightly upturned bill for probing deep mud and sand.
Marbled warm-toned body suited to open shore and prairie wetland camouflage.
Long-distance migration between breeding and coastal feeding grounds.
Steady shorebird rhythm shaped by tides and hidden prey.
interestingFacts: Marbled Godwits breed in prairie wetland regions and winter along coasts.
Their long bill lets them reach prey hidden beneath mud or sand.
They are among the larger North American shorebirds.
Their feeding rhythm often follows exposed flats and tide timing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, clams, crustaceans, insects, and aquatic invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Falcons, gulls, foxes, raccoons, skunks, habitat disturbance, and migration hazards threaten adults, eggs, or chicks.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Marbled Godwits are active by day and according to tides during feeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Banding records include a wild bird reported at about 29 years old, though most live far less. Typical lifespan has not been measured closely.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in ground nests in open prairie habitat, and chicks leave the nest soon after hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females often have longer bills than males, which can affect feeding depth and style.

marbled-newt.spotlight: Marbled Newt teaches Seasonal Passage through an amphibian that changes its life between damp woodland and breeding pond. Green marbling, aquatic courtship, male crest, eggs folded into plants, and terrestrial return make growth a seasonal route.
marbled-newt.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe. Woodlands, ponds, ditches, damp meadows, scrub, and shaded refuges.
signatureTraits: Green-and-black marbling blends beauty with damp woodland camouflage.
Adults move between terrestrial shelter and aquatic breeding ponds.
Breeding males develop a crest that makes seasonal change visible.
Eggs are placed carefully on aquatic plants, tying reproduction to pond structure.
interestingFacts: Marbled Newts spend part of life on land and return to water for breeding.
Males become more visibly crested during the breeding season.
Their eggs are often wrapped or placed among aquatic vegetation for protection.
They need connected wet habitats, so roads, drought, and pond loss can break the seasonal path.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, insects, larvae, crustaceans, tadpoles, and small aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, snakes, birds, mammals, beetle larvae, drought, traffic, and habitat loss threaten Marbled Newts. Their defense is partly timing: breeding when ponds are useful, hiding when land is safer, and avoiding places that no longer fit the season.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Marbled Newts are often nocturnal and strongly tied to moisture, becoming more visible during wet breeding periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Bone growth-ring studies of wild adults have found newts aged 10 years and more; captive animals have lived longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Over the spring breeding season a female typically lays a few hundred eggs, one at a time. Larvae hatch after roughly two to three weeks, grow in the pond for a few months, and leave the water after metamorphosis in summer or autumn.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males show stronger breeding-season crests and display features, while females are usually fuller-bodied when carrying eggs.

marbled-salamander.spotlight: Marbled Salamander teaches Quiet Season through an amphibian preparing before the pond returns. Black-and-white bands, autumn breeding, dry-basin eggs, and female guarding make the future placed in advance of rain.
marbled-salamander.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Deciduous forests, woodland pools, dry vernal pond basins, leaf litter, and damp lowlands.
signatureTraits: The belly is plain black, without markings.
Pale bands often merge along the sides, leaving black hourglass patches.
The body is stocky, usually 9 to 11 cm long.
The head is broad with a blunt snout, and the tail is short.
Newly transformed young are brown or grey with pale flecks, not banded.
interestingFacts: Because the larvae hatch months ahead of spring-breeding amphibians, they are large enough to eat the newly hatched larvae of spotted salamanders and wood frogs.
Adults spend most of the year out of sight in burrows and under logs, and rarely enter water.
North Carolina named it the official state salamander in 2013.
Like other mole salamanders, it is reported to raise and wave its tail when attacked; the tail carries glands with a distasteful secretion.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Earthworms, insects, slugs, small invertebrates, and larvae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, small mammals, fish if ponds connect, beetle larvae, and drought threaten salamanders or eggs. Seasonal timing reduces risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Nocturnal and most active in damp conditions, especially during autumn breeding rains.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults are estimated to live about 8 to 10 years, though few wild populations have been followed for long enough to be sure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating takes place on land. A clutch holds about 50 to 200 eggs, which hatch within days of being flooded. Larvae grow in the pool through winter and leave as small salamanders in late spring or early summer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have bright white crossbands; in females the bands are duller, silvery grey. Females also tend to be slightly larger.

margay.spotlight: About the size of a small house cat at 2.5 to 4 kilograms, this spotted forest cat ranges from Mexico to Uruguay and northern Argentina. It can hang from a branch by one hind foot. In Brazil one was recorded imitating the calls of young pied tamarins, apparently to draw the monkeys within reach.
margay.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Margays live in tropical and subtropical forests with dense canopy.
signatureTraits: Flexible rotating ankles
Long balancing tail
Large night-adapted eyes
Spotted arboreal coat
interestingFacts: Margays can descend trees headfirst thanks to ankles that can rotate up to about 180 degrees.
They are more arboreal than many small cats.
Their long tail, roughly two-thirds of their head-and-body length, helps them balance on branches.
They are threatened by forest loss and are listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small mammals are the main prey, among them climbing rats, mouse opossums and squirrels, followed by birds, eggs, lizards, tree frogs and large insects. Some fruit is eaten. Prey is caught both in the branches and on the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Heavy trapping for fur, which went on until the 1980s, is the best-recorded threat. Attacks by wild animals are rarely documented; ocelots and other larger cats, big snakes and raptors are thought to take some, the raptors chiefly kittens. It takes to the trees when threatened.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly between dusk and dawn. It spends the day asleep in vine tangles, on broad branches or in tree hollows, well above the ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to be about 10 to 15 years in the wild, though this is poorly documented; captive animals have lived for more than 20 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of about 80 days, females usually raise one kitten in a hidden den. Twins are rare. The kitten opens its eyes at around two weeks and starts on solid food at about two months. Females have a single pair of teats.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are larger; females provide kitten care. The size difference is slight and the coat is patterned alike, so the two are hard to separate on a wild sighting.

marine-iguana.spotlight: Large males swim out beyond the surf and dive, usually for a few minutes in the top few metres, cropping algae from submerged rock with a blunt snout and three-pointed teeth. Smaller animals and most females feed instead on algae exposed on the rocks at low tide.
marine-iguana.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america, south_pacific. Marine Iguana usually lives in Galapagos rocky shores, lava coasts, intertidal zones, and nearby sea.
signatureTraits: Only marine lizard, using a land body to feed in the sea
Salt glands that expel excess salt after ocean grazing
Flattened tail and strong claws for swimming and lava grip
Dark body that absorbs heat after cold dives
interestingFacts: Marine Iguanas sneeze excess salt out of nasal glands, often leaving white salt crusts on their heads.
They graze algae from rocks like underwater livestock of the lava shore.
Body size can shrink during severe food shortages and recover later.
They are found naturally only in the Galapagos Islands.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Marine Iguana feeds on marine algae scraped from rocks, especially in intertidal and shallow water.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Galápagos hawks, racer snakes and herons catch hatchlings and juveniles, and hawks also kill nesting females. Introduced cats, dogs, rats and pigs destroy eggs and young on some islands. In El Niño years the algae die back and large parts of a colony can starve.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Day-active, warming on black lava between cold-water feeding trips so a reptile body can repeatedly borrow strength from sun and sea.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 10 to 12 years on average in the wild. Maximum age is uncertain; some individuals are thought to live for several decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nests in sand or ash above the shore, leaving eggs to begin life on land before the young face a coastline of lava and waves.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger and may become more colorful during breeding season.

markhor.spotlight: A large wild goat of the mountains of Pakistan, Afghanistan, northern India and neighbouring parts of Central Asia. The horns of a mature male can measure up to about 1.5 metres along the curve. Markhor feed on near-vertical rock faces and will climb into evergreen oaks to reach the foliage.
markhor.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, south_asia. Markhor usually lives in rocky mountains, cliffs, scrub slopes, and open highlands.
signatureTraits: Corkscrew horns that turn strength into visible spiral form
Split hooves and balance for steep rocky slopes
Bearded mountain profile that signals age and presence
Seasonal browsing that follows what the high ground offers
interestingFacts: Markhor horns are among the most distinctive of wild goats.
Their name is often associated with snake-like or spiral imagery.
Cliff terrain helps protect them from many predators.
Their beauty is inseparable from balance on dangerous ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Markhor feeds on grasses, leaves, shrubs, and seasonal mountain browse.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snow leopards and wolves are the principal hunters of adults; lynx take some, and golden eagles carry off kids. An animal that spots danger gives a sharp nasal alarm call. Poaching for horns and meat and competition with domestic goats are the chief human pressures.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active mainly by day and rests on ledges or open slopes with views, letting height and balance guard the body.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: About 10 to 13 years in the wild; captive animals can live a few years longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one or two kids after moving to safer slopes, giving the young steepness as both nursery and shield.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with huge corkscrew horns and longer beards, while females carry a lighter version of the same mountain competence.

marsh-frog.spotlight: Generally regarded as Europe's largest native frog, this green or olive water frog has females that can exceed 12 centimetres. Males float at the surface in spring and call in chorus, inflating a grey sac at each corner of the mouth to produce a loud, cackling rattle. The scientific name ridibundus means laughing.
marsh-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia, north_africa_middle_east. Ponds, rivers, canals, reedbeds, marshes, and wet ditches fit Marsh Frogs because calls need water edges and breeding sites.
signatureTraits: Skin is green to olive-brown with dark blotches and is often warty.
Many have a pale green or yellowish stripe down the middle of the back.
Eyes sit close together near the top of the head.
Hind toes are webbed almost to the tips.
Backs of the thighs are marbled grey or whitish, without yellow.
interestingFacts: Crosses between marsh frogs and pool frogs produce the edible frog, a hybrid form that persists by breeding back with one of its parent species.
Winter is usually spent under water, buried in mud at the bottom of ponds, ditches and slow rivers.
Marsh frogs released in Kent in the 1930s founded a population that still occupies the marshes of south-east England.
It rarely strays far from water, basking on banks and floating plants and leaping in with a splash when disturbed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, spiders, small fish, other amphibians, and invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Herons, snakes, fish, mammals, raptors, and larger frogs threaten them. Leaps, water refuge, and loud group breeding help survival.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Marsh Frogs are active by day and night in warm wet seasons, calling heavily during breeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably about 5 to 10 years in the wild, judging by growth rings counted in the bones of sampled frogs; the figure varies between populations.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: In spring and early summer, females lay large jelly masses of eggs in water. One female can produce several thousand eggs in a season, in several clumps among water plants. Tadpoles hatch in about a week and most leave the water as froglets by late summer or autumn.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow noticeably larger than males. In the breeding season males develop dark, roughened pads on the thumbs and thicker forearms, which help them grip the female during spawning.

marsh-mongoose.spotlight: A stocky, dark brown mongoose with a shaggy coat, seldom found far from water. Its toes have no webbing; instead the long, soft-skinned fingers are spread and pushed under stones and into mud to feel for prey. Hard-shelled food such as mussels is hurled down against a rock until it breaks.
marsh-mongoose.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Wetlands, reedbeds, mangroves, streams, swamps, and muddy river edges fit Marsh Mongooses because their advantage lives between water and land.
signatureTraits: Semi-aquatic movement keeps the mongoose tied to wet edges.
Crab hunting turns muddy margins into useful ground.
Secretive night travel reduces exposure along reeds and streams.
interestingFacts: Marsh Mongooses are comfortable around water and wetlands.
Crabs and amphibians are important foods in many parts of their range.
They often forage alone along dense, muddy edges.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, frogs, fish, insects, rodents, eggs, and small reptiles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, large snakes, crocodiles, raptors, dogs, and humans can threaten marsh mongooses. Dense reeds, water escape, and secretive movement help protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Marsh Mongooses are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, moving when cover improves and wetland prey is active. Their rhythm belongs to the quiet edge.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Marsh Mongooses may live around a decade in safer conditions, though wild survival is often shorter.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in hidden dens or dense cover, and young depend on protected wet-edge shelter before foraging alone. The niche begins with concealment.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though males can be larger.

martial-eagle.spotlight: Martial Eagle teaches Martial Focus through a giant raptor narrowing a vast sky into one target. High soaring, enormous talons, sharp vision, and decisive descent make power disciplined by attention.
martial-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savanna, open woodland, semi-arid plains, thornveld, and large wild territories.
signatureTraits: Large African eagle with commanding wingspan and spotted underside
High soaring search over open woodland and savanna
Powerful talons used on birds, reptiles, and mammals
Long-distance vision that turns perspective into action
interestingFacts: Martial Eagles are among Africa’s largest and most powerful eagles.
They often hunt from high soaring positions, reportedly spotting prey from several kilometres away.
Their prey can include monitor lizards, birds, hares, and small antelope young.
They need large territories, making habitat quality important.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Birds, reptiles, hares, hyraxes, mongooses, small mammals, and young antelope.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but chicks and eggs can face other raptors, snakes, and nest disturbance. Human persecution and habitat loss are major threats to the eagle’s focused territory.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Martial Eagles are diurnal, soaring when thermals rise and hunting when visibility is strong.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Martial Eagles can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay one egg in a large tree nest, and the chick receives long parental care.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger than males, increasing nesting defense and prey-handling capacity. Both sexes share the high-soaring focus that defines the species.

mary-river-turtle.spotlight: Mary River Turtle teaches Aquatic Oddity through a river life so adapted it becomes unforgettable. Its algae-covered shell, long tail, underwater breathing ability, and river dependence show that strange appearance can reveal perfect fit.
mary-river-turtle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Clear flowing river channels, submerged rocks, sandbanks, basking sites, and the Mary River system fit Mary River Turtles because their oddity is fully aquatic.
signatureTraits: Algae can grow on the shell or head like a green crest
Ability to absorb oxygen through the cloaca underwater
Long tail, especially in males
Strong dependence on Australia’s Mary River system
interestingFacts: Mary River Turtles are found naturally only in Queensland’s Mary River.
They can stay underwater for long periods using cloacal respiration.
Males have especially long tails compared with many turtles.
The “punk” algae look comes from algae growing on the turtle, not from hair.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic plants, algae, fruits, small invertebrates, and river vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and young face goannas, foxes, dogs, fish, birds, and nest disturbance, while adults face river changes. Water and shell protect but cannot replace habitat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They spend long periods underwater and surface to breathe when needed, basking in safe windows. Their rhythm is river flow, breath, and hidden rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many decades, likely several tens of years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in sandy riverbanks, and hatchlings must reach the water safely. Nesting success depends on protected banks and river timing.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have very long tails and are often smaller, while females carry eggs and need nesting banks. The sex difference is unusually visible in tail length.

masked-owl.spotlight: A large, heavily built relative of the barn owl, found in Australia and southern New Guinea. Its legs and talons are much stronger than a barn owl's, and it kills prey as large as rabbits, bandicoots and possums, usually dropping on them from a perch at a forest edge or clearing.
masked-owl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Masked Owls usually live in forests, woodlands, farmland edges, and hollow-bearing trees.
signatureTraits: Heart-shaped sound-gathering face
Adapted to forests
Dark rim around a white to chestnut facial disc
Legs feathered down to the feet
Pale, intermediate and dark plumage forms occur
interestingFacts: Masked Owls are closely tied to forests, woodlands, farmland edges, and hollow-bearing trees.
Their food is mainly small mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects.
Major pressures include larger raptors, nest predators, habitat loss.
Its screech is louder, deeper and harsher than a barn owl's, a drawn-out rasping call given from perches at night.
Tasmanian birds are the largest of the species; females there have been recorded at more than a kilogram.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on small mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adult birds have few natural enemies, though a larger raptor may occasionally kill one, and climbing predators can reach eggs and chicks. Clearing of old hollow-bearing trees is the main threat; rodent poison and road traffic also kill birds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Strictly nocturnal. It passes the day in a large tree hollow, in dense foliage or, in treeless country such as the Nullarbor, in a cave, and leaves the roost after dark to hunt.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Banding has not set a published typical lifespan; large Australasian barn-owls hunting open woodland by night remain lightly aged.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Nests are in large hollows of old trees, occasionally in caves. The female lays two to four white eggs and incubates them for about five weeks while the male brings food. Young fledge at roughly 10 to 12 weeks and stay with their parents for some time afterwards.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger and darker.

mata-mata.spotlight: Mata Mata teaches Leaf Illusion through a turtle that makes its body read like drowned forest debris. Fringed skin, leaf-shaped head, still water, and sudden suction show how perfect disguise can turn patience into a trap.
mata-mata.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Slow Amazon and Orinoco backwaters, swampy channels, muddy pools, flooded forest, and leaf-littered water.
signatureTraits: Leaf-like triangular head and fringed skin for debris mimicry
Vacuum-like suction strike that pulls fish inward
Long snorkel-like snout for breathing while mostly hidden
Extreme stillness in muddy, slow, plant-filled water
interestingFacts: Mata Matas catch prey by rapidly expanding the mouth and sucking water in.
Their rough head and skin can resemble leaves, bark, and submerged debris.
They are poor active swimmers compared with many turtles, relying on still ambush.
The long snout lets them breathe while staying mostly concealed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish and aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Caimans, large fish, birds, mammals, and humans can threaten eggs, young, or adults. Camouflage and stillness protect the turtle by making danger overlook it as part of the water’s clutter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mata Matas are often most active in dim, quiet periods but spend long hours still.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Mata Matas can live for decades in stable conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on land in sheltered nest sites, leaving young to enter the water where disguise becomes survival.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle, though males may have longer tails. The main identity is shared: both sexes are shaped by disguise, mud, and suction.

matschies-tree-kangaroo.spotlight: To climb, this tree kangaroo hugs the trunk and pushes up with both hind feet, and unlike ground kangaroos it can move its hind legs one at a time to walk along a branch. It lives only on the Huon Peninsula of north-eastern Papua New Guinea, in mountain forest from about 1,000 to 3,300 metres.
matschies-tree-kangaroo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. New Guinea cloud forest canopy fits because body reimagined needs branches that reward climbing rather than open hopping.
signatureTraits: Back is chestnut to red-brown; limbs, belly and tail are golden yellow
Face and ear edges are pale yellow
Ears are small and rounded
Hind feet are short and broad, with rough soles
interestingFacts: It is also called the Huon tree kangaroo.
The name honours the German zoologist Paul Matschie.
It has been reported to jump to the ground from 15 metres or more without injury.
Local landowners set aside the YUS Conservation Area, created in 2009, largely to protect it.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, fruit, flowers, shoots, and bark.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large pythons, raptors on young, humans, and forest loss threaten tree kangaroos, making height and concealment essential.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Matschie’s Tree Kangaroos are often crepuscular or nocturnal, resting in trees and moving carefully through cloud forest when safer.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live many years, especially in protected conditions, giving the reimagined climbing body time to master canopy routes.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise a single joey in the pouch, then guide it into climbing life after long protected development.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, though males are often larger; both share the gripping paws, tail balance, and upward body plan.

meerkat.spotlight: Meerkat teaches Vigilance through a group that buys freedom with watchfulness. Upright sentries, alarm calls, digging claws, social foraging, and rotating duty show safety as a shared responsibility.
meerkat.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Dry savannas, scrub, desert edges, open plains, and burrow systems fit Meerkats because food is found in exposed ground while safety depends on nearby tunnels and sentries.
signatureTraits: Rotating sentries: individuals take watch while others forage.
Burrow mob life: safety is organized around tunnels, calls, and group roles.
Upright posture: standing high turns a small body into a horizon scanner.
interestingFacts: Meerkats use different alarm calls for different kinds of threats.
They can eat scorpions and other difficult desert prey after careful handling.
Young meerkats learn foraging skills through social teaching and practice.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, scorpions, spiders, lizards, eggs, small mammals, and roots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, hawks, jackals, snakes, and wild cats pressure Meerkats constantly. Rotating sentry behavior lets the group feed without everyone being blind to danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Meerkats are diurnal, warming up near burrows before foraging and returning underground to rest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Meerkats often live around 6 to 10 years in the wild, with longer lives possible under safer care.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth in underground burrows, and the group helps babysit, feed, and guard the pups. Offspring survival depends on the mob turning watchfulness into shared labor.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though dominant breeding animals shape the group’s reproductive structure. The useful difference is less visual than social: who watches, who breeds, who helps, and when.

mexican-beaded-lizard.spotlight: Mexican Beaded Lizard turns Beaded Slow Venom into consequence: a heavy body, bead-like scales, and venomous bite show that slow power still deserves distance.
mexican-beaded-lizard.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Mexican Beaded Lizards live in dry forests, thorn scrub, and rocky slopes where shade, burrows, and seasonal food matter.
signatureTraits: Bead-like armored scales
Venomous defensive bite
Heavy slow movement
Dry rocky habitat
interestingFacts: It is one of the world’s venomous lizards.
Its scales contain small bony deposits that create a beaded texture.
It stores fat in its thick tail, helping it survive long periods without food.
It belongs to the genus Heloderma, the same genus as the Gila Monster of the south-western United States.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat eggs, nestlings, small vertebrates, insects, and carrion when available. This diet fits slow venom because they do not need constant chase; they need timing and a serious bite.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large predators, humans, habitat loss, and persecution threaten them. Their warning colors, tough skin, and venomous bite turn slow movement into protected movement.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often crepuscular or nocturnal in hot seasons and may shelter for long periods.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for decades in captivity and many years in the wild. Long life matches a slow strategy built around energy storage and careful emergence.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in hidden nests, with young hatching already marked and equipped for caution. Reproduction is seasonal, tied to safe heat and shelter.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, though males may be larger or more robust. The shared beaded body makes consequence the main signal.

mimic-octopus.spotlight: Slender and boldly banded in brown and white, this octopus of silty sea floors reaches about 60 centimetres in total length. When harassed by damselfish it has been seen to push six arms into a burrow and wave the other two in opposite directions, so that they resemble a banded sea snake, a predator of those fish.
mimic-octopus.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, southeast_asia_coastal. Open sand and silt sea floors, often near river mouths and in estuaries, in warm tropical waters, especially around Indonesia and the Philippines. Most records come from shallow water a few metres to a few tens of metres deep.
signatureTraits: Shape-shifting posture
Color and texture change
Intelligent exploration
Open-sand mimicry
interestingFacts: It can resemble several different animals, including lionfish, flatfish, and sea snakes.
It was scientifically described only in 2005, although divers had reported it years earlier.
Its mimicry combines body posture and swimming movement with changes in color.
It forages in the open on sandy and muddy seabeds around river mouths in the Indo-Pacific.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small crustaceans, worms and fish. It forages across open sand, pushing arm tips down burrows and holes, and spreads the web between its arms over a patch of sediment to trap whatever is flushed out.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators have rarely been observed directly; large fish hunting over open sand are the main danger. Apart from its impersonations it bolts down the nearest burrow or sinks into the sediment until only the eyes show.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Forages in daylight, which is when most sightings are made. It withdraws into a burrow or tube in the sediment to rest, and is thought to spend the night there.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan has not been measured for this species; it is thought to be short, probably a year or two at most.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Once mated, females lay and guard eggs, then usually die after reproduction. Breeding in this species has seldom been observed; the hatchlings are thought to be tiny and to drift in the plankton before settling on the sea floor.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar externally; reproductive roles differ sharply at egg guarding. As in other octopuses, a mature male has one arm modified for passing sperm packets to the female.

mississippi-kite.spotlight: Mississippi Kite teaches Air Ease through a raptor that makes work look light when the sky fits its body. Long pointed wings, buoyant glide, aerial insect catching, and smooth turns make strength feel effortless because the medium is right.
mississippi-kite.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Open woodland, river groves, prairies, towns, parks, and warm skies with flying insects.
signatureTraits: Long pointed wings for graceful gliding
Aerial insect hunting with agile turns
Light buoyant flight that uses warm air efficiently
Social nesting or loose colony behavior in suitable places
interestingFacts: Mississippi Kites often catch insects while flying and usually eat them in mid-air without landing.
They can look almost effortless as they circle and glide in warm air.
They migrate long distances between breeding and wintering areas.
They may nest in neighborhoods and parks as well as open woodland.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasshoppers, dragonflies, cicadas, beetles, and other flying insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Great horned owls, hawks, snakes, raccoons, crows, and storms can threaten nests or young.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mississippi Kites are diurnal, especially active in warm daylight when insects rise. Their rhythm follows lift, heat, and moving prey.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Banding records show wild birds reaching at least 11 years. Most probably live well short of that, and typical lifespan has not been measured closely.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree nests, and both parents feed and defend the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males have a paler, almost whitish grey head, while females have a darker grey head and often show faint pale bars under the tail. Females are slightly larger.

mole-viper.spotlight: The Mole Viper is subterranean power with a specialized edge. Its side-stabbing fangs and underground hunting show that strength can gather where the surface never thinks to look.
mole-viper.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east. Mole Vipers live in savannas, grasslands, scrub, and loose soils where burrows and underground prey are available.
signatureTraits: Burrowing snake body
Side-stabbing fang mechanics
Specialized skull for confined spaces
Hidden underground hunting style
interestingFacts: Mole vipers can bite sideways without opening the mouth as widely as many snakes.
Their unusual fang action helps them strike in tight burrows.
They spend much time underground or under cover.
They prey on burrowing rodents, reptiles, and other small animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat small mammals, lizards, and other burrow-associated prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators may include raptors, mongooses, larger snakes, and humans. Their defense is secrecy, venom, and underground movement, showing that hidden power is strongest when it avoids unnecessary exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are secretive and often active at night or underground, with surface sightings uncommon.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Exact wild lifespan is not well known, but similar snakes can live for many years under suitable conditions. The uncertainty itself fits the hidden principle: much of the life remains out of sight.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Like most burrowing asps it is thought to lay eggs, probably in soil or under cover, but clutch size, incubation time and the size of hatchlings have been little documented for this species.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are not usually obvious in casual observation. The shared underground anatomy matters more than visible male-female contrast.

monarch-butterfly.spotlight: Monarch Butterfly teaches Inherited Migration through orange warning wings, milkweed dependence, and multi-generation travel. Small bodies carry enormous direction because the route is stored across seasons, not one individual alone.
monarch-butterfly.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Milkweed patches, meadows, fields, gardens, migration corridors, and overwintering forests.
signatureTraits: Long-distance migration completed across generations.
Bright orange-and-black warning coloration tied to milkweed chemistry.
Milkweed-dependent caterpillars that make habitat specific.
Seasonal navigation using environmental cues.
interestingFacts: Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed plants, storing toxic cardenolides that make them distasteful.
Their orange-and-black pattern warns many predators of chemical defenses.
Some eastern North American monarchs migrate thousands of miles to overwinter in fir forests of central Mexico.
The generation that returns north may be several generations removed from the one that left.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars eat milkweed, while adults drink nectar from many flowers.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, wasps, weather, pesticides, habitat loss, and climate shifts threaten monarchs. Warning color helps, but migration depends on whole landscapes staying connected.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Monarchs are diurnal, flying and feeding in daylight while roosting at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults of the summer breeding generations usually live about 2 to 6 weeks. The late-summer generation that migrates and overwinters can live for about 6 to 9 months.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on milkweed, giving caterpillars the only food they need to begin.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males have scent-scale spots on the hindwings and slightly different vein patterns. Both sexes carry the warning route.

monkey-tailed-skink.spotlight: Reaching 70 to 80 centimetres with the tail, this is the largest living skink, found only in the forests of the Solomon Islands. It spends its life in the trees and eats almost nothing but plants, which is rare among skinks. Small groups share a tree, behaviour seldom seen in lizards.
monkey-tailed-skink.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Solomon Islands forest canopy fits because grasp turns height from danger into home.
signatureTraits: Body is olive to grey-green with darker flecks
Head is large, blunt and wedge-shaped
Scales are smooth, glossy and overlapping
Hisses loudly and may lunge when threatened
interestingFacts: Females give birth to live young, usually a single large baby and occasionally twins, after a pregnancy of six months or more.
Young skinks eat adult droppings, which is thought to supply the gut microbes they need to digest leaves.
It is mainly active at dusk and night, resting by day in tree hollows or among epiphytes.
Heavy collection for the international pet trade led to its listing on CITES Appendix II.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruit.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, humans, and introduced predators threaten Monkey-tailed Skinks, making grip, tree hollows, and family defense important.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, resting in tree hollows and climbing carefully when cooler forest hours make feeding safer.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild is unknown. Captive animals commonly live 15 to 20 years, and some are reported to have passed 25.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to large live young, investing heavily in offspring that are already built for branch gripping and canopy life.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, though males may have broader heads.

monocled-cobra.spotlight: Monocled Cobra teaches Hooded Warning through a snake that makes the line visible before conflict begins. Raised posture, hood spread, eye-like mark, venom, and retreat options show that clear warning can prevent worse contact.
monocled-cobra.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia. Rice fields, wetlands, scrub, forests, villages, farmland, and water edges.
signatureTraits: Distinctive monocle-like mark on the back of the hood.
Raised forebody and hood display used as a threat warning.
Venomous defense paired with attempts to deter before striking.
Flexible use of fields, wetlands, forests, villages, and edges.
interestingFacts: Monocled Cobras are named for the circular mark on the hood.
They often rear up and spread the hood as a warning display before striking when threatened.
They can live around wetlands, farmland, forests, and human edges.
Their warning posture makes the body look larger and harder to ignore.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Rodents, frogs, fish, lizards, snakes, birds, and eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Mongooses, raptors, humans, larger snakes, and habitat conflict threaten them. Hooding creates hesitation before contact, making the warning valuable to both snake and threat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Monocled Cobras may be active by day or night depending on temperature and disturbance.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is not well documented. Captive monocled cobras have been reported living about 20 years, though most wild snakes probably live far less.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected warm sites, and hatchlings are independent immediately.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though size can vary.

monte-iberia-eleuth.spotlight: Monte Iberia Eleuth teaches Micro Significance through a frog so small that a leaf-litter world becomes enormous. Its pin-sized body, damp forest dependence, tiny prey, and extreme rarity show that meaning is not measured by body size.
monte-iberia-eleuth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Moist Cuban rainforest, leaf litter, shaded soil, mossy cover, and humid microhabitats fit Monte Iberia Eleuth because a tiny body dries out quickly and needs a miniature world.
signatureTraits: One of the world’s smallest frogs
Life hidden in moist Cuban leaf litter
Bright markings on a tiny dark body
Extreme dependence on a small forest range
interestingFacts: Monte Iberia Eleuth is famous for being among the smallest known frogs.
It lives in a very limited area of eastern Cuba.
Its tiny body makes moisture and leaf-litter cover especially important.
Small frogs like this often feed on tiny invertebrates that larger animals overlook.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mites, springtails, tiny ants, and minute invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Spiders, insects, small reptiles, birds, and drying conditions can threaten tiny frogs. Leaf litter and hidden scale are the main protections.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active in damp conditions and likely retreat during dryness or heat. Their rhythm follows moisture more than the human clock.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Exact lifespan is not well documented, but tiny frogs often live only a few years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay very small clutches compared with larger frogs, and development is tied to protected damp places. Offspring begin life already dependent on the leaf-litter world.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle to a casual observer. Females are often larger in many frogs, while males may call, but the species’ main message is smallness rather than display.

moorish-idol.spotlight: Moorish Idol teaches Reef Icon through a fish whose banner-like shape stays recognizable in coral complexity. Bold stripes, trailing dorsal filament, and graceful reef turns make presence a moving signature.
moorish-idol.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean, coral_triangle, red_sea. Coral reefs, lagoons, rocky reefs, and clear tropical reef slopes.
signatureTraits: Long trailing dorsal filament that gives the body a banner-like profile.
Bold black, white, and yellow striping visible in reef complexity.
Graceful turning movement through coral and rocky structures.
Narrow reef-foraging body that picks across surfaces and growth.
interestingFacts: Moorish Idols are visually iconic reef fish because of their shape and stripes.
Their long dorsal filament gives them a banner-like look.
They are often confused with similarly patterned butterflyfish, but their body form is distinctive.
They forage across reef surfaces for sponges, algae, and small invertebrate growth.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sponges, algae, tunicates, small invertebrates, and reef growth.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large reef fish, eels, sharks, and habitat loss threaten Moorish Idols. Speed and reef structure provide escape, showing that graceful identity needs a place to move through.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Moorish Idols are diurnal, foraging by day and sheltering in reef structure.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan is not known for wild Moorish idols, and the species rarely survives long in aquaria, so captive records give no useful figure.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning takes place in open water above the reef, and the fertilised eggs float away on the current with no parental care. The larvae spend a long time drifting and reportedly settle onto reefs at a comparatively large size.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look very similar, so the species lesson is not about dimorphism. The shared body shape, stripe, and banner fin carry the iconic signal.

moose.spotlight: Moose teaches Heavy Passage through a giant browser crossing swamp, snow, forest, and water with calm length. Long legs, broad hooves, aquatic feeding, and male antlers make large movement deliberate rather than rushed.
moose.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia. Boreal forest, wetlands, willow thickets, lakes, rivers, muskeg, and snowy woodland fit Moose because swamp and snow make the long stride meaningful.
signatureTraits: Humped shoulders standing higher than the rump
Long, overhanging muzzle with a broad upper lip
Flap of skin, the bell, hanging from the throat
Pale grey-brown legs below a dark brown body
Very short tail, barely visible
interestingFacts: It is the largest living member of the deer family, with big bulls standing about 2 metres at the shoulder.
It can close its nostrils and feed on water plants with its head fully submerged.
Hearing and smell are keen, while its eyesight is thought to be fairly poor.
Over short distances it can run at roughly 50 kilometres per hour.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Willow, birch, aspen, aquatic plants, twigs, bark, and leaves.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves and bears are major predators, especially for calves; ticks, heat, vehicles, and humans add risk. Size helps, but passage still requires caution.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Crepuscular in many areas, feeding in cooler hours and resting when heat or insects intensify. The rhythm conserves a large body.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many wild individuals live 8 to 15 years, and a few reach about 20; heavy predation or hunting shortens this in many populations.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After about 8 months' gestation, cows give birth in late spring to one calf, sometimes twins. Calves follow their mother within days, stay with her through their first winter, and are driven off shortly before she calves again.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Bulls are much larger than cows and grow antlers each summer, shed in early winter; many bulls have broad, palm-shaped antlers, while others carry narrower, branched ones. Cows have no antlers and a pale patch below the tail.

moray-eel.spotlight: Moray Eel teaches Lair Strategy through a reef predator winning from the right hiding place. Long body, crevice life, open-mouth breathing, strong jaws, and sudden strikes make the hole part of the method.
moray-eel.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_africa_middle_east, south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia, australia_oceania, indian_ocean, north_pacific, coral_triangle, red_sea. Coral reefs, rocky crevices, lagoon walls, caves, and reef slopes.
signatureTraits: Long muscular body built for reef crevices
Ambush hunting from holes and caves
Strong jaws and specialized feeding mechanics
Open-mouth breathing posture that can look threatening
interestingFacts: Moray Eels often sit with mouths open to move water over their gills, not simply to threaten.
Their long bodies let them use reef spaces other predators cannot enter.
Some morays cooperate with other predators such as groupers in reef hunting systems.
Their second set of throat jaws helps pull prey inward.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, octopus, squid, crustaceans, and reef animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large groupers, sharks, humans, and larger morays can threaten them. The crevice defends and attacks at once, showing why the right place can become stronger than constant motion.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Moray Eels are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, sheltering by day with the head exposed. Their rhythm is hidden readiness followed by night movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Moray Eels can live for many years, making Lair Strategy a long relationship with territory, hiding places, and repeated reef routes. The lesson deepens because patience must be maintained over time.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females release eggs into the water, and the young begin life as drifting larvae before settling into reef habitats.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are usually not obvious to casual observers.

mossy-frog.spotlight: Much of its time is spent part-submerged in flooded rock crevices and tree holes, with little more than the eyes above water. Adults measure about 6 to 9 centimetres, the back raised into warts and small spines.
mossy-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Mossy Frog usually lives in cool wet forests, limestone pools, rocky streams, and mossy caves.
signatureTraits: Bumpy green-brown-black skin that resembles moss and lichen
Wet-rock hiding style that turns body texture into landscape
Damp forest dependence that makes moisture part of disguise
Stillness that completes the camouflage pattern
interestingFacts: Mossy Frogs can resemble a clump of moss on wet rock.
They are native to parts of northern Vietnam and nearby areas.
When threatened, they may curl up and rely on camouflage.
Their skin texture is as important as their color.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mossy Frog feeds on insects, worms, and small invertebrates captured near wet stone and vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tree snakes, birds and small mammals are the likely predators, though attacks are rarely witnessed. Forest loss and collection for the pet trade are the recognised threats to wild populations.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal, hiding by day and becoming active in damp darkness, when being part of the wet wall matters most.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around ten years is reported by keepers for captive frogs; wild frogs have not been aged.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs near water, where tadpoles develop in pools or cavities, beginning life inside the same wet stone world the adults imitate.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger; males may call around breeding sites, but camouflage remains the main shared language.

mouflon.spotlight: Mouflon teaches Horn Boundary through a wild sheep whose curled horns make conflict legible before it becomes chaos. Rocky footing, herd awareness, rut contests, and visible male horns turn boundary into structure, not random force.
mouflon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east. Rocky hills, dry mountains, open woodland, and grassy slopes.
signatureTraits: Large curved horns in males make dominance contests visible and structured.
Sure-footed movement helps the flock use rocky slopes as refuge.
Herd vigilance turns individual boundaries into shared safety.
Dry-hill grazing keeps the animal moving between food, cover, and contest ground.
interestingFacts: Mouflon are often treated as one of the wild ancestors or close relatives behind domestic sheep.
Males clash horns during the breeding season, but the ritualized contest helps sort dominance without constant disorder.
Their rugged habitat makes balance part of survival, not just an athletic trait.
Females and young rely more on flock movement and terrain than on the dramatic horns of adult rams.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, herbs, shrubs, leaves, and bark.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, lynx, bears, eagles for lambs, dogs, and humans can threaten Mouflon. Herd vigilance, speed, rocky refuge, and the visible force of adult rams make protection a layered system rather than a single weapon.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mouflon are mainly active by day and around cooler dawn or dusk periods, feeding and resting according to heat and safety.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Mouflon can live around a decade in the wild, with longer lives possible under protected conditions. That span gives repeated seasons for young animals to learn routes, flock rules, and the difference between panic and a clear horn line.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one lamb after the breeding season, choosing cover and flock proximity so the young can stand and follow quickly. Offspring survival depends on early footing, watchful mothers, and the herd’s shared sense of danger.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger and carry the most dramatic curled horns, while females are smaller and may have small horns or none depending on population.

mountain-beaver.spotlight: The Mountain Beaver is primitive fit without apology. Its ancient rodent line, wet-forest burrows, and plant-chewing life show that an old design can survive when it still fits the ground perfectly.
mountain-beaver.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Mountain Beavers live in moist forests, brushy slopes, streamside thickets, and dense vegetation of the Pacific Northwest.
signatureTraits: Primitive rodent lineage
Moist-forest burrow systems
Ever-growing gnawing teeth
Vegetation-heavy diet
interestingFacts: Mountain Beavers are not true beavers and do not build dams.
They are often called living fossils because their lineage retains ancient rodent traits.
They need moist environments and are poor at conserving water compared with many rodents.
They cut and carry vegetation into burrows for feeding and nesting.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat ferns, leaves, stems, bark, and many kinds of forest vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Coyotes, bobcats, owls, weasels, and other predators may take them when they leave cover. Their protection is burrowing and thick vegetation, showing that an old design survives by staying close to the ground it understands.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are often active around dawn, dusk, and night, moving between burrow entrances and feeding areas.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Mountain Beavers usually live only a few years in the wild, though some may survive longer. Even a modest lifespan can carry an ancient design forward when the fit is exact.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in burrows, usually to a small litter that develops in hidden nests. Offspring inherit not just a body, but a damp underground architecture that makes that body work.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, with no showy sex difference. The species' identity is ecological fit, not ornament.

mountain-goat.spotlight: Mountain Goat teaches Cliff Footing through a white alpine body making steep fear feel stable. Split hooves, rough pads, thick coat, and ledge discipline turn cliffs into usable ground.
mountain-goat.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Alpine cliffs, rocky ridges, snowfields, mineral licks, and high meadows.
signatureTraits: Split hooves with rough pads for gripping rock
Thick white coat suited to snow and alpine cold
Powerful shoulders and balance for steep climbs
Use of cliffs as both feeding ground and predator refuge
interestingFacts: Mountain Goats are not true goats, but goat-antelopes.
Their hooves are highly adapted for steep rocky terrain.
Kids can follow their mothers on difficult slopes very early.
Cliffs protect them from many predators that cannot climb as well.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, lichens, mosses, herbs, shrubs, and alpine plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, bears, cougars, eagles for kids, avalanches, falls, and harsh winters threaten them. Good footing protects, but the mountain still punishes careless movement.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mountain Goats are diurnal, feeding and resting on cliffs while shifting with weather and temperature.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild animals commonly live 10 to 13 years; females tend to outlive males, and some reach their late teens.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to kids that must quickly stand and climb.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females both have horns, though males are usually larger.
