fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Lions, wolves, large dogs, humans, and conflict around settlements can threaten them. Their defense is nocturnal secrecy, strong jaws, mane display, and avoidance, showing that useful power does not need constant confrontation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal, resting in dens or shelters by day and ranging at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Striped Hyenas may live around 10 to 12 years in the wild and longer in care. A long scavenging life is built on repeated practical choices rather than one heroic hunt.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth in dens to small litters, and young depend on protected shelter while they grow. Offspring begin life hidden, learning a world where food may be found in unlikely places.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, with size differences usually not dramatic. The species' main signal is the striped, useful night-worker body shared by both.

striped-skunk.spotlight: Striped Skunk teaches Boundary through a warning system designed to prevent conflict before spray is spent. Bold stripes, raised tail, stamping feet, arched posture, and chemical defense all say the same thing: notice the line before you cross it.
striped-skunk.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Forests, grasslands, farms, suburbs, gardens, and urban edges fit striped skunks because they are flexible foragers that need den sites and nighttime food. Their boundaries travel with them through human and wild edges.
signatureTraits: High-contrast striping advertises chemical defense before a predator gets close.
Tail raising, stamping, and arched posture give several warnings before spray.
Chemical spray is powerful but costly, so prevention is built into the display.
interestingFacts: Striped Skunks usually warn before spraying by stamping their front feet, hissing, and raising the tail.
The spray takes time and energy to replenish after use.
Great Horned Owls are one of the few regular predators that often ignore the warning.
They can aim their spray at an attacker's face from a distance of roughly three metres.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, grubs, small mammals, eggs, fruit, carrion, and plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Great Horned Owls, coyotes, foxes, bobcats, dogs, and humans create danger, but most predators learn to respect the stripe. Warning prevents wasteful fighting.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Striped Skunks are mainly nocturnal, moving under cover of darkness to forage.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild skunks often live only a few years, though they can live longer in safer conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to litters of kits in dens and care for them until they can follow and forage. Young skunks learn that warning, staying close, and using scent carefully are survival tools.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females, but both carry the same striped warning system and spray defense. Boundary is species-wide protection rather than a male-only display.

sulphur-crested-cockatoo.spotlight: Sulphur-crested Cockatoo teaches Transmission through a loud, social mind that turns discovery into shared behavior. Its crest, strong beak, gripping feet, flock calls, and problem-solving show that intelligence becomes more powerful when one bird’s trick can travel to another.
sulphur-crested-cockatoo.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Woodlands, forest edges, farms, parks, cities, and open tree country fit the cockatoo because intelligence needs both tools and witnesses. The habitat gives objects to open, food to learn, and flocks to teach.
signatureTraits: Flock Learning: useful behavior can spread through watching, testing, and copying.
Beak-and-Foot Tools: the cockatoo manipulates the world with a strong hooked beak and zygodactyl feet.
Loud Contact: sharp calls keep the flock connected across trees, distance, and disturbance.
interestingFacts: Sulphur-crested Cockatoos are highly social parrots with strong problem-solving ability.
They can manipulate objects with both beak and feet.
Their loud calls help maintain contact in open woodland and urban settings.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, nuts, roots, fruit, crops, and insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large raptors, snakes, nest predators, humans, and habitat loss create pressure around feeding and nesting. Flock alarm, loud contact, and learned caution make survival social rather than solitary.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sulphur-crested Cockatoos are diurnal, feeding, calling, flying, and investigating during daylight. The day becomes a classroom where discoveries can be seen, repeated, and passed on.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for decades, especially in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree hollows, and both parents may care for the young. Nest cavities make learning begin in protected darkness before the young join the louder intelligence of the flock.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though eye color can differ in adults.

sumatran-orangutan.spotlight: Sumatran Orangutan teaches Canopy Thought through a mind that shapes rainforest one branch at a time. Its long arms, tool use, nest building, fruit knowledge, and slow maternal learning show intelligence as patient craft.
sumatran-orangutan.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra. Sumatran rainforests, peat swamp forest, fruiting canopy, and tall connected trees fit Sumatran Orangutans because careful thought works through branches.
signatureTraits: Long arms and grasping hands for canopy travel
Daily nest building from branches and leaves
Tool use and complex foraging knowledge
Slow childhood with long maternal learning
interestingFacts: Sumatran Orangutans are more arboreal than Bornean orangutans.
They build fresh sleeping nests in trees each night by bending and weaving branches together.
They have been observed using tools for feeding and comfort.
Young orangutans learn survival skills from mothers for many years.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, young leaves, bark, insects, flowers, and occasional honey or seeds.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tigers, clouded leopards, snakes, and humans can threaten orangutans, especially young. Height, intelligence, and maternal care provide protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, feeding and traveling by day, then building nests to sleep at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Orangutans can live for several decades, with long childhoods and slow reproduction.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single infant after long intervals. Young stay with mothers for years, learning food, routes, tools, and nest craft.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males can develop large cheek pads and throat sacs, while females remain smaller and raise young. The contrast shows intelligence as both display and deep care.

sumatran-rhinoceros.spotlight: Sumatran Rhinoceros carries Rhino Ancient Strength as a small, hairy forest tank, holding old lineage power in a wet, dense world that demands endurance over display.
sumatran-rhinoceros.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra, borneo. Sumatran Rhinoceroses live in dense tropical forests, hills, and swampy areas where cover and browsing routes matter. The habitat turns ancient strength into quiet movement through wet vegetation.
signatureTraits: Smallest living rhinoceros
Hairy reddish-brown body
Two horn structure
Dense forest browser
interestingFacts: It is the hairiest living rhino, with reddish-brown hair that is thickest on young animals.
It is the closest living rhino relative to extinct woolly rhinos.
It is among the most threatened large mammals.
Only a few dozen are thought to survive, in small scattered groups on Sumatra and in Indonesian Borneo.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They browse leaves, shoots, twigs, fruits, and bark. This diet fits old strength because the rhino must steadily process forest growth rather than dominate open grassland.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but poaching, habitat fragmentation, and isolation are severe threats. Ancient power cannot survive if individuals are too separated to breed.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly solitary and often active during cooler periods, wallowing and browsing through dense cover.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for decades, with slow reproduction.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf after a long gestation and nurse it for an extended period. Each calf is rare and carries enormous conservation weight.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females both have two horns, though males often have larger horns. The sex difference is less important than the shared ancient, hairy forest form.

sumatran-tiger.spotlight: Sumatran Tiger carries Dense Stealth as compact jungle power, using dark tight stripes and a smaller body to fit a forest where every opening is narrow.
sumatran-tiger.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra. Sumatran Tigers live in lowland forest, peat swamp, mountain forest, and dense jungle on Sumatra.
signatureTraits: Compact tiger body
Dense dark striping
Solitary ambush hunting
Tropical forest specialist
interestingFacts: It is the smallest surviving tiger subspecies, with males often weighing about 100 to 140 kilograms.
Its stripes are often darker and closer together than many mainland tigers.
It lives only on Sumatra, the last surviving Sunda island tiger since the Javan and Bali tigers vanished.
The IUCN lists the Sumatran Tiger as Critically Endangered, with only a few hundred thought to remain.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They hunt deer, wild pigs, monkeys, birds, and other animals. The diet fits Dense Stealth because the tiger must get close before power becomes useful.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have no regular natural predator, but habitat loss, poaching, conflict, and prey decline threaten them. The forest is as important as the claws.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly crepuscular and nocturnal, resting in cover and hunting when stealth improves.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live more than a decade in the wild and longer in care. A solitary hunter’s lifespan depends on territory, prey, and avoiding people.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to small litters in hidden dens and raise cubs alone. Cubs learn stealth slowly from the mother’s forest routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger than females and hold larger territories. The difference reflects solitary command, while both sexes carry the same striped ambush design.

sun-bear.spotlight: Sun Bear teaches Hidden Honey through a small forest bear opening hard places for sweetness. Long tongue, curved claws, strong jaws, and tree climbing make value accessible where bark, logs, and bee nests hide it.
sun-bear.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Tropical rainforests, lowland forest, fruiting trees, logs, and cavity-rich woodland.
signatureTraits: Very long tongue for reaching honey and insects
Strong claws and jaws for opening logs and tree cavities
Compact body suited to climbing tropical forest trees
Bright chest patch that gives each bear a distinct mark
interestingFacts: Sun Bears are the smallest bear species, with adults commonly reported at about 25 to 65 kilograms.
Their tongues can reach deep into nests and cavities for honey and insects.
They are excellent climbers and often forage in trees.
The pale chest patch varies in shape between individuals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Honey, bees, termites, ants, beetle larvae, fruit, figs, small vertebrates, and eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Tigers, leopards, large pythons, humans, and habitat loss threaten Sun Bears. Climbing, claws, and hidden forest movement protect a bear that survives by getting into places others cannot.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sun Bears can be active by day or night, often shifting with disturbance and food. Their rhythm follows fruiting trees, insect nests, and the quiet chance to open hard places.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Sun Bears can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to one or two cubs in sheltered dens or tree-related cover, nursing and guarding them closely.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger, but both sexes share the long tongue, climbing ability, and extraction tools that carry the principle.

sun-conure.spotlight: Golden-yellow with an orange face and belly, this small long-tailed parakeet lives in a limited part of north-eastern South America centred on Roraima in Brazil and neighbouring Guyana. Flocks call with shrill, grating screeches in flight, then fall almost silent once they settle to feed. Young birds are largely green and gain the yellow as they mature.
sun-conure.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Sun Conure usually lives in tropical forests, savannas, palm groves, and woodland edges.
signatureTraits: sun-bright plumage
loud calls
social flocking
quick flight
interestingFacts: Far more sun conures now live in aviaries and homes than in the wild, where only a few thousand are thought to remain.
It has been listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2008.
The scientific name solstitialis means 'of the summer solstice', a reference to the sun-like colouring.
Its nearest relatives are the jandaya and golden-capped parakeets of eastern Brazil, which share its yellow and orange tones.
At Karasabai in southern Guyana, villagers protect a wild flock and guide visiting birdwatchers to it.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sun Conure feeds on fruit, seeds, flowers, berries, and plant foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation on wild birds has been little studied. Hawks and falcons are the likely hunters of flying flocks, and snakes and small mammals can reach eggs and chicks in nest holes. A disturbed flock leaves together, screeching. Trapping for the cage-bird trade has done the greatest damage.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sun Conure is diurnal, calling and feeding in active flocks.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Sun Conure can live for decades in good conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Wild pairs nest in cavities and raise small clutches. Most details come from aviaries, where females lay 3 to 5 eggs and incubate for about 23 to 27 days, and the chicks fledge at around eight weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look very similar. No plumage feature separates them reliably, so aviary birds are sexed by DNA test.

sunbeam-snake.spotlight: Sunbeam Snake teaches Hidden Radiance through a burrower whose rainbow only appears when light finds it. Smooth scales, soil movement, wet-ground cover, and quiet strength make low life shine.
sunbeam-snake.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Wet soil, rice fields, forest edges, gardens, leaf litter, and humid lowlands.
signatureTraits: Highly iridescent smooth scales that flash rainbow colors
Burrowing body suited to soft soil and leaf litter
Nocturnal or secretive movement near wet ground
Quiet nonvenomous constrictor strategy
interestingFacts: Sunbeam Snakes are famous for rainbow-like iridescence in sunlight.
They spend much time hidden in soil, leaf litter, or loose ground.
They are nonvenomous constrictors, subduing prey in their coils before swallowing it whole.
Their smooth scales help them move through earth.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Frogs, lizards, small snakes, rodents, and other small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, mammals, larger snakes, humans, and habitat change threaten them. Burrowing and hidden movement protect the radiance from constant exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sunbeam Snakes are mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, often emerging after rain.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Captive lifespan looks scarce and wild ages are unpublished; fossorial iridescent snakes of Southeast Asian soils often fare poorly in tanks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in protected warm sites, and hatchlings begin life small and secretive. Offspring fit the principle because the shine is inherited before the world notices it.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Outwardly the sexes are alike in colour and sheen; as in many snakes, males tend to have a longer, thicker tail base, which is seldom noticeable.

sunbittern.spotlight: Sunbittern teaches Revelation through a quiet riverside bird hiding a sunburst in its wings. Cryptic walking, river margins, sudden eye-like wing display, and timing make the hidden gift powerful.
sunbittern.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Shaded tropical streams, forest rivers, quiet banks, wetlands, and creek edges.
signatureTraits: Hidden sunburst wing pattern revealed in display
Quiet cryptic walking along tropical water edges
Eye-like wing markings used in threat and courtship display
Slender riverside body suited to careful foraging
interestingFacts: Sunbitterns usually look cryptic until they open their wings.
Their wing displays can reveal bold eye-like patterns.
They live along shaded streams and forest water edges.
Their dramatic display is useful because it is not shown all the time.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, fish, frogs, crustaceans, and small aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raptors, snakes, mammals, and nest predators threaten Sunbitterns or chicks. The eye-like wing flash can startle danger, turning beauty into a defensive interruption.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sunbitterns are diurnal, walking and foraging quietly by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Reliable year totals are unpublished; streamside birds that flash sunburst wing eyespots along Neotropical creeks are scarcely aged.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in nests built near water, and both parents may help raise the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, so the species lesson is not based on one sex showing off more than the other. The same hidden sunburst belongs to the shared body plan.

sunda-pangolin.spotlight: A scaly anteater of Southeast Asian forests, the Sunda pangolin usually weighs 4 to 7 kilograms. Pangolins are the only mammals armoured with scales, which are made of keratin, the material of fingernails. It is a capable climber and spends much of its time in trees.
sunda-pangolin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra, borneo. Tropical forest, plantations, burrows, tree hollows, and termite-rich ground.
signatureTraits: Overlapping brown scales from head to tail tip
Small, pointed head with a narrow snout
Long tail that grips branches
Large curved claws on the forefeet
Walks with the front claws curled under
interestingFacts: Pangolins have no teeth, and swallowed grit and horny spines lining the stomach grind up the insects instead.
The tongue is anchored deep in the chest, near the last ribs, and not in the mouth.
It can close its nostrils and ears to keep out ants while it feeds.
The word pangolin comes from the Malay pengguling, meaning one that rolls up.
International trade in all eight pangolin species was banned in 2016, after years in which pangolins were among the most heavily trafficked wild mammals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Ants and termites.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large cats, pythons, dogs, and humans threaten pangolins. Curling works against many predators, but trafficking turns protection into vulnerability.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly nocturnal, resting hidden by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild and captive lifespan records for Manis javanica are few; this scaled mammal is notoriously hard to keep and forages mainly for ants and termites.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually carry one pup on the tail or body, curling around it when threatened.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger and heavier than females, but the two otherwise look alike in scales and colour.

suni.spotlight: Suni teaches Cover Passage through tiny size, shy movement, and narrow routes under dense vegetation. Smallness becomes power because the hidden path opens only to bodies light enough to use it.
suni.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Coastal forest, thickets, dense woodland, scrub, and forest edges.
signatureTraits: Tiny antelope body suited to dense cover and narrow paths.
Low-profile movement through thickets and forest edges.
Sharp alertness that avoids exposure before flight is needed.
Browsing diet taken from protected understory.
interestingFacts: Sunis are very small African antelopes, with adults typically weighing only around 5 kilograms.
Males have short horns while females usually do not.
They rely heavily on dense cover and secrecy.
They browse leaves, shoots, fruit, fungi, and fallen plant material.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, shoots, fruit, flowers, fungi, and fallen vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards, eagles, pythons, small carnivores, humans, and dogs can threaten them. Dense cover and small paths are the first protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Sunis are mostly crepuscular or nocturnal, feeding when cover and low light help.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented. Captive suni have lived about 9 to 10 years, and a few somewhat longer.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to a single fawn hidden in vegetation.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry short horns while females usually lack them. The difference matters in display, but both sexes depend on small hidden movement.

sunset-moth.spotlight: Tailed hindwings and a wingspan of about 7 to 9 centimetres mark this large moth of the family Uraniidae. Its populations shift across Madagascar: adults fly in large numbers between the eastern rainforest and the western dry forest, a movement thought to track the condition of the plants their caterpillars feed on.
sunset-moth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Sunset Moths live in Madagascar forests and areas with larval host plants.
signatureTraits: Iridescent rainbow wings
Day-flying moth habits
Madagascar origin
Structural coloration
interestingFacts: Its colors come largely from wing structure, not just pigment.
It is often mistaken for a butterfly because it is brightly colored and flies by day.
Its caterpillars feed only on Omphalea plants, and adults are thought to retain some of the plants' toxins.
Adults are reported to make large movements across Madagascar as their Omphalea host plants change in availability.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Adults drink nectar, mostly from white or pale flowers; recorded nectar plants include mango, eucalyptus, Indian almond and Weinmannia. Caterpillars feed only on Omphalea, shrubs and trees of the spurge family, eating leaves, flowers, fruit and tender stems.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards and spiders are the likely predators, though few attacks are documented. The food plant is poisonous, and toxins taken in by the caterpillar are thought to persist in the adult, whose bright wings advertise that it is distasteful.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Adults fly and feed in daylight, mostly in sunshine. They roost among foliage overnight and in dull or wet weather.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The caterpillar stage lasts about two to three months and the pupa about three weeks. How long adults live in the wild is not well established.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After mating, females lay eggs on host plants for caterpillars to feed. Eggs are laid in batches, often of around 80, usually on the underside of a leaf. Young caterpillars eat only the tissue between the leaf veins, and the full-grown caterpillar pupates in an open-mesh silk cocoon.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are similar, with wing color and pattern central to both. No dependable difference shows on a flying or feeding moth.

superb-bird-of-paradise.spotlight: To court a female, the male of this New Guinea songbird swings the long feathers of his nape forward until they form a black disc around his head. Two pale blue spots near the top look like eyes. He then hops in tight arcs around her on a log or low branch.
superb-bird-of-paradise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Superb Bird-of-paradise usually lives in New Guinea forests and display courts in dense vegetation.
signatureTraits: black cape display
blue breast shield
dance
shape change
interestingFacts: A 2018 study found that the black display feathers absorb more than 99 per cent of the light striking them head-on, because of their microscopic structure.
At rest the cape lies folded over the back, so the male looks like a compact black bird with a blue-green breast.
It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, being widespread in the mountains of New Guinea.
Some authorities now treat birds from the Vogelkop Peninsula and from eastern New Guinea as separate species, narrowing what is called Lophorina superba.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Superb Bird-of-paradise feeds on fruit, insects, and small forest foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predation has seldom been seen directly in this species. Snakes, hawks and other forest hunters are thought to take eggs and chicks. People hunt adult males for their display feathers, worn in highland headdresses.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Superb Bird-of-paradise is diurnal, with males displaying by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Nobody has followed wild birds of this species long enough to say how long they live. Males need several years to grow adult plumage, so any displaying male is already at least that old.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: As in most birds-of-paradise, females nest and raise young alone after courtship. The nest is an open cup holding one or two eggs. Incubation is thought to last about two and a half to three weeks, with a similar period before the chicks fledge.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are ornate displayers; females are plainer brown. She is barred dark on pale buff below and has a pale stripe over the eye. Young males resemble females before moulting into black.

superb-lyrebird.spotlight: Superb Lyrebird teaches Sound Mimicry through a forest performer turning the whole world into vocal material. Layered songs, copied calls, environmental sounds, display mound, and lyre-shaped tail make creativity a gathered archive.
superb-lyrebird.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Wet forests, fern gullies, temperate rainforest, dense gullies, and leaf-littered woodland fit Superb Lyrebirds because sound, cover, and foraging material surround the performer.
signatureTraits: Exceptional mimic capable of copying many bird calls and other sounds.
Male has elaborate lyre-shaped tail feathers used in courtship display.
Forages by scratching through leaf litter on the forest floor.
Courtship display combines voice, movement, and visual performance.
interestingFacts: Superb Lyrebirds can imitate complex sound sequences from their environment.
They are native to forests of southeastern Australia.
Their scratching helps turn leaf litter while searching for invertebrates.
Young males take years to develop full adult tail display.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, worms, spiders, larvae, centipedes, and soil invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, cats, dogs, raptors, snakes, fire, and habitat loss threaten lyrebirds or nests. Dense forest cover protects the performer behind the famous voice.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Superb Lyrebirds are diurnal, foraging and displaying by day. Their rhythm gives time to collect sound, rehearse, and turn attention into performance.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Long-lived for a songbird: ages of more than 20 years have been reported, and around 30 years is sometimes quoted.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build domed nests and raise a single chick with heavy investment. Offspring survival depends on hidden nesting and long learning before performance becomes possible.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the famous ornate tail and display behavior, while females are plainer and handle nesting.

surinam-horned-frog.spotlight: Surinam Horned Frog teaches Mouth Surprise through leaf-colored stillness, horn-like eyes, and a huge sudden bite. Great action begins from stillness because the whole body is built around the moment prey comes close.
surinam-horned-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Rainforest leaf litter, damp forest floor, stream edges, and muddy cover.
signatureTraits: Wide mouth built for sudden ambush feeding.
Leaf-like camouflage with horned head outline.
Sit-and-wait hunting on rainforest floors.
Explosive lunge after long stillness.
interestingFacts: Surinam horned frogs are close relatives of other Pacman frogs.
They have very wide mouths for taking large prey relative to body size.
Their camouflage helps them resemble forest floor debris.
They are ambush predators rather than active chasers.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, spiders, small frogs, lizards, and other small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, larger frogs, drought, and habitat loss threaten them. Camouflage and moisture-seeking behavior keep stillness from becoming exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Surinam Horned Frogs are mostly nocturnal or moisture-linked, waiting in cover and feeding when humidity supports movement.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Keepers' reports suggest roughly 5 to 10 years in captivity. Wild longevity is unrecorded.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in water, where tadpoles develop before moving into ground-level ambush life.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males in many horned frogs. The difference supports egg production, while both sexes share the ambush body.

surinam-toad.spotlight: The Surinam Toad is strange care made unforgettable. Eggs held in the female's back turn parental protection into a living surface, proving care does not have to look familiar to be complete.
surinam-toad.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Surinam Toads live in slow-moving streams, ponds, flooded forests, and muddy tropical freshwater in northern South America.
signatureTraits: Flattened leaf-like aquatic body
Eggs brooded in female's back skin
Fully aquatic lifestyle
Star-shaped sensitive fingertips
interestingFacts: During breeding, eggs become embedded in pockets on the female's back.
Young develop in those pockets and emerge as small toads.
Surinam Toads are highly aquatic and rarely move like typical hopping frogs.
Their flat bodies help them blend with leaves and debris underwater.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat small fish, aquatic invertebrates, worms, and other prey captured underwater.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators can include fish, birds, caimans, and larger aquatic animals, especially for young. Their defense is camouflage, aquatic stillness, and unusual reproduction, showing that protection can be built into the body itself.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly aquatic and active in water, often resting quietly against the bottom.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live for many years, with captive individuals often reaching a decade or more. A long life makes the strange care more than a curiosity; it is a repeated strategy.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry fertilized eggs embedded in the skin of the back until young emerge as small toads.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally smaller and call or clasp during breeding, while females perform the remarkable back-brooding role. Here, sex difference is central because female reproduction defines the species' signature care.

swallow-tailed-kite.spotlight: Swallow-tailed Kite turns open air into a path. Long wings, a scissor tail, insect-catching flight, and thermal steering make control look effortless because the body is shaped for it.
swallow-tailed-kite.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Open woodlands, river forests, swamps, wetlands, and warm skies.
signatureTraits: Deeply forked tail acts like a steering blade in the air.
Long pointed wings support buoyant gliding and sharp turns.
Feeds on insects and small prey while still flying, reducing wasted landings.
Soaring movement lets it cover forest and wetland edges efficiently.
interestingFacts: Swallow-tailed kites can eat prey on the wing.
Their black-and-white plumage and deeply forked tail make their shape unmistakable overhead.
They migrate long distances between breeding and wintering areas.
They often drink in flight by skimming the water surface with the bill.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Flying insects, lizards, frogs, small snakes, nestling birds, and other small prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, larger raptors, raccoons at nests, storms, habitat loss, and human disturbance threaten them. High nests and flight skill reduce ground exposure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, most active when thermals and daylight support soaring and visual hunting.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Poorly measured. About 6 years is often quoted as an average, though firm data are scarce and some birds probably live well beyond that.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in high tree nests, and young depend on precise parent flight bringing food back through the canopy.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females share the same plumage. Females average slightly larger, but the difference cannot be judged in the field.

swamp-harrier.spotlight: Swamp Harrier teaches Low Search through a raptor that sweeps close enough to read the ground. Long wings, low quartering flight, marsh routes, and repeated passes show hidden things found by staying near the surface.
swamp-harrier.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Wetlands, reedbeds, swamps, grasslands, farmland, estuaries, and open marsh edges fit Swamp Harriers because their hunting method needs wide low search lanes.
signatureTraits: Low quartering flight: repeated passes search reeds and grass.
Long wings: the body is shaped for slow sweeping rather than sudden stoop only.
Ground nesting: the hunter of cover also depends on cover.
interestingFacts: Harriers often hunt by quartering low over open ground.
Swamp Harriers use wetlands, grasslands, and farmland edges.
Swamp Harriers nest on the ground among reeds or rank grass, where concealment protects eggs and chicks.
It occurs in Australia, New Zealand, and several Pacific islands, and is New Zealand's most common bird of prey.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small birds, eggs, rodents, rabbits, reptiles, frogs, insects, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger raptors, foxes, cats, snakes, and humans can threaten harriers, especially ground nests. Low flight helps hunt, but nesting on the ground requires concealment.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Swamp Harriers are diurnal, flying low over wetlands and fields in daylight. Their rhythm is patient sweeping until movement betrays itself.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Swamp Harriers can live several years, with success tied to wetland health, prey supply, and safe nesting cover.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in nests placed on the ground or low in dense vegetation. Offspring make the low-cover world both hunting ground and nursery.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger and often darker, while males may be lighter or more agile-looking depending on age and region. Size difference matters in hunting, nesting, and pair roles.

sword-billed-hummingbird.spotlight: A large hummingbird of the high Andes, found from Venezuela to Bolivia. Its bill, roughly 9 to 11 centimetres long, is too long to preen with, so the bird grooms its plumage by scratching with its feet.
sword-billed-hummingbird.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Sword-billed Hummingbirds usually live in Andean cloud forest, edges, and long-tubed flower habitats.
signatureTraits: Perched birds hold the bill tilted steeply upward.
The black bill is straight and slender.
A small white spot sits just behind the eye.
It hovers beneath hanging flowers and probes them from below.
interestingFacts: The passionflower Passiflora mixta has a floral tube too long for most other pollinators and relies largely on this hummingbird to carry its pollen.
Both parts of its scientific name, Ensifera ensifera, mean sword-bearer, after the bill.
Its closest relative is thought to be the great sapphirewing, another large hummingbird of the high Andes.
It is classed as Least Concern, as it has a wide range along the Andes and is not thought to be declining quickly.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on nectar from deep tubular flowers plus tiny insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Small Accipiter hawks may take adults at Andean forest edges, while snakes and arboreal mammals can raid cavity or nest sites for eggs and chicks. Loss of montane forest removes the long-tubed flowers this bill is built for.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, feeding along a regular circuit of scattered flowers and resting on a perch between visits. It roosts at night and, like other high-Andean hummingbirds, probably enters torpor on cold nights, though this has been little studied in this species.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Measured ages are unpublished; hummingbirds whose bills exceed body length at Passiflora flowers may live several years by size analogy alone.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding is scarcely known and few nests have been described. They are reported as mossy cups, and the clutch is assumed to be two white eggs, incubated and raised by the female alone as in other hummingbirds.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar, though females are often duller.

tailless-whip-scorpion.spotlight: Tailless Whip Scorpion teaches Dark Tactile Mapping through a flattened arachnid feeling its way across walls. Antenniform legs, cave stillness, spiny grasping arms, and sideways movement turn fear into direction.
tailless-whip-scorpion.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, north_africa_middle_east. Caves, bark, tree hollows, rock walls, humid forests, and dark crevices.
signatureTraits: Long whip-like sensory legs used to map surfaces
Flattened body for bark, cave, and rock shelter
Spiny pedipalps that grab prey at close range
Nocturnal movement guided more by touch than sight
interestingFacts: Tailless Whip Scorpions are arachnids, but they are not true scorpions.
They have no venomous tail or stinger and are harmless to people despite their fearsome look.
Their long, thin front legs are not used for walking but work like sensory feelers.
Females carry young on their backs after hatching.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crickets, cockroaches, moths, small insects, and other arthropods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, reptiles, mammals, larger arthropods, and habitat disturbance threaten them. Flattening into crevices and sensing early make darkness safer.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tailless Whip Scorpions are nocturnal, waiting and moving in darkness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Tailless Whip Scorpions can live for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry eggs under the body and later carry young on the back until they disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences can include size or pedipalp differences.

tailless-whip-spider.spotlight: Tailless Whip Spider teaches Tactile Mapping through a strange hunter turning darkness into a touch map. Antenniform legs, flattened body, cave walls, bark surfaces, and spiny pedipalps make touch reach farther than sight.
tailless-whip-spider.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Caves, hollow trees, bark, limestone walls, tropical forest crevices, and dark shelters fit Tailless Whip Spiders because Tactile Mapping needs surfaces that can be read by touch. The habitat makes darkness navigable.
signatureTraits: Long antenniform legs used as sensory feelers
Flattened body for slipping along walls and crevices
Spiny pedipalps for grabbing prey at close range
Nocturnal navigation through caves, bark, and dark shelters
interestingFacts: Tailless Whip Spiders are arachnids, but they are not true spiders.
They do not have a venomous stinger or tail like scorpions.
Their long front legs act like feelers rather than walking legs.
They are often more strange-looking than dangerous to humans.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crickets, cockroaches, moths and other small arthropods. It finds prey at night by sweeping with its long, whip-like first legs, then seizes it with a fast grab of the spiny pedipalps and tears it apart with the jaws.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, reptiles, mammals, larger arthropods, and habitat disturbance threaten them. Flattening into crevices and early sensing reduce danger, proving that sensitivity can be defensive power.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tailless Whip Spiders are nocturnal, and their long sensory legs matter most when light is limited. Their rhythm is feel, map, wait, and grab.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Tailless Whip Spiders can live for several years, especially compared with many small arthropods.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females carry eggs under the body and later carry young on the back until they disperse.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes are very similar and hard to tell apart in the field; adult males may have relatively longer pedipalps. Reliable sexing is done by examining the genital plate on the underside of the abdomen.

takahe.spotlight: Takahe turns Grounded Thriving into a blue, heavy, wingless confidence, proving that a bird can master tough alpine grass without needing the sky.
takahe.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Takahe live in alpine tussock grasslands, wetlands, and protected island or sanctuary habitats. The habitat makes grounded life meaningful because the food and shelter are underfoot.
signatureTraits: Flightless rail body built for walking through vegetation
Thick red bill cuts tough grasses and sedges
Deep blue-green plumage gives a grounded bird royal presence
Rediscovery and protection turned absence into recovery
interestingFacts: It was once thought extinct before being rediscovered in New Zealand
It uses a strong bill to cut tough alpine grasses
It is a flightless rail that survives through protected management

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat grasses, sedges, shoots, and plant stems, often cutting tough vegetation with a strong bill.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Stoats, cats, dogs, habitat limits, and food competition threaten them. Flightlessness needs protected places where the ground is safe enough.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are diurnal, walking, feeding, calling, and defending territories by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many years and breed across repeated seasons. Longevity matters for a slow-recovering species rebuilt one protected territory at a time.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in ground nests, and both parents care for chicks. Offspring begin life grounded, hidden among vegetation rather than lifted into trees.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike in plumage and bill colour, and cannot reliably be told apart in the field; males are reported to average slightly heavier.

takhi.spotlight: Takhi teaches Wild Return through a stocky horse lineage restored to the steppe after disappearance. Upright mane, strong herd bonds, winter endurance, and protected grassland make return a living act of room given back.
takhi.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, east_asia. Mongolian steppe, semi-desert grassland, open plains, and protected reserves.
signatureTraits: Stocky wild horse body with upright mane and no forelock
Steppe herd structure shaped around stallions, mares, and foals
Hardy grazing life across cold, dry open country
Conservation return from extinction in the wild
interestingFacts: Takhi, the Mongolian name for Przewalski's Horses, is often translated as spirit or worthy.
They were once extinct in the wild before reintroduction programs restored free-ranging herds.
Their upright mane gives them a different silhouette from domestic horses.
Przewalski's Horses have 66 chromosomes, two more than domestic horses, yet the two can interbreed.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, sedges, herbs, shrubs, and tough seasonal forage.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves can threaten foals, while harsh winters, drought, disease, and human pressure challenge herds.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Takhi graze and rest in shifting daily rhythms, often moving with weather, water, and herd safety. Their rhythm fits Wild Return because freedom must be practiced every day on real ground.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 20 years is typical in zoos, where some are reported to have lived beyond 30; figures for free-living herds are still few.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to one foal that must stand and follow the herd quickly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Stallions are larger and defend bands, while mares carry herd continuity through foals and movement knowledge.

takin.spotlight: Herds climb to alpine meadows near 4,000 metres in summer, sometimes a hundred or more together, then split into small groups and descend into forested valleys for winter. This thickset hoofed mammal lives in the eastern Himalaya and the mountains of western and central China. Its swollen, arched muzzle holds large sinuses, thought to warm cold air on the way to the lungs.
takin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia, south_asia. Takins live in cold mountain forests, bamboo thickets, and steep brushy slopes.
signatureTraits: Heavy mountain body
Thick insulating coat
Curved horns in both sexes
Brush-pushing movement
interestingFacts: Takins are related to goats and sheep and belong to the same subfamily, Caprinae.
Their oily coat helps shed rain and fog in wet mountain forests.
Both sexes carry horns, which rise from the center of the head and curve outward and back.
They can move surprisingly well on steep ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: A very wide range of plants is eaten: leaves of willow, oak and rhododendron, bamboo, grasses and herbs in summer, twigs and evergreen leaves in winter. It rears on its hind legs to reach foliage, pushes over saplings and visits mineral licks for salt.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves, dholes, snow leopards and leopards take mainly calves and weakened animals, and Asiatic black bears may do the same. An alarmed takin gives a loud cough and the herd crashes into dense thickets. Hunting and habitat loss are the wider threats.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active in cooler parts of day, resting and ruminating in cover. This rhythm supports the principle because timing decides when the animal hides, searches, rests, or acts.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to be about 12 to 15 years in the wild, based on few data; zoo animals have reached around 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding females usually bear one calf that follows the herd. Mating takes place in summer and the calf is born in early spring after about seven to eight months. It can keep up with its mother within roughly three days.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: In this species, both sexes have horns; males are larger and heavier. Bulls can weigh up to about 350 kilograms, cows around 250 or less.

tapanuli-orangutan.spotlight: Tapanuli Orangutan turns Highland Nestcraft into rare intelligence above the ground, building night shelter with careful hands in one of the smallest great-ape ranges on Earth.
tapanuli-orangutan.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, sumatra. Tapanuli Orangutans live in highland forest of Sumatra, where canopy routes, fruit trees, and nesting branches define survival. The habitat turns home building into a nightly act of intelligence.
signatureTraits: Rare Sumatran great ape
Daily tree nest building
Long arboreal arms
Restricted highland forest range
interestingFacts: It was described as a distinct orangutan species in 2017.
It has one of the smallest ranges of any great ape.
Like other orangutans, it builds nests in trees.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fruits, leaves, bark, flowers, insects, and seasonal forest foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Habitat fragmentation, human conflict, and slow reproduction are major threats. Their intelligence cannot protect them without continuous forest to build in.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly diurnal, traveling, feeding, and building sleeping nests before night. The day ends by making a home with intention.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Orangutans can live for many decades. Long life gives learned routes, nestcraft, and food knowledge great importance.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually raise one infant at a time with long maternal care, teaching movement, food choice, and forest life. Each offspring represents years of investment.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males become much larger than females and may develop cheek pads, while females remain smaller and carry young. The contrast shows different roles within a slow, intelligent life history.

tarantula-hawk-wasp.spotlight: Tarantula Hawk Wasp teaches Skilled Courage through a wasp that faces a larger spider with exact technique. Long legs, blue-black wings, painful sting, and larval provisioning make courage precise.
tarantula-hawk-wasp.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Deserts, scrub, grasslands, open woodland, and tarantula-rich ground.
signatureTraits: Specialized hunt that targets tarantulas for offspring
Powerful sting used to paralyze rather than immediately kill
Long legs that help handle dangerous spider prey
Bright dark-and-orange warning appearance
interestingFacts: Tarantula Hawk Wasps are known for one of the most painful insect stings.
Females hunt tarantulas as food for their larvae.
Adults often feed on flower nectar and fermenting fruit, while only their larvae feed on spiders.
Their bright wings and body act as warning signals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Nectar feeds adults, while larvae feed on paralyzed tarantulas.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, lizards, mammals, spiders, and humans may threaten them, though warning colors and sting deter many. Courage is safer because the warning is honest.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tarantula Hawk Wasps are mostly diurnal, searching in warm conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Adults are thought to live only a few weeks to a few months during the warm season. Most of the life cycle is spent as a larva and pupa inside the spider's burrow.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay an egg on a paralyzed tarantula sealed in a burrow or nest site.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females differ in behavior: females perform the tarantula hunt, while males often focus on mate searching.

tasmanian-devil.spotlight: The largest living carnivorous marsupial, a stocky animal of roughly 5 to 12 kilograms that today lives free in the wild only in Tasmania, apart from small reintroduced groups. It trots many kilometres a night along regular paths, finding food by smell, and at a carcass can swallow a very large meal, by some accounts up to 40 per cent of its own weight.
tasmanian-devil.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, tasmania. Tasmanian Devils usually live in Tasmanian forests, scrub, farms, and coastal edges.
signatureTraits: Crushing jaws and noisy scavenging
Adapted to Tasmanian forests
Black coat, usually with white marks on chest or rump
Large head and thick neck on a squat body
Ears flush red when the animal is agitated
interestingFacts: Tasmanian Devils are closely tied to Tasmanian forests, scrub, farms, and coastal edges.
Their food is mainly carrion, small animals, birds, insects, and bones.
Major pressures include eagles for young, dogs, vehicles, disease, and humans.
Devils died out on mainland Australia about 3,000 years ago.
Young devils climb trees well, but adults become too heavy to do so easily.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on carrion, small animals, birds, insects, and bones.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have no regular natural predator; wedge-tailed eagles, owls and quolls can take small young. Far more devils die from a contagious facial cancer passed on by biting, from road traffic and from dogs. A frightened devil gapes widely and gives off a strong smell.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: By day it lies up in a den, which may be an old wombat burrow, a hollow log, a cave or thick scrub. It emerges after sunset and is busiest in the hours after dusk and before dawn, though devils sometimes sun themselves in quiet places.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Up to about 5 or 6 years in the wild and 7 or 8 in captivity. Where facial tumour disease is present, few live beyond 3.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a pregnancy of about three weeks the female gives birth to 20 or more young, each the size of a grain of rice. She has only four teats, so at most four survive. They leave the pouch at about four months and are independent at around nine.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger.

tasselled-wobbegong.spotlight: Tasselled Wobbegong teaches Reef Concealment through a shark that lets the reef mistake it for itself. Flattened body, mottled pattern, facial tassels, and sudden ambush show that patience wins when the setting belongs to you.
tasselled-wobbegong.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, australia_oceania, coral_triangle, australia_coastal. Coral reefs, reef flats, lagoons, caves, ledges, sandy patches, and Indo-Pacific reef floors.
signatureTraits: Flattened shark body that lies close to the reef floor.
Fringed facial tassels that break up the outline.
Mottled pattern that blends with coral, sand, and rock.
Ambush strike from stillness when prey comes close.
interestingFacts: Wobbegongs are carpet sharks, named for their patterned, flattened appearance.
The tasselled wobbegong has elaborate lobes around the mouth and head.
It can ambush prey from close range after lying still.
Its camouflage is so strong that prey may approach too closely.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Reef fish, crustaceans, cephalopods, and bottom-moving animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger sharks, humans, habitat damage, and fishing pressure threaten wobbegongs. Camouflage reduces many risks, but stillness cannot protect against every disturbance.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tasselled Wobbegongs are often nocturnal or crepuscular hunters, resting camouflaged by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long this wobbegong lives is unknown; no reliable figures have been published from the wild or from aquariums.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young, which must immediately rely on camouflage and small-scale ambush.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though females may grow larger.

tawny-frogmouth.spotlight: Often taken for an owl, this stocky night bird is closer to the nightjars and has weak feet that cannot grip prey, so it seizes food in its bill instead. Even at its day roost it is not asleep: through eyes narrowed to slits it keeps watching whatever approaches.
tawny-frogmouth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Woodland, eucalyptus forest, parks, gardens, and branches fit frogmouths because broken-bark stillness needs tree structure.
signatureTraits: Silver-grey plumage is streaked and mottled with black.
Bill is very broad, hooked at the tip and topped by bristles.
Large yellow eyes face forward.
Pairs roost side by side, often touching.
Call is a low, repeated 'oom-oom-oom'.
interestingFacts: Pairs stay together for years and often use the same nest site in successive seasons.
Many are killed on roads, where they hunt insects drawn to headlights and street lamps.
It usually hunts by watching from a low perch and dropping on to prey on the ground.
On cold winter nights and mornings it can enter torpor, lowering its body temperature for a few hours to save energy.
A bird threatened at close range opens its bill wide to show the pale yellow-green lining of the mouth.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Moths, beetles and other insects, spiders, frogs, and small animals such as mice. At night it watches from a low, hidden perch, then drops or sallies out to seize prey with its broad bill, mostly on the ground.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Owls, foxes, cats, snakes, and corvids threaten adults or nests. Daytime camouflage protects them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are nocturnal, hunting at night and freezing like branches by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Banded wild birds have reached about 14 years; how long most live in the wild is not well measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: From August to December, both parents incubate eggs on branch nests. The nest is a loose platform of sticks in a horizontal fork, holding one to three white eggs. The male sits by day. Eggs hatch after about 30 days and chicks fledge around a month later.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look much alike. Males are slightly larger with a heavier bill, and females often show more rufous or chestnut tones in the plumage.

tawny-owl.spotlight: Tawny Owl teaches Attention through a woodland hunter shaped to hear what the noisy world misses. Its round head, dark eyes, soft feathers, and dusk perch all point toward quiet power that waits until sound reveals the next move.
tawny-owl.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east. Woodlands, parks, gardens, old trees, hedgerows, and forest edges fit Tawny Owls because layered cover holds hidden prey and safe roosts.
signatureTraits: Soft flight feathers reduce sound while moving through trees.
Large dark eyes and strong hearing support hunting in low light.
Perch-and-listen hunting turns stillness into information.
interestingFacts: The classic hooting call is strongly associated with Tawny Owls in Europe.
Tawny Owls often nest in tree cavities but also use old buildings, abandoned crow nests, and nest boxes.
Their hunting can be focused on small mammals but shifts with local prey.
Pairs are strongly territorial and often keep the same territory for many years, rarely moving far from it.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Mice, voles, small birds, frogs, beetles, and other small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger raptors, foxes, martens, cats, crows, and human disturbance can threaten owls or nests. Concealment, night hunting, and careful nest placement protect the quiet hunter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tawny Owls are mainly nocturnal and crepuscular, calling and hunting through dusk and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically about 4 to 5 years in the wild; the oldest ringed birds have passed 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in tree cavities or similar sheltered sites and brood the young while food is delivered. Offspring make listening practical because hidden prey must become steady meals at the nest.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger than males, a common owl pattern.

tayra.spotlight: Long-legged for a member of the weasel family and weighing about 3 to 7 kilograms, the tayra hunts and forages both on the forest floor and high in the trees. In Costa Rica, tayras have been watched picking unripe plantains and hiding them, then coming back days later to eat them once they had ripened.
tayra.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america, north_america. Tropical forests, edges, plantations, river corridors, and canopy routes fit tayras because curiosity uses many levels.
signatureTraits: Slim dark brown to black body ends in a long bushy tail.
Head and neck are paler than the body, often grey or tan.
A yellow or whitish patch usually marks the throat or chest.
Small rounded ears sit low on a broad head.
It bounds along with the back arched and the tail held out.
interestingFacts: Strong claws and a long balancing tail let it run along branches and leap from one tree to the next.
Tayras usually travel alone or in pairs, though small family groups are sometimes seen.
Its eyesight is thought to be relatively poor, and it finds much of its food by smell.
Raids on fruit crops and beehives bring it into conflict with farmers in parts of its range.
The species occurs from Mexico south to northern Argentina, and on the island of Trinidad.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, honey, small mammals, birds, reptiles, insects, and eggs.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas, large raptors, snakes, and humans can threaten tayras. Agility and tree movement help escape.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tayras are mainly diurnal with active searching through the day. Their rhythm is restless movement through forest layers.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not measured in the wild. Captive tayras have lived for around 18 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: After a gestation of 63 to 70 days, females raise kits in dens or tree hollows. Litters number one to three. The young are born blind, open their eyes at about five weeks, leave the den at around two months and are weaned by about three months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are somewhat larger and more heavily muscled than females. Coat colour and markings are alike in both sexes.

tent-tortoise.spotlight: Tent Tortoise teaches Slow Continuance through a patterned shell crossing dry ground without needing speed to prove movement. Small steps, armor, camouflage, and drought-wise patience make progress quiet but real.
tent-tortoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Karoo scrub, dry grassland, sandy flats, rocky patches, and low shrubland.
signatureTraits: Patterned domed shell that blends with dryland texture.
Slow terrestrial movement through arid South African habitats.
Protective withdrawal instead of fast escape.
Patient grazing and browsing tied to seasonal plant growth.
interestingFacts: Tent Tortoises are small dryland tortoises from southern Africa.
Their shell patterns can help break up the body shape against dry ground.
They rely on patience, cover, and shell defense rather than speed.
Activity often depends on temperature and rainfall patterns.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Grasses, succulents, flowers, herbs, leaves, and dryland plants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jackals, mongooses, birds, monitor lizards, fire, drought, vehicles, and collecting threaten tortoises and eggs. Shell protection helps adults, but slow life still needs safe ground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tent Tortoises are diurnal in suitable temperatures, resting during extremes and moving when warmth and moisture allow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Lifespan in the wild has not been measured reliably. It is probably long-lived, perhaps a few decades, but figures for this species are lacking and it rarely survives long in captivity.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in shallow nests dug into the ground, where hatchlings emerge small and vulnerable.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences can include size, shell shape, or tail differences, but both sexes share the same patterned slow-distance strategy.

tentacled-snake.spotlight: The Tentacled Snake is prediction turned into anatomy. Its strange snout feelers and fish-startle ambush show that strategy can aim not where danger is now, but where fear is about to move.
tentacled-snake.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia. Tentacled Snakes live in slow-moving freshwater, flooded vegetation, ponds, and swampy habitats in Southeast Asia.
signatureTraits: Paired snout tentacles
Aquatic ambush posture
Fish-startle prediction strategy
Rough water-adapted body
interestingFacts: Tentacled Snakes are fully aquatic and rarely leave the water.
They can strike toward where a startled fish is about to flee.
Their tentacles likely help sense movement in murky water.
They often hold a J-shaped posture while waiting for prey.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fish, using ambush rather than chase.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, birds, bigger snakes, and habitat disturbance may threaten them. Their defense is concealment, aquatic specialization, and stillness, showing that knowing the environment can be safer than overpowering it.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Its daily activity cycle in the wild is poorly documented. Fully aquatic, it rests and hunts from the same spot, anchored by the tail among submerged plants, and rises to the surface at intervals to breathe.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for years in stable aquatic habitats, and captive snakes may reach a decade or more. The lifespan note reinforces the slow craft of prediction: repeated stillness trains the strike.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, so offspring enter the water already shaped for aquatic life.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are not obvious in casual viewing, though females may be larger in many snakes. The important shared feature is the unusual tentacled sensing system.

termite.spotlight: Termite carries Ventilated Labor through a specific body plan, habitat choice, and survival rhythm. The principle is visible in how it feeds, moves, avoids danger, and places the next generation.
termite.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa, south_asia, southeast_asia. Savannas, woodlands, soil mounds, and decaying plant zones.
signatureTraits: Large fungus-growing Macrotermes mounds of packed clay
Soldiers with oversized cutting mandibles
Workers tending underground fungus gardens
Ventilated nest chambers that exchange stale air
Winged alates emerging in brief rainy-season swarms
interestingFacts: Termite shows Ventilated Labor through concrete biology.
Its daily rhythm connects food, shelter, and risk.
Young survive best when placed in the right habitat.
Predators explain why the principle matters.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Plant fiber, dead wood, grasses, and fungus gardens.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Ants, aardvarks, birds, reptiles, mammals, and mound damage threaten termites; walls, soldiers, and tunnels protect labor.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Termite colonies work day and night in shifts, with workers maintaining tunnels, fungus, brood, and ventilation continuously.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Individual workers may live months, while queens and colonies can persist for years, making Ventilated Labor larger than one body.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Queens lay huge numbers of eggs, while sterile workers and soldiers care for brood and defend the colony structure.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Castes differ strongly: queens, kings, workers, soldiers, and winged reproductives have different bodies and jobs.

thorny-devil.spotlight: Thorny Devil teaches Water Harvesting through spines, grooves, and a desert body that channels tiny droplets toward the mouth. Small systems solve enormous thirst when every surface has a job.
thorny-devil.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Australian deserts, sandy plains, spinifex, scrub, and arid woodland.
signatureTraits: Grooved skin that helps channel moisture toward the mouth.
Spiny armor and false-head posture for predator confusion.
Slow desert walking that conserves energy.
Specialized ant-eating diet in arid Australia.
interestingFacts: Thorny devils can collect moisture through capillary channels in the skin.
They feed mainly on ants, often eating many small prey items in a day.
They have a false head-like knob that may distract predators.
Their spines protect them and break up their outline on desert ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Almost nothing but small ants, chiefly of the genus Iridomyrmex. It stands beside an ant trail and picks them off one at a time with a short sticky tongue; a single meal is estimated at several hundred to a few thousand ants.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, goannas, snakes, and feral animals can threaten them. Spines, camouflage, slow movement, and false-head display reduce the chance of a clean attack.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Thorny Devils are diurnal but adjust activity to desert temperature, often moving when heat is manageable.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often said to reach up to 20 years, but lifespan in the wild is poorly documented and most individuals probably live much shorter lives.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in burrows dug into sandy soil.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look broadly similar, though females are often larger.

three-toed-sloth.spotlight: Three-toed Sloth teaches Slow Camouflage through a canopy life moving at leaf speed. Algae-tinted fur, long claws, slow digestion, and upside-down resting turn calm into a predator-avoidance system.
three-toed-sloth.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Tropical rainforest canopy, mature trees, vine tangles, and humid crowns fit Three-toed Sloths because leaves, hanging routes, and visual cover all work together.
signatureTraits: A dark stripe runs back from each eye across a pale face.
The throat and sides of the face are brown.
Forelimbs are much longer than the hind limbs.
The head is small and round, with ears hidden in the fur.
A short, blunt tail shows below the rump.
interestingFacts: Three-toed sloths have eight or nine neck vertebrae, where nearly all other mammals have seven, and can turn the head much further than most mammals.
About once a week it climbs down to the ground to defecate, digging a small hollow at the base of the tree with its tail.
It swims well, pulling itself through the water with its forelimbs, and can cross rivers and flooded forest.
Body temperature rises and falls with the surrounding air, so sloths move into sunlit branches to warm up.
Small moths live in the coat and lay their eggs in the sloth's dung.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Leaves, buds, and tender shoots.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harpy eagles, jaguars, ocelots, snakes, and humans threaten sloths. Slow motion and algae-tinted fur reduce detection in trees.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Rest is spread across day and night; activity is slow and energy-limited. The rhythm is an energy budget, not laziness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well measured in the wild. Estimates of 20 to 30 years are often quoted, and because three-toed sloths survive poorly in captivity, zoo records add little.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single young is born after a gestation of roughly six months. It clings to the mother's belly, begins tasting leaves within weeks, and rides on her for around five to six months before living alone.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males carry a patch of short orange-yellow fur with a dark central stripe between the shoulders. Females lack it; otherwise the sexes are alike in size and colour.

thresher-shark.spotlight: The largest of the three thresher sharks, reaching five metres or more, found in temperate and warm seas worldwide. Longline fishers often find it hooked by the tail instead of the mouth, a sign that it hits bait with the tail first. It can also leap clear of the water.
thresher-shark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Thresher Sharks live in open ocean and coastal waters where schooling fish gather.
signatureTraits: Extremely long upper tail lobe
Tail-slap hunting strategy
Streamlined shark body
Schooling-fish predator
interestingFacts: Its tail can be as long as much of its body.
It may stun schooling fish with whip-like tail strikes, and many are caught hooked by the tail.
It gives birth to live young, usually two to four pups per litter.
Warm red muscle along its body keeps its swimming muscles warmer than the surrounding water.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small schooling fish such as anchovies, sardines, herring, mackerel and hake make up most of the diet, with squid taken as well. It is thought to circle a school to pack it tighter before attacking.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural enemies, possibly orcas and the largest sharks, and larger sharks eat pups and juveniles. Fishing is the main threat: the species is caught for its meat and fins and as bycatch, and it breeds too slowly to recover quickly.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: It swims continuously and has no known resting place. Fish tagged off California made deeper dives by day and stayed nearer the surface at night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: At least 20 years, judged from growth bands in the vertebrae. Some studies suggest 35 years or more, and the true maximum is uncertain.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The embryos have no placenta and feed on unfertilised eggs the mother keeps producing, and females give birth to live pups after internal development. Pregnancy is thought to last about nine months. Litters are small, usually two to four, and pups are over a metre long at birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: As in many sharks, females may be slightly larger, but both sexes share the long-tail hunting design. Males carry a pair of claspers behind the pelvic fins and mature at a smaller size than females.

tiger-salamander.spotlight: Tiger Salamander teaches Two-World Belonging through an amphibian that lives underground yet returns to water to begin life again. Burrows, rain migration, striped body, ponds, and aquatic larvae make flexibility a home in more than one world.
tiger-salamander.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Grasslands, woodlands, prairie edges, burrows, leaf litter, ponds, and temporary wetlands fit Tiger Salamanders because survival depends on land shelter connected to breeding water.
signatureTraits: Bold yellow or olive markings break up the body like tiger patterning.
Spends much of adult life underground or under cover.
Migrates to fishless ponds or wetlands for breeding.
Aquatic larvae show the water side of an otherwise hidden land life.
interestingFacts: Tiger Salamanders are among the largest land salamanders in North America.
They often use burrows made by other animals rather than digging everything themselves.
Some populations can remain aquatic in larval-like forms under certain conditions.
Rainy nights are important triggers for movement to breeding ponds.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Worms, insects, slugs, spiders, small invertebrates, and aquatic prey as larvae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, fish, larger amphibians, drying ponds, roads, and habitat loss threaten them. Burrowing and rainy timing help reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Mostly nocturnal and moisture-linked, especially during migrations. Their rhythm waits underground until weather opens the path between worlds.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild adults are usually credited with 10 to 16 years. Captive animals have lived past 20.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in ponds or wetlands where larvae hatch into aquatic hunters. The future begins in water even when the adult spends much of life hidden in soil.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, though males may show breeding-season features such as swollen cloacal areas.

tiger-shark.spotlight: Tiger Shark teaches Range through a predator built for wide opportunity. Its striped juvenile pattern, powerful body, broad diet, coastal cruising, and ability to move through different ocean zones make survival less about one perfect prey and more about using many doors the sea opens.
tiger-shark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Tropical and subtropical coasts, reefs, open ocean, lagoons, and estuaries.
signatureTraits: Broad opportunistic diet across many marine prey types.
Large cruising body suited to coast, reef, and open water movement.
Tiger-like striping most visible in younger sharks.
Powerful jaws and senses used across varied hunting situations.
interestingFacts: Tiger Sharks are known for having one of the broadest diets among large sharks.
Young tiger sharks show stronger stripes, which fade with age.
They travel through coastal, reef, and open-ocean habitats.
They are important apex predators in many warm marine systems.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, turtles, rays, birds, seals, dolphins, crustaceans, carrion, and many other foods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few predators besides orcas and humans, while young face larger sharks. Human pressure is the major risk, showing that even wide-ranging power has limits in a changed ocean.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Tiger Sharks are active by day and night, often patrolling widely.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Age estimates from growth bands in the vertebrae show that some live 20 to 30 years or more, and a few estimates exceed 40. Maximum age is uncertain because growth bands are hard to read in old sharks.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to live young after carrying embryos internally.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger than males in many shark species, including tiger sharks. The difference matters for reproduction, while both sexes carry the same wide-ranging predator design.

titicaca-water-frog.spotlight: A large, wholly aquatic frog of Lake Titicaca, about 3,800 m up in the Andes on the border of Peru and Bolivia. It takes most of its oxygen through loose, heavily folded skin, and its lungs are much reduced. When oxygen runs low it bobs up and down on the bottom, washing water over the folds.
titicaca-water-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Cold high-altitude Lake Titicaca shallows, rocky bottom, and oxygen-rich water.
signatureTraits: Broad, flat head with a rounded snout
Colour varies from olive-green to dark brown, often mottled
Large hind feet with full webbing
Body length typically about 8 to 14 cm
interestingFacts: A 1970s expedition led by Jacques Cousteau reported frogs about 50 cm long with legs outstretched; animals that large are no longer reported.
Its red blood cells are among the smallest measured in any amphibian, and it has a great many of them.
In 2016 around 10,000 dead frogs were reported along the Coata River, which flows into the lake; pollution was suspected.
In parts of Peru and Bolivia the frogs are blended into a drink sold as a tonic.
Zoos and breeding centres in Peru, Bolivia and the United States now breed it as a safeguard against loss in the wild.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic invertebrates, worms, small crustaceans, and small fish.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large fish, birds, snakes, and humans threaten them; pollution and harvest are especially serious because skin-breathing animals cannot ignore water quality.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are aquatic and rest or move underwater through day and night, with activity shaped by oxygen and safety.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How long this frog lives is unknown. Conservation breeding in Peru and Bolivia is recent, and none of it appears to have reported a longevity figure yet.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in water where tadpoles develop aquatically.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are similar, though breeding condition can differ; the important difference is less visual than ecological.

toco-toucan.spotlight: The largest of the toucans carries an orange bill roughly 20 centimetres long. Perched on a stout branch, it stretches out to pick fruit from twigs too thin to bear its weight, gripping each one in the tip of its saw-edged bill.
