fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults face few natural predators, but eggs and chicks may face ravens, monitors, storms, and human pressure. Height protects but does not remove risk, so command still requires nest defense and timing.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wedge-tailed Eagles are diurnal, soaring when thermals build and visibility improves. Their rhythm is wait for lift, rise, scan, and descend only when the move is worth it.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Thought to reach 20 years or more in the wild, although many young birds die before they are old enough to breed. Captive eagles have lived about 40.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, often high in trees or on cliffs, and both parents help rear the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger than males, as in many raptors. The difference can sharpen nesting and hunting roles, but both sexes share the same thermal-soaring command.

weedy-seadragon.spotlight: A relative of seahorses and pipefish found only in the cool coastal waters of southern Australia, it grows to about 45 centimetres. Small leaf-shaped flaps on stalks along the neck, back and tail break up its outline. It moves by rippling nearly transparent fins, so the body appears to sway with the weed instead of swimming.
weedy-seadragon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania, australia_coastal. Weedy Seadragons usually live in southern Australian reefs, seagrass, and kelp beds.
signatureTraits: Leafy appendages and seaweed mimicry
Adapted to southern Australian reefs
Long tube-like snout with a small mouth at the tip
Reddish-orange body with yellow spots and violet-blue bars
Tail cannot grip weed, unlike a seahorse's
interestingFacts: Weedy Seadragons are closely tied to southern Australian reefs, seagrass, and kelp beds.
Their food is mainly tiny crustaceans and planktonic prey.
Major pressures include larger fish and habitat degradation.
It is the official marine emblem of the Australian state of Victoria.
The pattern of spots and blotches differs from one animal to the next, so divers' photographs are used to recognise individuals over several years.
It has no teeth: prey such as mysid shrimps is sucked whole through the snout with a sudden gulp.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on tiny crustaceans and planktonic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Few predators have been documented; larger fish are assumed to take some, young ones above all. It swims too slowly to flee and relies on a body cased in bony plates. Storms that strand animals ashore and the loss of kelp and seagrass are heavier pressures.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: By day it feeds among the weed. After dark it is reported to settle low among kelp or seagrass and move little, though its behaviour at night is less well studied.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at around 5 to 7 years in the wild, though this is not well measured; aquarium animals have lived up to about 10 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: The female presses roughly 100 to 250 pink eggs onto a spongy patch of skin under the male's tail, where each sits in its own cup. They hatch after about one to two months, and the young, a few centimetres long, fend for themselves at once.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males brood eggs; females deposit them. Outside the breeding season the sexes are hard to separate, though mature females tend to be deeper in the body and males narrower.

wels-catfish.spotlight: Wels Catfish teaches Deep Economy through a giant river predator saving motion until the signal comes close. Barbels, smell, vibration sensing, huge mouth, and deep-channel cruising make strength economical.
wels-catfish.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe. Large rivers, deep channels, reservoirs, lakes, backwaters, and murky waters.
signatureTraits: Large freshwater predator with massive mouth
Long barbels used for sensing in murky water
Low-light and deep-channel hunting style
Energy-saving cruising and ambush rather than constant chase
interestingFacts: Wels Catfish can grow to enormous sizes compared with many freshwater fish.
Their barbels help them sense prey in dark or murky water.
They often feed most actively in low light or at night.
Large individuals can take surprisingly varied prey, including fish, frogs, water birds, and small mammals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, crayfish, frogs, birds, rodents, carrion, and shoreline animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Young face larger fish, birds, otters, and cannibalism; adults mainly face humans and habitat change. Size eventually protects, but deep cover and sensing matter before dominance arrives.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wels Catfish are often nocturnal or crepuscular, resting deep by day and feeding in low light.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Many live 15 to 30 years, and ages beyond 30 have been reported for very large fish. Claims of 50 years or more are poorly supported.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay many eggs in nests or guarded areas, and males may protect the nest in some breeding behavior.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females may become large and heavy with eggs, while mature males may show breeding-related roles around nests. The main lesson belongs to the shared giant sensing body.

western-crowned-pigeon.spotlight: A blue-grey pigeon with a maroon back and red eyes, confined to the lowlands of far western New Guinea and a few islands offshore. Both parents feed the chick on crop milk, a rich secretion from the lining of the crop. Its call is a deep, hollow booming unlike the cooing of smaller pigeons.
western-crowned-pigeon.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: southeast_asia, australia_oceania. Western Crowned Pigeons live in New Guinea lowland rainforest floors.
signatureTraits: Lace-like blue crest
Large ground pigeon body
Quiet forest walking
Fruit-and-seed foraging
interestingFacts: It is one of the largest pigeons in the world, roughly the size of a small turkey.
Its crest of lacy, fan-shaped blue feathers stands upright on the head.
It spends much time on the forest floor.
Pairs usually raise a single chick from one egg laid in a nest built in a tree.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fallen fruit, seeds and berries form most of the diet, probably with some small invertebrates. Small parties walk slowly together, pecking up what has dropped from the canopy.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: People are the main threat: it is hunted for meat and plumes, and lowland forest is being logged. Natural predators are poorly documented but probably include large raptors and snakes. A disturbed bird flies up with loud wingbeats to a branch and sits there, which makes it easy to shoot.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day, spending most of the daylight hours on the ground. At dusk the birds fly up into trees to roost, well clear of the forest floor.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Crowned pigeons are long-lived for pigeons: in zoos this species is reported to have exceeded 20 years, but its survival in the lowland forests of western New Guinea has never been measured.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Breeding females usually lay a single egg in a simple nest. It is a platform of sticks and stems built in a tree. In captivity both parents incubate for about four weeks, and the chick leaves the nest at around a month old but is fed for some weeks longer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look similar, with shared crowned beauty and parental care. Males average slightly larger and perform the bowing courtship display, lowering the head and pumping the fanned tail.

western-hognose-snake.spotlight: Western Hognose Snake teaches Death-Feigning Theater through defense that becomes performance. Upturned snout, flattened neck, hissing, mock strikes, rolling over, and playing dead show protection created by convincing danger the chase is not worth it.
western-hognose-snake.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Prairies, sandy plains, scrub, grasslands, open woodlands, and loose soils fit Western Hognose Snakes because they dig, search, and perform best on workable ground.
signatureTraits: Upturned snout: the nose is built for digging in loose soil.
Flattening display: the body imitates a more dangerous snake before contact.
Death-feigning: the final act tries to make predators lose interest.
interestingFacts: Western Hognose Snakes are famous for playing dead when threatened.
They specialize heavily on toads in many areas.
Their dramatic bluff often looks more dangerous than the snake really is to people.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Toads, frogs, lizards, eggs, small rodents, and amphibians.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Hawks, owls, foxes, coyotes, snakes, badgers, and humans threaten hognose snakes. Bluff, burrowing, and death-feigning reduce the need for real combat.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Western Hognose Snakes are mostly diurnal, active in warm daylight after basking. Their rhythm gives the body heat to dig, search, and perform when needed.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Western Hognose Snakes can live several years in the wild and much longer under care. Survival favors a snake that can dig, bluff, and avoid real fights.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in hidden, warm, loose soil or protected places. Offspring hatch with the same upturned snout and defensive theatre already built into the species pattern.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are usually larger and heavier than males, while males may be slimmer and more mobile in mate searching. The theater belongs to both, but egg production changes female size.

western-lowland-gorilla.spotlight: Western Lowland Gorilla teaches Gentle Strength through a massive social body whose power is organized around protection. Silverback leadership, plant feeding, nest building, and family bonds show that strength is most complete when it guards peace.
western-lowland-gorilla.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Lowland rainforest, swamp forest, forest clearings, and fruit-rich understory.
signatureTraits: Silverback leadership that protects and guides social groups
Great physical strength paired with mainly plant-based feeding
Complex family bonds, grooming, play, and communication
Night nest building from vegetation on ground or in trees
interestingFacts: Western Lowland Gorillas live in social groups often led by a mature silverback.
They eat large amounts of fruit, leaves, stems, and other plant foods.
They build fresh sleeping nests from leaves and branches each night, on the ground or in trees.
Young gorillas spend years learning social life through play and closeness.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, leaves, stems, shoots, bark, herbs, and occasional insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Leopards may threaten young, while humans, disease, and habitat loss are major dangers. Silverback defense and group awareness make strength protective, not merely impressive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Western Lowland Gorillas are diurnal, feeding and resting through the day, then building nests for night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Western Lowland Gorillas can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to one infant after a long pregnancy and nurse for years, with the group’s structure supporting the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males become much larger and develop silver backs with maturity, while females carry intensive infant care. The difference makes protection and nurture visible as two sides of the same strength.

whale-shark.spotlight: No living fish is larger: adults can reach 10 to 12 metres or more, and lengths of about 18 metres have been reported. It feeds by swimming open-mouthed through dense patches of plankton or by hanging upright and gulping, and the water is strained through sieve-like pads in front of the gills before it leaves through the gill slits.
whale-shark.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, south_atlantic, north_pacific, south_pacific, indian_ocean. Whale Shark usually lives in warm tropical and subtropical seas, reefs, and plankton-rich waters.
signatureTraits: huge filtering mouth
spotted skin
slow cruising
vast size
interestingFacts: The arrangement of pale spots behind the gills differs on every animal, and researchers identify individuals from photographs of it.
The jaws hold thousands of tiny teeth set in hundreds of rows, none of which is used to bite or chew food.
Tagged whale sharks have been recorded diving deeper than 1,500 metres, although most of their time is spent near the surface.
Small tooth-like scales cover the surface of the eye, and the eyeball can be pulled back into its socket.
Off Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia, whale sharks gather each year in the months after the mass spawning of corals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Whale Shark feeds on plankton, small fish, fish eggs, and tiny drifting animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Small whale sharks have been found in the stomachs of a blue shark and a blue marlin, and orcas have been recorded killing larger ones. Size, skin several centimetres thick and deep dives protect adults. Ship strikes, fishing nets and hunting for fins and meat kill far more.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: No rest period has been described. Tagged sharks keep swimming through day and night, and feeding follows the plankton, whether that is richest near the surface by day or rises towards it after dark.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Probably long-lived. Growth bands in the backbone, shown in one study to form yearly, suggest ages of 50 years or more, and some estimates run to about 100 years; no reliable maximum is known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: As far as is known, females give birth to live young after eggs develop inside the body. The one pregnant female examined in detail, caught off Taiwan in 1995, carried about 300 embryos at different stages of growth. Newborns are roughly 40 to 60 centimetres long, and no parental care is known.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males carry a pair of claspers, finger-like organs on the pelvic fins that are visible from below and become long and hardened at maturity. Records suggest that females tend to grow larger than males.

wheel-bug.spotlight: Wheel Bug teaches Piercing through a strange tool built for one exact purpose. The cog-like crest, assassin beak, spiny legs, slow stalk, and enzyme injection show power that reaches precisely where it must.
wheel-bug.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Woodland edges, gardens, shrubs, fields, orchards, and areas near outdoor lights fit Wheel Bugs because prey insects gather on plants and lit edges.
signatureTraits: Cog-like crest: the raised wheel shape makes the body instantly recognizable.
Piercing beak: prey is stabbed and liquefied rather than chewed.
Slow stalk: patience matters more than chase speed.
interestingFacts: Wheel Bugs are assassin bugs, true bugs with piercing beaks, not beetles.
Their bite can be painful to humans, so they should be left alone.
They are useful garden predators because they eat many plant-feeding insects.
Wheel Bugs are among the largest assassin bugs in North America, with adults reaching roughly three to four centimetres long.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Caterpillars, beetles, flies, aphids, bees and other insects. It seizes prey with its forelegs, stabs it with a sharp beak, injects saliva that paralyses and liquefies the tissues, then sucks out the contents.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Birds, spiders, mantises, rodents, and larger predatory insects can threaten Wheel Bugs. Armor, camouflage, a painful bite, and deliberate movement help protect them.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wheel Bugs are mostly diurnal in warm seasons, slowly patrolling vegetation and striking when prey comes within range. Their rhythm favors patience over chase.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wheel Bugs usually live through one warm-season generation, with eggs carrying the next cycle forward. The short adult window makes each slow patrol and precise strike count.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clusters of barrel-shaped eggs, often on twigs or surfaces where young can hatch near prey-rich plants. The next generation begins as tiny predators already built for piercing work.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often larger-bodied because of egg production, while males may be slimmer.

whirligig-beetle.spotlight: Whirligig Beetle teaches Dual Sight through an insect built for the water’s border. Split eyes, spinning movement, surface skating, and group swarms show how navigation improves when one body reads above and below at once.
whirligig-beetle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Ponds, streams, lakes, quiet river margins, and calm water surfaces fit Whirligig Beetles because their power lives exactly on the boundary between air and water.
signatureTraits: Divided eyes read above-water danger and below-water movement at the same time.
Surface spinning can confuse predators and coordinate group movement.
A slick oval body is specialized for skating at the water-air boundary.
interestingFacts: Whirligig Beetles often gather in groups on calm water surfaces.
Their eyes are physically divided into upper and lower viewing zones.
They can dive below the surface when threatened.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small insects, trapped surface prey, larvae, and floating organic material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Fish, frogs, birds, aquatic insects, and spiders pressure whirligigs from above and below. Their spinning groups confuse attackers and turn vision into collective safety.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Whirligig Beetles are active by day and in calm surface conditions, often gathering in groups. Their rhythm follows light, water surface stability, and predator pressure.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Whirligig Beetles usually live through short seasonal cycles, but the adult strategy is highly specialized. Dual Sight matters because every active moment is spent at a risky border between two predator worlds.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs on aquatic plants or submerged materials, tying the next generation to the same water-edge system.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sex differences are subtle to casual observers, though males may have modified forelegs for mating.

white-backed-vulture.spotlight: White-backed Vulture teaches Scavenger Convergence through many wings reading the same thermal sky. Pale back, broad soaring wings, social feeding, and carcass cleanup make hidden death visible and useful to the land.
white-backed-vulture.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, open woodland, grassland, protected areas, and nesting trees.
signatureTraits: Broad wings for soaring on thermal columns
Social carcass feeding with strong visual cue-following
Bare head and neck suited to scavenging hygiene
Ecological cleanup role that reduces disease risk from carrion
interestingFacts: White-backed Vultures often locate food by watching other scavengers.
Their soaring depends heavily on rising warm air called thermals.
Bare head skin helps keep feeding on carcasses cleaner than feathers would.
Vulture declines can affect carcass cleanup and disease dynamics.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carrion from large mammals and other dead animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and chicks may face eagles, snakes, and mammals, while adults face poisoning, collisions, persecution, and food-chain toxins.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: White-backed Vultures are diurnal, waiting for thermals before soaring and feeding.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: White-backed Vultures can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay one egg in a tree nest, and both parents invest heavily in the chick.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females have the same plumage and are nearly the same size, so they cannot be told apart in the field. Age is easier to judge: adults show the white back and a pale body, while young birds are darker and streaked.

white-bellied-sea-eagle.spotlight: White-bellied Sea Eagle teaches Coastal Vantage through a broad-winged hunter turning coast, river, and island movement into one readable map. High perches, white body, talons, and water patrol make perspective decisive.
white-bellied-sea-eagle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, australia_oceania, australia_coastal. Coasts, islands, estuaries, rivers, lakes, mangroves, and reservoirs.
signatureTraits: Broad wings for soaring above coasts and rivers
High perches used to read water movement
Strong talons for fish, reptiles, birds, and carrion
White head and belly giving a clear coastal silhouette
interestingFacts: White-bellied Sea Eagles are widespread around coasts and large waterways of southern Asia and Australasia.
They hunt fish but also take birds, reptiles, mammals, and carrion.
Pairs may use large nests over repeated seasons.
Their loud calls are often associated with coastal skies.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, sea snakes, birds, turtles, mammals, carrion, and shoreline prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults have few natural predators, but eggs and chicks face monitor lizards, crows, storms, and disturbance. Human activity and habitat loss can weaken the vantage system.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: White-bellied Sea Eagles are diurnal, hunting and patrolling when light makes water readable.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: White-bellied Sea Eagles can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, often reused, and both parents care for the young.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger than males, common in raptors.

white-faced-capuchin.spotlight: White-faced Capuchin teaches Manipulation through a primate solving the forest with hands, teeth, memory, and social learning. Turning objects over, testing food, and watching others make intelligence physical.
white-faced-capuchin.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Tropical dry forest, rainforest, mangroves, secondary forest, and canopy edges fit Capuchins because varied structure gives the hands constant problems to solve.
signatureTraits: Black body, limbs and tail contrast with white to cream shoulders and throat.
A black cap covers the crown.
The face is pink and mostly bare of fur.
The tail can grip and is often carried coiled at the tip.
Usually seen in noisy groups of about 10 to 30 moving through branches.
interestingFacts: They rub strong-smelling plants such as citrus fruit and pepper leaves into their fur, a habit thought to repel insects.
In some Costa Rican groups, pairs have been recorded sniffing each other's hands or holding fingers in each other's mouths, habits that spread and later died out.
On islands in Panama's Coiba National Park, white-faced capuchins have been filmed using stones to break open nuts and shellfish.
Males leave the group they were born in at around four years old and may change groups several times in their lives, while females usually stay.
Different alarm calls are given for birds of prey overhead and for threats on the ground.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, insects, nuts, seeds, eggs, crabs, small vertebrates, and plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, ocelots, harpy eagles, boas, crocodilians, and humans threaten Capuchins. Group vigilance and learning protect the experimenter.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, moving in social groups by day and resting in trees at night. The rhythm creates daily chances to learn by watching.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: The oldest captive animals passed 50 years. Few wild individuals have been followed from birth to death, so a typical wild lifespan cannot yet be given.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single infant is born after a pregnancy of about five and a half months, usually two years or more after the previous birth. It rides clinging to its mother's back, and other group members, especially females, often carry and groom it.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are noticeably larger and heavier than females, with a broader, more muscular head and shoulders and bigger canine teeth. Colour and pattern are the same in both sexes.

white-faced-saki.spotlight: White-faced Saki turns contrast into presence. The male's pale mask, powerful leaps, seed-cracking teeth, and canopy life show how an unusual face can be remembered without needing constant noise.
white-faced-saki.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Tropical rainforests, mature canopy, riverine forest, and dense South American woodland.
signatureTraits: Male white face creates a memorable signature against a dark body.
Strong hind limbs launch long leaps through broken canopy routes.
Heavy jaws and teeth handle tough fruits and seeds that softer feeders may avoid.
Pair or small-group living keeps the mask tied to social recognition, not just display.
interestingFacts: White-faced sakis are important seed predators and dispersers in South American forests.
Males and females look very different, making the species a strong example of visual identity.
They often move by powerful bounds rather than constant branch-by-branch climbing.
Their bushy tails help balance but are not prehensile.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruits, seeds, leaves, flowers, and insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harpy eagles, large raptors, big snakes, cats, and habitat loss threaten them. Leaping, canopy cover, and alert group life protect the memorable face.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, moving and feeding by day while sleeping in trees at night where height reduces ground danger.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around 15 years in the wild and longer in care; the mask gains meaning over many years of route memory, pair bonds, and canopy feeding.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually give birth to one infant, carrying and nursing it while the young learns the canopy paths that make the family visible but safe.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males have the dramatic white face and dark body, while females are more muted.

white-faced-whistling-duck.spotlight: White-faced Whistling-duck teaches Flock Contact through a voice that keeps company together. Its whistling calls, long-necked flock movement, communal resting, and wetland travel show that connection has to be repeated to hold.
white-faced-whistling-duck.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america, sub_saharan_africa. Marshes, lagoons, floodplains, rice fields, and wet grasslands.
signatureTraits: Distinct whistling calls that keep flock contact alive
Long-necked, upright duck shape suited to wetland movement
Large social flocks for feeding, resting, and travel
Comfort in marshes, lagoons, rice fields, and floodplains
interestingFacts: White-faced Whistling-ducks often gather in large flocks, sometimes numbering thousands of birds.
Their calls sound more like whistles than typical duck quacks.
They may feed by day or night depending on conditions.
Their white faces make flock members visually distinctive even at a distance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic plants, seeds, grasses, grains, and invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eagles, crocodiles, snakes, foxes, rats, humans, and nest predators threaten ducks or nests. Flocking and whistling keep awareness moving through the group before danger breaks the surface.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They may feed by day or night and rest communally.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No good measure exists for wild birds. In captivity this duck has lived for 10 to 15 years or more.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in nests near water or vegetation, and ducklings soon need the safety of group awareness and wetland cover.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: The sexes look alike; they cannot be separated reliably by plumage or size in the field.

white-headed-vulture.spotlight: White-headed Vulture teaches Necessary Work by doing the clean-up others avoid. Bare head, hooked bill, open-country searching, and carrion feeding turn unglamorous work into ecological service.
white-headed-vulture.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Savannas, open woodland, dry grassland, and lightly wooded African landscapes.
signatureTraits: Bare head stays cleaner when feeding around carcasses.
Hooked bill cuts scraps and carrion efficiently.
Soaring search turns wide open country into a work route.
Scavenging role helps recycle nutrients and reduce waste.
interestingFacts: White-headed vultures are among Africa's more distinctive vultures, with a pale head and dark body contrast.
They may arrive at carcasses alone or in small numbers rather than huge crowds.
Like many vultures, they are vulnerable to poisoning and habitat pressure.
Their work is necessary precisely because it is not pretty.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Carrion, scraps, small dead animals, and occasionally live small prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Adults face few natural predators, but eggs and chicks may face raptors or mammals; poisoning, electrocution, and habitat loss are the larger dangers.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, soaring when thermals rise and feeding when visibility and air lift make searching efficient.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Not well documented for this species. Large vultures are long-lived, and 20 years or more is considered likely for birds that reach adulthood.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females typically lay one egg in a tree nest, so each chick represents a slow replacement for a bird doing a critical job.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar in appearance, so the principle rests on the shared scavenging role rather than display difference.

white-nosed-coati.spotlight: White-nosed Coati teaches Troop Curiosity through many noses searching one path. Long snouts, digging claws, raised tails, female troops, and forest-floor movement show curiosity traveling farther when shared.
white-nosed-coati.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Tropical forests, dry woodland, canyons, scrub, river edges, and forest floors fit White-nosed Coatis because food hides in soil, bark, fruiting trees, and leaf litter.
signatureTraits: White snout markings: the face highlights the searching tool.
Troop movement: females and young often forage socially.
Claws and nose together: digging and smelling turn curiosity into food.
interestingFacts: White-nosed Coatis are relatives of raccoons and belong to the same family, Procyonidae.
Females and young often travel in bands, while adult males are more solitary.
Their raised tails help group members track one another in vegetation.
Their range extends from the southwestern United States through Mexico and Central America to northwestern Colombia.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, insects, eggs, small vertebrates, larvae, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, pumas, ocelots, coyotes, eagles, snakes, and humans threaten coatis. Troop vigilance and climbing help make curiosity safer.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: White-nosed Coatis are mostly diurnal, especially social troops, moving with raised tails through daylight.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: White-nosed Coatis often live around 7 to 10 years in the wild, with longer lives possible under protection. A long-lived coati can learn fruiting trees, trails, and safe sleeping places.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually leave the troop to give birth in a tree nest or protected den, then return with young when they are ready. Offspring rejoin curiosity as a social path.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are larger and often solitary, while females and young form troops.

white-rhinoceros.spotlight: Bulls can weigh more than two tonnes, which makes this the largest rhinoceros and one of the heaviest land animals after the elephants. All of that bulk is built on grass. A long head hangs from a muscular hump on the neck, keeping the mouth at ground level as the animal walks slowly forward, feeding as it goes.
white-rhinoceros.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Short-grass savanna and open grassy woodland on flat or gently rolling ground, with water for drinking and mud wallows within reach and patches of bush for shade. It favours closely grazed lawns of short grass and avoids dense thicket and steep slopes.
signatureTraits: Square mouth and massive calm grazing
Adapted to African grasslands and savannas with water and grazing
Two horns rise from the snout, the front one usually longer.
Long, tube-shaped ears swivel independently.
Skin is slate grey to yellowish brown, often coloured by mud.
interestingFacts: Their food is mainly short grasses cropped by a square lip.
The name probably has nothing to do with colour; a popular explanation traces it to a Dutch word for wide, though this is disputed.
Southern white rhinos were reduced to fewer than a hundred animals in one corner of South Africa around 1900 and have since recovered to many thousands.
Only two northern white rhinos, both females, were known to survive after the last male died in Kenya in 2018.
Territorial bulls mark their boundaries with dung heaps, scattered by kicking, and with sprays of urine.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They feed on short grasses cropped by a square lip.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Healthy adults have no regular natural predators. Lions and spotted hyenas occasionally take calves, which run ahead of the mother where she can see them; a threatened group may stand rump to rump, horns outward. Poaching for horn causes far more deaths.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Grazing is concentrated in the early morning, late afternoon and evening and continues after dark. The hottest hours are spent lying in shade or wallowing in mud, and sleep comes in bouts by day and night.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Typically 35 to 45 years in the wild. Captive animals have reached about 50.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single calf is born after a gestation of about 16 months, weighing roughly 40 to 65 kilograms. It stands within hours, begins to graze at about two months and suckles for a year or more. The mother drives it off shortly before her next calf arrives.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are larger with heavier horns and territorial behavior.

white-stork.spotlight: Adult white storks are almost voiceless: pairs greet each other at the nest by throwing the head back and clattering the bill. European breeders winter mainly in Africa, and because they depend on rising warm air, which does not form over the sea, they go round the Mediterranean, funnelling over Gibraltar or the Bosphorus instead of crossing open water.
white-stork.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, north_africa_middle_east, sub_saharan_africa. Wet meadows, farmland, villages, marshes, river plains, and rooftops fit White Storks because feeding grounds and high nesting platforms must connect.
signatureTraits: Rooftop and platform nests mark repeated seasonal return.
Broad wings use thermals for long migration.
Pair and nest fidelity connect distance with home.
interestingFacts: White Storks often reuse and enlarge nests over years.
They migrate long distances using soaring flight on thermals, which funnels them across short sea crossings like Gibraltar.
Their association with rooftops has made them culturally significant in many regions.
Some White Storks now skip part or all of their migration, wintering at landfill sites in Spain and Portugal.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, frogs, rodents, worms, fish, reptiles, and small animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, martens, eagles, crows, humans, and nest disturbance threaten eggs or young. High nests and repeated site fidelity help protect the family route.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: White Storks are diurnal, foraging by day and migrating on thermals. Their rhythm follows sunlight, air lift, and the pull back to the nest.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: White Storks can live for decades, especially when migration hazards are survived. Long life supports route memory, nest fidelity, and repeated seasonal return.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in large stick nests, and both parents incubate and feed the chicks. The family begins on a high platform built for return.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look alike, though males are usually larger.

white-tailed-tropicbird.spotlight: The smallest of the three tropicbirds, a white seabird of warm oceans whose two central tail feathers are drawn out into streamers about as long as its body. In courtship, pairs and small groups circle near the nesting cliffs calling, and one bird glides above another with its streamers bent down towards its partner.
white-tailed-tropicbird.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_atlantic, indian_ocean, south_pacific. Open tropical and subtropical ocean, usually far from land outside the breeding season. It comes ashore only to nest, on oceanic islands with sea cliffs, rocky crevices and caves or, on some islands, tree hollows and sheltered ground beneath vegetation.
signatureTraits: A black bar runs diagonally across each inner upperwing.
A black stripe curves back through the eye.
The bill is yellow to orange, stout and slightly downcurved.
The outer wing tips are black above.
Flight is direct, with quick, steady wingbeats and little gliding.
interestingFacts: On land it can barely walk: the legs are set so far back that it pushes itself along on its belly.
In Bermuda it is called the longtail, and its return each spring is a traditional sign that winter is over.
Birds breeding on Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean have an apricot-gold wash to the plumage and are known locally as golden bosuns.
Artificial nest domes have been installed on Bermuda to replace cliff cavities lost to erosion and hurricanes.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish, especially flying fish, and squid. It hovers briefly, then plunges from up to about 20 metres with wings half folded, seizing prey just below the surface; flying fish are sometimes caught in the air.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: At sea adults have few enemies. On breeding islands introduced rats, cats and dogs take eggs, chicks and sitting adults, and crabs may take unguarded eggs. A bird on the nest defends it with harsh screams and jabs of its sharp bill.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Foraging is done by day. Breeding adults spend the night in the nest cavity; away from the colonies the birds live on the open ocean and rest floating on the sea with the tail cocked up.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan is poorly documented. Adults have high yearly survival and many probably live more than 10 years, but reliable ringing figures are few.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: A single egg is laid on bare ground in a crevice, cavity or sheltered scrape, with no nest material. Both parents incubate for about 40 days and feed the chick by regurgitation until it fledges at roughly 10 to 12 weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are alike in plumage, and both carry full tail streamers; they cannot be told apart in the field.

whooping-crane.spotlight: Whooping Crane teaches Return Call through a white wetland giant whose voice helped carry recovery. Its bugling call, migration, pair bond, and conservation story show that a clear signal can help life find its way back.
whooping-crane.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Northern marshes, prairie wetlands, migration stopovers, coastal marshes, and shallow feeding areas fit Whooping Cranes because return depends on connected safe wetlands.
signatureTraits: Tall white crane with black wingtips in flight
Loud bugling call that carries over wetlands
Long migration between breeding and wintering grounds
Conservation recovery symbol with guided population work
interestingFacts: Whooping Cranes are the tallest birds in North America.
Their bugling calls can carry over long distances.
Whooping Cranes nearly disappeared in the twentieth century, falling to only around twenty wild birds in the early 1940s.
Conservation programs have helped rebuild migration knowledge and populations.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Crabs, insects, fish, frogs, berries, roots, grains, and wetland animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, coyotes, bobcats, eagles, raccoons, and humans can threaten eggs or young. Tall vigilance and wetland nesting reduce risk.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Whooping Cranes are diurnal, feeding and traveling by day and roosting in shallow water.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Whooping Cranes can live for decades, especially in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females usually lay two eggs, though often one chick survives. Both parents incubate, defend, and teach the young migration routes.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, with males often slightly larger. Pair calling and shared parenting matter more than visual difference.

wild-yak.spotlight: Wild Yak is Plateau Fortitude grown into muscle, lungs, hair, and horn. It does not survive the high cold by wishing conditions away; it carries the plateau on its body.
wild-yak.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: central_asia, south_asia, east_asia. Wild Yaks live on the Tibetan Plateau, alpine steppe, cold deserts, and high grasslands.
signatureTraits: Dense shaggy coat for high-altitude cold
Large body and strong lungs for thin air
Powerful horns and herd defense
Grazing life on open Tibetan Plateau
interestingFacts: Wild Yaks are ancestors of domestic yaks and are larger and wilder than most domestic forms.
They are adapted to cold, high-altitude environments with thin air.
Their long hair helps protect against wind and extreme temperatures.
They graze grasses, sedges, and alpine plants across open plateau.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They graze grasses, sedges, herbs, and hardy alpine vegetation.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include wolves and snow leopards, especially for calves, while humans are a major pressure. Their defense is size, horns, herd vigilance, and the ability to occupy ground that is already difficult for enemies.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active through cold days and seasons, resting and grazing according to weather and forage. Their rhythm shows fortitude as routine: the yak does not wait for easy weather before living.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 15 to 20 years where conditions allow. The lifespan why is that protection repeated over years becomes a way of life, turning severe climate into a long-term home.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to sturdy calves timed for better forage and herd movement. Offspring must quickly learn cold, altitude, and herd safety, making fortitude a family inheritance.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are much larger and more heavily horned, while females anchor calf survival in herds. Both sexes carry the plateau design, but in different forms of strength.

wilsons-bird-of-paradise.spotlight: Wilson's Bird-of-paradise teaches Stagecraft through a jewel-colored male who prepares the forest floor before performing. Cleared court, blue crown, curled tail wires, and precise display show that rare beauty needs a made space.
wilsons-bird-of-paradise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Lowland and hill rainforest on Waigeo and Batanta, dense understory, and cleared display courts.
signatureTraits: Male’s vivid red, yellow, green, blue, and curled-tail display
Carefully cleared court on the forest floor
Female choice shaped by color, posture, movement, and preparation
Small island forest life with extreme visual specialization
interestingFacts: Male Wilson's Birds-of-paradise have a bright bare blue crown.
The male clears leaves from a display court before courtship.
Females are much plainer, helping with nesting camouflage.
The species is native to islands off western New Guinea.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit and arthropods.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, raptors, mammals, and habitat loss threaten birds and nests. Court preparation must be balanced with secrecy because a stage attracts attention from more than mates.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wilson's Birds-of-paradise are diurnal, feeding and displaying by day when color can be judged.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: How many years Cicinnurus respublica lives is unpublished; males on Waigeo and Batanta clear forest-floor courts before jewelled displays.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build nests and raise chicks alone after choosing males by display.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are spectacularly colored, while females are brownish and cryptic. The contrast is central: display and concealment are both necessary for the species to continue.

wolf-eel.spotlight: Wolf Eel teaches Crushing Pressure through a rocky-reef fish that opens hard food by steady jaw strength. A long crevice body, blunt head, shell-breaking teeth, and patient den life show that pressure works when it is aimed and sustained.
wolf-eel.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_pacific. Cold rocky reefs, kelp forests, crevices, caves, and North Pacific coastal bottoms fit Wolf Eels because Crushing Pressure needs hard prey and hard shelter. The habitat makes jaw strength more valuable than speed.
signatureTraits: Strong jaws and teeth adapted for crushing hard-shelled prey.
Long eel-like body that lives in rocky dens and crevices.
Pair bonding and repeated use of den sites in reef habitat.
Slow pressure strategy focused on shells rather than chase.
interestingFacts: Wolf Eels are not true eels; they are wolffish relatives.
Adults often live in rocky dens and may form long-term pairs.
Their jaws can crush sea urchins, crabs, clams, and other hard prey.
Young wolf eels look more orange and pelagic before settling into reefs.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails, and other hard-shelled animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large fish, seals, sea lions, sharks, humans, and egg predators can threaten wolf eels or their young. Crevice living and pair defense help turn a dangerous reef into a workable home.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wolf Eels are often active in low light or around den areas, with feeding shaped by opportunity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Estimated at 20 years or more. Ageing studies on wild fish are limited, so the upper limit is not firmly known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay egg masses in dens, and adults may guard or tend the eggs until hatching.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, though mature males may develop heavier heads.

wolverine.spotlight: Built like a small bear, this is the largest land-living member of the weasel family; most adults weigh about 7 to 18 kilograms, males much heavier than females. Its jaws and neck muscles can shear meat that is frozen solid and crack the bones of reindeer and moose.
wolverine.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, east_asia, arctic_antarctic. Wolverines live in boreal forests, tundra, alpine zones, and snowy northern wilderness.
signatureTraits: Large snowshoe-like feet
Powerful jaws
Thick cold-weather fur
Wide-ranging tenacity
interestingFacts: Wolverines can travel huge distances for food, with some individuals covering dozens of kilometres in a day.
They cache food in cold places such as snow and rock crevices, which helps preserve it for later.
Their large, broad feet help them cross deep snow without sinking far.
Wolverines are the largest land-dwelling members of the weasel family.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Scavenged remains of reindeer (caribou) and moose, often wolf kills or animals dead from accidents or cold, are the main winter food. It also hunts hares, rodents, marmots and ground-nesting birds, eats eggs and berries in summer, and can kill animals as large as reindeer when deep snow slows them.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Wolves are the predator most often recorded killing adults, and bears, cougars and golden eagles take some, mainly kits. A threatened animal growls, bares its teeth and gives off a strong musk, and may climb a tree. Trapping and the loss of late spring snow are the main human pressures.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Active by day or night, alternating a few hours of travel with a few hours of rest instead of keeping a fixed schedule. It does not hibernate. Resting animals lie up in snow holes, under boulders or beneath fallen trees.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly 7 to 12 years in the wild for animals that survive to adulthood; captive wolverines have lived past 15.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Mating is in summer but the embryos do not implant until winter; females den in snow and raise small litters of kits. Two or three kits are usual, born white-furred from February to April and weaned at about ten weeks.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Across the range males are larger and range more widely; females carry the denning work. A male is about a third heavier than a female, and his territory overlaps those of several females. Coat colour and markings are alike.

wood-duck.spotlight: Wood Duck teaches Descent through young life that begins high in a tree and survives by dropping toward water. Tree cavities, sharp claws, colorful adults, soft ducklings, and the first brave jump show that some beginnings require falling into the next world.
wood-duck.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Wooded swamps, forested wetlands, ponds, rivers, beaver marshes, and tree-lined water fit Wood Ducks because their life connects height and water. The habitat makes descent necessary.
signatureTraits: Tree-Cavity Nesting: eggs are laid above ground in hollows near water.
First Drop: ducklings leap from the nest shortly after hatching.
Waterward Following: the mother leads the brood from tree shelter to aquatic safety.
interestingFacts: Wood Ducks nest in tree cavities or nest boxes.
Ducklings can jump from elevated nests soon after hatching.
Males are known for vivid multicolored breeding plumage.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Seeds, acorns, fruits, aquatic plants, insects, and invertebrates.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, snakes, owls, hawks, foxes, snapping turtles, and large fish threaten eggs, ducklings, or adults. The first drop is risky, but staying in the tree is not the future.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wood Ducks are mostly diurnal, feeding in wetlands and resting in sheltered cover. Their rhythm follows water, cover, and brood movement rather than open-field exposure.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wood Ducks may live several years, though many young do not survive their first season.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Clutches usually hold about 9 to 14 creamy white to tan eggs in a down-lined tree cavity, and other females often add eggs. Only the female incubates, for about 30 days. The day after hatching she calls from below and the ducklings leap from the cavity to ground or water, then feed themselves.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are brightly colored, while females are more camouflaged for nesting. The difference supports the species’ design: display has its season, but hidden maternal cover carries the descent.

wood-frog.spotlight: Wood Frog teaches Revival through a body that can pause almost completely and answer spring again. Freeze tolerance, cryoprotectants, leaf-litter hibernation, explosive breeding, and thawed movement show life returning after deep stillness.
wood-frog.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america. Northern forests, vernal pools, leaf litter, bog edges, and cold woodland wetlands fit Wood Frogs because they need freezing winter shelter and temporary spring breeding water.
signatureTraits: Freeze tolerance: parts of the body can ice over while life pauses.
Cryoprotectants: body chemistry helps cells survive winter freezing.
Explosive breeding: spring thaw triggers a fast return to pools and calls.
interestingFacts: Wood Frogs can survive being frozen during winter.
They breed early in spring, often gathering in temporary pools that lack predatory fish.
Their dark eye mask makes them easy to recognize among many frogs.
Their range reaches farther north than that of any other North American amphibian, extending beyond the Arctic Circle.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, spiders, worms, small invertebrates, and larvae.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Snakes, birds, mammals, fish, insects, and amphibian predators threaten Wood Frogs, eggs, or tadpoles. Temporary pools reduce fish predation but demand fast breeding.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Wood Frogs are active in spring and warm wet months, then freeze-tolerate winter in sheltered litter.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Most live about 2 to 4 years in the wild, and few survive beyond 5. Many males breed first at one or two years old, females usually a year later.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay masses of eggs in vernal pools soon after thaw, giving tadpoles a fish-free but temporary nursery. Offspring must develop before the pool disappears.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually smaller and call during breeding season, while females carry egg masses. Sex difference becomes most visible in the urgent spring chorus.

wood-stork.spotlight: Wood Stork turns sensitivity into a feeding method. Its open bill, touch-trigger snap, slow wetland steps, and flock nesting show that what cannot be seen can still be found by feel.
wood-stork.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, south_america. Shallow wetlands, marshes, swamps, mangroves, flooded fields, and drying pools.
signatureTraits: Touch-sensitive bill snaps shut quickly when prey brushes it.
Slow wading turns shallow water into a search field.
Bald head and long legs suit messy wetland feeding.
Colony nesting ties individual sensitivity to group survival.
interestingFacts: Wood storks often feed by tactolocation rather than sight alone.
Falling water levels can concentrate fish and make feeding more efficient.
They nest in colonies in trees over or near water.
Their breeding success depends heavily on wetland timing.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish, frogs, crustaceans, insects, and aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Raccoons, snakes, alligators near colonies, raptors, storms, drought, and wetland loss threaten them. Nesting over water helps reduce some ground danger.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal, feeding by day when shallow-water conditions allow slow sweeping and quick snapping.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often 10 to 20 years or more; sensitivity matters through many wetland cycles where timing decides whether chicks are fed.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick nests, and both parents feed chicks; successful offspring depend on the right water level as much as parental effort.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes look similar, though males may be larger; the important difference is not sex but the bill's shared sensitivity.

woolly-monkey.spotlight: Among the largest monkeys of the Amazon basin, it is thickset with dense, short fur, and adults weigh roughly 5 to 10 kilograms. The underside of the tail tip is bare skin, ridged like a fingertip, and the tail alone can bear the animal's whole weight while both hands are free to pick fruit.
woolly-monkey.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Woolly Monkey usually lives in Amazon rainforest canopy and mature tropical forest.
signatureTraits: woolly fur
prehensile tail
strong limbs
social travel
interestingFacts: Females leave the troop they were born in when they mature, while males generally stay.
It sometimes stands upright on its hind legs, bracing with the tail, to look around or reach food.
In Brazil it is called barrigudo, meaning big-bellied, after the rounded abdomen of well-fed adults.
Large troops split into smaller parties to feed and come together again later.
Troops are large for a Neotropical monkey, commonly of about 10 to 40 animals.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Woolly Monkey feeds on fruit, leaves, seeds, flowers, and occasional insects.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Harpy eagles and other large eagles take monkeys from the treetops; jaguars are a lesser danger. Troop members bark in alarm and move off through the branches. Hunting is the most serious threat: adults are shot for meat and infants sold as pets, and losses are replaced slowly.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Woolly Monkey is diurnal, moving and feeding through trees by day.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Wild lifespan has not been measured well. In captivity, where the species is hard to keep, individuals have lived to about 25 to 30 years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Births are about three years apart: females usually bear one infant after long care. Gestation lasts roughly seven to seven and a half months. The newborn clings to the mother's belly and later rides on her back.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Adult males are often larger, but both share the gripping tail design. Males are more heavily muscled and have longer canine teeth; coat colour does not differ.

woylie.spotlight: Woylie turns Fungal Stewardship into hidden service: small paws dig for underground food while spreading spores and turning soil for a forest that may never see the work.
woylie.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Woylies live in woodlands, shrublands, and forest edges with soil rich in underground fungi. The habitat is a hidden pantry where searching feeds both the animal and the ecosystem.
signatureTraits: Truffle-digging marsupial
Strong small forepaws
Brush-tipped tail
Ecosystem spore spreader
interestingFacts: Woylies help spread fungal spores through their droppings.
They carry bundles of nesting material by curling their prehensile tails around them.
Their digging for fungi turns over soil, with each animal reported to shift several tonnes of soil a year.
Woylies are also called Brush-tailed Bettongs, and their numbers fell by roughly ninety percent in the early 2000s.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat underground fungi, seeds, tubers, insects, and plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Foxes, feral cats, habitat change, and disease threaten them. Their night activity and cover use help, but small stewards need protected ground.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Woylies are mainly nocturnal, resting in nests by day and digging after dark. Night work makes the future happen quietly below notice.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live several years in the wild, though predation can shorten life. Their impact comes from repeated small digs across many nights.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise a tiny joey in the pouch, then shelter it as it grows. The pouch protects the next digger before it can search on its own.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, with males often slightly larger. The important identity is shared: both are small ground workers with ecological consequence.

x-ray-tetra.spotlight: X-ray Tetra teaches Transparency through a clear-bodied fish that becomes braver in a school. Its translucent body, small size, coordinated swimming, and freshwater groups show vulnerability made safer by staying close and readable.
x-ray-tetra.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Slow streams, floodplains, clear or blackwater creeks, planted aquarium-like shallows, and vegetated freshwater edges fit X-ray Tetras because small fish need cover and group space.
signatureTraits: Translucent body tissues make the small fish look glassy in water.
Schooling reduces individual risk and improves coordinated movement.
Small size makes vegetation, group spacing, and quick response essential.
interestingFacts: X-ray Tetras are popular aquarium fish because of their clear bodies and peaceful schooling behavior.
Their native habitats include slow, vegetated freshwater in northern South America.
They scatter eggs rather than guarding a nest.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Tiny insects, worms, crustaceans, larvae, and plant particles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger fish, birds, aquatic predators, and amphibians pressure small tetras. Schooling makes one delicate body less obvious and many bodies more responsive.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: X-ray Tetras are diurnal, schooling and feeding when light helps coordination.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 4 to 5 years in aquariums, where almost all records come from; lifespan in the wild has not been documented.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females scatter eggs among plants or fine cover, and the young begin as tiny vulnerable fish.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are often fuller-bodied, especially when carrying eggs, while males may be slimmer.

xeme.spotlight: Xeme teaches Arctic Distance through a light gull body traveling enormous seasonal routes. Forked tail, delicate flight, tundra breeding, and ocean wandering make lightness a form of endurance.
xeme.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: north_america, europe, central_asia, arctic_antarctic, arctic_ocean. Arctic tundra pools, coastal marshes, pack-ice edges, and open ocean.
signatureTraits: Forked tail gives the bird a light, elegant outline in flight.
Long migration connects Arctic breeding grounds with far ocean routes.
Small seabird build favors efficiency over force.
Seasonal plumage and movement tie identity to change.
interestingFacts: Xeme is another name for Sabine's gull, and it is the only species in the genus Xema.
It breeds in the high Arctic but spends much of the year over oceans.
In flight its wings show a bold tricolored pattern of grey, black and white triangles, distinctive among gulls.
It often nests near wet tundra and coastal pools.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Insects, aquatic invertebrates, small fish, crustaceans, and marine food.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Skuas, gulls, foxes, jaegers, storms, and climate pressure threaten eggs and chicks. Distance helps adults, but nesting exposes the next generation.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Diurnal in the long Arctic day and flexible at sea, following feeding opportunities rather than a simple clock.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Often around a decade or more if it survives migration.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay small clutches in ground nests, and chicks must grow quickly during the brief Arctic summer.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are similar.

yacare-caiman.spotlight: Yacare Caiman teaches Armored Waiting through low eyes, tough scales, marsh concealment, and sudden ambush. Stillness is not emptiness; it is a protected readiness held just below the surface.
yacare-caiman.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Marshes, rivers, lakes, floodplains, and the Pantanal.
signatureTraits: Armored crocodilian body suited to marsh and river edges.
Low floating posture with eyes and nostrils above water.
Ambush feeding on fish, invertebrates, and small vertebrates.
Wetland patience supported by strong jaws and concealment.
interestingFacts: Yacare caimans are common in parts of South American wetlands such as the Pantanal.
They feed heavily on fish and aquatic animals.
Their armored body helps protect them in crowded wetland systems.
Females build nests and guard eggs and young.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, snails, crustaceans, insects, birds, mammals, and reptiles.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Large jaguars, anacondas, humans, and other caimans can threaten them, while eggs and hatchlings face many predators. Armor helps adults, but nest guarding protects the young.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yacare Caimans are active by day and night depending on temperature and hunting conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Yacare Caimans can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females build mound nests and guard eggs and hatchlings.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are usually larger than females. Size affects dominance, but both sexes share armored wetland patience.

yangtze-finless-porpoise.spotlight: Yangtze Finless Porpoise carries River Smoothness through a rounded back, echolocation, and quiet freshwater agility, moving through pressure without needing a dorsal fin.
yangtze-finless-porpoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: east_asia. Yangtze Finless Porpoises live in the Yangtze River system and connected lakes, where murky water rewards sound and smooth maneuvering. The habitat makes silence and sensing essential.
signatureTraits: No dorsal fin
Rounded smooth back
Freshwater echolocation
Small river porpoise body
interestingFacts: It is the only porpoise that lives entirely in freshwater, in the Yangtze River and its connected lakes.
It lacks a dorsal fin, giving the back a smooth profile.
It uses echolocation clicks to find prey and navigate in turbid river water.
The IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered, with roughly a thousand left in the wild.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fish, shrimp, and small aquatic animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Boat traffic, fishing gear, pollution, prey loss, and river modification threaten them. A smooth body cannot glide around every human-made pressure.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are active through day and night in water, surfacing to breathe and using echolocation while moving. Their rhythm is continuous river awareness.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They may live for decades in suitable conditions, though survival is now difficult. Longevity matters because slow-breeding river mammals need stable water over time.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females give birth to a single calf that nurses and stays close to the mother. Offspring learn the river as a moving sound-map before independence.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar externally, with size differences subtle. The defining feature is shared smoothness, not display.

yellow-anaconda.spotlight: Yellow Anaconda teaches Marsh Coil through a heavy snake whose strength belongs to water’s edge. Camouflage, semi-aquatic movement, thick body, and constricting coils make power effective in the right element.
yellow-anaconda.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Swamps, marshes, slow rivers, flooded grasslands, and aquatic vegetation fit Yellow Anacondas because weight, ambush, and camouflage work best there.
signatureTraits: Ground colour is yellow to greenish yellow, marked with black blotches.
Dark stripes on top of the head converge towards the snout.
Eyes and nostrils sit high on the head.
The belly is yellow with scattered black flecks.
Adults typically measure about 2.5 to 3.5 metres; large females exceed 4.
interestingFacts: Another widely used common name for it is the Paraguayan anaconda.
At mating time several males may coil around a single female in a tangle known as a breeding ball.
It has long been hunted for its skin, and in Formosa, Argentina, a managed harvest has been run with local hunters.
The United States listed it as an injurious species in 2012, which banned its import.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Birds, fish, mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and wetland animals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Caimans, jaguars, large birds, humans, and other predators can threaten young or adults. Water concealment is protection.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Often most active at night or cooler periods, resting concealed in water or vegetation.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Around 15 to 20 years is usual for well-kept captive snakes. How long wild ones survive is not known.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Young are born live, not hatched from laid eggs. After a pregnancy of about six months a female bears from a handful to several dozen young, each around 60 cm long and independent from birth.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females grow longer and far heavier than males. Males have larger spurs beside the vent, used to stimulate the female during courtship.

yellow-billed-stork.spotlight: Yellow-billed Stork teaches Tactile Search through a bill that finds what eyes cannot. Open-bill sweeping, shallow-water walking, yellow bill, and snap-shut reflex show hidden value discovered through patient contact.
yellow-billed-stork.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Shallow lakes, wetlands, floodplains, marshes, lagoons, and muddy pools fit Yellow-billed Storks because their feeding method needs water thin enough to sweep.
signatureTraits: Tactile bill sweep: touch triggers the feeding strike.
Shallow-water walking: the body searches where hidden prey moves.
Colony nesting: safety grows through many tall nests together.
interestingFacts: Yellow-billed Storks often feed by sweeping an open bill through water.
Their bill can snap shut quickly when prey touches it.
They are strongly tied to changing wetland water levels.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fish, frogs, crustaceans, insects and other aquatic animals. It wades with the bill held partly open in the water, often stirring with a foot, and snaps it shut as soon as touch reveals prey, so it can feed in muddy water.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Crocodiles, eagles, hyenas, snakes, and nest predators can threaten storks, eggs, or chicks. Colonies and tall nesting sites help protect young.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yellow-billed Storks are diurnal, feeding in shallow water when prey movement and water levels allow sweeping. Their rhythm follows floods, pools, and touch.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: No published typical lifespan exists; tactile foragers that sweep yellow bills through African floodplain shallows leave few long-term ring recoveries.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay eggs in stick nests, usually in colonies with other waterbirds. Chicks depend on adults finding hidden prey by touch and returning repeatedly.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females look similar, though males may be slightly larger.

yellow-footed-tortoise.spotlight: The Yellow-footed Tortoise carries steady color through the forest. Its slow walk, domed shell, and golden scales make patience feel warm rather than dull — a reminder that brightness can travel slowly.
yellow-footed-tortoise.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Yellow-footed Tortoises live in humid tropical forests, forest edges, and nearby clearings in northern South America.
signatureTraits: Yellow-orange scales on limbs and head
Domed protective shell
Slow forest-floor movement
Omnivorous tropical tortoise diet
interestingFacts: Yellow-footed Tortoises are among the larger South American tortoises.
They live more in humid forest than many dry-country tortoises.
They eat fruit, leaves, flowers, fungi, and sometimes carrion or invertebrates.
Their yellow markings make a slow animal feel visually alive and memorable.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat fallen fruit, leaves, flowers, fungi, and occasional animal matter.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Eggs and young are vulnerable to birds, mammals, reptiles, and ants, while adults rely heavily on the shell.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: They are mostly active by day, especially when humidity and temperature are suitable, and rest under cover during harsh conditions. Their rhythm shows steady progress tuned to comfort rather than urgency.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: They can live for many decades, often 40 years or more in protected conditions.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females lay clutches of hard-shelled eggs in nests on the ground, leaving young to hatch independently. Offspring begin small and vulnerable, so the slow adult shell represents protection earned over time.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males may be larger with a more concave plastron and longer tail, but both sexes carry the yellow-marked forest identity. The color belongs to the species as a whole.

yellow-spotted-river-turtle.spotlight: Yellow-spotted River Turtle teaches River Nesting through a freshwater turtle reading water levels before trusting the sand. Yellow head spots, river life, basking, and seasonal sandbank eggs make the future depend on choosing the right shore.
yellow-spotted-river-turtle.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_america. Amazon and Orinoco rivers, floodplain lakes, oxbows, channels, basking logs, and exposed sandbanks.
signatureTraits: Yellow head markings, especially clear in young animals
Amazon and Orinoco river life tied to water levels
Sandbank nesting during suitable dry-season windows
Basking and aquatic movement between feeding and nesting sites
interestingFacts: Yellow-spotted River Turtles nest on exposed river sandbanks.
River height can decide whether a nest stays safe or floods.
Females come ashore to lay eggs, leaving hatchlings to reach water.
They are strongly affected by egg harvesting and river disturbance.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Aquatic plants, fruits, seeds, leaves, small invertebrates, and carrion.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Jaguars, caimans, large fish, birds, tegus, raccoons, humans, and egg predators threaten turtles or nests. Choosing the right sandbank is defense before the hatchling has any strength.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yellow-spotted River Turtles are diurnal, basking and feeding by day while resting in water or cover. Their rhythm follows sun, river height, and nesting season.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Yellow-spotted River Turtles can live for decades.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females dig nests in sandy banks and lay clutches timed to river conditions.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Females are generally larger than males, fitting the heavy work of egg production and nesting journeys. Males remain smaller and more aquatic.

yellow-throated-marten.spotlight: Yellow-throated Marten teaches Bold Pursuit through a bright-throated hunter rushing across trees and ground. Speed, social boldness, agile climbing, and fearless foraging turn opportunity into motion.
yellow-throated-marten.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: south_asia, southeast_asia, east_asia. Forests, mountain woods, mixed canopy, forest edges, and valleys.
signatureTraits: Bright yellow-orange throat marking that gives visual confidence
Fast movement between canopy and forest floor
Fearless opportunistic hunting and foraging
Agile mustelid body suited to pursuit and exploration
interestingFacts: Yellow-throated Martens are among the larger marten species, with a long body and a tail roughly two-thirds of its length.
They move well in trees and on the ground.
They eat fruit, small animals, birds, eggs, insects, and carrion.
They may travel in pairs or small groups more often than many mustelids.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Fruit, rodents, birds, eggs, insects, reptiles, carrion, and small mammals.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger carnivores, raptors, snakes, humans, and habitat loss threaten them. Speed and canopy-ground switching help turn danger into another route.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Yellow-throated Martens are often diurnal or crepuscular, with flexible activity.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Yellow-throated Martens can live for several years.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Females raise kits in dens or tree cavities.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males are generally larger than females. The difference can affect range and competition, while both sexes share the same bold movement design.

zander.spotlight: Zander teaches Dim-Light Patience through eyes built for the signal in dark water. Its low-light vision, sudden strikes, long predatory body, and murky-water confidence show that preparation becomes real when the dark finally gives the opening.
zander.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: europe, central_asia. Lakes, rivers, reservoirs, turbid water, and deep edges.
signatureTraits: Strong low-light vision suited to dusk, night, and murky water
Predatory body built for sudden strikes at fish
Preference for deeper, turbid, or dim habitats
Patience that turns poor visibility into advantage
interestingFacts: Zander, also called pike-perch, belong to the perch family Percidae and are among its largest members.
Their eyes are adapted for feeding when visibility is low.
They often become more active around dusk or in cloudy, turbid water.
Their fang-like canine teeth help grip slippery fish prey.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: Small fish and aquatic prey.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Larger predatory fish, birds, otters, humans, and cannibalism can threaten zander or young. Depth and dim water become protection, showing that patience is also a hiding strategy.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Zander often feed at dusk, night, or in murky conditions.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Commonly up to about 10 years; the oldest fish on record were aged at about 17.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: Spawning comes in spring as the water warms to roughly 10 to 14 °C. The male clears a shallow nest on gravel, sand or plant roots; a large female lays several hundred thousand sticky eggs there, and he guards and fans them until they hatch within about a week.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Males and females are broadly similar, though reproductive roles differ during spawning.

zebra-duiker.spotlight: Zebra Duiker makes a paradox useful: its stripes are bold, yet they help a shy forest body vanish by breaking its outline into the understory.
zebra-duiker.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: sub_saharan_africa. Zebra Duikers live in dense lowland rainforest, understory, and shadowed forest floor.
signatureTraits: Bold zebra-like stripes across the back
Small secretive body for dense West African understory
Forest-floor browsing and fruit feeding
Shape-disrupting pattern that turns contrast into cover
interestingFacts: Zebra Duikers are among the most distinctly striped duikers.
They live in dense Upper Guinean forests of West Africa.
Their stripes likely help break the body's outline in filtered forest light.
They are shy and usually difficult to observe in the wild.

fieldGuide.dietSummary: They eat leaves, shoots, fruit, seeds, and other forest plant material.
fieldGuide.predatorsSummary: Predators include leopards, crowned eagles, pythons, and humans. Their defense is secrecy, quick movement, and body patterning that makes pursuit harder in the broken forest scene.
fieldGuide.sleepPattern: Likely crepuscular or partly nocturnal, resting in dense cover and moving when visibility favors concealment. The rhythm deepens the lesson: boldness becomes safest when timed with shadow.
fieldGuide.lifespanEstimate: Likely several years in the wild, with survival strongly tied to intact forest. The lifespan why is that a rare pattern only works as long as the forest remains complex enough to hide it.
fieldGuide.femaleOffspringNotes: One calf is usual. It spends its early weeks tucked motionless in thick undergrowth, and its mother comes back to it to suckle; captive records put pregnancy at about seven months.
fieldGuide.sexDifferenceNotes: Sexes are broadly similar, though males have small horns. The stripes matter more than sexual display, making identity and concealment the same visual language.

zebra-finch.spotlight: Zebra Finch teaches Bonding through a small desert bird whose voice keeps closeness alive. Learned song, contact calls, pair connection, flock movement, and seed-searching life show that a tiny signal can hold a group together across dry country.
zebra-finch.typicalHabitat: Native range keys: australia_oceania. Dry grasslands, scrub, open woodland, waterholes, and aviaries fit Zebra Finches because bonding matters most where resources can be scattered. The habitat makes voice and flock contact practical.
signatureTraits: Learned Song: males develop song through listening and practice.
Contact Calling: short calls help flock members and pairs stay connected.
Dryland Flocking: social life makes scattered food and harsh weather easier to face.
interestingFacts: Zebra Finches are social seed-eating birds from Australia.
